With the next update comming soon this game is going to be fantastic, and I highly recommend this game to any mature player who loves realistic and challenging shooters.

It's definitely a head-turning title, isn't it? It seems cynical, it implies the developer knows that the genre is oversaturated.
Unfortunately, this really is a run of the mill zombie defence game.
There is no plot, you just pick a character (A man, a woman or a soldier) and get thrown into a grey plane with an infinite-ammo handgun and two dozen zombies heading your way.
As a proof of concept this could actually work, it could have been an interesting game and not... well, not yet another zombie defence game.
There is a variety of weapons you buy between rounds, either for your own use or to mount on fragile turrets and some barricades to build. It is, however, nowhere near enough to make this game more than a short-lived distraction.
Sure, it's cheap, but that shouldn't be enough.
Go play something more interesting instead.

It is a good game for combined arms. Huge battles, with a real wow factor for number of players in a fight. I would avoid if you like run and gun style shooters. Time to live is very low, so cover is essential. You will die... a lot, but that is okay. It doesn't mean you are bad, rather it is just part of the game. If you have a k/d of 1 then you are doing pretty good.
Lvl 1 noob syndrome is not a thing in this game. Grinding to be effective is not really a thing. While there are tons of weapons and suit upgrades that you can unlock, most are side-grades, not upgrades. They wont make you better, rather they make you different/specialized. Some of the best weapons in the game are the ones that you start with and you are able to do almost everything right out of the gate. It is all just about player knowledge. None of the "premium" (read store bought) weapons are any better than the base guns. They are literally just a color change.
Best advice I can give for new players is start out as a medic or an engineer. Watch the players around you; notice how they move, and what the sight lines are. Most importantly, find a sight that you like and cert into it first. You can use the VR (globe terminals at the warpgate) to test out different things. Everything is cert free in VR.
Good luck and see you out there!

A 3D puzzle platformer disguised as a way to inquire into some of the deepest philosophical questions is how I would summarize Talos Principle. It was definitely an unique experience and it led me to believe that the fact that this narrative piece was expressed in the form of a game of solving puzzles was done purposefully and quite brilliantly at that.
Let's start off with what probably caught most of our attention - what IS this game all about? It is an exploration of purpose, meaning, existence and humanity (all of the good stuff that can lead to either nihilism or some form of existentialistic crisis). It is a collection of bits and pieces of various ideas packaged up and slowly delivered as the player progresses through 100+ puzzles. The puzzles are quite unique, I have seen a fair amount of the individual elements used in these puzzles in other games (except a few), but their solutions arrangement in the 3D environment are both very new and challenging for me. But hear me out - this game is not at all about the puzzles. The puzzles themselves are used tacticfully for the main role of giving the player tasks and to make the player suffer. If by the 100+ (or however many) puzzle you feel exhausted, tired and not wanting anymore, then that's what is expected!
I have not written much with regards to the storyline because I do not want to spoil anything. This game should be played with an open mind, fresh and unspoiled, and with your critical thinking mode turned on. Also keep in mind that if you think and/or read a lot, then a lot of the ideas expressed in the game might not be new, however the best part about it is the narrative and perspective in which these ideas are conveyed from. It is one thing to read a philosophical text and another to engage in a philosophical construct.
Visuals? Stunning. Sounds? Colourful. Controls? Fluid and mostly intuitive. Why do I recommend this game? Let's just say it had left an impact during and after completing it. I had learned something from it and I dear say that what I've learned from it influenced both my worldview and my approach in life. If a game can have an everlasting effect after 30-50 hours of time spent on it, then what more can I say to convince you to get it?

The sheer awesomity of this game is easily on par with the Portal series. The Talos Principle is gorgeous, thrilling and clever.
One thing which sets this game apart from other action-puzzle titles (including the aforementioned Portal 1 and 2) is the difficulty level. In order to beat the game completely, you'll need to actually think, not just throw stuff together until it works (that's how I remember beating Portal, anyway — and that's not necessarily a bad thing either, just very different).
Levels are beautifully designed, minimal, and very accessible — no lava floor, no trick jumps, getting the timing right to a millisecond isn't at all necessary. If you've had the miserable experience of playing the fan-made Portal: Prelude mod, you know what I'm talking about.
The writing is also solid.
To summarize, I enjoyed The Talos Principle immensely, and you probably should too. Recommended/10.

In Age of Empires II, each of the civilzation's has hundreds of possible traits, including a unique selection of: units, buildings, and technologies.  WIth 31 civilizations, even skilled veterans have not mastered every civilization in the game.  Because the civilizations use the same base units, buildings, and technologies, knowledge of one civilization is somewhat applicable to another.  There is no "best way to play this game", as every style can be countered.  As each "type" of unit can be countered by another "type"; it is really important to have a military composition that contains different "types" of units.
Early game demands: setting up, and planning out your economy; exploring the map for resources and choke points; as well as communicating with your team mates, and planning out your overall strategy.  You must balance your time: perfecting the efficiency of your economy, while advancing and managing your military interests.  Upgrading and maintaining complex military compositions, formations, and unit countering demand attention: and only the most experienced and efficient players can manage their economy and military simultaneously.

Remember when Max Payne was a badass in the first two games... yeah, you won't find that guy here.  I don't even recognize who the guy in this game is supposed to be, because it's not Max Payne, it's gotta be some fake who happens to have the same name.
The most annoying aspect of the game may be the non-stop cutscenes.  Cutscenes happen over and over again every level.  Some cutscenes end with you already being shot at, so you're already taking damage when you gain control.  During every cutscene, the game switches your weapon to the pistol you have in your first slot.  So after every cutscene, you have to switch back to your primary weapon.  Thanks fake Max, I fully intended to engage these 6 enemies with your pistol that holds 8 rounds instead of the 30 round assault rifle you're now holding in your offhand.
The story in this game is incoherent at best, it's like they didn't even bother trying.  You can't have me running around killing hundreds of bad guys, then suddenly have a cutscene where Max decides he's a ♥♥♥♥♥boy who can't handle 6 bad guys and gets captured. I also had plenty of gameplay nitpicks.  If Max gets close to a wall with a gun, he'll point the weapon up in the air.  This is very problamatic since they turned this game into a cover shooter.  Sometimes you'll pop out of cover to shoot and Max will point his weapon up at the ceiling... Thanks fake Max, that's what I wanted to do, shoot the ceiling instead of the bad guys in front of me.
You're also limited in the arsenal you can carry, 2 pistols/smgs and a primary weapon.  If you ever want to dual wield pistols, which is the only real fun in the game, Max has to drop whatever the primary weapon he is carrying. Thanks fake Max, for not allowing me to actually have fun using the dualies.

Thanks fake Max, for waiting to dive until I've already been shot up, gotten to cover, and then randomly activating and diving out into the open again.

The sheer awesomity of this game is easily on par with the Portal series. The Talos Principle is gorgeous, thrilling and clever.
One thing which sets this game apart from other action-puzzle titles (including the aforementioned Portal 1 and 2) is the difficulty level. In order to beat the game completely, you'll need to actually think, not just throw stuff together until it works (that's how I remember beating Portal, anyway — and that's not necessarily a bad thing either, just very different).
Levels are beautifully designed, minimal, and very accessible — no lava floor, no trick jumps, getting the timing right to a millisecond isn't at all necessary. If you've had the miserable experience of playing the fan-made Portal: Prelude mod, you know what I'm talking about.
The writing is also solid.
To summarize, I enjoyed The Talos Principle immensely, and you probably should too. Recommended/10.

Easily one of the best games I've ever played, and definitely the best puzzle game.
And I thought Portal was good. The Talos Principle blows Portal out of the water in terms of complexity, story, and immersion. Not to mention the beautiful graphics.
Many puzzle games provide a relatively weak storyline to drive your progression, but The Talos Principle is not one of them. If anything, I began to want to know MORE about the story and played the game less for the mental challenge of the puzzles, and more just to know what was going to happen, what it all meant.
Highly recommended to anyone who likes a bit of a mental challenge, and loves the feeling of victory after overcoming a particularly hard series of challenges. Lots of Easter Eggs and hidden gems in this game too. And multiple endings definitely keep the game interesting.
I give this game 10/10 across the board -- graphics, story, replay value, complexity, etc. There is almost nothing I can crticize about this game. Some of the sigil puzzles are insanely complex, and some of the Easter Eggs are almost impossible to find without prior knowledge of where they are..... but man, it feels good when you do figure it out on your own.

My educational background is in philosophy and I've got a PhD in the subject so while I no longer work as a professional philosopher I do have a fair idea what I'm talking about. My opinion: it is good! It isn't perfect of course but I wouldn't hesitate to put it on a list of things that philosophy students might like to look at. One thing that did irritate me was an over-reliance on ancient sources. I'd have preferred it if the game had acknowledged its debt to more recent philosophy and I feel that it a barrier to taking this as a first step into the subject and kind of insulting to the modern scholars who are actually taking on the intellectual challenges the game gestures at.
I'm particularly impressed that there wasn't any real tension between the philosophy (or theology) and the gameplay. The Swapper for instance made a good attempt at tackling a philosophical debate but there was a major clash between the philosophy and the gameplay. The philosophy was essentially that of the real world and the questions that would be raised by the gameplay mechanics (if they were real) went untouched. The Talos Principle on the other hand feels almost entirely consistent.

Pros:
Fantastic story and narrative. Good cinematics. Bullet time (player activated slow-mo) is fun. Good music and mostly nice environments.
Cons:
This game becomes tiring. At the START of the game you could kill enemies by one shot in the head. Later on some enemies need 5+ shots in the head to finally die, when they are wearing nothing on the head, or just a basebul cap. It takes the fun out of things when you don't know after how many shots to the head will kill the enemy. This ruins bullet time too. Massively disappointing if you start the game on the hardest difficulty and progress.
Bullet time was more fun in previous max payne games. Bullet time adds fun, so why reduce the amount of time you can bullet time? There was clearly more of it in previous games.
The engine this game was built on just is not fluid enough. The RAGE engine is not even remotely as good as some modern engines. It's great for GTA, but a FPS? Compare this to the Source engine, Unreal engine, Frostbite engine.... It's just kind of poor in comparison. Less fluid, more bugs, more glitches, worse AI, bulky. Lacking optimization.
You can just look at the game size to see how bulky it is. 33gb +? Really? The graphics and cinematics arn't that great. This game could be compressed down to 10gb. We all see what you are trying to do here Rockstar...
No tactics (again due to the engine and AI).
Point and shoot. Use bullet time. Repeat. Point and shoot use bullet time. repeat. Endless chases with the enemy escaping in the last second.
The story is WAY too slow. If it were 70% faster and the game 70% shorter, it would be a lot better. It feels like a constant chore to continue. This is a prime example of a producer over prolonging a story to justify a higher price tag.
oh... and F**k off Social club. Signups/Signings and additional bloatware installations and DRM suck.

*Update for latest release*
Almost all of the negative points I had made below can be considered null, especially with the addition of vehicles. I would also like to point out, I was indeed wrong about bullet drop entirely, and it is quite a factor in the game.
Now, with the addition of vehicles, the game has become class, especially the artillery. It's terrifying to be holding an enemy outpost, capturing it after decimating the Squad - before the recent updates, you knew there was going to be a counter-attack before you could successfully capture the point, it was only a matter of time when. Now, you hear the vehicles rolling up, or the sound of an artillery barrage about to land on your head, and it's absolutely f**** terrifying. 10/10.
--------------------------------------------------------
I don't regularly write reviews - but I figured I would make the effort for this game for several reasons, namely that it's an alpha or early access game, it's price is over the $40 mark, and .. it's really good. Most of my FPS experience lays with games like RO2, Rainbow Six, Day of Defeat, and so on.
Having said that, and moving onto Squad - this game meets my expectations and then some, and as far as I know (though I may be wrong) they are only on the seventh version, with vehicles coming in at the end of the month. The community is as good as a FPS can get - and I say that coming from RO2 which at the end of the day, on the right servers has some great folks playing. The more experienced players are willing to help with the learning curve (and trust me, there is one), and the newer players tend to listen. The graphics are.. well, Unreal Engine 4, which as someone who's developed on, I may have a bit of  a bias for, but they are phenominal. I run around high settings and am getting about 50fps on a a 960 GTX and an i7 intel processor - so the game runs well enough with the right equipment, and I haven't yet had frame rate or stuttering issues outside of some server lag when connecting to overseas servers.
- the firefights are insane. Coming from R02 I was worried I would be less than thrilled - the bullet supression in that game, and the general sense of fear when you were being shot at compounded with the system of heavy breathing and fear they designed for that game was great - HOWEVER, Squad just does it better. How? Thanks to UE4's capability to create sound thresholds and dynamic noises fairly easy - the sheer amount of firepower, explosives and bullets whizzing off in every direction, coupled with a surpression system that does a good job of mixing a "blurred" screen with that feeling of anxiety just makes for amazing firefights.
- I get that this is sort of something to be judged on a case by case basis, and everyone's experiences vary, but in general the people who take squad lead positions tend to be communicative, as do the squad members. The ability to kick troublemakers from squads also helps. There's rarely any hesitation to listen to SL's, even when it means switching roles (I've many times seen people switch out of preferred roles to play the SL's asked role), which might seem petty to some but.. let's be honest, this wouldn't happen in many others games.
-  I'm using a second point for this because I feel it needs to be seperate - the teamwork is outstanding when the interplay between squads connects, and you have 2 or 3 different squads linking up to attack or defend, flank or what have you an enemy position. The way it's broken down requires you to listen to your SL, as only SL's can talk among eachother, but squad members can't talk to other squad members unless they're local. (Again, the sound threshold, it's really cool to hear people's voices moving closer and further away, or to hear another squad yelling as you approach in combat. Also creates the need for "radio silence," which all IMO lends to the immersion.)
- Really fun to set up FOB's, (forward operating base) and then lay down the "deployables," sandbags, bunkers with weaponry, ammo caches, etc. etc. The way the squad lead sets up rally (spawn) points or FOBS (also spawn points) is crucial to the capture or defense of certain points - vulernable to the enemy and can completely change the outcome of a match. Fortification of places is great, and the freedom to make your moves as you see fit allows for an open world sort of feel to it - maybe fortifing the hill overlooking the town is better than taking the town itself?
- The map is HUGE.  Regardless of whether you are in an Eastern European countryside or the poppy fields of Afghanistan - the scale is phenominal. The variety is great, the scenery, landscape, shrubbry, everything looks beautiful. *This works into the cons later, but in a super minimal way.
- Sound - Models: Gun models are top notch, the sounds are accurate, realistic and scary as hell when you're getting shot at.
- Populated servers, I'm N/A and there is several servers that run with great low-ping. I also often find Euro servers and the ping is acceptable as well, which really means it's a playable game 24/7. Tons of people on.
- This is great, because it really makes the medic role important. Medics HAVE to stay alive with their squad, and do their best to keep their squad members alive for the duration of their mission - all on limited supplies. (Each troop is equipped with bandages to stop the bleeding, only medics have med bags however.) The fact that the matches are based on not only objectives but tickets also stops people from constantly dying and respawning - along with the size of the map. It's often times more beneficial to you, your squad and your team to wait it out until a medic arrives.
- This goes along with the open world, but there are many many different options for winning, that at the end of it are only determined by the abilities of the squads on your team. There are no set "objectives" outside of capturing towns or depleting the enemy - so the methodology of how your team goes about doing that is completely up to you. Often times, you'll have SL's coordinated, and have several squads split off for defense, several for attack, several for recon, so on and so forth - it's a unique experience to play a game with as many others as this one, and have that level of coordination and planning.
-
Note, these are all issues related to the fact that it's an early build, and are certainly not game breaking issues by any means.
- the server browser can be a little wack sometimes, and show a lot more empty servers than servers with anyone playing. Having said that, a few refreshes generally always gets me a good server.  -UPDATED- MUCH, MUCH better!
- playing with friends can be tedious because of the above issue, and the fact that "join friends game" through steam currently doesn't work. (Again, I'm sure this will be resolved), so right now it's a matter of "What server are you on?" which really isn't a hassle.
- I don't really want to put this a con, but some people complain anyways. The map size is huge, and with no vehicles it takes some time to traverse. (The first vehicles are coming at the end of July, so this will be an invalid point soon.)
- This game has a bit of a steep learning curve. Its not your usual FPS in the sense that, you can somehow zoom in with your eyeball 10 miles and see a dude laying on a hill. (Unless you have an ACOG.)
Buy this game, and feel free to add me! Hope to see you in game!

If you've never heard of Age of Empires II, this is probably not for you.
If you're a long time fan and player, this is for you, but you're probably better off sticking to the original.
I must have just turned 9 years old when I spent my entire allowance on a 2 CDROM box of AoE II Gold edition. I still have the box and the discs and every now and then I return to this game I grew up with. It felt only right that I should get a renewed version that wouldn't rely on a dedicated user base to fix things like resolution problems and low population caps. In fact, I'm pretty sure this entire product floats on the nostalgia of players like myself.
Overall though, I must say I am disappointed. Of course, the game itself is still fantastic and I dare say timeless. However, it seems that everything that was done to rebrand it as HD Edition has been to the game's detriment. It is far buggier than before, performs far worse than before (and no, it is not my pc) and new additions, from interface to units, are executed in a sloppy / rushed manner. Whoever worked on this can't possibly have been a fan of the game, as they did it a great injustice by treating it so carelessly.
In the end, there is just no way to justify the price this is going for on Steam and I sure am glad I got it on sale at the time.

Saw this was £0.39 on Steam (75% off) and thought YOLO how bad could it be!
This game is actually pretty good for a small simple game that it is. The goal is to survive hordes of zombies trying to kill you and you have some variety of weapons and defenses to help you.
There are two game modes, Defense and Endless Night.
First of all you can choose to play solo or allow others to join you when choosing this game mode or you can choose to find a game hosted by another player. Playing with others does help survivability however only the host can buy items such as walls, weapons, turrets and ammo.
You start with only a pistol to defend yourself and earn $ by killing zombies. You can buy weapons, walls and even turrets which can have any weapon mounted on them as you see fit. You do need to make sure that you buy ammo for all of the guns that are in use however because turrets will be useless if they are not shooting because of ammo shortages. In the later levels repairing walls and resupplying ammo can start to get very expensive since the zombies also progressively get faster, tougher and stronger.
The area you have to build is a little smaller than the edge of the map where the zombies will be spawning and you have a single lamppost in the center of the map providing some light. The very edge of the map is an invisible barrier and zombies will just spawn instantly so can occasionally block you if you happen to be running the edge of the map.
Lastly the items that you can buy to help your survivability sometimes can be bought slightly cheaper because they go 'on sale' which can be helpful but sometimes it can take a while for them to do so, in which case it might be more viable to buy them at their full prices.
In this mode you can also choose to play solo or allow others to join you when choosing this game mode or you can choose to find a game hosted by another player. Again playing with others can help survivability but in this mode you cannot build defenses, you can only run around so make sure not to run into each other with a horde of zombies either side of you and get trapped!
This game mode runs 'endlessly' until you die, there is no daytime in which you can buy weapons or defenses or ammo, there is just one single night that lasts until you die. You can however pick up weapons dropped by zombies upon their death but the ammo is very limited for these so you will run out and your pistol (which has infinite ammo) will be pulled out again.
Great game for only £0.39 that i bought it for, does have achievements that took me only 5 hours to achieve but its a very simple fun game and for that price you can not go wrong!
For reviewing completeness the game does also have Steam Badges if you are interested in those too!

This is without a doubt the greatest real-time strategy game I have ever played. It's challenging and spontaneous and if I win I feel a grand sense of accomplishment and pride, knowing that I did it myself without the game's help. When I lose I don't give up until it's truly over, even if I have to seek refuge in the forest on a far corner of the map with my few remaining villagers and one man-at-arms to defend them, slowly rebuilding my once-great civilization. This game is unbelievably well-balanced - each civilization in the game has its own ups and downs but ultimately it is the player that causes his/her own victory. You can build great fortifications of walls and towers around your city, creating an enormous and impenetrable stronghold. You can chop down an entire forest and manage fifty farms and ten mines, stimulating an economy that will allow you to recover rapidly from countless battles, which will in turn let you slowly weaken your opponents through unrelenting raids. You can act peaceful while amassing a secret army of knights, battering rams, archers, cavalry, and petards (self-destructing bomb guys), then blitzkrieg straight through the middle of somebody's village, destroying houses and mills not because you need to but because you want to, and then when all is said and done tear down every last castle and town center within their walls. You can take an island for yourself and create a perimeter of walls and guard towers along the shore, then defend it with a diverse navy of flamethrower boats and massive warships, occasionally sending a small force of twenty galleons to harass your enemies into submission. You can accumulate enough resources to construct and defend a structure of such greatness that your civilization will eventually be recognized as the ultimate empire, claiming victory by sheer impressiveness. You can have your city study smithing and academics so that despite having the smallest army you may still pose the greatest threat to your enemies. You can BUILD A GREAT WALL. You can practice devout faith in your God, so much so that the soldiers of your enemies will convert and join alongside you in your quest which is truly the most righteous. And if none of that appeals then you can always just say ♥♥♥♥ it and go out with a bang. The possibilities are limitless in this game.

*Update for latest release*
Almost all of the negative points I had made below can be considered null, especially with the addition of vehicles. I would also like to point out, I was indeed wrong about bullet drop entirely, and it is quite a factor in the game.
Now, with the addition of vehicles, the game has become class, especially the artillery. It's terrifying to be holding an enemy outpost, capturing it after decimating the Squad - before the recent updates, you knew there was going to be a counter-attack before you could successfully capture the point, it was only a matter of time when. Now, you hear the vehicles rolling up, or the sound of an artillery barrage about to land on your head, and it's absolutely f**** terrifying. 10/10.
--------------------------------------------------------
I don't regularly write reviews - but I figured I would make the effort for this game for several reasons, namely that it's an alpha or early access game, it's price is over the $40 mark, and .. it's really good. Most of my FPS experience lays with games like RO2, Rainbow Six, Day of Defeat, and so on.
Having said that, and moving onto Squad - this game meets my expectations and then some, and as far as I know (though I may be wrong) they are only on the seventh version, with vehicles coming in at the end of the month. The community is as good as a FPS can get - and I say that coming from RO2 which at the end of the day, on the right servers has some great folks playing. The more experienced players are willing to help with the learning curve (and trust me, there is one), and the newer players tend to listen. The graphics are.. well, Unreal Engine 4, which as someone who's developed on, I may have a bit of  a bias for, but they are phenominal. I run around high settings and am getting about 50fps on a a 960 GTX and an i7 intel processor - so the game runs well enough with the right equipment, and I haven't yet had frame rate or stuttering issues outside of some server lag when connecting to overseas servers.
- the firefights are insane. Coming from R02 I was worried I would be less than thrilled - the bullet supression in that game, and the general sense of fear when you were being shot at compounded with the system of heavy breathing and fear they designed for that game was great - HOWEVER, Squad just does it better. How? Thanks to UE4's capability to create sound thresholds and dynamic noises fairly easy - the sheer amount of firepower, explosives and bullets whizzing off in every direction, coupled with a surpression system that does a good job of mixing a "blurred" screen with that feeling of anxiety just makes for amazing firefights.
- I get that this is sort of something to be judged on a case by case basis, and everyone's experiences vary, but in general the people who take squad lead positions tend to be communicative, as do the squad members. The ability to kick troublemakers from squads also helps. There's rarely any hesitation to listen to SL's, even when it means switching roles (I've many times seen people switch out of preferred roles to play the SL's asked role), which might seem petty to some but.. let's be honest, this wouldn't happen in many others games.
-  I'm using a second point for this because I feel it needs to be seperate - the teamwork is outstanding when the interplay between squads connects, and you have 2 or 3 different squads linking up to attack or defend, flank or what have you an enemy position. The way it's broken down requires you to listen to your SL, as only SL's can talk among eachother, but squad members can't talk to other squad members unless they're local. (Again, the sound threshold, it's really cool to hear people's voices moving closer and further away, or to hear another squad yelling as you approach in combat. Also creates the need for "radio silence," which all IMO lends to the immersion.)
- Really fun to set up FOB's, (forward operating base) and then lay down the "deployables," sandbags, bunkers with weaponry, ammo caches, etc. etc. The way the squad lead sets up rally (spawn) points or FOBS (also spawn points) is crucial to the capture or defense of certain points - vulernable to the enemy and can completely change the outcome of a match. Fortification of places is great, and the freedom to make your moves as you see fit allows for an open world sort of feel to it - maybe fortifing the hill overlooking the town is better than taking the town itself?
- The map is HUGE.  Regardless of whether you are in an Eastern European countryside or the poppy fields of Afghanistan - the scale is phenominal. The variety is great, the scenery, landscape, shrubbry, everything looks beautiful. *This works into the cons later, but in a super minimal way.
- Sound - Models: Gun models are top notch, the sounds are accurate, realistic and scary as hell when you're getting shot at.
- Populated servers, I'm N/A and there is several servers that run with great low-ping. I also often find Euro servers and the ping is acceptable as well, which really means it's a playable game 24/7. Tons of people on.
- This is great, because it really makes the medic role important. Medics HAVE to stay alive with their squad, and do their best to keep their squad members alive for the duration of their mission - all on limited supplies. (Each troop is equipped with bandages to stop the bleeding, only medics have med bags however.) The fact that the matches are based on not only objectives but tickets also stops people from constantly dying and respawning - along with the size of the map. It's often times more beneficial to you, your squad and your team to wait it out until a medic arrives.
- This goes along with the open world, but there are many many different options for winning, that at the end of it are only determined by the abilities of the squads on your team. There are no set "objectives" outside of capturing towns or depleting the enemy - so the methodology of how your team goes about doing that is completely up to you. Often times, you'll have SL's coordinated, and have several squads split off for defense, several for attack, several for recon, so on and so forth - it's a unique experience to play a game with as many others as this one, and have that level of coordination and planning.
-
Note, these are all issues related to the fact that it's an early build, and are certainly not game breaking issues by any means.
- the server browser can be a little wack sometimes, and show a lot more empty servers than servers with anyone playing. Having said that, a few refreshes generally always gets me a good server.  -UPDATED- MUCH, MUCH better!
- playing with friends can be tedious because of the above issue, and the fact that "join friends game" through steam currently doesn't work. (Again, I'm sure this will be resolved), so right now it's a matter of "What server are you on?" which really isn't a hassle.
- I don't really want to put this a con, but some people complain anyways. The map size is huge, and with no vehicles it takes some time to traverse. (The first vehicles are coming at the end of July, so this will be an invalid point soon.)
- This game has a bit of a steep learning curve. Its not your usual FPS in the sense that, you can somehow zoom in with your eyeball 10 miles and see a dude laying on a hill. (Unless you have an ACOG.)
Buy this game, and feel free to add me! Hope to see you in game!

Roofs are broken. They don't get built. Also, You can't prioritize more than one task for a charater to do, manually. Like, you can't say "cut down three trees" then go back to whatever. You have to click and prioritize, wait for them to cut one down, click and prioritize, wait, etc. etc. Or you can delete all other things they may be trying to do in work, and then put them back later. It's really really tedious. I find myself struggling not because I don't know what to do, but because I can't command the people to do it easily, so it takes a lot more micromanaging than it should. You also can't rearrange the priority from right to left or left to right. For example, in work, if something is to the left, it's higher priority if you give it equal number (1-4) priority. So can't really customize the characters to work the way you want them to. Like if I want art to be the highest priority along with hunting (whichever is available) the character will hunt first if both are available, but what if I want the character to do art first if both are available? I think the characters are supposed to have a free will of sorts, but they generally follow priority exactly. You can give things higher and lower scores, but you can't move them left (higher if both are equal) or right (lower if both are equal). That makes things a huge pain. Every game starts with a different combination of strengths and weaknesses, but I can't get the game to function properly if I've got a bad combo that doesn't function well within the work system. The game can be lots of fun, but basic interaction is tedious. It's really clumsy. Not being able to stack commands (like go get that gun, then finish planting crops, then go to bed) makes it so you have to focus on the one character and you can't enjoy the bigger pictures.
Another problem is combat. There needs to be an option that says 'if im probably gonna shoot my own guy, don't take the shot.' Don't get me wrong, it's funny when grandma headshots grandpa cause what idiot gave her a pistol? Me. Would be nice to say, if the enemy gets in a certain range, run away, or engage in melee as well. Another problem, if I set two different buildings up to get built, they'll start working on both at the same time. I can't say, build everything in this one first, then the other one. That would be a huge help.
Generally my experience in the game is this - crazy stuff happens and that's fun, but then when that's not happening, I'm wrestling with overly complicated ways of getting the characters to do what I want them to. I can do it, but it takes way more time and energy than it should.

Wolfenstein:The New Order is a first-person shooter developed by Machine Games and published by Bethesda Softworks. The game features a single-player mode with 16 chapters,each ranging from 20-40 minutes long,and bringing the total game time to about 10-11 hours of pure unadulterated Nazi-blasting fun.You play as Nazi killer B.J Blazkowicz in an alternate history where the Nazi's won the Second World War under the spearhead of the infamous General William "Deathshead" Strauss. The game features both your typical run-and-gun way of fighting as well as stealth gameplay,though it's incredibly average in regards to the latter. There's aso a perk system that includes small trees for stealth,tactical,assault,and demolition playstyles. Each tree has eight perks in it but most are just small passive upgrades like increased mag size or extra throwing knives.
So,as I mentioned before,there's two ways to play TNO: stealthily or by going loud. Almost every level has paths built into the map to make it so both ways of play can work but there are some scripted scenes where you have to use one or the other. Loud gameplay mostly consists of what you'd expect from a Wolfenstein game as you'll be gunning down hordes of nazi's and their assorted technological monstrosities. Stealth gameplay consists of a more refined way of killing in the form of  slitting throats,throwing knives,and using suppressed weaponry. Honestly the stealth is a viable way to play the game but it can get incredibly boring since Wolfenstein is clearly meant to be played in a run-and-gun sort of fashion. The stealth isn't bad but it's just so overwhelmingly average that there's really not much point of using it when compared to the nazi-blasting action that comes with going loud. Speaking of going loud,this is probably the most fun and also the intended method of play in Wolfenstein. You get an assortment of weapons to use ranging from a sniper/laser rifle combo to a gigantic shotgun. Every weapon in the game can be dual-wielded and,as you would expect, this is crazy fun to play around with. Sure,it eats up ammo like a ♥♥♥♥♥ and it's incredibly inaccurate unless used in very close quarters but you'll have so much fun using it you won't care. The game also has some perk trees which are very useful for augmenting your gameplay with passives but are incredibly boring in what they have to offer.
The story was probably the most suprising aspect of TNO because I just haven't played too many FPS games with such a well-made story as this. The story begins with you,B.J Blazkowicz, in a plane with your pilot and friend, Fergus Ried during the allied invasion of Deathshead's compound. The invasion is doomed to failure from the very start it seems, as allied planes begin falling from the skies like crippled birds. You are forced to make a mid-air jump onto the wing of another plane after yours takes a critical hit and it is there that you meet Private Probst Wyatt III. The plane crashes and you end up underwater surrounded by gunfire and corpses. You swim ashore and get inside of another crashed plane where you make contact with Fergus and his squad who've got a Panzerhund (A Nazi Robot Dog) keeping them inside of their downed plane.You take the beast off of them and kill it and charge full-on into the trenches in order to disable a nazi MG nest. You then meet back up with the squad and get briefed,by Fergus,on who your target is and on the plan to take him out. You rappel up the side of a building and make it inside the facility. You make your way through the floors,take out the artillery guns,and reach Deathshead's own laboratory while meeting up with your squad along the way. Wyatt accidentally activates the incenerators and you are discovered by Deathshead while trying to find the key to shut them off. Deathshead orders his Supersoldaten to hold you down and he forces you to pick who he will experiment on:Fergus or Wyatt. Worst comes to worst and you end up in an insane asylum 14 years later. From a quest borne of senseless murder comes,well, more senseless murder.
Wolfenstein,as you know, takes place in an alternate timeline where the Nazi's won WWII. There aren't a whole lot of games that are willing to take on such an interesting concept but TNO does it exceptionally well. They really make the world feel as if it's occupied and that rebellion is only being kept down through use of exceptional force. There are 3 different record albums that you can find that are Nazi versions of famous american songs such as Mond, Mond, Ja, Ja by Die Kafer. The world as a whole feels incredibly well detailed and this adds so much to the overall experience. You might be walking through the hallways and see pictures of things like propaganda for the German Moon Landing project or different bulletins. The environments in TNO are all breathtaking as well. Ranging from a skyscraper that grabs at the sky over the streets of Berlin to a Nazi Concentration camp these environments are all very well done. The game as a whole is just so interesting and I would totally read a book about just the world of TNO if they had one.
TNO is the best Wolfenstein game to date with gameplay that's perfection incarnate,a world and setting that sets a chilling alternitive ending to WWII,and a suprisingly good story.

- I must say something: it's hard to start this game out, as there are some people that are level 100+. You've been warned for the first time, but there is no going back once you've been consumed into the game. Also, this is completely free to play, you can get to insane levels by just playing without subscribing, as all it does is give you the developer currency and increased cert/experience gain.
is a fast paced, first person, open world shooter that would lift one's experiences if they had interests in any of those genres of games. The intensity itself is jaw-dropping, especially when some of the battles can possibly be big enough to have an epic battle to control a continent containing over five hundred players, in which fight non-stop until their empire has total control.
There are plenty of pros just like there are cons. For a starter, this game is widely open-world and it's an amazing feeling to get into a harrasser (gokart/car-like battle car) and soar to the horizan, exploring the amazing world with your friends. The first pro we will be talking about is, in fact, the open world. Despite it's somewhat sharp boundaries, it isn't like Call of Duty and other first-person shooters. It has four HUGE maps, like, multiply the maps on Battlefield One by a hundred and you get one PlanetSide 2 map. These maps go by the name of Indar, an arid climate map; Amerish, a more foresty/plain map with more terra life; Esimar, a cold polar typed map; and Hossin, a jungle map. All of these maps are LIVE, and it is all on one server. There are no "in between map pauses" like Call of Duty or Battlefield, as everything is LIVE. You can 'warp' between each continent at your friendly warpgate. Each continent as its own daily quest/objectives, as well as different alerts and objectives. For example, the biggest ones always end up being the ones where you capture the most land in the limited ammount of time given, or to capture the entire continent (or capture the most territory). Those are basically the main pinned things, I don't really know what else to say about the open-world besides it's really freaking awesome. ^^'
The gameplay has its ups and downs, but we're just focusing on it's ups for right now. As I said, it's fast paced and action-packed, and it
promise to give you time in between kills. You must always be watching your enemy's every move, because it's most likely that if you stop to reload, you'll be shot and killed. So cover is always key to surviving throughout the battles. I highly recommend that if you're trying to find cover, if you're a light assault, it's always best to stay on the higher ground as much as possible. That's really all I can think of again.
There are 6 different classes that you can choose from, and each has its own different playstyle and weaponry-choosings. For example, the infiltrator is based off supporting the front-line troops while they push, staying back and picking off the low-barring enemy infintary that are trying to use heavy weaponry to surprise your allies while they're busy with an objective. Light assault is self explanitory, except that they have a jetpack that they can fly around in, same thing with combat medic. You heal people. The engineer can fix (heal, I suppose) machinery such as vehicals and MAX infintary, as well as place down turrets that only they can use to gun down the enemy. The heavy assault is basically just a heavy assault, having heavy armor and an LMG/rifle to take agro off of the medics and engis while they get busy. The MAX itself is a beast, a huge monster that will tear through infintary like they're pawns on a chess table, if they have an engineer at their back.
Vehicals are very diverse, from infantary transport to heavy machinery, they can be the key to taking objectives and crushing your foe. Each empire has one unique heavy tank and it's own fighter-plane, in which could possibly tilt the tide to your likings. I can't go into much depth with each vehical, as it would take a lot of time to do so, and I'm a
tight schedule! You can't just spawn as many vehicals as you want, sadly, you do require recourses (in which come in "supply drops" for your own personal use, though they're not unpacked, the vehical recourse autimatically gets put in your inventory) to build them. Now, to explain what they are. There is your average four-wheeler, which can hold two people - a driver and a gunner - as somekind of light assault to make a quick and swift base-steal. The Harrasser, as said before, is basically just a car with three spaces, a driver, gunner and a carrier. The Sunderer is  basically its own spawn spot (if deployed) and can be used as a heavy troop transport, holding up to 12 people including two gunners and a driver. The Lightning is a light tank, but what it lacks in damage it makes up for in speed. (Insert name for each team's heavy tank) is a heavy tank, which can be used for damage, and even could be used for simple transport if you're into wasting recourses! The planes include your average single-player fighter, six-person transport, three-person attack plane and a huge twelve person transport called the Galaxy, and I don't want to take the time and space needed to describe each of them.
Basically your in-game currency for buying weapons, weapon parts, and vehical parts. They're slow to make, as PlanetSide 2 is a time consuming game, you could imagine that it takes a while to make just a thousand of them. They can be earned by capturing bases, killing people, completing objectives, finishing alerts and getting to specific levels (if I'm not wrong, you can get them for every ten levels).
Whew! That took some time and effort to make. Thank you for reading this, if you found this helpful, press the helpful button and follow me (if you want), and if you thought this was funny somehow (insert cringe-worthy pun), then press the funny button! ^^

*Update for latest release*
Almost all of the negative points I had made below can be considered null, especially with the addition of vehicles. I would also like to point out, I was indeed wrong about bullet drop entirely, and it is quite a factor in the game.
Now, with the addition of vehicles, the game has become class, especially the artillery. It's terrifying to be holding an enemy outpost, capturing it after decimating the Squad - before the recent updates, you knew there was going to be a counter-attack before you could successfully capture the point, it was only a matter of time when. Now, you hear the vehicles rolling up, or the sound of an artillery barrage about to land on your head, and it's absolutely f**** terrifying. 10/10.
--------------------------------------------------------
I don't regularly write reviews - but I figured I would make the effort for this game for several reasons, namely that it's an alpha or early access game, it's price is over the $40 mark, and .. it's really good. Most of my FPS experience lays with games like RO2, Rainbow Six, Day of Defeat, and so on.
Having said that, and moving onto Squad - this game meets my expectations and then some, and as far as I know (though I may be wrong) they are only on the seventh version, with vehicles coming in at the end of the month. The community is as good as a FPS can get - and I say that coming from RO2 which at the end of the day, on the right servers has some great folks playing. The more experienced players are willing to help with the learning curve (and trust me, there is one), and the newer players tend to listen. The graphics are.. well, Unreal Engine 4, which as someone who's developed on, I may have a bit of  a bias for, but they are phenominal. I run around high settings and am getting about 50fps on a a 960 GTX and an i7 intel processor - so the game runs well enough with the right equipment, and I haven't yet had frame rate or stuttering issues outside of some server lag when connecting to overseas servers.
- the firefights are insane. Coming from R02 I was worried I would be less than thrilled - the bullet supression in that game, and the general sense of fear when you were being shot at compounded with the system of heavy breathing and fear they designed for that game was great - HOWEVER, Squad just does it better. How? Thanks to UE4's capability to create sound thresholds and dynamic noises fairly easy - the sheer amount of firepower, explosives and bullets whizzing off in every direction, coupled with a surpression system that does a good job of mixing a "blurred" screen with that feeling of anxiety just makes for amazing firefights.
- I get that this is sort of something to be judged on a case by case basis, and everyone's experiences vary, but in general the people who take squad lead positions tend to be communicative, as do the squad members. The ability to kick troublemakers from squads also helps. There's rarely any hesitation to listen to SL's, even when it means switching roles (I've many times seen people switch out of preferred roles to play the SL's asked role), which might seem petty to some but.. let's be honest, this wouldn't happen in many others games.
-  I'm using a second point for this because I feel it needs to be seperate - the teamwork is outstanding when the interplay between squads connects, and you have 2 or 3 different squads linking up to attack or defend, flank or what have you an enemy position. The way it's broken down requires you to listen to your SL, as only SL's can talk among eachother, but squad members can't talk to other squad members unless they're local. (Again, the sound threshold, it's really cool to hear people's voices moving closer and further away, or to hear another squad yelling as you approach in combat. Also creates the need for "radio silence," which all IMO lends to the immersion.)
- Really fun to set up FOB's, (forward operating base) and then lay down the "deployables," sandbags, bunkers with weaponry, ammo caches, etc. etc. The way the squad lead sets up rally (spawn) points or FOBS (also spawn points) is crucial to the capture or defense of certain points - vulernable to the enemy and can completely change the outcome of a match. Fortification of places is great, and the freedom to make your moves as you see fit allows for an open world sort of feel to it - maybe fortifing the hill overlooking the town is better than taking the town itself?
- The map is HUGE.  Regardless of whether you are in an Eastern European countryside or the poppy fields of Afghanistan - the scale is phenominal. The variety is great, the scenery, landscape, shrubbry, everything looks beautiful. *This works into the cons later, but in a super minimal way.
- Sound - Models: Gun models are top notch, the sounds are accurate, realistic and scary as hell when you're getting shot at.
- Populated servers, I'm N/A and there is several servers that run with great low-ping. I also often find Euro servers and the ping is acceptable as well, which really means it's a playable game 24/7. Tons of people on.
- This is great, because it really makes the medic role important. Medics HAVE to stay alive with their squad, and do their best to keep their squad members alive for the duration of their mission - all on limited supplies. (Each troop is equipped with bandages to stop the bleeding, only medics have med bags however.) The fact that the matches are based on not only objectives but tickets also stops people from constantly dying and respawning - along with the size of the map. It's often times more beneficial to you, your squad and your team to wait it out until a medic arrives.
- This goes along with the open world, but there are many many different options for winning, that at the end of it are only determined by the abilities of the squads on your team. There are no set "objectives" outside of capturing towns or depleting the enemy - so the methodology of how your team goes about doing that is completely up to you. Often times, you'll have SL's coordinated, and have several squads split off for defense, several for attack, several for recon, so on and so forth - it's a unique experience to play a game with as many others as this one, and have that level of coordination and planning.
-
Note, these are all issues related to the fact that it's an early build, and are certainly not game breaking issues by any means.
- the server browser can be a little wack sometimes, and show a lot more empty servers than servers with anyone playing. Having said that, a few refreshes generally always gets me a good server.  -UPDATED- MUCH, MUCH better!
- playing with friends can be tedious because of the above issue, and the fact that "join friends game" through steam currently doesn't work. (Again, I'm sure this will be resolved), so right now it's a matter of "What server are you on?" which really isn't a hassle.
- I don't really want to put this a con, but some people complain anyways. The map size is huge, and with no vehicles it takes some time to traverse. (The first vehicles are coming at the end of July, so this will be an invalid point soon.)
- This game has a bit of a steep learning curve. Its not your usual FPS in the sense that, you can somehow zoom in with your eyeball 10 miles and see a dude laying on a hill. (Unless you have an ACOG.)
Buy this game, and feel free to add me! Hope to see you in game!

So, first of all: Buy it!
Secondly, I take a little tour around the game:
The (basic) gamemode is as classic as seen in thousands of games before: You're stranded in foreign lands (here, a planet, hence rimworld) and you need to survive somehow. Unlike most other games however, you start with 3 guys and gals in a customly selected biome and you don't control the colonists directly. And you can set a narrator, defining how often and hard events like pirate raids occur. Honestly: That's a gimmick, but most reviewers love it for some weird reason.
Well, as soon as you're on the surface, you do the standard mine / grow crops / build houses stuff. So what's so special?
The details are. I've never seen a game this dedicated to details like wounds and with such an amount of emo moodswing guys going berserk ten times in a row because of really interesting reasons like "my bedroom isn't impressive enough", just like your classic CoD kid. 10/10 for realism.
Jokes aside: You can ampute basically pretty much everything of your colonists and reattach pigslegs or wooden legs, you can imprison raiders (but don't kill them, because your colonists are humanist af and will be sad if the guy that 3 mins ago shoot them will die) and you can sell your peoples organs.
If you mine too much under a mountain, your miners might get smashed and you can send a cute couple cuddling. No kids though, sadly. You can tame animals, hunt them, create a city of buildings and you can let your people make art, you can experience the freezing cold or the tropically hot biomes, or something in between, you can craft bows, pistols all up to miniguns and rocket launchers, you can explore caves with ancient cryosleep people and you can trade with other factions or travellers. You can build your powergrid and even set automatic sprinklers. You can experiment and experience different kind of people with different kind of properties like the mentioned depressive emo guy or a prostetic-hating girl. This game is so rich, its possibilities are only limited by your time.
But it isn't all gold and glory;
A major bummer for me was that the game tended to freeze on my Debian Stretch GNOME system, while it runs fine on Debian Stretch KDE.
Technical issues aside:
The game is sometimes horribly unbalanced and two mins of actions might doom your entire colony. Your guys will miss so much on reasonable distances you could be faster killing the enemies by making a snapshot of your RAM and finding the enemy in the hexdump manually.
Your resources can run out because even though the game creates a huge map for you to pick one square from, you can't colonize but this one square. But raiders can travel. Cool, amirite?
Also, there's quite a rush in the beginning of the game as you have to collect resources and build housing and prepare for pirate attacks quite quickly, and you need to hunt but as food will spoil, you'll also need a fridge but if you're in a cold biome you'll also need heaters and so on and so forth.
Speaking of which: The temperature system is more than broken as walls, no matter how thick they are, can't really keep heat out and cold in.
Also, trading via radio the traders asked me to give them a present of 300 silver first. I'm no trader, but I'm pretty sure that's not how trade works.
Also, things aren't properly explained. It took me 5 hours to realize you can change materials of walls and co.
But these are minor things.
As most games recently, this one also has mod support, but I haven't tried any of them (yet).
The game itself is nice, but it can be very unfair / frustrating. But I guess this is just because you get to love every each and one of your people, and thus it's a good, rather than a bad sign for this game.
I think this game is what Factorio should have been. 9/10.

So I’ve never really been a guy who plays sandboxy games and has a good story to tell afterwards, maybe because I’m playing them wrong or whatever.
Well, I have a good one from Rimworld.
So, I was made up a kinda cheaty scenario, where I was basically playing as a bunch of entitled children who ran away from home and crashed their spaceship, but started with a bunch of really good♥♥♥♥♥♥ While I didn’t include this in the scenario rules, I’m choosing to do research for the spaceship stuff (presumably to leave the planet we crash landed on) last, and focusing on the important things like television. These kids all all beautiful, have good skills, though some of them have issues with sociability where they’re just anti-social, or apathetic to the feelings of everyone around them. Half of them also refuse to fight fires.
So, fast forward a few days, to when I have a base built up from all the wood I have around, a few types of crops going, and preparing to start crafting some tools, when suddenly a drifter shows up to join the colony. Why, it’s the inventor Strick Santos, brother of one of my colonists (Henry Santos). How great! I decide to go look at Strick’s (now referred to as Santos for the rest of this post) skills, and it seems like he’s good at research, crafting, and medicine. What a great, well rounded guy to have in our colony. I did not notice his traits, or what he is incapable of at the time. I did notice later that he was also incapable of fighting fires.
Fast forward, a couple more days, and I’m having my colonists mining for steel in an outcropping to the south. A notification pops up in the corner: Santos has had a psychotic break. Santos decided to set a bunch of fires.
Turns out Santos is a pyromanic. He likes to set fires and refuses to put them out. As it happens, my base is built out of wood, and I have a bunch of fields full of crops that could catch on fire. So, I was faced with two choices: Let Santos keep going until he got bored and stopped, or try to arrest him and hope it ended up alright. I had one of my colonists try to arrest him while the others started to work on putting out the fire (keep in mind: half of them refuse to be fire fighters!). Santos is beaten half to death and stops his rampage, so the game refuses to let me arrest him. While he recovers, I start trying to reach a decision on what to do with him, and come to the conclusion that I need to try arresting him again.
Unfortunately, this may not have been the greatest idea. When one of my colonists tries to arrest Santos, they beat him to death. Santos is dead, and I’m not sure how his brother is going to react.

I'm not usually one to review games I enjoy, hate, love, or anywhere inbetween. Rimworld however is a game that I keep finding myself dropping back into for a good many reasons. On the surface without really digging Rimworld is your rather basic Colony Simulator game that harkens to others in the genre with the standards of a few settlers, enough resources to build enough to get started and the world is your oyster from there, the setting is in itself nothing ground breaking it's randomly named Rimworld (hence the name of the game) your plucky, or downright depressive, survivor settlers are stranded on. What at the more basic level sticks out is the story the game weaves, upon creating a new colony you're presented in Vanilla with three choices, Cassandra Classic, Phoebe Chillax, and Randy Random, each a storyteller with a different twist to the story itself. Cassandra will slowly increase the difficulty and add challenge over time and as her name suggests is the more standard game type for the full Rimworld experience, Phoebe tends to be more laid back in the situations she throws at you but with sufficient difficulty or time can pile on the situations as much as Cassandra can, and then Randy oh this guy. Randy is unpredictable to the extreme, he doesn't follow a rule of any narrator with peaks and troughs he throws whatever he fancies at you because it's all a story in the end. This is of course what the true meat of Rimworld is, a story of your making with twists thrown at you in such a fashion that you can't possibly prepare for every single one because it's out of your control. This of course is only at the most basic level of the game, not accounting for mechanics indepth elements, or gameplay itself. It is also worth noting that to add flavor to the story at the generation of each world a relationship 'tree' so to speak is generated, at any time a random wanderer, survivor, tribal, or trader could have a previous relationship with one of your colonists; be it an ex-lover, a brother, even a significant other who crash landed on the other side of the planet or remained in your old tribe.
Now to get to the nitty gritty. As of this review Rimworld is currently version Alpha, yes that's right Alpha, 14. This game makes no mystery over the fact it is not currently and utterly feature complete and just requires bug testing and polish. That is however not to say that the game is a buggy mess, personally I've not run into anything that was broken or acted wholly incorrect from it's intention and design. While the game itself doesn't have a traditional tutorial ala a pre-generated level or a hand holding amount of gameplay time, it does however have an intutive 'teacher' which picks up on what you have and have not done and tries it's best to nudge you towards what you need to learn. But don't worry if more then a couple colonies come and go while you learn, they've had their story it's on to the next story! The interface itself is easy to follow and while minimalistic it's to the benefit of the player over detriment from it's minamalistic simplicity. The game itself also offers a scenario editor that allows you to disable, add, or remove specific elements of your start. Don't like fighting raids at all? You can disable them. Want to create your own cloisted Militarized Utopia with no random wanderers? Done and done. Doing so disables those elements from being thrown at you by any storyteller as events even if you meet the threshold for them. In the same vein you can begin with pre-defined technologies, added supplies. Whatever scenario you wish or even let the game cook up a random scenario with limiters or an imposed time deadline to get off the planet before everything's destroyed. Of course if all this gets boring for you Rimworld has a pretty robust modding community that adds a pretty vast array of new elements to gameplay over at the forums as well as the steamworkshop.

This is without a doubt the greatest real-time strategy game I have ever played. It's challenging and spontaneous and if I win I feel a grand sense of accomplishment and pride, knowing that I did it myself without the game's help. When I lose I don't give up until it's truly over, even if I have to seek refuge in the forest on a far corner of the map with my few remaining villagers and one man-at-arms to defend them, slowly rebuilding my once-great civilization. This game is unbelievably well-balanced - each civilization in the game has its own ups and downs but ultimately it is the player that causes his/her own victory. You can build great fortifications of walls and towers around your city, creating an enormous and impenetrable stronghold. You can chop down an entire forest and manage fifty farms and ten mines, stimulating an economy that will allow you to recover rapidly from countless battles, which will in turn let you slowly weaken your opponents through unrelenting raids. You can act peaceful while amassing a secret army of knights, battering rams, archers, cavalry, and petards (self-destructing bomb guys), then blitzkrieg straight through the middle of somebody's village, destroying houses and mills not because you need to but because you want to, and then when all is said and done tear down every last castle and town center within their walls. You can take an island for yourself and create a perimeter of walls and guard towers along the shore, then defend it with a diverse navy of flamethrower boats and massive warships, occasionally sending a small force of twenty galleons to harass your enemies into submission. You can accumulate enough resources to construct and defend a structure of such greatness that your civilization will eventually be recognized as the ultimate empire, claiming victory by sheer impressiveness. You can have your city study smithing and academics so that despite having the smallest army you may still pose the greatest threat to your enemies. You can BUILD A GREAT WALL. You can practice devout faith in your God, so much so that the soldiers of your enemies will convert and join alongside you in your quest which is truly the most righteous. And if none of that appeals then you can always just say ♥♥♥♥ it and go out with a bang. The possibilities are limitless in this game.

Wolfenstein: TNO is a totally fine game. It's hard to give it a review more glowing than "surprisingly decent," but it's an across-the-board solid shooter. Just make sure that your computer is up to snuff, because this does not seem to be very well optimized for PC.
It's more cover-oriented than you'd expect of the franchise (or of any game that lets you dual-wield shotguns), but the gunplay feels good and occasional stealth bits provide a much-needed bit of pacing. The story is completely ridiculous pulp and the character are mostly thin sketches, but the presentation of both is slick enough to make everything go down smoothly. All in all, it's not something worth going out of your way for, and it's certainly not something I'd pay $60 for, but if you're tempted it won't let you down.

Dirty bomb is a game that takes the cake when it comes to it's free to pay modelling, core gameplay loop, and the rulesets it puts in place for the players to tinker around with. Yes, I did type; "free to pay." At any point, you can pay money to do things faster, like unlocking mercs, unlocking loadout cards, and maybe some crafting can be done quicker using a bit of dosh as well, but I've never felt the need. You aren't ever paywalled, and mercs don't get more expensive as you buy them with either free currency, or real dollariodoos. Instead, they're put at a pretty decent cost, 50k ingame credits, where usually, if you play all day, you can easily make at least 30. And it doesn't have to be 24/7 topfragging gameplay either. The game provides you with missions every 3 hours, first win, and first game type of the day. Ontop of normal gameplay offering around 100 to 500 credits, depending on whether you perform well (You DON'T have to be a pro genji,) and whether or not you have a booster, which the game is very generous in rewarding the player with. In my honest opinion, mercs on their own are frick-frack-snick-snacking ridiculously expensive, seriously. 10 bucks for a character you may very well not like is a very ♥♥♥♥♥♥ deal, at least, it feels that way. Normally, it's best to try out mercs on free rotation every two weeks before you buy, or, buy the Elite Starter Pack, and never have to worry about mercs again, which definitely feels fair for the price, as all those mercs together would cost a great deal more if you bought them individually.
Money, and how you are encouraged to spend it in a free to play game, is very important, but now that I'm finished discussing that, let's talk about NOT spending money. You will NOT feel like you are "grinding" for characters. You will NEVER feel as though you're just "slogging through another ftp grind", as this game is so god damn fun it made my
feel like paying around 60 bucks, and I genuinely want to slap more dosh on the table for this game.
The simplified core gameplay loop is as follows, choose what mercs you want to play, their loadouts, then press "quick join", select whichever gamemode you want, often depending on your missions, then play. You play the objective, get sniped a few times, kill the sniper, plant the bomb, listen to Jackal praise your goody gumdrops, and unless you're playing stopwatch, you get to do that again. That sounds like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, doesn't it? It kinda is. Dirty Bomb doesn't offer♥♥♥♥♥♥for a metagame, don't let anyone tell you otherwise. Buying, crafting, and getting card drops is fun, but it is not the same as adding a fooking laser sight to your golden mp7, as there is no real customization for your mercenary, or their guns. Mercs all have their abilities which cannot be changed under any circumstance, and then they have loadout cards that decide their guns, and minor passive abilities that everyone simply ignores 9 times out of 10. This is done over like 5 seconds of menuing, and most of the time for new players will only ever yield lead or iron "scrap" cards most people just insta recycle. If you like the gun however, keep it and use it until you have a shinier card.
Playing the game itself is of course, pretty darn fun. You have the ability to jump off of walls, perform an HL1-esque long jump, and shoot bad guys with a wide-enough assortment of deagle brand deagles, ar-1500 future funz, and slav-cyberpunk toys. Sniping feels responsive if not only occasionally unrewarding when attacking full health characters. If you have better tracking than the guy you're shooting at, only a red beam of death is going to save that man from having his dome splattered onto that EV. Shotguns are not something I enjoy, as I can never understand where and how you're meant to use them, but I see people loving them enough often that you probably would give it a try just to see why that lil medic grill was able to put the scotsman down like old yeller with such ease. Movement is as useful as good aim, and in some cases, being better than your opponent at moving your character, eg, performing long jumps, wall jumps, and of course the timing and knowledge necessary to know when to go full phoon, and where to rush down their connector like a speed demon; will undeniably net you a victory some way or another.

The game gives each character limits, detriments, as well as bonuses that make them better or worse at doing X, Y, or Z than the next guy. You have the full gamut of roles, Support, Murderlater, and Engineer. Supports heal other people, each medic does it different than the next. Aura has a healing station, Sawbonez has a slow healing medpack, and Phoenix has a pulse. They all lead to different ways to play that medic, usually coinciding with their health values, speed, and arsenal. Murderlaters can technically be supports to, as some of them, while really good at murderlating innocent mcguffins, are also really ♥♥♥♥ing good at giving people ammo.
Anyways, meme aside, murderlater type characters usually have assault rifles, and abilities that help them murder people. Fragger tosses and cooks zesty nades, while showering freedom and headshots with his REAL F*CKING NATO. Skyhammer drops the hammer, and by the hammer, I mean roughly 12-20 50kg bombs onto to unsuspecting vehicles. Nader has a grenade launcher, and is the token ruski lady. Thunder CONCUSS YOU ALL. These abilities are easy to understand, and in a vacuum, easy to avoid or counter, of course, there are more, but I don't like talking about Kira, or snipers as a whole because genuinely they have little to no valid place in this game. /salt. Lastly, there are the engineers, or, objective specialists, whatever you want to say. These three have special abilities that let them handle objectives faster. A lot faster. Fletcher, Proxy, and Bushwhacker are the best and fastest at planting objectives, so whenever you've got 3 seconds left in the round, hotswap to them and go plant the charge, because they do it that fast. Fletcher is a good trapper, planting bombs he can use to FIRE IN YOUR HOLE. Proxy is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bushwhacker sets down turrets and locks down an area as he has a pretty serious array of submachine guns to easily out DPS even the most prudent of benchlifting, minigun wielding brits. Of course, as with supports, sometimes there's a bit of overlap with other murderlater characters. Characters like Skyhammer and Stoker are capable of destroying EV's with only one use of their respective abilities. This technically makes them objective based characters.
Because I'm a lazy piece of filth, I'll finish this review later, but as it stands, I'd rate this game a very solid 8/10, as its worst issues are almost no fault of the developer, but they are still issues. Usually, my biggest problem with the game is matchmaking, as you can easily get paired against extremely high level players once you pass level 6.
