Squad is a tactical and supposably realistic first person shooter set in a modern warfare environment. This game has its upsides and also its downsides, but really the question is which one of the two has the higher quantity. Lets start with the details, the menu's as a menu should be (which is always good), the game gives you 'okay' control on the settings such as graphics ect. Now lets move on the gameplay, which most would argue this to be the most important feature of a game such as this if not any game. The server hosting in my opinion is one of the worst for shooters, as it is a gurantee that you have serveral lag spikes per match, somtimes even going passed ten, when playing as squad leader (to play as a squad leader you can 'command' your own squad and cominicate with other squad leaders throughout the game) you are given options to place down "buildings" as such, for example a F.O.B (Forward Operating Base) or sand bags and ladders ect. But this can be buggy as the menu will often be brocken, contantly talking you out of the menu and back the the main HUD screen. Overall the way the game was designed to be played was ambitious but was pulled off, for the most part, in order for this gameplay design to work, you need players to live up the the standards of an actul army man, and me saying this alone sounds ridicolous, but some times, every blue moon, all the players "turn up" and play the way its meant to be played giving you the best gameplay experience. The game offers you a Test range area seperate from the online servers, allowing you to inprove your skills on the battlefeild, which for me is a good feature to have. The game's controls are complex at first which could steer away new players but once you've had around 1-2 hours gameplay it will feel as if you've been playing for years (although controls can change for different classes, as each class has acess to different equipment but the controls stay more or less the same, the biggest problem with this is that items will change bind to equip them, which can be anoying). On the note of controls the game allows you to lean left and right which is a good feature, but the animations for that are of a game made in the early 2000's. Design wise i think this game has good graphics but has a few bugs with map props disapering, even so much as an entire building was not loaded in. As a whole i think this game is an okay game, not the best, definatly not work £30, but if the game is inprooved i think it will become a much better game, Inproovemnts would consist of 1) Better game servers 2) more game servers, as it is somtimes hard to find a game 3) better graphics rendering 4) needs to remove the little bugs such as the game taking you out of the "buildings" menu and somtimes when crouching/prone you may "jutter" around a bit. 5) get rid of the lean animation and replace it with somthing which looks better than the pathetic exuse of an animation they have currently. (earlier on the the reveiw i labled Command in a sarcastic manor with inverted commas, this is because of the players, you need a mic for this game, most dont have one, if they do its buggy or they play LOUD music through it on top of speaking, or they are eating, either way, and everyone else if either brand new and will♥♥♥♥♥♥up or just a general troll). Overall i think this game is the baby of Battlefeild and Arma III with a couple of little bugs in the middle making it not as good as other games under the same genre. I give this game a 4/10 but with inproovements it could score an 8/10. P.S: this game could use a carry mechanic to carry your wounded allies to safety simular to Arma III's mechanic.

Max Payne 3's got a different tone than the previous two Max Payne titles; some people didn't like the departure from the noir-esque setting. The plot is still dark and serious, though, and Max comes across some pretty emotionally disturbing♥♥♥♥♥♥over the course of the game.
If you're in it for the gameplay, this game is one fantastic third person shooter. The addition of a cover system to the Max Payne series might seem like a turn-off at first, but it works very nicely since it's mainly there just as a way to give you a few precious seconds to plan your next move; if you try to sit and camp like it's any other traditional cover shooter, the AI will severely punish you by either strategically flanking you or flushing you out with explosives. Some cover is destructable anyway, which pushes the player to always be on the move. The bullet-time/shootdodge mechanics are still all there and they feel as good as ever, and you'll probably end up relying on them more than the cover system anyway. The soundtrack compliments the feel of the game perfectly, the sound design is top-notch, and the level design is great too; it's pretty linear, but that's just the kind of game Max Payne's always been. And the set peices for intense firefights are layed out pretty much perfectly.
The only negative things that I can think of are the fact that multiplayer is pretty dead, and the story's departure from the tone of the original games. However, both of those things didn't matter too much to me, and gameplay-wise Max Payne is phenomenal. Pick it up if you're looking for a fresh old-school shooter.

Wolfenstein: TNO is a totally fine game. It's hard to give it a review more glowing than "surprisingly decent," but it's an across-the-board solid shooter. Just make sure that your computer is up to snuff, because this does not seem to be very well optimized for PC.
It's more cover-oriented than you'd expect of the franchise (or of any game that lets you dual-wield shotguns), but the gunplay feels good and occasional stealth bits provide a much-needed bit of pacing. The story is completely ridiculous pulp and the character are mostly thin sketches, but the presentation of both is slick enough to make everything go down smoothly. All in all, it's not something worth going out of your way for, and it's certainly not something I'd pay $60 for, but if you're tempted it won't let you down.

Castle Crashers, a lovely little beat-'em-up that understands that soft spot in gamers' hearts for air-juggling four enemies simultaneously with awesomely extensive air combos and knocking them all back a screen and a half.
Yup, this game is 98.5% sterling fun, designed simply to put a smile on your face without even attempting to take itself seriously. The controls are responsive (though I've accidentally used an item more than once), the art style charming, and that sense of humor and heart that categorizes the best of indie gaming are on full display.
Yes, yes, there is that 1.5% that annoys me - some parts of the game are a nightmare to play solo, the first phase of the Necromancer boss comes to mind. The nadir of the whole game for me was that accursed volleyball section, but I had the fortune of playing as Orange Knight, so I just kept the ball up and my opponents alight with my Y magic like the good sport I was. Also, while the sort-of 2.5D perspective reminiscent of games like Turtles in Time is pretty cool, it sometimes makes it hard to hit anything due to your attacks being on a 2D plane.
That aside, though, this game was a blast - now I just need to get 3 friends to play with.

Pros:
-Well optimized, by Rockstar standards anyway.
Cons:
-Bad controls. They don't feel like they were tuned for the keyboard and mouse at all. Max moves like a tank and aiming is weird. The game can't seem to make up it's mind about the sinsitivity ratio. Sometimes you need to drag the mouse all the way accross the room for the crosshair to point where you want it to, other times you need MLG 360 no-scope reflexes to do it, and disabling Acceleration from Settings doesn't seem to actually disable it.
-Very linear and scripted gameplay, although I use that term loosely since it's mostly cutscenes. I'm pretty sure there's actually more cutscene time than gameplay time in this "game". I'm not exaggerating.
-Uninteresting story. Feels more like a mixture of Far Cry and Call of Juarez: The Cartel than Max Payne. That includes the cringe.
-You can only carry two weapons at once (most people will say you can actually carry three, but trust me on this one). This wouldn't be a bad thing if you at least had more ammo, but you actually seem to carry less ammo than in previous games, and back then you could carry every weapon in the game with you, and between levels.
-Takes up a sh*tload of space and loads slow as hell even on an SSD. What makes matters worse is the fact that about 15 out of 33 GB of space that the game takes up are actually the stupid pre-rendered cutscenes that for some reason had to be super-high-res, even though they run at 30 FPS and actually look worse than the game itself.
-Rockstar Games Social Club, aka Games For Windows Live 2.0. To be fair, it's actually gotten better after GTA V's release, but back when Max Payne 3 first came out on PC it was a disaster, especially if you had Steam to deal with as well. I remember prior to GTA V's release and RGSC getting a makeover, I actually couldn't run the game at all 'cause RGSC and Steam couldn't get along.
TL:DR: It doesn't resemble a Max Payne game in the slightest, gameplay or story. Feels like Rockstar tried to reinvent the wheel and ended up making it square.

ESCAPE
My stepfather always hated me. When my mother married him and he moved into our house, my life became a living hell. He found fault with every little thing I did and was constantly shouting at me and calling me names. In his eyes, I could never do anything right.
Pretty soon, all of the chaos at home began to affect my schoolwork. I found it impossible to study and my grades started slipping. At the dinner table, I was so nervous that I hardly ate a thing. I gradually withdrew into myself and stopped hanging around with my friends.
Things began to grow worse and worse. I became my stepfather’s punching bag. He started beating me at the slightest excuse. He was a strong man and I was too small to fight him off. Each punch and kick he delivered hurt me emotionally as well as physically. It wasn’t long before I was diagnosed with depression and the doctors put me on medication.
Through all this, my mother stood by and refused to intervene. She chose her new husband over me. That hurt me more than anything else. I gave up hope and prayed for the day when I could escape.
One day, I couldn’t take it anymore and ran away from home. I made it as far as the city, when the police found me and brought me home. When they took me back to my house, my stepfather was standing at the door waiting for me. His face was twisted in anger and rage.
As soon as the police left, he turned to me and said, “Did you think you could escape?”
That night, he beat me twice as bad as before. I cried myself to sleep. After that, the violence escalated. Every evening when he came home from work, I tried to avoid him, but it was no use. He began inventing excuses to beat me. I never understood how anyone could be so mean and cruel. It seemed like it was all a big game to him. Each time he hit me, I could see how much he was enjoying it. My body was covered in bruises and it hurt to breathe.
Eventually, he went too far. One evening, he beat me so badly that I couldn’t move. I just lay on the floor of my bedroom, staring at the ceiling. I didn’t know it at the time, but I was bleeding internally. My mother begged him to bring me to hospital, but he just ingored her. He said I was faking it. During the night, I lay on the floor of my bedroom, moaning in pain and slowly slipping into unconsciousness. The next morning, my mother came in to check on me, but by then, I was already dead.
Time passed…
I don’t know how much time passed…
Suddenly, I saw a bright light.
I heard a voice announce, “It’s a healthy baby boy!”
I started crying loudly.
Slowly, ever so slowly, I opened my eyes.
A man and a woman were staring at me.
They were smiling from ear to ear.
The man leaned down and touched my cheek.
In a gentle voice, he said, “Did you think you could escape?”.

Having finally had a chance to play this game, I was pulled in immediately to a much deeper experience than I expected from a game that was billed to me as being "like Portal." My Master's thesis was on cyberpunk novels, so I was very familiar with The Talos Principle's philosophical questions regarding the nature of humanity and the slim divide between man and machine, so much so that I've gotten pretty tired of it being so popular in video games. If there's anyone out there like me, let me assure you that The Talos Principle decidedly takes a different tack.
While some of the discussions were a bit heavy-handed and limited, I was pleasantly surprised at how well this game handles the deep questions and draws the player through them to question everything as an extension of gameplay, exploration, and the same problem-solving and investigative skills we have been learning from puzzle games since Myst. It gets the usual "shattering revelations!!!" found in other cyberpunk games out of the way pretty quickly and moves on to much more interesting questions, teasing out more world-building the deeper you go and the more you explore.
This is a slow-building game, and if you want to find EVERYTHING, you'd better get used to exploring every nook and cranny of some well-crafted but often sprawling set-pieces, and to read a LOT of text documents. To me, it was worth the extra work to get to a very interesting perspective on the Singularity and the Man / Machine questions found everywhere in video games today. If you played SOMA for the story, go back and play The Talos Principle for what I consider to be a much more mature and complete handling of similar concepts.

Widely praised as the game of the year of 2014, The Talos Principle is a puzzle-platformer which can probably be summarized in the following way:
The Good: It reminded me of Portal 2 in a good way.
The Bad: It was not Portal 2.
The Ugly: It kind of wanted to be Portal 2.
Its similarities to – and differences from – Portal 2 are instructive. Some of these were solid choices which helped to differentiate it, but some of its differences were failures on its part which diminished it as an experience.
However, perhaps the most salient difference is this: Portal 2 is about 8 hours long. The Talos Principle took me 26 hours to complete.
Now, you might think that this means that The Talos Principle had massively more content than Portal 2. In a strict sense, this is true; The Talos Principle has about twice as many levels as Portal 2 did, with Portal 2 clocking in at 64 in the single-player campaign and The Talos Principle clocking in at 138, more counting the Easter eggs – little (and sometimes big) things hidden in the various levels.
However, even with twice the content, that would leave The Talos Principle at only about 18 hours in length. Whence the extra 8 hours?
The answer to that is, sadly, “running around looking at walls”. And it is actually probably more than that, as the first half of the game is primarily spent on that activity, with far more time spent trying to find hidden puzzles than is spent on solving the actual puzzles themselves.
And worse still, despite taking nearly three times as long to beat, The Talos Principle doesn’t feel like it has more content than Portal 2 – indeed, in many ways, it feels like it has less, as you don’t interact with the characters as often, nor do the environments feel as varied as they did in Portal 2.
Through the course of the game, the player travels through a number of different environments themed around ancient civilizations – Greek ruins, Egyptian ruins, ruins of European churches, and even ruins of castles and forts high in snowy mountains. This contrasts sharply with the obviously technological nature of the player and of the various puzzles in the game, revealing a dichotomy between the pseudo-religious nature of Elohim, and the reality of the technological reality you inhabit. All of this contrasts sharply with the overworld hub – a place full of what look like beautiful ancient places from the inside, but which it quickly becomes clear are naught but replicas built in concrete bunkers in a snowy place from the outside. The tower dominates your view in the overworld hub, an enormously tall spire of concrete and steel that towers over all else, containing an elevator with the higher floors locked out – to begin with. Unlike everything else in the game, there is a sort of grubby reality to the tower, which hints at its true nature and purpose.
The story aspect of the game is quite good, and the whole game does a great job of invoking a feeling of profundity but also underlying desperation. You find messages left behind by various previous people, with version numbers after their names, and, if you pay close attention, you might notice a name or two from your Steam friends list. This is no coincidence – it is possible for you yourself to find paint buckets to leave behind messages to future folks who go through. Interestingly, this also hints at the nature of the world – as well as where you’re going in the end – and as you progress through the game, you unlock more and more messages you can leave behind for your buddies.
The game also has some meta aspects to it. I have seen some reviews which claim that the whole game is meta-commentary about video games, but it really isn’t. That said, it certainly contains meta-commentary about video games, and there are a lot of in-world meta explanations for the nature of the world and even why names from your Steam friends list are appearing in the world – this is not an artificial contrivance, but an actual part of the world you inhabit, and there’s a reason for it. There are also in-game Easter eggs, some of which are quite brilliant, and as you progress through the game the reason that those Easter eggs exist is again explained in-game as being an organic (if silly) part of the world.
What the game is really about is the central question of what it means to be human. The titular Talos Principle is a concept from Greek mythology – Talos being a massive automaton made of bronze, animated by ichor put in his body by Zeus (or Hephestus, depending on the myth) himself to animate him and give him life. In the end, when the ichor is drained from his body, he dies as a human would if they exsanguinated, thus proving him to be “human” in a sense. Much of the game’s philosophical conversations with Milton – and many of the documents in the computer – talk about the question of what it means to be human, and the question of whether or not the AIs they are creating – which you are one of – are “human” in a sense.
As you might guess, this is incredibly pretentious, but on the whole, the game makes it work. Milton is a lot of fun to interact with, and the unfolding of the project – and the hopes and dreams of the human scientists working on it in hopes of creating something to carry on their legacy into the future as a person themselves – is a strong current which carries the game along. The game relies on serious philosophical questions in order to carry it, as opposed to the humor prevalent throughout Portal 2, but it works well enough, and it contains its moments of levity just as Portal 2 contained its moments of seriousness.
A lot of the puzzles are in fact reasonably clever, even if they are never as engrossing or as exciting as Portal’s puzzles – carrying around items and setting them up simply does not carry the same sort of weight that hurling yourself through portals at high speeds does, and it shows, with the game feeling much slower paced as a result. And unlike Portal 2, the game is non-linear, with the ability to skip puzzles and come back to them as needed, and the various hub and sub-hub areas leading to the puzzles allowing you to attack them in a variety of orders, as well as explore the (mostly) empty world in search of the bits of content.
That said, there are three real problems with the puzzles in the game:
•	The game runs out of interesting ways to recombine the pieces about halfway through the game. You might think that this means that it stops introducing new ideas at that point, but instead, the middle part of the game is the part where new ideas for combining the pieces ends – the final few sets of puzzles in the third area of the game, as well as in the tower, proves that they knew of other ways to combine many of the pieces, but rather than run out midway through, they threw in a lot of boring, repetitive puzzles into the middle and then made the end better. This makes the mid part of the game a drag.
•	Some of the harder puzzles in the game are harder not because they require you to think, but because they’re long, and thus feel like a repetitive grind as you repeatedly backtrack to adjust your pieces.
•	Some of the star puzzles are puzzles of the “we hid the puzzle piece under the couch cushion” variety rather than the “you have all the pieces and need to figure out how to use them” variety.
But I have to say in the end, I really liked this game, and its use of serious, philsophical questions as compared to Portal's humor actually works really well. The moment to moment gameplay is all a blur in memory, but the story stands out, and I reflect fondly on this game, for all its problems with its puzzles.

I don't usually take time to write reviews, let alone finish a game start to end, but The Talos Principle deserves another voice added to its already large chorus of praise.
The Talos Principle is a masterfully-crafted, thoroughly enjoyable, challenging, and ultimately satisfying game to play.
+ Wonderfully engaging story
+ Puzzles challenging enough to provide a real sense of accomplishment when solved
+ Beautiful environments (your PC will need to be up to scratch to fully appreciate it)
+ Exquisite soundtrack and solid sound design
- Tetris-style minigame unnecessarily tough (I actually used a guide to skip these sequences)
- "Puzzle fatigue" - there isn't much variety to the core game mechanic of "enter world, solve puzzles, leave"
- Fast-forward and third-person-view not standard config on XBOX controller (I figured this out around halfway through!)
If you're looking for a story and puzzle play akin to Portal 2, or are just looking for an easy-to-play story-driven singleplayer game, this is definitely worth a look.
Overall, I would thoroughly recommend this game and give it a score of 8.5/10.

My Squad Leader experiances so far:
30% intense RP guy who thinks he's in the Marines, Soviet Red Army, or ISIS
40% guy who was randomly chosen, who doesnt care, is beyond stupid, or never communicates
20% 12 year old Squeaker-Rager who thinks he knows EVERYTHING
10% Cool guy who knows his stuff, makes good calls, and sucessfully leads the Squad and reminds everyone how awesome this game can be.
First of all if you dont enjoy realisticish shooters Squad is not for you. However, if you like Insurgency, RO2, or Arma then you're in luck.
WARNING: If you are not used to playing with a small team of people who can be either way too intense or careless that might be an issue,(After playing 1000+ hours of DOTA 2 it doesnt really bother me)  Be prepared to verbally communicate- it is essential.
-+Right now Squad is pretty basic, there are four factions, classes, some constructable objects like sandbag cover, HMG emplacements, barbed wire etc., a few gamemodes, and a few maps.
-There are NO weapon mods, vehicles, or multiple weapon options per class yet. (Vehicles are coming soon though:))
+Maps are BIG you may get Dayz/Arma walking simulator flashbacks early game, Watch out for Flanks!!!
+I'd put the combat system at a level similar to insurgency and RO2, way better than Arma/Dayz but not perfect.
+The damage model and medical system is similar to Red Orchestra on Realism mode 1-2 hits= dead or bleeding, every unit has bandages but medics can also revive downed teammates and regen health by using the Force
-Performance: it runs smoothly for me on a GTX 970, but if you have a low/mid level pc or AMD card at the moment you're kinda screwed
+ The controls are simple and easy to remember and fully customizable
-The UI is OK, I find it annoying when playing medic (switching from bandages to medpack is frustrating), but it should be changed to a much smoother radial system some point in July
Overall the game is fun and enjoyable most of the time and the community is OK (unless you're in Australia), If you want to join Isis, Blackwater/Academi, fight for Putin, or feel like you're in Black Hawk Down get this game.

Widely praised as the game of the year of 2014, The Talos Principle is a puzzle-platformer which can probably be summarized in the following way:
The Good: It reminded me of Portal 2 in a good way.
The Bad: It was not Portal 2.
The Ugly: It kind of wanted to be Portal 2.
Its similarities to – and differences from – Portal 2 are instructive. Some of these were solid choices which helped to differentiate it, but some of its differences were failures on its part which diminished it as an experience.
However, perhaps the most salient difference is this: Portal 2 is about 8 hours long. The Talos Principle took me 26 hours to complete.
Now, you might think that this means that The Talos Principle had massively more content than Portal 2. In a strict sense, this is true; The Talos Principle has about twice as many levels as Portal 2 did, with Portal 2 clocking in at 64 in the single-player campaign and The Talos Principle clocking in at 138, more counting the Easter eggs – little (and sometimes big) things hidden in the various levels.
However, even with twice the content, that would leave The Talos Principle at only about 18 hours in length. Whence the extra 8 hours?
The answer to that is, sadly, “running around looking at walls”. And it is actually probably more than that, as the first half of the game is primarily spent on that activity, with far more time spent trying to find hidden puzzles than is spent on solving the actual puzzles themselves.
And worse still, despite taking nearly three times as long to beat, The Talos Principle doesn’t feel like it has more content than Portal 2 – indeed, in many ways, it feels like it has less, as you don’t interact with the characters as often, nor do the environments feel as varied as they did in Portal 2.
Through the course of the game, the player travels through a number of different environments themed around ancient civilizations – Greek ruins, Egyptian ruins, ruins of European churches, and even ruins of castles and forts high in snowy mountains. This contrasts sharply with the obviously technological nature of the player and of the various puzzles in the game, revealing a dichotomy between the pseudo-religious nature of Elohim, and the reality of the technological reality you inhabit. All of this contrasts sharply with the overworld hub – a place full of what look like beautiful ancient places from the inside, but which it quickly becomes clear are naught but replicas built in concrete bunkers in a snowy place from the outside. The tower dominates your view in the overworld hub, an enormously tall spire of concrete and steel that towers over all else, containing an elevator with the higher floors locked out – to begin with. Unlike everything else in the game, there is a sort of grubby reality to the tower, which hints at its true nature and purpose.
The story aspect of the game is quite good, and the whole game does a great job of invoking a feeling of profundity but also underlying desperation. You find messages left behind by various previous people, with version numbers after their names, and, if you pay close attention, you might notice a name or two from your Steam friends list. This is no coincidence – it is possible for you yourself to find paint buckets to leave behind messages to future folks who go through. Interestingly, this also hints at the nature of the world – as well as where you’re going in the end – and as you progress through the game, you unlock more and more messages you can leave behind for your buddies.
The game also has some meta aspects to it. I have seen some reviews which claim that the whole game is meta-commentary about video games, but it really isn’t. That said, it certainly contains meta-commentary about video games, and there are a lot of in-world meta explanations for the nature of the world and even why names from your Steam friends list are appearing in the world – this is not an artificial contrivance, but an actual part of the world you inhabit, and there’s a reason for it. There are also in-game Easter eggs, some of which are quite brilliant, and as you progress through the game the reason that those Easter eggs exist is again explained in-game as being an organic (if silly) part of the world.
What the game is really about is the central question of what it means to be human. The titular Talos Principle is a concept from Greek mythology – Talos being a massive automaton made of bronze, animated by ichor put in his body by Zeus (or Hephestus, depending on the myth) himself to animate him and give him life. In the end, when the ichor is drained from his body, he dies as a human would if they exsanguinated, thus proving him to be “human” in a sense. Much of the game’s philosophical conversations with Milton – and many of the documents in the computer – talk about the question of what it means to be human, and the question of whether or not the AIs they are creating – which you are one of – are “human” in a sense.
As you might guess, this is incredibly pretentious, but on the whole, the game makes it work. Milton is a lot of fun to interact with, and the unfolding of the project – and the hopes and dreams of the human scientists working on it in hopes of creating something to carry on their legacy into the future as a person themselves – is a strong current which carries the game along. The game relies on serious philosophical questions in order to carry it, as opposed to the humor prevalent throughout Portal 2, but it works well enough, and it contains its moments of levity just as Portal 2 contained its moments of seriousness.
A lot of the puzzles are in fact reasonably clever, even if they are never as engrossing or as exciting as Portal’s puzzles – carrying around items and setting them up simply does not carry the same sort of weight that hurling yourself through portals at high speeds does, and it shows, with the game feeling much slower paced as a result. And unlike Portal 2, the game is non-linear, with the ability to skip puzzles and come back to them as needed, and the various hub and sub-hub areas leading to the puzzles allowing you to attack them in a variety of orders, as well as explore the (mostly) empty world in search of the bits of content.
That said, there are three real problems with the puzzles in the game:
•	The game runs out of interesting ways to recombine the pieces about halfway through the game. You might think that this means that it stops introducing new ideas at that point, but instead, the middle part of the game is the part where new ideas for combining the pieces ends – the final few sets of puzzles in the third area of the game, as well as in the tower, proves that they knew of other ways to combine many of the pieces, but rather than run out midway through, they threw in a lot of boring, repetitive puzzles into the middle and then made the end better. This makes the mid part of the game a drag.
•	Some of the harder puzzles in the game are harder not because they require you to think, but because they’re long, and thus feel like a repetitive grind as you repeatedly backtrack to adjust your pieces.
•	Some of the star puzzles are puzzles of the “we hid the puzzle piece under the couch cushion” variety rather than the “you have all the pieces and need to figure out how to use them” variety.
But I have to say in the end, I really liked this game, and its use of serious, philsophical questions as compared to Portal's humor actually works really well. The moment to moment gameplay is all a blur in memory, but the story stands out, and I reflect fondly on this game, for all its problems with its puzzles.

I don't usually take time to write reviews, let alone finish a game start to end, but The Talos Principle deserves another voice added to its already large chorus of praise.
The Talos Principle is a masterfully-crafted, thoroughly enjoyable, challenging, and ultimately satisfying game to play.
+ Wonderfully engaging story
+ Puzzles challenging enough to provide a real sense of accomplishment when solved
+ Beautiful environments (your PC will need to be up to scratch to fully appreciate it)
+ Exquisite soundtrack and solid sound design
- Tetris-style minigame unnecessarily tough (I actually used a guide to skip these sequences)
- "Puzzle fatigue" - there isn't much variety to the core game mechanic of "enter world, solve puzzles, leave"
- Fast-forward and third-person-view not standard config on XBOX controller (I figured this out around halfway through!)
If you're looking for a story and puzzle play akin to Portal 2, or are just looking for an easy-to-play story-driven singleplayer game, this is definitely worth a look.
Overall, I would thoroughly recommend this game and give it a score of 8.5/10.

I have been a huge fan of Max Payne games since I was a kid. In fact the first Max Payne brought me into PC gaming and simply blew me away. The Second one took everything great about the first one and made it even better. The third one feels really different than the first two.
It lacks the feel of its Film Noir roots, it is more punishing and the first two games while dark still made you care and wanted you to find out more about the world around you.
In this game the people around you are Rich Snobs that spend their time reveling in their dubious gained wealth, or poverty stricken drug dealers and other worse scum. As a result it is really hard for you to care about anything in this game.
Even Max feels like a completely different character compared to the first two games. The introduction of the covering system was a nice touch but it is negated by the fact that you can only carry 4 weapons with you, where in the previous titles you were a walking armory.
This game is not bad by any means, but it simply feels too different and in some ways limiting to be called Max Payne. I think that if this was a new game rather than a sequel that came almost a decade after the last one it would have been an excellent game that could be rated 10 out of 10 easily.
However the change in style, the limiting weapon system and a dark story filled with unlikeable characters makes this a 7/10.

I felt compelled to write a short review for The Talos Principle (TTP) since it provided me with a memorable experience for an extremely reasonable price (5 USD).
Pros:
Absolutely stunning graphics - I was not sure what other games CroTeam had developed but as soon as I started playing, I noticed a remarkable similarity with Serious Sam 3. It turns out TTP also uses the Serious Engine which would also explain how well it performs. (Although for the very same reason, I expected monsters to pop out for the first few hours) This game looks even more amazing than Serious Sam 3 due to the carefully crafted environments.
Story - I agree with what others have said: it is most like the Portal series for being a first person view puzzle game (although you can change to third person view in the settings) but the difference is that the plot is significantly more involving. Although it lacks the humour and playfulness of the Portal series, TTP has you conversing with an AI on rather philosophical ideas, such as the concept of conciousness and your purpose.
Decent game length - According to Steam, I have finished the first playthrough of The Talos Principle in 14 hours which seems especially long for a puzzle game where every level had to be designed and tested meticulously. Despite its length, I did not feel bored at any stage as I had access to different puzzles in the other worlds/buildings in case I was ever stuck.
Cons:
Tedious puzzles - The more complex puzzles require the use of several items. Unfortunately, you are only able to pick up items one at a time so there is usually a lot of back and forth in order to get all of the items into their desired place. This is where Portal shines since your Portal gun does most of the work for you.
Puzzle resets on death - If you die, the puzzle 'room' resets to the original state. Usually this is fine especially if you have messed it up irreversibly (although you can always reset it yourself manually). However, it also resets the other 'rooms' so if you are trying to collect the hidden stars which may span multiple puzzle 'rooms', this may become quite frustrating.
All in all, the pros outweigh the cons by tonnes and I would not hesitate to recommend this game to anyone looking for a puzzle game and/or likes to ponder philosophical ideas.

Great game.
Puzzle games tend to be rather hit or miss for me. Even though The Talos Principle's puzzle mechanics aren't particularly innovative, the game still managed to hold my interest thanks to an engaging story and some good design choices. The puzzles aren't strictly linear - which gives you some flexibility if you come across a stumper and need to take a break - and the levels are designed such that it's easy to see what challenges are complete and what still remains. The difficulty curve is also reasonable. The only quibble I have is that some of the mechanics are poorly explained. Axes, for example, just appear randomly at one point and it's not obvious what they can and can't be used for. Not that it's the hardest thing in the world to figure these things out, but it hurts the pacing.
I enjoyed the more challenging star puzzles as well, which require more out-of-the-box thinking, although some of them feel copy-pasted. At least half of them use the same two or three major gimmicks. It would also have been nice if there were better indicators as to where the stars are located. Getting to them is challenge enough; having to scour the map to find them as well is a bit of a chore. I won't lie, I resorted to GameFAQs to get a few hints in this regard.
The vague story pieces add some much-needed motivation. The puzzles themselves are rewarding enough, but the game would feel rather hollow if not for the little bits of information the game rewards (one could also say teases) you with. The philosophical discussions are entertaining too, though I felt a bit constrained having to participate in such open-ended discussions while limited to only a handful of scripted responses.
It was still a fun, rewarding, and engaging ride that I can wholeheartedly recommend.

The game limits your graphics settings based on the amount of dedicated, on-card video RAM you have.  While this ensures smooth graphics performance, it also forces players with obsolescent, obsolete, or unanticipated-by-the-developer hardware to endure lower quality graphics than their systems may be capable of.
The control scheme is non-standard, and the tutorial is inadequate in teaching you to use it.
The developer fails to understand the point of difficulty levels, and there's tremendous variance in the difficulty of given campaign maps.  While I am not a "play for the challenge" gamer, I am not incompetent, yet I am unable to complete the game even on "casual" difficulty setting, which I feel should be easy enough for a casual gamer to complete the game without ever dying in the same spot twice.  Why else, after all, is it called "casual"?
Some chapters have too much cutscene.  Some enemies are ridiculous bullet sponges.  There are a lot of design inconsistencies and outright flaws.  For example, part of the metagame involves finding clues and pieces of golden guns throughout the game, which requires carefully searching each level.  However, the game provides no indication of which area is the "trigger cutscene and you never get to come back to this area again" spot, so you end up missing these collectibles.
When it's fun, it's a lot of fun.  When it's frustrating, it's REALLY frustrating.
If you're playing because you want to fail and be challenged, this is a great game for you.  If you're an adult with limits to your gaming time, you're going to feel like a lot of time was wasted repeating parts for no reason other than cheap shots on the part of the developer.  At one point, you must kill one specific enemy on an invisible countown timer of roughly 3-4 seconds, but YOU CAN"T EVEN SEE HIM, so you repeately kill every enemy you can see and still fail.
Need to pause the game to take a phone call or use the bathroom?  Better do it fast.  Pausing the game longer than 5 minutes or so results in the the video no longer being updated upon returning and unpausing, so you can hear what's going on while looking at the pause menu.

REVIEW FOR B18:
Development on this has continued, and after my review, A15 came out and released drugs.  That didn't do much to change my feelings and I felt it was gimmicky.  Since then, there has been an update that added a world and caravans to the game which definitely adds more depth.  I still have some issues with strange pathfinding issues and other frustrating issues, but I want to reiterate the game is completely playable and enjoyable.
Many features that were once mods have been incorporated into the game. However, I still feel the game relies way too heavily on mods to provide features that should be in the base game.  I have approximately 20 mods installed, and another 10 that haven't been updated.
I've changed my rating to recommend, but I'd still consider my feelings about the game neutral.
ORIGINAL REVIEW (for A13/A14):
I wish there was a nutral rating.  I've been waiting for this to come to steam for a while after watching some let's play videos.  I also own Gnomoria and Prison Architect.  I probably paid about $15 combined for them.
I understand that the $30 price point is to honor early backers, and I respect that.  However, if you read the Early Access description closely it specifically says to buy the game based on its current state.  They may or may not continue development.
Bottom line, when comparing the game to Gnomoria and Prison Architect (even during early access) this game lacks content.  Prison Architect is still being actively developed too.  It also feels like this game leans on modders a little too much to make up for the lack of content.
Will I continue to play this game?  Yes.
Do I enjoy it?  Yes.
Are mods for this game great?  Yes
Do I recommend this game in it's current state at the $30 dollar price point?  No.
Edit to make clear:  I definately would recommend you follow/wishlist this game and take a wait and see approach about further development and/or price.

The New Order is a game attempting to walk in various directions at once. It's also a title attempting to maintain old conventions of particular shooters whilst adopting modern expectations of what constitutes an FPS experience.
On the one hand, you can dual-wield shotguns and speed-run a level. On the other, you can forego the craziness and take a safer, more cerebral approach to the killings, with single fire options available on your automatic rifles and the option to lean in and out of cover. Then there's the ability to stealth your way through the entire level, with suppressed handguns and silent take-downs with knives.
You can generally play to whichever of the three conventions you wish to adhere to, but the first is somewhat of an illusion. This is one of my few critiques on the game: The New Order gives you the option to Serious Sam your way through a level, but it feels rather tacked on and counter-intuitive when you can steadily die if you decide to run through the whole ordeal. Sure, you can Rambo your way through a level, but in-between spurts of action you'll need to take cover and let the health-regen kick in. You'll also need a substantial amount of armor gathered to be able to take enough damage to do any sort of dent in the enemies defenses while you're running all over the map. Armor that needs to be collected by foregoing the action, which, from a design perspective, ensures that the player is at least encouraged to try a stealithier approach and play the game in more than one way. Not that this encouragement is necessary as the game has plenty of sections that require you to stealth your way through a map, due to the absence of weapons other than knives.The game is ultimately meant to be a light cover based shooter with stealth elements, consider the 'Rambo' option more as an option that comes with conditions.
That critique aside, there's not much more to pick at. The stealth and gunning elements work well in-tandem, and the maps are created in such a way to allow either option to be viable. I wish the stealth portion had a few more mechanics at play, since Metal Gear proves you can have robust stealth elements whilst maintaining FPS elements without sacrificing from either. Otherwise, there's nothing to really exalt in this department; the maps allow tackling tasks in a few different ways and allow for diverging paths but there's nothing extraordinary to report. This isn't a critique, it's a standard all games should strive towards, which is competency and congruety.
The New Order is a competent shooter that entertains throughout its duration, but there's nothing particularly eye-catching or ground-breaking here. But there doesn't need to be to justify a purchase, whilst nothing is eye-catching its akin to a summer movie that's still worth the price of admission for entertainment's sake alone, which this title fulfills in spades.

I think the best way of describing RimWorld is Prison Architect with more going on and less control. If this game appeals to you solely through that sentence, buy it. You'll love it. If not, then let me go into more detail.
First, let's take the assumption you have seen what Prison Architect is, a top-down view with people wandering around and surviving in a realistic way, you overseeing them. This game stays true to that, just with many more hurdles.
Think of it as doing a 200m Hurdle Dash. Except there is a hurdle every three steps. You could get over most of them, but a lot of them you're going to stumble through, until eventually you trip up. That is this game. Struggling through an onslaught of challenges, just making it through, until one gets you.
There is room for improvement. Tutorial is non-existent, luckily I am a souper-jenius and managed to understand it from messing around, but it could require some learning to get started.
The game is viartually bug-free. Which is a bonus.
I'm struggling for bad points, but it's really just the Anti-Beginner Missiles. Lots of people compare it to Dwarf Fortress. I am not one of these people.

Let me start by saying I am a huge fan of the Max Payne franchise. It has been a
phenominal story driven noir experiance that is unmatched in gaming to this day.
I was apprehensive to say the least when I heard that Remedy lost the rights
to the Max Payne name to Rockstart studios. When I heard the game would be
set in Brazil I was even more apprehensive. How can you have a Max Payne set
not in the iconic New York city. I was afraid they would trash the franchise and
turn it into a new money grubbing copypasta game series that forgets what it
was all about.
To be fair, the game blew away my expectations. In every aspect the game is
solid and quality. The graphics, story, pacing, gameplay and voice acting are
top notch. Worthy of a Max Payne game. First the good.
The game itself is incredibly well put together. The story is tight but the weak
est entry in the series. However it is quite enjoyable hearing Max chew through
his lines and wit as sharp as ever. The graphics are using the RAGE engine and
it is truly stunning. The physics are the best on the market. I do miss the story
board way of telling a story. It is sorely missed in Max Payne 3. The "new age"
way of doing the story convence is okay but it can be a little annoying. People
complain that there are too many cinematics in MP3, but its a story driven game
and so I think it makes sense. I enjoy seeing the beauty of the game unfold with
excellent voice acting and animations. It all comes together incredibly well.
The gameplay and particularly the gunplay is BY FAR the BEST part of this
game. It is the BEST 3rd person shooter ever made. The combat is a true
pleasure. The bullets showing where you hit enemies, how the bullets hit the
targets, how their bodies react. Its an incredible ballad of death.
I don't think I really have to write much more. Simply put Max Payne 3 is the
best 3rd person shooter I have ever played. It is also a damn fine entry in an
incredibly franchise. I honestly hope Rockstar is not done with Max Payne.
Seeing as 3 was as solid as it was. Max Payne 3 from a die hard fan is a must
buy.
9/10 A MUST BUY.

On a serious note, Rimworld has the best procedural storytelling of any game I have ever played, and this is a story that I am dealing with at the moment.
John, a rich colonist, crashlands on Rimworld with all of his riches and boundless enthusiasm as an explorer.  He specializes in construction and mining, hand picked by myself after looking through many random applicants.  John's life was simple at first.  He found an abandoned slate house which he claimed as his own, only needing to add a door to it to make it complete and save time constructing.
John, being as he was brilliant at construction, was quickly able to build defenses and set up most of the power of his colony, but just after completing his defenses, John received a distress call.  Looking at the personality of the person in question, it was deemed that one of them was not worth it, as he was lazy and had no expertise, so John left him to die.   Soon after, we had someone else join our colony in exchange for getting bandits off of his back.  Although Matthew only had mediocre traits, he had just enough for John to accept the invitation, and the invaders were repelled with ease with the defenses John had built up.
Not long after, things started to go south, particularly for John.  It all started when we mistakingly gave many of our resources to a surviving refugee that had no interest in joining the colony.  After one day of constant treatment and nurturing, the refugee suddenly left and followed up very quickly by John getting the plague.  After hours of attempted treatment and excruciating pain, John, the original colonist died.  Matthew, who was only intended to do cleaning duties, was now required to do all the work that John once did.  The colony went from a speedy development in efficiency to a true survival situation.  Fortunately, Matthew had great defenses built up and nearly all of the power grid, thus was able to repel all of the raids (and scare the ones he couldn't kill with his charge rifle off).
After a couple of days of very little progress, a new colonist joined, Yates, who was far more competent in construction, and the colony started to improve.  The power grid was finished and slowly, we added two bedrooms and a kitchen.
But not all was well still.  Matthew continued to mill on about John's death and how he could not take care of him.  Matthew's mood became more and more foul as the days passed, particularly also because food resources were diminishing and the survival meals were no longer there.  Additionally, the colony started to become repulsive because current work didn't allow for cleaning (as there was much else to finish up).
We leave off with Matthew going through fits of rage.  Matthew nearly turned on his colonists last night, the only saving grace being as his mental breakdown was after a session of mining, but this also left him without sleep, thus immediately after recovery, he went through another mental breakdown.  This time, however, it's in the actual home, and this is where it leaves off.
I doubt I will write the conclusion of this (I will if I think about it), but the point of this is that you can tell rich stories with this game.  The survival elements are there, but the elements combine to tell this emergent story more than any game I have played except for maybe Prison Architect.
But, this game is a very different experience than Prison Architect, because Prison Architect is a management game, and this is a survival game.  The steps you take in both games are very different from one another.
EDIT://
The story finished, with a fitting ending for this game:
Matthew went through another mental breakdown, but fortunately nobody was harmed this instant.  He sat in an isolated spot with his gun until he calmed down.  Both breakdowns let out a lot of steam, so for a time, the colony went on normally.  We got the first signs of our kitchen, with at least something to feed us, and things were going well.
A new recruit, a pacifist named Chaz joined our camp.  He was fairly decent and well rounded in terms of construction and medicine, so he was worth keeping around.  Unfortunately, he never did get along with Yates, although with a severe infection during the waning hours of the colony, her injuries were treated.
Then, the raid came...
At first, they seemed like they wanted no part of the defenses.  They wandered about in the northeast part of the area aimlessly.  At the exact same time, Yates father, Jupiter, landed in a pot looking for his daughter.  We decided to take care of him, but in doing so, forgot about the raid just enough to allow the raiders, three with SMGs, one with a grenade luncher, to get close enough.  They attacked the point which had poor turret coverage, and although we had sandbag defenses, because we reacted so late, one of them was able to walk over and do severe damage.
The invaders did eventually get defeated ... just.  Yates was dead, Matthew was critically injured, and to compound the situation of already-near mental breakdown, a grenade had exploded near the house, causing a fire.
With Matthew incapacitated, Yates dead, and Jupiter not yet being part of the colony, all that was left was the new recruit, Cortez.  Being a pacifist, he was unable to bring himself to fight a fire that likely wouldn't be put out to begin with.  In desperation, two emergency sleeping spots were set up between two abandoned ruin walls where there were few trees to prevent forest fire risk.  Matthew was set down and Cortez went out to collect what supplies he could to at least try to start elsewhere, resigned to the fact that most possessions would be lost.
And then the final blow.
Jupiter, with his daughter dead and left to burn alive in a fire that there was no time to save him from, got his revenge.  On Cortez way back, he witnessed it perfectly, Matthew being punched to death by Jupiter, in a berserk mental state.
Cortez, out of resources, out of options, freezes to death in the night being chased by the raging Jupiter.
And this, my friends, is all less than a day of playing RimWorld.  Get this game.

The only things in the store are cosmetics and loadout cards which you can gain during normal play anyway. Bronze cards give you all the extra augments and anything above that are purely cosmetic, these augments are slight bonuses to specific things such as faster reloading or faster repairing. You may think that that makes certain people with cards with good augments can overpower all those that do not but that is not the case. This is a game of skill and you can have the default cards and still carry the team. Sadly they removed the ability to trade up cards and replaced it with crafting cards which no one I have talked too seem to like, me included. While i can understand why those who were massive fans of the original Max Payne games by Remedy with the very diffirent settings, direction, music and a lot of other elements that made those games fantastic in thier own way (and are still great games anyway that have aged superbly for the time in thier own right) and while i can see people not enjoying MP3 as a Max Payne game, i will make this clear: This is still a fantastic game and honestly in terms of quality i think honestly surpasses the originals.
While next to everything in this game was diffirent from the originals such as again the visuals, the music and so-on i found next to all of the new things and the old tricks still in to be absolutely incredibly well done to make one of the most well crafted and satisfying third person shooters ever.
The settings while diffirent at least were absolutely gorgeously visually designed with tons of detail everywhere around and all coming together to create a beautiful looking game, which i honestly found to work with the contrast of the video filters. The music once again while diffirent was incredibly catchy and fit beautifully with the enviroments you were in never feeling out of place (Just listen to some of these especially "Panama" and "Tears" two of my favourites
. The Gameplay was just THE best of the MP series with some of the tightest shooting ever with all the guns feeling like they had weight to them and fun to mess around with and the bullet time was the coolest to pull off with Max's more weighty control as the visual effects with a bullet time stunt.
If there was a issue with MP3 it would probaly have to be the story. Not that it was anything awful, it had its moments (most of them in the flashback bits the best parts to replay easily, due to me being such a big fan of the originals) and the writing was solid overall espacially with Max's narrations (which never failed to crack me up) being spoken incredibly well by James McCaffrey along with the voice acting in general being great, but considering that the game before truly delved into Max's psyche about him blaming himself for his wifes death and him breaking down to a point where he would go after Mona a criminal who he wouldve brought to justice if still basically sane so he could fill his hollow existance with the death of those he loved and knew, MP3's story does feel 'bland' in comparison especially for a series with such intresting plots and characters, allthough i personally enjoy plots that focus on the characters turmoils and how the character deals with them without other plot points going on like in 1 so i enjoyed it for what it was with the great setups themself.But the end was pretty good and satisfying rounding off Max's arch well.
But outside of the story everything else checks out to make a fantastic game and even though there is a chance that you might not end up liking it if you are a truly dedicated fan of the originals and the styles that were there, its still worth a shot either way. A incredibly fun, well made shooter by Rockstar and a great way to finish a trilogy and story that i have replayed many times before i bought it on steam (which is the BEST way to play it).

On a serious note, Rimworld has the best procedural storytelling of any game I have ever played, and this is a story that I am dealing with at the moment.
John, a rich colonist, crashlands on Rimworld with all of his riches and boundless enthusiasm as an explorer.  He specializes in construction and mining, hand picked by myself after looking through many random applicants.  John's life was simple at first.  He found an abandoned slate house which he claimed as his own, only needing to add a door to it to make it complete and save time constructing.
John, being as he was brilliant at construction, was quickly able to build defenses and set up most of the power of his colony, but just after completing his defenses, John received a distress call.  Looking at the personality of the person in question, it was deemed that one of them was not worth it, as he was lazy and had no expertise, so John left him to die.   Soon after, we had someone else join our colony in exchange for getting bandits off of his back.  Although Matthew only had mediocre traits, he had just enough for John to accept the invitation, and the invaders were repelled with ease with the defenses John had built up.
Not long after, things started to go south, particularly for John.  It all started when we mistakingly gave many of our resources to a surviving refugee that had no interest in joining the colony.  After one day of constant treatment and nurturing, the refugee suddenly left and followed up very quickly by John getting the plague.  After hours of attempted treatment and excruciating pain, John, the original colonist died.  Matthew, who was only intended to do cleaning duties, was now required to do all the work that John once did.  The colony went from a speedy development in efficiency to a true survival situation.  Fortunately, Matthew had great defenses built up and nearly all of the power grid, thus was able to repel all of the raids (and scare the ones he couldn't kill with his charge rifle off).
After a couple of days of very little progress, a new colonist joined, Yates, who was far more competent in construction, and the colony started to improve.  The power grid was finished and slowly, we added two bedrooms and a kitchen.
But not all was well still.  Matthew continued to mill on about John's death and how he could not take care of him.  Matthew's mood became more and more foul as the days passed, particularly also because food resources were diminishing and the survival meals were no longer there.  Additionally, the colony started to become repulsive because current work didn't allow for cleaning (as there was much else to finish up).
We leave off with Matthew going through fits of rage.  Matthew nearly turned on his colonists last night, the only saving grace being as his mental breakdown was after a session of mining, but this also left him without sleep, thus immediately after recovery, he went through another mental breakdown.  This time, however, it's in the actual home, and this is where it leaves off.
I doubt I will write the conclusion of this (I will if I think about it), but the point of this is that you can tell rich stories with this game.  The survival elements are there, but the elements combine to tell this emergent story more than any game I have played except for maybe Prison Architect.
But, this game is a very different experience than Prison Architect, because Prison Architect is a management game, and this is a survival game.  The steps you take in both games are very different from one another.
EDIT://
The story finished, with a fitting ending for this game:
Matthew went through another mental breakdown, but fortunately nobody was harmed this instant.  He sat in an isolated spot with his gun until he calmed down.  Both breakdowns let out a lot of steam, so for a time, the colony went on normally.  We got the first signs of our kitchen, with at least something to feed us, and things were going well.
A new recruit, a pacifist named Chaz joined our camp.  He was fairly decent and well rounded in terms of construction and medicine, so he was worth keeping around.  Unfortunately, he never did get along with Yates, although with a severe infection during the waning hours of the colony, her injuries were treated.
Then, the raid came...
At first, they seemed like they wanted no part of the defenses.  They wandered about in the northeast part of the area aimlessly.  At the exact same time, Yates father, Jupiter, landed in a pot looking for his daughter.  We decided to take care of him, but in doing so, forgot about the raid just enough to allow the raiders, three with SMGs, one with a grenade luncher, to get close enough.  They attacked the point which had poor turret coverage, and although we had sandbag defenses, because we reacted so late, one of them was able to walk over and do severe damage.
The invaders did eventually get defeated ... just.  Yates was dead, Matthew was critically injured, and to compound the situation of already-near mental breakdown, a grenade had exploded near the house, causing a fire.
With Matthew incapacitated, Yates dead, and Jupiter not yet being part of the colony, all that was left was the new recruit, Cortez.  Being a pacifist, he was unable to bring himself to fight a fire that likely wouldn't be put out to begin with.  In desperation, two emergency sleeping spots were set up between two abandoned ruin walls where there were few trees to prevent forest fire risk.  Matthew was set down and Cortez went out to collect what supplies he could to at least try to start elsewhere, resigned to the fact that most possessions would be lost.
And then the final blow.
Jupiter, with his daughter dead and left to burn alive in a fire that there was no time to save him from, got his revenge.  On Cortez way back, he witnessed it perfectly, Matthew being punched to death by Jupiter, in a berserk mental state.
Cortez, out of resources, out of options, freezes to death in the night being chased by the raging Jupiter.
And this, my friends, is all less than a day of playing RimWorld.  Get this game.

It's amazing that a 17 year old video game can still keep me enthralled for hours on end. I remember being shown this game at a friends house when I was a teenager, and I was immediately captivated by the medieval setting. I would spend hours in the Scenario maker designing my own medieval lands and the online games I played with my friends were so fun we would talk about it the day after at school. I couldn't wait to get home and play AOE2, again!
I played AOE3 a bit and AOM quit extensively, the latter being a very good game in it's own right, but there's just something about AOE2 that resonates something deep inside me to this day. I didn't know about the HD remake until last year, and when I found it I had to get the game, again! The graphics still hold up, and with hundreds of community mods in the workshop the game has a lot of appeal to almost anyone out there. I'm impressed with the amount of attention Creative Assembly have poured into the game, most notably the new expansions and added units and civilizations, new maps and map sizes, the game really feels twice as much more than it did in the past.
The only thing that irks me about the game, and has done so since day one, are the vast array of units that every civilization shares. There are a few unique units that each civilization has all to their own, but it's still a little off putting seeing an army of European man-at-arms being recruited from a Japanese barracks or swarming the jungles of the Aztecs and Mayans. But that's what AOE2 has always been about, I suppose. It's a small complaint and doesn't take away at all of the true core gaming experience. And with the aforementioned community mods available, a lot of fine folks have alleviated this problem, a bit.
If you're a huge fan of medieval gaming, you may want to check this one out. If you enjoy real time strategy games, well this is one of the most classic examples of the genre and you would be doing yourself a disservice if you passed AOE2 up.
If you can stomach the price for a 17 year old game, it is worth it, but if you're patient enough to wait for it to go on sale it would truly be a steal. It would be most worthwhile to purchase all of the added expansions as well to get the full AOE2 experience. I waited until the Summer Sale because I wanted to also purchase it for my girlfriend, who I am trying to get into the game and although she really doesn't play any games whatsoever, she can't resist just how damn fun this one is, especially playing online, together.
Online is a whole other story. Personally I haven't dabbled too much into online with people I didn't know, as my skills aren't quite up to par to the general level. But I'm starting to be a little more brave and I really don't mind getting my butt handed to me as it's quite a learning experience and still much fun to be had, as long as it doesn't happen too often!
So long story short, if you haven't heard of this game before, get out from under that rock you've been living under and experience one of the most timeless, funnest, most in depth games ever created. And for those who have played the original before but felt they've grown out of it, well be prepared to spend more countless hours falling in love with it all over again, as I have!

Many of the reviews for this game truly don't do the game much justice. First, some negatives about the game.
1. Game can be a bit choppy at times with the larger scale battles
2. The occasional, but entertaining, glitches in the game. (Like any other game)
3. The semi-toxic community, though you always can find a variety of helpful, friendly, and humorous players
Positives:
1. Battles that can last anywhere from about 15 minutes to an hour plus
2. A sense of community with the various platoons in the game
3. Large scale battles can be anywhere from 48 on 48 to 100+ on 100+
4. Game is made well with generally well-programmed physics
5. Platoons do have an overall effect on the outcome of a battle (An example of this: I was previously part of BWC, the general command of the platoon would always send us to the battles that we were losing or where we needed the territory and we would almost always succeed in changing the outcome of a battle.)
6. Huge room for advancement in the game both for the developers, and as players.
7. Game for all ages and skill groups. Everyone can be used somewhere for something and be proven useful in that field.
All-in-all, this game has been one of my most favorite games since I've started PC gaming. It is also one of the few games that I have been able to keep myself up all night playing. The game truly never gets old, theres always ways to advance.
On a side-note, I have seen a few reviews saying that the game is pay-to-win. That is entirely no the case. Yes, you can pay for items in the game. But, all of those items are also obtainable through hours put into the game. No items are overpowered. The only factors into how well a player does is skill and knowledge of the game. And, of course, the occasional lucky play. But yes, the game is not pay-to-win. I have put money into the game, to obtain items that I simply did not feel like grinding for. Now, even with these items, people who have put no money into the game, had generic starting loadout, etc. Have killed me without issue. It simply depends on the player behind the keyboard.
Of course, this game could improve in many ways. Like any other game, it has the occasional game-breaking glitch that is generally fixed immediately. Apart from that, there are generally very few issues within the game from what I have experience.

Our tale begins when a group of 3 crash landed on a mostly barren world one day.  With her was a middle aged architect and a "computer" (researcher). As more survivors showed up, Sparkles became obsessed with cleaning blood, which was an ever present stain on the compound, and if it didn't get cleaned up, time for a mental breakdown. Though frail and demented, Sparkles was a hard worker, usually forgetting to eat as she was so wrapped up in cleaning the never ending blood pools.

For those not familiar with what Squad is, it's essentially the new version of Project Reality, which was a BF2 mod back in the day and is now a stand alone title that focuses on realism, patience and teamwork. However the game is quite dated now and has needed a serious upgrade like this for a while.
Squad is currently in its Alpha and while it looks much better than PR, it's stripped of a lot of the features that make PR so great, but rest assured these will be coming in the future, i.e vehicles.
Even in Alpha, the game is WELL worth the price, you're not going to find a more realistic, team based modern shooter/simulator outside of Arma; but in many ways this is much more accessible than Arma, as you don't need a clan or a good sized party to enjoy the full experience.
If you have yourself a good team, who work together and know what they're doing, then you're going to have a lot of fun with the game, however, there are a lot of new players right now who don't know how to play the roles, so some games can get frustrating. (Most players here, as in Project Reality use mics and you're not really going to get by without one, so I recommend you have one before purchase.)
DISCLAIMER, this game requires teamwork, communication and patience, you might go an hour without getting a single kill and that's fine, this isn't Battlefield, do not purchase this if you're not familiar with the likes of Arma, Project Reality or Red Orchestra OR if you're not willing to learn.
The maps are huge with thousands of possibilities and choices when it comes to strategy and tactics,  the weapons are accurate, sound effects are almost too real, teams work together and you can see some amazing things in this game with a little initiative from squads. the community is friendly, supportive and willing to help always.
This is only Alpha and there's so much more to come. But for now, what other game on Steam can let you build a .50 cal position on a mountain top and rain fire on enemies kilometres away while your buddies help you with targeting and adjustments?

Max Payne 3 is a third person, action shooter with a very addicting bullettime mechanic and a good story to boot.
Developed by Rockstar Studios in 2012, this game is no doubt a wonderful expansion to the already amazing series, and is a contender for one of the best in its genre.
The game series has you playing as (you guessed it) Max Payne, a pill addict and someone who should already be dead due to physical trauma. If you haven't played any of the previous games, you won't quite know what he went through, but take it from me, this guy is hard as nails. After losing his wife, (and every other main woman in his life) he goes on an endless killing spree to 'right the wrong'; or so he'd think.
In this game, your journey takes you to Brazil, nine years after the events of Max Payne 2. Max Payne, a middle aged man by now, is a tired, booze addict who simply wants a life free of action. If you ever hated pills and booze then this guy is going to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. Max Payne consistently makes questionable choices and many of them don't seem to go his way, but if there's anything I'd commend is his persistence and commitment to whatever he's doing. As far as badass protagonists go, he's definitely close to the top of the list. Max Payne continually makes almost poetic comments about various situations he encounters, bringing an element of depth to a man who ruthlessly guns down those in his way.
In brazil, Max Payne wants an easy job, to get away from the horrors of the past. A friend of his, Passos, enlisted him for an 'easy' job of protecting the Branco family. Without revealing much, you'll discover that nothing is ever easy in the world of Max Payne. Almost anything that can go wrong, usually does. The story is pretty believable if you ignore the fact that he goes up against so many enemies with various high powered weapons, and is captivating enough for you to continue playing it.
In this story, nothing comes easy to Max, and you're sure to endure many painful/frustrating moments as you see just how human this guy is. But if you like a story of a man fighting till the very end, this is one hell of a treat.
Max Payne's shooting is pretty satisfying. Headshots with most guns will instantly kill a target, while body shots may simply knock them down for a while. Some enemies will try to shoot at you if they aren't killed, incentivizing the player to ensure they are killed. I liked the fact that enemies were so dynamic, as they would try to take a shot at the player from wherever they could. They utilized cover pretty well, and would sometimes not even lean their body out to take a shot. As the enemies got tougher, their body armor and intelligence got better as well. Sometimes they would jump between cover slowly inching their way towards you, sometimes they would simply rush you down. It all depended on the type of enemy faced.
Using the bullet time mechanic, combat was always fun. Seeing the bullets whizz right past my face as I took out five enemies in a single dive was definitely satisfying. One welcome feature was the ability to shoot on the ground after I had done a bullet jump. This was helpful because there were some areas of cover that would be too low for a crouch but just right on the ground. Sadly the lack of a prone button was disappointing, as there's no reason why he couldn't have that.
The shooting recticle was a very simple dot in the middle of the screen, which incentivized proper aiming. This game, even more than previous games, focused a lot on utilizing cover and bullettime mechanics, as enemies could shred you in almost no time at all. Avoiding damage was the best way to progress through levels, but even so I found myself dying at various points and I enjoyed the feeling of satisfaction beating the enemies. Healing up was done through the signature painkillers, which I'm currently sick of (please no more painkillers, just let me die). Dying didn't totally leave you in a pickle, as you'd slowly gain more benefits to make a retry easier every time you died; more painkillers, ammo, etc. Overall, gameplay was quite fun, but definitely had a lot of challenge to it, perfect for people who are tired of the easy-mode shooters out there.
Max Payne 3's visuals were both good and bad. The visuals were well done, and the environments were impressive enough, but for the love of all that is holy,
. This cinematic effect, used no doubt for a 'drunken' feel, was the bane of my existence in this game. It's terribly annoying on the eyes and it needs to stop, like yesterday. That alone ruined a lot of the game for me.
I actually liked the music and voice-overs in MP3. I think enough effort was put into this aspect for it to warrant a thumbs up. Some aspects didn't exactly stand out, but I guess everything fulfilled its purpose well enough.
Sadly, multiplayer is dead, with one group out there dedicated to

Max Payne 3 is a brilliant 3rd person shooter, with unique mechanics and a thrilling story. The audio and visuals are nothing to scoff at, but where this game shines is it's core gameplay and badass protagonist. Though the chromatic aberration and drug overdose nearly killed me inside, Max Payne 3 is a game you'll regret not playing.
9/10 Worth a Buy.
