Great game killed by poor decisions.
1. Ranked play has a tiny player base, but the devs allowed 5 man teams to queue together. This usually results in groups of high ranked players ganking unranked noobs. This was previously limited by only allowing smaller groups in ranked so that high lever players would be spread across both teams, not stacked.
2. Some of the mercs are just horrible, get a few thunders in your match and your screen is just white constantly.
3. Server locations aren't great for many countries. Australia has some casual servers, but they moved the ranked servers to Singapore, so ping there is as bad as the USA.
Outside of all that, the game play is fast with a high skill ceiling, there's lots to learn and the learning curve feels pretty good IMHO. The loadout card system never feels P2W, you get the same level of power from bronze up (the other grades are purely cosmetic) and bronze cards are trivial to earn. You can unlock all characters and play for free if you really desire.
The devs are working on the game still, so hopefully they will fix some of these issues in future.

Alternate history of the after effects of World War II had the Nazi's won and Joe America, the reluctant hero destroys a nation and the tyranny sought by those who wish to see you beg.
I was first interested in this game because I'd heard that many folks were surprised at the character depth and downtime spent with the people in your bunker. As Wolfenstein of the past is more or less just a twitch-y first person shooter and this one has more cut-scenes than it did previously. The gameplay loop goes something like this; Shoot all the things, make it go boom. America is the best. BJ Blazkowicz regrets his past, walk around with some people that are vaguely interesting. Maybe collect something for one or more of them. Shoot all the things, make it go boom.. America..
And it just goes on like that. There is nothing wrong with this game. Its just innocuous. I am neither mad at the time I spent playing it nor am I glad I bothered to take the time. It has it moments, its a true summer blockbuster. I personally just didn't care for it in the end. But it is extremely competent mechanically. The stealth feels good. Weapons feel properly powerful. You get to cut metal with a plasma cutter that would make Issac Clarke jealous; but it all comes to together in this package that feels immediately forgettable. I'm tired of shooting Nazis; no matter how cool it feels to do while a rocking soundtrack blares as you move in slow motion. This was obviously a game with a huge budget. Its a shame they didn't do much to make it unique.
There is a faintly interesting moment where you make a relatively prominent choice in where the story goes. One that might make some of you go back and replay the entire game to see what changes but for me; I'm satisfied.

After giving this review a lot of thought, I can't reccomend this game for a few major and a few minor reasons.
1. You are going to need a pretty good PC to run this game at all. I have a decent PC and I still dip into the low 20s even on medium quality. Sure there are mass battles that can be fun, but you can't experience them at 10 FPS.

The Talos Principle already has a great reputation, so there's not much I can really add to the conversation. The first half of the game is, quite frankly, amazing and perfectly executed all around; gameplay, setting, narrative, aesthetic, etc. are all clearly highly polished and worthy of extreme praise. Puzzle games are not really my forte, but I had fun most of the time.
I do have some issue around the 10 hour mark or so. The puzzles, while thought provoking and challenging, ramp up difficulty rather quickly or have obscure or illogical solutions. More times then not, I found myself looking up a guide for a puzzle, only to find I had an incorrect placement of an object of about half an inch. Over extended playtime, the music feels a bit repetitive, but not unpleasant. Rarely, I find puzzles to be redundant or tedious.
A major issue I have with the game is the star system (for those unfamiliar, stars are hidden collectibles in each world) and how difficult some of the puzzles are. For example, one of the puzzles involves using a QR code reader, a hex converter, and an encyclopedia if you're unfamiliar with US history. Some stars are so well hidden, I don't know if I would ever find them without using a guide. After spending hours with a guide, I would not recommend going after them, just look up the ending on Youtube.
However, despite these seemingly sizable complaints, the game is quite good - definitely within my top 25 games of all time. The story is though provoking and well written; it draws heavily from ancient Greek and Egyptian(?) texts, along with contemporary philosophy.  The ideas tossed around are significantly deeper than other story focused games I've played recently (not to name any specific games, but think popular 2015 story-heavy games).  Regardless, the story had me rushing through the game just so I could see the next 'chapter', if you will.
The gameplay, while not particularly innovative, is challenging and satisfying. Think Portal meets Half Life 2 meets a theoretical co-op Braid meets that one Wind Waker temple with the mirror shield, for about 20 hours. The most interesting mechanic, the jammer, is used frequently for the first act, but largely forgotten about in acts two and three, which is a shame.
All in all, while I had some significant issues with the game while playing, The Talos Principle was a thought provoking and interesting experience. If you want a more detailed review of this game and how I felt regarding it, I would recommend watching Yahtzee's Zero Punctuation episode on this game, as he has a similar stance to me and describes it more eloquently.

Sometimes a game is really just a cheap aimless unpretentious passtime. This is a good thing.
- no intricate storyline or cutscenes to suffer through
- no huge open world to travel
- no claustrophobic disorienting dungeons to explore
- no complex dialogs with NPCs
- no quest grinding to get your level ups
- no sophisticated graphics
- no pompous soundtrack
- no DLC (no DLC!)
- no gimmicky fad-of-the-day description with overused meaningless keywords
Just a simple game. Survive the zombie onslaught at night, rebuild and restock at day, rinse and repeat with stronger zombies and better stuff. Graphics, sounds, settings menu, user interface, environment, goal... all minimalistic but perfectly functional, no need for more. It's like Skyrim without Skyrim.
Run it, and blow off some steam, or laugh your hiney off, or alleviate some real world frustrations. Or all of those at the same time. There's no shame in it. Deep down inside, you want to, and you know it. Do it alone, do it together. It's ok. The zombies won't complain.
One gripe:
- Zombies should never, ever be allowed to run. Ever. Seriously, what were you thinking?

Let me tell you the story of Andy.
Andy was one of three lucky souls who survived a crashlanding. Another of those three souls was his fiance'.
Things were going well; a small complex was built, animals were hunted, crops were sown. Trees were chopped, ores and rocks were mined.
Andy lost his right eye (crushed in a terrible mining accident!).
A wandering soul joined, the group grew stronger. Andy even got a handy eye patch, as not to frighten anyone with a nasty face-cave.
Over the weeks, a couple♥♥♥♥♥holes got jealous of this awesome and productive colony growing on their planet. They attacked, and were beaten back. A couple prisoners taken here n there. A greater number of those♥♥♥♥♥holes buried.
One of those♥♥♥♥♥holes had chopped off Andy's hand!
So he got himself a hook hand attached. Not so great for ya know, grabbing stuff... But he'd put some extra holes into the next set of jealous♥♥♥♥♥holes that mosey'd on by! Tell you what...
Andy's lovely lass never lost her feelings for this now one-eyed, hook handed dude she'd crashlanded with. A good, productive, and true-aiming woman she was!
... And then, she was gone. Infection I'm afraid.
Andy, to say the least, was distraught. Over the following days and weeks, he'd fall into states of sadness, wandering about, dropping random items, such as his weapon, or his pants.. Ya know, whatever he happened to be carrying or wearing.
Lumi, one of the souls who'd wandered into and joined this blossoming colony, saw his suffering. She'd known his first love. She'd respected that gal, shared a few laughs with her, had fought back raiding♥♥♥♥♥holes side-by-side her and Andy. She felt this loss too personally.
She didn't mind his eye-patch or hook-hand. She found it a bit comical actually, calling him a pirate on occaision. She said she'd tame a parrot for him one of these days. He would grin and laugh, keeping a sense of humor through all these dark times.
They became an item, and Andy and Lumi became engaged! Oh, what joy, to find a second chance at love on this Rimworld.
Another day, another crop sown, another raid repelled. It had become routine, the blood-letting, the survival, the raw grit of this new, unforgiving existance.
Lumi got Malaria...
Andy and his few remaining fellows tended to her as best they could. Day after day, they cared for her. Fed her, hoping she'd survive, pull through, exhibit that surviving spirit that was essential now. She was on the upswing it seemed, they hoped and prayed for the best.
It wasn't enough. She passed, and Andy wept from his one eye, and gouged his nose as he tried to wipe the tears away with his hook hand. He was quite distraught you see; probably better than him at this point!
At this point, a simple hole in the ground wasn't enough. No, Lumi, and another one of the five colonists when the Malaria had hit, had been true survivors. They'd held onto life as long as they could, until the last of the red-threads had frayed and snapped, falling into infinity.
They'd be set to rest in marble sarcophogi, in a tomb pecked into the mountain. No chance for desecration, by foul raider or dirty wolf alike.
And so it was.
Andy, was distraught. He went into a blind rage a day or so later, attacking both of his fellow colonists. Their small, patch-work, tight-knit family that had been through Hell and back was falling apart!
He died of blood loss, as Artemis was carrying him back to camp.
Artemis, and her last fellow, were never heard from after this.

I have no doubt that The Talos Principal is, if not the, most accomplished game I have ever played. This admittedly simple game is technically amazing, from the environmental art to the puzzle mechanics. That being said, what is on screen is a distraction from The Talos Principal itself. It does not matter that your are in the ruins of a roman garden, getting hints from "God" nor is it important that your ancestor (you being a sentient robot) is trapped in hard network.
The allegory of you, a lone thinking being is lost in a world of building puzzles, with only a vague voice of encouragement, and warning to guide you as you discover each small challenge only prepares you for what is next. Add to this that the essence of all humanity echoes through the terminals in a broken way, filled with missing conclusions, and place it all in a dreamscape.
What The Talos Principal is, is a literal walk through existential reality. Unfortunately, that is where my problems with the game start. For starters, every question the game has posed, I have already answered for myself years ago. I accept that the world is chaos, and that by being the only thinking creature (at least to this level) we are going to question reality. I accept that I may not exist, or that my existence is only a blip, that there is nothing before or after. I also accept that life in this from may be a long elaborate test, that the human species is a prototype, and that the "soul" is being "beta tested" before transcending into an ethereal cloud. I accept that that does not matter, we are here, and the only thing we can prove is what we accept.
Additionally, the game seems to hold that the rise and fall of the Roman Empire is a allegory for existence. It is not, in the course of human events there is a grand cycle:
Dissatisfaction with the status quo breeds resentment.
Resentment breeds revolution.
Revolution breeds new structures, and new challenges based on the victors ideals.
The human condition compels us to solve these challenges.
When the challenges are done, we are dissatisfied.
The Roman Empire was an example, not an allegory. The game does a good job of starting us in that cycle, and having not finished the game (only 90 minutes as of this review) the tower represents the ultimate reward. Once we have attained that, there is no longer a point. We have won, there is nothing left to conquer, we are bored.
The fact that this game exists thrills me, and I hope other people struggling to understand the great why of life can find it here. Only because I have already realized what I accept as the meaning of life, I give the Talos Principal a 4 out of 5. I will update as I play through, and I may award the fifth point if it brings a question I cannot answer.

Alternate history of the after effects of World War II had the Nazi's won and Joe America, the reluctant hero destroys a nation and the tyranny sought by those who wish to see you beg.
I was first interested in this game because I'd heard that many folks were surprised at the character depth and downtime spent with the people in your bunker. As Wolfenstein of the past is more or less just a twitch-y first person shooter and this one has more cut-scenes than it did previously. The gameplay loop goes something like this; Shoot all the things, make it go boom. America is the best. BJ Blazkowicz regrets his past, walk around with some people that are vaguely interesting. Maybe collect something for one or more of them. Shoot all the things, make it go boom.. America..
And it just goes on like that. There is nothing wrong with this game. Its just innocuous. I am neither mad at the time I spent playing it nor am I glad I bothered to take the time. It has it moments, its a true summer blockbuster. I personally just didn't care for it in the end. But it is extremely competent mechanically. The stealth feels good. Weapons feel properly powerful. You get to cut metal with a plasma cutter that would make Issac Clarke jealous; but it all comes to together in this package that feels immediately forgettable. I'm tired of shooting Nazis; no matter how cool it feels to do while a rocking soundtrack blares as you move in slow motion. This was obviously a game with a huge budget. Its a shame they didn't do much to make it unique.
There is a faintly interesting moment where you make a relatively prominent choice in where the story goes. One that might make some of you go back and replay the entire game to see what changes but for me; I'm satisfied.

On the surface,
is a game about killing Nazis and in this it most certainly excels, with immensely rewarding and fluid gameplay that rewards specific play styles and thus replay value. Whoever thought it'd be a great idea to dual-wield pretty much every rifle in the game is a genius, as this features some of the best shooting mechanics I've personally experienced. If you wish to play this simply for the bloody and glorious action, then you certainly won't be disappointed.
But more than that,
is a FPS about humanity and how we behave in the face of overwhelming adversity. It avoids the pitfalls of the genre that often portray such evils in superficial and one-dimensional ways and suffer from bad writing as a result.
is the complete opposite.
When it comes to depicting the horrors of a technologically advanced Nazi regime, Machine Games must be greatly applauded for handling the subject matter with a fine precision. This is predominantly achieved through the remarkable cutscenes and soundtrack. As one of the greats of the shooter genre, the re-incarnation of
often feels like a great film and work of art rather than what could be misinterpreted as a brainless shooter, and is a far-cry from the days of
or
. The extraordinary direction of the cutscenes is reinforced by the top notch score throughout, which really does capture and engross the player. Complementing the fantastic range of weaponry and upgrades, the sound design in general is phenomenal. This is a very intense game in a lot of ways but remains captivating from start to finish. The single-player campaign is remarkable, and well-worth the omission of any multiplayer component.
The Nazis are, of course, the enemy faction but the game also provides significant commentary on the nature of war itself, as well as granting a voice to those often unheard during the conflicts. While certainly focused on a small range of characters, in areas outside of combat even level design provides a fleshed-out and believable world, one that allows for the grand narrative to play out.
As a protagonist, William Joseph "B.J." Blazkowicz is fascinating. Seen by his comrades as the walking death machine and embodiment of shock-and-awe tactics, throughout the game he is given remarkable depth and provides poignant insight into the horrors he constantly experiences. He does not shy away from the horrible things he committs but retains his morality without having to personally justify the things he does.
He is the flawed hero of the
series and receives his greatest outing yet here.
Deviating to technical comments quickly, I did frequently experience huge issues with texture popping and stuttering; an issue that apparently continues to plague the engine despite my own attempts to tweak or fix them. The stealth system was fairly robust with decent AI, if somewhat simplistic. Another thing to consider is the price, which remains very high for a game that is more than a year old now... but that is a comment for Bethesda/Zenimax games in general. But I've rambled on long enough though, so let's conclude.
is a landmark for the shooter genre, boasting top-notch gameplay across the board. It is a narrative done right, portraying the unimaginable horrors of totalitarian cleansing in a believable and uncompromising way. Packed full of detail with a superb soundtrack from start to finish, this stylish shooter is unlike any other.
It is not
but it is thrilling and deeply satisfying, and gaming is all the better for it.

I was looking for a new puzzle fps game like the Portal games, and then Talos principle came out. I couldn't understand all the excitement and the awards about this game, but I decided to trust them. I didn't regret this...
- Puzzles, lots of puzzles, and many of them get really complicated as well
- Ambience. Graphic may not be the best engine ever, but the Serious Engine shows some very neat worlds, it's a pleasure to move around.
- The Story. It's very simple but the way it's being unveiled is really great: you have to look for documents, audio logs and other texts that, little by little, tell a very small portion of the story.
- The Computer. I've never argued about philosophy and logic so much as with that computer... And he won, that b@$t@rd...XD
- The Ending. Spoilerless: the game is such a quiet puzzle game that you'd never expect such a final intense rush. Loved it.
- Nice Soundtrack
- The Italian translation for the most important part (The texts and dialogues with the computer) were ridiculous. Google translate could teach a few lessons to the guys who did that terrible job. And looks like Italian isn't the only language horribly translated. Almost all the languages (except for English) are wrong. Luckily seems like the community submitted various amateur translations that definitely work.
- Unfortunately it lacks the presence of charming and overwhelmingly funny characters as GlaDOS or Wheatley from portal 2... But maybe they wouldn't fit in this context so it's better this way...

This game is not for everyone.
That being said, it is a very good game. If you have any idea what Dwarf Fortress is, think of it as a much more accessible cousin of DF. It combines strategy, simulation, and management nearly flawlessly into a game that you absolutely don't need multiplayer in; it'd be fun to be able to share the experiences, but 1.) that's where you work on your storytelling skills and 2.) you'll get so wrapped up in your colony it won't matter.
One thing I love about this game is that you will constantly learn new things - you might be doing something one way, but there might be a more efficient way that you'll figure out on your next colony.
It is a very unforgiving game, though; if you are on a harder difficulty, even one wrong step can put your entire colony in danger (from within or without).
I definitely recommend this game to strategy/simulation game players.

Another Day in Rimworld.
Explosion rocks the colony compound walls as a conduit wire short circuits, starting a small fire. Emmie wakes up from the shockwave to beat the flames out, only to greet a berserking John by receiving a swift knee to the face, destroying her nose. The local militia rouses from the screams, trying to shuffle off the dizzying effects of moderate exposure to toxic fallout, and rushes across the compound to Emmie's aid. John kicks a door open, Emmie shrieking the garbled rimworld dialect equivalent of "kick his teeth out" before she passes out from shock. John gets no such warm treatment: the militia open fire with their pistols and survival rifles and shred the disgruntled colonist's arms, torso, and eyes.
John's dead. Five colonists left.
Emmie's engulfed in flames as the fire reaches the blades of leaves from nearby strawberry bushes, and quickly spread across the entirety of the wooden wall. Her last reactions were mixed anguish and unbridled rage, claiming that she'd be back again, as her psychosis takes her to the void. The flames take her to ashes, though, so fat chance on that.
Night falls as the militia, having recently drafted a researcher who can't stop his hands from shaking as he grips his rifle, scrambles to beat the flames out. Batteries only stored enough energy to power one turret for 30 seconds, or the compound's turret gallery for about, let's say, five seconds.
The pirates terrorizing the rimworld decide this is an opportune moment to attack... from afar.
Another Day in Rimworld.

One day an angry monkey attacked my camp and my band of tribespeople had to fight him off, thus injuring the monkey's shoulder. After seeing the monkey in pain and incapacitated, Camblar decided he would help the monkey. A day or so later Camblar names the Monkey Baldy and he becomes the tribe's best friend/mascot.
Time passes and Camblar develops a crush on Trout, a gatherer, and they share their feelings of love as the tribe continues to expand there village. However the tribe failed to plant crops earlier in the year and suddenly the food is running out. As everyone stuggles to survive and find a way to get more food, Camblar is taken ill with some sort of plauge due to malnutrition. For the next few days Camblar can do nothing but rest in bed while the rest of his tribe is scrounging the jungle around them for berries and animals to hunt. Trout tries her best to tend to Camblar, bringing him food and medicine, and Baldy sleeps curled up next to him every night...but he doesn't seem to be improving...
As Trout goes out on an ill-advised hunting mission with her friend Scorpion, the healer, her thoughts still dwell on her love, Camblar. Unfortunately her fragile state leads her to sustain a nasty scratch on her leg from a capybara, and soon after as she lies in a bed next to Camblar, trying to recover, she develops an infection. Things are looking grim and the herbal remidy supplies are running out, so Grey does the only thing he can do and builds a statue with some marble they had cleared away earlier. He creates a fair likeness of Camblar and Trout, symmetrically lying next to eachother in bed. In hopes of raising their spirits he puts the statue right next to their beds.
But hope is not lost! Camblar's condition seems to be improving, as though he has developed an immunity to the plague! As he recovers he starts to do everything he can to help Trout, who is still bedridden; he cleans, he hunts, he builds, and he brings her food every day. And amazingly, Trout begins to recover as well, surving the infection some how and regaining her strength. The tribe can now celebrate at last as the crops are almost ready to harvest, everyone is in good health, and Baldy the monkey helps keep everyone happy.
All is well in the village of Antioch.
[...]
Until there's a heatwave and everyone dies of heatstroke in their beds because they don't know how to swim, except for poor poor Camblar, whoose heat tolerance and non-violence meant he survived long enough to watch all his friends and loved ones die. Finally, depressed and alone (except for Baldy), went out into the jungle and got bitten by a cobra.
A raider comes to the empty village and sets the crops on fire, incapacites Baldy, and leaves.
And then a panther finishes Baldy off and eats him.
And at last, Camblar dies.
The End.

Planetside 2 is a MMOFPS where 3 different factions fight for control over several continents.
Each continent supports hundreds of players for every faction. The gameplay consists of
players from one empire fighting players from the other two empires (or in case of the NC
all three *wink*) to take or hold bases for their empire to ultimately take control of
the continent. The game features 6 different infantry classes and several air and ground
vehicle types to fight together as combined arms.
As mentioned there are 3 different factions with access to different weapons and each faction
having a different theme to it.
The Terran Republic is using fast firing weapons with the lowest damage up to medium damage tier.
The Vanu Sovereignty uses plasma based weapons that are generally the middle ground in terms of fire rate and damage. Some of their weapons have no bullet drop.
The New Conglomerate has the hardest hitting weapons but mostly also the slowest firing ones.
Despite the different themes of the factions the weapons are generally well balanced with often similar weapons being available to the other empires. Some weapons like the bolt action sniper rifles are also direct clones stats wise. You have also access to weapons from Nanite Systems which can be uses by all factions. You can always try out weapons in the VR training area or trial them in the field before purchase.
There are 6 different infantry classes you can choose from with different abilities.
These beeing infiltrator who can cloak, snipe, support their faction with recon devices and
hack turrets and terminals.
Light assault with a jet pack ideal for flanking and with C4 able to hunt vehicles.
Medic with the ability to revive and heal other players is an important part in every battle
over taking the control points but also packing quite a punch with it's assault rifle.
Engineer to repair vehicles, structures and the below mentioned MAX unit. He can also lay down mines and use different personal turrets against infantry or vehicles.
The Heavy Assault is the backbone of every fighting force with it's better survivability via an extra personal shield and the ability to carry anti vehicle launchers.
Last but not least is the MAX unit, an exoskeleton that can be outfitted with 2 guns and is useful for breaking into held enemy bases or defend points against attacks from infantry or vehicles depending on your choice of weapons.
Well the game comes down to shooting stuff, stuff shooting you or you doing various tasks so other guys can continue to shoot stuff.
Like other MMOs the game has clans/guilds which are called outfits. Depending on your playstyle you can probably find an outfit for that. They range from very serious attitude to casual to specialised in infantry /vehicle play to general. It is a good idea for a new player to join an outfit or at least a squad to learn the game and to not get lost. Coordinated play makes the most impact in the game and securing a base at the last second via hot drop from a Galaxy transporter or holding a base against overwhelming numbers with your outfit sure is fun.
But even a solo player can leave a mark and get fun out of the game. Infiltrate a base behind the enemy line and hack out a vehicle at which other players can spawn or take over enemy turrets and shoot them in the back. Disrupt the enemy attack waves by destroying one of their spawn points. Support your troops by healing and reviving or lay down mines.
The important part is to take a look at the map, see where you could be useful and go there.
Apart from the usual PVP gameplay on the live servers, there are frequent competetive
matches carried out by the player community on a different server. If you're into such things you can find matches ranging in size from squad (12 players) vs squad , platoon (up to 48)
vs platoon or server vs server with usually 280 players per side.
Is this game perfect? No it's not. It has it's flaws like performance problems from time to time though the devs will try to fix them quickly. They are also very vocal on reddit. Speaking of performance you will need a good cpu to get the best out of it and even then some of the big fights might drop your fps down so take a look at various performance guides.
It might be a little steep and overwhelming at first so getting help from an outfit is advised. The devs also made the game easier for new players with giving them extra certs for leveling up at the first 15 levels and some class specific unlocks which weren't present in the past. While tempting don't waste your certs on guns right away. Find a class you like and ask which skills you should buy. They have by far the most impact on the game.
This game can get frustrating from time to time. Like if you are outnumbered and the enemy
is blasting you with vehicles. Just leave the fight instead of getting farmed over and over again. Dying over and over this way is probably the biggest reason why new players give up on the game. So if you feel outnumberd just spawn at a different base when you're dead or use the redeploy button.
Many frustrated players say this game is P2W. Getting killed by high level players with weapons that are available via money and fully certed characters sure seems that way at first glance. Yet all these weapons are avaiable for cert points and while having a fully certed skill makes the character a little better, it's by no means the deciding factor in an engagement. The first ranks of skills give you already a good bonus and are cheap. Also you can only ever
wear one suit item at the same time so choosing the best one for the moment is important. A vet bringing a flak armor to a gunfight will be dead just as fast as the newbie next to him.
Paying for weapons is only a shortcut though personally I find the weapons quite expensive for real money. Certs can't be bought directly though XP bonuses can which give you a higher cert gain. Weapons are sidegrades, meaning they are specialised in one area while having drawbacks in others. The starting weapons are for the most part jack of all trades while beeing not specialised in one area.
Here is a short example of a weapon and a suit slot.
It's just a rough estimate but you get the gist.
Most weapons cost 1000 certs, seems much at first but it will pretty much pay for itself.
You get a copper, silver, gold, auraxium medal for 10, 60, 160 and 1160 kills with that weapon giving you 2,10,20 and 200 bonus certs. A kill also nets you 100 xp so from 1160 kills alone you get 464 certs (250 xp = 1 cert). For every 10 kills you will also get 250xp in form of a service ribbon giving you 116 certs. That alone is more than 800 certs, not to mention the bonus xp for headshots, killing high threat players, kill streaks and so on plus the regular xp you get for taking bases or holding them.
In terms of suit slots take Nanoweave armor as example. It reduces small arms damage by some percentage but doesn't help against headshots. To fully buy Rank 5 for a class you pay 1211 cert points and lets you survive 2 more bullet from most weapons. Yet rank 2 only cost 11 certs and lets you survive 1 bullet more.
So in short is the game fun? Yes it is.
Can it be frustrating? Yes, sometimes.
Has it flaws? Yes of course.
Is the game for you? That depends. If you are the kind of player who values his KDR way to much than probably not. If you don't mind dying often or even better know when to pick a fight and when to retreat then yes. And if things get too tough you still can be a delivery man. Sitting in vehicles all day long sure is hard work so send the drivers some love and gift them a pizza or some presents.
Finally do I think this game deserves to be tried? Absolutly.

The game itself feels very much an odd mix of Bioshock and Dishonored, (Yes, there are stealth elements and a lot of knife play. (This game gets a whole point for having throwing knives alone.)) "Is this real life?"
As a piece of art, The Talos Principle works magic engaging the player in a lush, beautiful atmosphere with deep, thought provoking messages. Is there such thing as free will? What is the essence of humanity? All questions presented through both the in-game narrative as well as the excerpts found on the terminals while exploring the game.
However, as a puzzle game, The Talos Principle actually falls short of itself later on in the game. Where puzzles at the beginning of the game gave you all the information you needed and it was up to the player to use said information, puzzles closer to the end of the game have more of a challenge of not presenting necessarily all the information to the player when needed. This is not always a bad thing, but the lack of conveyance through level design actually left a sour taste in my mouth after completing some of the later puzzles. On a side note, the grid sigil puzzles felt unneccessary to me, although others may disagree (stating that they raise the difficulty ceiling in the late game).
With that in mind, the rest of the puzzles in the game are extremely rewarding without being too difficult. Often, the puzzles will build upon previously learned mechanics which were purposefully taught through the level design. Completing a red sigil puzzle early in the game, for example, feels incredibly rewarding when you finally piece together all the small little intracacies of the puzzle and collect your sigil. Star puzzles and a lot of the easter eggs in the game also offer a feeling like this, however, they rely sometimes on breaking the game's continuity as well as the previously mentioned problem with conveyance (which is to be expected since they encourage exploration most of the time rather than problem-solving).
Even with its slight problems in design, The Talos Principle was probably one of the best games I played all year, and I cannot wait to jump into the DLC when I have a chance!

"Not a Portal clone but an innovative, interesting puzzle game of its own genre".  9/10
Many people compare Talos Principle to the Portal series.  While they are both 3D puzzle games, beyond that they are two very different types of game.  Talos Principle is less vertical than Portal.  It also doesn't poke holes in the time-space continuum with portal guns.  Instead, it allows you to overlap a copy of yourself in time, thus allowing you to access to places which you usually cannot!  The underlying themes of the two games are also very different.  Talos Principle focuses on what it means to be a human being and whether or not we could duplicate it in machines.  Whereas Portal series is about machines gaining self awareness as more tasks become automated.
The reason I'm not giving a 10/10 to this game is because some of the secrets are so hard to find, the game itself offers almost no clues on how to find them.  So you either come across them by blind luck or have to look it up in a guide.  The soundtrack is superb and fits the game very well.

That being said, it is a very good game. If you have any idea what Dwarf Fortress is, think of it as a much more accessible cousin of DF. It combines strategy, simulation, and management nearly flawlessly into a game that you absolutely don't need multiplayer in; it'd be fun to be able to share the experiences, but 1.) that's where you work on your storytelling skills and 2.) you'll get so wrapped up in your colony it won't matter.
One thing I love about this game is that you will constantly learn new things - you might be doing something one way, but there might be a more efficient way that you'll figure out on your next colony.
It is a very unforgiving game, though; if you are on a harder difficulty, even one wrong step can put your entire colony in danger (from within or without).
I definitely recommend this game to strategy/simulation game players.

A rental. 100%. I was having a blast for the first couple of hours, when I wasn't mashing the keys while trying to remember how to sprint-slide. (Shift+Ctrl. Yecch.) The KB+M controls deserve special mention for being even worse than Borderlands.
Halfway through, this game's gunfights start to feel like rock+paper+scissors. You gotta switch to your laser gun to kill these guys, then to your AR to mow down the grunts, then back to laser, then use your shotty on these armored dudes, then back to AR and hit the button to switch to rockets.....after the 20th death caused by frantic weapon-swapping attempts, I switched to my 360 controller. Died a lot less, but was bored a lot more.
With a few exceptions, like that great collapsing bridge level, Wolfenstein: The New Order follows the modern FPS style. Narrow corridors and wide rooms built for big firefights. None of the exploration that made Wolfenstein 3-D or DOOM so great, just mowing people down and then combing the area for ammo and collectibles. Oh, the collectibles. Enigma codes, Nazi gold, record albums, they add replay value, right?
Speaking of replay value, you make a crucial decision in the first hour and the game splits into 2 timelines, meaning you gotta play twice to see everything. What are the differences?
-1 timeline you can pick locks, the other you can hotwire keypads.
-1 timeline has Nikola Tesla, the other has Jimi Hendrix.
-1 timeline has a guy who thinks he's too young to lead the resistance, the other has a guy who thinks he's too old to lead the resistance.
-1 ending has....just kidding! The ending is the same in both timelines!
The story. Oh my god so much praise has been heaped on this story. Remember when Futurama did that parody of M*A*S*H* and that robot had the dial to switch between "irreverent" and "maudlin?" Sometimes you're piloting a robot and mowing Nazis down with mounted chainguns, and sometimes you're stuck underneath corpses and headed for a furnace. Those 2 examples are from the same level. The main baddie (returning from RtCW) encapsulates this perfectly: for almost the entire game he's GENERAL DEATHSHEAD, but his real name is Wilhelm Strasse. WILHELM STRASSE.
The characters are all cartoons. A girl who nursed you back to health and naturally has 2 sex scenes with you, an ultra-badass woman in a wheelchair, an ultra-badass Nazi woman who just won't die, the Nazi woman's aryan boy toy (who sounds like Mike Myers from those old Sprockets skits) an ex-Nazi resistance fighter named Klaus, a big strong dumb guy with part of his brain missing, the Jewish resistance fighter who calls you "Shimshon." The game flings all kinds of blood and guts and sad backstory at you to make you care, but it all feels so banal and familiar. Mumbling about how hellish war is while you're dual-wielding ARs and gunning down dozens of The Enemy. Come And See, this ain't.
It's not all bad, though. It's still worth renting, not avoiding entirely. The graphics really are impressive. There are occasional fun firefights in between all the scrounging for loot, cutscenes, and Press X To Setpieces. Some of those Press X To Setpieces really ARE good. It feels like a Wolfenstein game and deserves a spot in the series. The easter eggs and references to past titles feel earned, and not tacked-on hackwork. The world is solidly constructed, and when you're not shut up in generic locations like sewers or U-Boat corridors it really shines.  The soundtrack is excellent, bringing back memories of older games without just copy-pasting the old leitmotifs. The German versions of 60's pop songs are a nice touch, and the Volksmusik take on "House of the Rising Sun" has been in my head for days.
Wolfenstein: The New Order was worth 1 playthrough, but in the future I'm gonna stick to wolf3d.exe.

I dont care that it has good writing. Or a setting that was interesting for an hour or two.  Wolfenstein: The New Order is a terrible shooter, and is simply not fun to play.
Its shooting mechanics are a complete mess, and no amount of mix-matching from eras and playstyles can hide the fact that the developers had no idea what they were doing.
First, as per usual, you only have two weapon slots. However, despite carrying hundreds of rounds for other gun types you cannot access these weapons.  If you attempt to pick up the guns that you see right there on the ground by the soldier who used it to shoot you, you will usually find yourself the owner of 8 more shells, but still not the gun.
Except youre actually carrying four weapons.  One of them is the knives, which has no point as you can use the knives while using guns, and the other is a laser cutter.  The laser cutter is basically a skeleton key for chains and chain fences.  Except, because you only have two weapon slots, you either always have one taken up by a laser cutter with no use in combat, or everytime you want to use it you have search for a recharge station, which is the only way of bringing it back into one of your two slots.
At which point it will continue to occupy one of those slots until you find a weapon cupboard.
And then there is the health. Your health recharges but only partially. Basically, it rounds up to the nearest 20.
The problem with this is the same reason almost every other shooter series abondoned static health meters. Because some sections are virtually impossible to do without losing at least 30ish health. Which means you can easily become a dead-man walking, forcing you to play through the whole mission again, and hope you do better next time.
This problem contributes to a general feeling of trial and error that permeates the entire game.  The stealth sections are often so claustrophic that the only way of completing them is simply bumping into enemies and dying until you know the layout. Its not like you would have many tactics anyways though; the game has a quiet crouch, and silent takedowns from beyond and at range, and THATS IT. Cover peekarounds exist, but happen on their own.  This is a problem when good cover is as rare as it is in this game, so ultimately the cover system is just another way for the game to take you off guard.
By the way, do you, like I do, switch weapons when you run out of ammo because it saves time versus reloading in a pinch? Well ♥♥♥♥ YOU.  BJ will reload his weapon, and THEN switch weapons because thats what you wanted right?
There is also a tacked on rpg element.  Basically, if you complete some insipid challenges you will get upgrades that really wont matter.  The challenges are a mix of the incredibly easy, and those that you would never attempt to do if the system didnt bottleneck your progress on them.
At its most basic level The New Order is an expose on why its developers should never make a shooter again.  Within the game is almost every core mechanic shooters have used, all handled so ineptly that no story could possibly be worth slogging through it.

The Talos Principle is a first-person puzzle game following in the footsteps of Portal.  Overall, I think it's a very well done game with clever puzzles, a great story, and excellent audio.
Ultimately, because of the lack of diversity in the settings you'll be solving puzzles in, I don't feel the mechanics alone support the length of this game (assuming you're going for collectiong most of everything). Fortunately, an excellent story penned, in part, by Tom Jubert who wrote the excellent story for the surprisingly philosophical "The Swapper."  In The Talos Principle, the story explores philosophical ideas about identity, existence, the self, and morality.  While not revelatory to anybody versed in the field, for those who know little or have only a limited, casual interest in philosophy, there is interesting ideas to be explored within this game.
The difficulty curve for the puzzles is excellent, and if you want to find some of the more hidden collectables, you'll need to really think inventively and outside the box with how to utilize your limited tools.
Overall, I had fun. Near the end I was finishing it more for the story than out of pure enjoyment of the puzzles, but that still carried me through with the desire to see some of the alternate endings as well.  If you enjoy puzzles or if you found the fusion of story-driven narrative mixed with puzzles compelling, it's definitely worth checking out!

Max Payne 3 provides a unique side of Rockstar that isn't often seen. While GTA and Red Dead feature 3rd person shooters, Max Payne works on this genre by providing very unique and detailed environments, while giving a different style to how the 3rd person shooter works.
MP3 does not have replenishable health over time, unless you find pills to recover your health. This provides great emphasis and stress on moments, which prevent you from playing very carelessly; although there are a few moments where those moments are provided.
MP3 also provides bullet time, which allows you to slow down time and have greater emphasis on accuracy in order to take down hard to hit/multiple targets.
The story is a bit lack-luster, with the families often being very air-headed, although the look into Max's personal life and past help make for some interesting moments.
Definitely worth a purchase at sale price.

One of the best things that I like about the game in general is that it rarely makes you feel safe if you ramp up the difficulty - Randy Random / Extreme / Permadeath here we go - until you actually beat it, i.e. get enough colonists, infrastructure, gear and research progress to be able to deal with any kind of event in the game at that point.
And even when you feel like you can beat the game already on any difficulty, there is still a huge variety of mods for the game to make it seem like a completely new game and a fresh kind of challenge.

TL:DR Good game so far, worth a try if you're fence sitting.
So far this game is quite good, it is a puzzle solving game akin to portal in it's problem solving style but with less jumping and a supportive voice rather than a mocking one.
The play style is fun with a casual no consequence for death making it great for those who need that sort of game.
I can already tell that there will be limited replayabliity but such is the case for most if not all puzzle games as once you have solved them there is little to no challenge in beating them again.
Graphicly the game is good, it is set in a soothing environment that evokes a feeling of peace and as such makes it easier to lose an hour and feel refreshed at the end.
The story so far has me already involved with the environment making me guess as to whats happening later on as well as to contemplating why I am there, whether its all real or in my head. I has me hooked to want to keep playing the game so it serves its purpose admirably.
The cost of this game particularly during sales is pretty low, low enough that I would say give it a shot even if you are on the fence a bit on this one but I'll update later as I make my way through the game.

I'm going to look at
from two points of view: casual and hardcore. Now I'm fully aware that "casual" is a dirty word when it comes to videogames. Honestly, I think a game being casual is a good thing. If I'm playing a lot of hardcore games, the kind with a lot of depth, high punishments for failure, and an extreme level of difficulty; I'm going to want something to fall back on. In this regard,
fits the bill.
However, a lot of games - sometimes the best ones - can appeal to both the casual and hardcore gamers. These titles offer a perfect learning curve and are enjoyable at any skill-level. There are multiple methods for playing through them. The challenge can range from easy to improbable. It all depends on how the player approaches these games. Though it tries,
can't bridge this gap. It's a fine game for a friendly get-together, or a time-sink on a slow day. If you're looking for a quality brawler, the kind you can keep coming back to again and again, then look elsewhere.
I hate to say it, but this review isn't over yet.
Looking further,
works as a casual game due to the constant thread of "niceties". These are moments that make you say "Oh. That's nice." when they happen. Leveling up, the discovery of a new weapon or animal, a dead enemy dropping a valuable crystal instead of a mere coin; these are all examples of niceties. The game is further bolstered by simplistic but charming hack & slash action. Through the combination of both elements, as well as flavor touches like the set-piece battles and action sequences, this game works. It just plain works.
Even with this casual approach, you're still bound to run into problems. The balance between strength, magic, and agility is crap. Magic and agility require huge investments to attain any noticeable effect. Strength is an absolute necessity, unless you want to juggle foes for several minutes at a time. The ranged options are only forced onto the player by the rare appearance of giant enemies. You know who these jerks are, because you can't get close to them, without being grabbed and thrown.
Also, while the niceties are appreciated, I believe that Behemoth could have done a little better. Character-unlocking is just plain awful after a certain point. Having to replay the entire game with character F to unlock character M is maddening. It's especially bad when A) all characters behave the same outside of spells B) every character starts at level 1 and C) there aren't any methods for passing experience onto new characters. Dynasty Warriors is a franchise with gobs of playable heroes, and usually there's some method for strengthening unused characters, so everyone remains at a level playing field. In
, this -admittedly not all that important - element was overlooked, and it's pretty annoying.
The insane mode is ironically where hardcore gamers are liable to get the door slammed in their faces. This is also where the game almost completely falls apart. A high difficulty mode is fine, but it needs to make sense. Insane difficulty features faster and more aggressive enemies, so it's good on that front. Unfortunately, their HP and especially their strength have recieved a massive multiplier, and that's really bad. A number of enemies and bosses go from non-threatening to entirely absurd. For most players, insane mode ends with the large troll of the Thieves' Forest.
This is my third play-through of the game, and I still don't understand why insane mode exists. In the original Xbox 360 version, insane mode was somewhat mitigable, due to a prevalent experience glitch (involving the troll boss). This is one of those rare glitches that actually made the game worse when it was fixed. Depending on how you look at it, abusing an XP glitch to make a game easier probably isn't very hardcore. As far as I'm concerned, insane mode is where the game actively cheats. Everyone has too much HP and does too much damage, but apparently it's unfair for players to have something to fall back on.
Personally, I would have suggested difficulty modifiers (ala
) instead of a difficulty mode, but this a 20/20 hindsight suggestion. I certainly didn't have the idea, when
was released, back in 2008. All told, this game is still pretty enjoyable and even better with friends. Just don't invest too much of your energy, because the pay-off isn't worth the effort.

Played it for many hours at first on Xbox 360 and some time after, at some sale, started to play it again on PC. I can say for sure that Castle Crashers is one of most interesting beat 'em up games I have ever played. Graphics might look like some kind of game for kind but don't be mistaken - kids, teenagers, adults, everyone will have great time playing this game. With so many characters (few at start, many to unlock) to play, so many levels to make, many weapons and secrets to find, you won't be bored after beating once, or twice, or until you will reach max level with every character. You can enjoy it alone, or with friends on 1 PC or over internet. Castle Crashers isn't not only filled with action, but also with humour, and what's better, the one that will for sure make you laught, unless you take everything too serious. Sure, some people will say it get's boring quickly or it's repetitive but if you ask me, I didn't get bored even once in those 50 (at the moment I'm making this review) hours. And I'm sure I will play it at some point again, and again, and again... and again. It's really easy to get addicted to this game.
In my opinion, it's worth full price but sure, there are people who might not know what Castle Crashers is, or what kind of people made this game. If you are fan of beat 'em up games, then you must grab it at sale. Look at the number of reviews this game have received, and look at what number of those are positives ones - there is high chance that another positive review will be coming from you.

One of the best modern single-player FPS, stays true to the Wolfenstein spirit. The story is solid with great characters and cutscenes; the gameplay frantic and fast-paced like in the good ol' times; the universe seems a bit too over-the-top at first, but shockingly close to reality once you realize this is about WW2 and the atrocities of the 30's and 40's. It's bound to raise the hairs on your back quite a few times along the campaign.
My only complaint is the presence of quick time events. I ♥♥♥♥ing hate quick time events. But they're only here and there and in no way influence the gameplay (unless you don't notice the prompt :P )
Later edit: I just finished it and I have to say it's one of the best games I have ever played. The second half of the game is amazing. I won't spoil anything, but the locations, the level design, the boss fights, the weapons, they are all very well made. A lot of games run out of juice towards the end and start feeling rushed, but NTO keeps pushing up the difficulty, while still delivering incredible content. In the end it's short, but very satisfying.
It's really good. Don't worry too much about the philosophy, but push yourself to make your own.

In the very short ammount of time I (thankfully) spent playing this game, I was surprised time and time again - and not by a thrilling storyline or astounding graphics - but by the sheer lack of depth this game offers. Needless to say, I didn't expect much going in, as the title and price surely indicated.
But a part of me, maybe niavely, at least expected some basic core elements of a shoot em' up waze-based zombie survival game, such as noise made by either the zombies, my character, or guns. Nope. The best you get is a single monotous thud sound when firing some of the weapons - which sounds less like an actual gunshot, and more like the sound of your heart sinking at the sight of this game.
Another basic feature that is missing altogether: a point. Sure, it's called Yet Another Zombie Defense for a reason, and that's exactly what one should expect from it. But the utter lack of depth to the game - besides a handful of guns to buy and a few player upgrades (which are unlocked here and there, but don't provide much difference to the game) leaves you bored after only 5 or 10 minutes.
Ultimately, if you buy this *flash game*, here's what you can expect: running in circles in an extremely limited, un detailed environment, shooting identical zombie after ifdentical zombie silently, while a repetative music track from some royalty-free music site plays endlessly. Oh, and keep an eye on your health, because there's no sound or visual indication that you are being hurt, other than the small red bar in the top corner of your screen disappearing with each hit, making you question if you're really playing a game from the 21st century or not.
However, I understand the limited capabilities of independent developers, and for that I feel this review may be a bit harsh. But, then again, independent or not, if you want good reviews and happy players, make a decent game.
Thankfully, I only payed about $1 for this game, and I do know that you get what you pay for. But, then again, I've played free flash games that are 5+ years old that are easily 100 times better than this garbage. Don't waste your time or money here.

Rockstar pulled it off.
They created an epic Max Payne game, which somehow remains as grim as ever, despite losing the everlasting night to the sunny Sao Paulo.
"Brasil? Sao Paulo? Max Payne? Nah, that ain't gonna work..." And boy, am I glad I was wrong. The story is dark and depressing, violent and bloody.
Pros:
-The levels are diverse
-Great Graphics
-Body physics and bullet hit reaction are second to none
-The score is memorable and fits perfectly.
-Mature storyline, good writing, memorable quotes
-varied enemies
-Flashy and brutal
Cons:
-The realistic physics can get in the way though. In previous titles Max would always quickly recover after a bullet time dodge. In MP3 however, how quickly you get back on your feets depends on how you landed. So sometimes it can take seconds, which usually ends up with Max getting killed.
-The loading levels can be a bit of a payne(pun intended), as you always have to sit through the rather long - but very well done- in engine cinematics. For replaying levels, this can get tedious (although you can skip some, whilst others you can't).
-Rockstar Social Club. On numerous occassions I couldn't log in, sometimes blocking me from running the game (it would hang up at the title screen with an endless attempt to connect to RSC). Playing Steam in offline mode can solve this quickly.
-Some might consider the extreme violence a downside.
-Some of the tougher armoured enemies are bullet sponges. This didn't bother me, but others might see this as a downside.
-----
Summing up: Rockstars unique approach to Max Payne has brought us one the the most memorable and violent shooters in the last years.
The bar has been raised.

Extremely good singleplayer experience that blends classic and modern FPS elements together nearly flawlessly. The story is surprisingly good, the mechanics are solid and visually/artistically the game is a treat for the most part. The art design and direction is absolutely incredible.
The only real problems I have are the length, the limited FOV and the view bob. I played on "I Am Death Incarnate", searching for as many secrets as possible and died a pretty decent amount of times, yet on my first playthrough I managed to beat the game in about 8 hours, possibly less if I hadn't been AFK. The game features two timelines though with different pathways and experiences starting from the first mission.
The FOV is limited to a max of 100, but it doesn't FEEL like 100. It feels more like around 80 or 90. I would have preferred 120. Finally, the viewbob is overdone to the point of absurdity at times. This combined with the FOV weirdness can lead to a headache over time at the very least.
I enjoyed it very much, but I bought it when it was on sale recently for about under 10 bucks or something like that. I can recommend this game on a sale, but not at full price. There's no modding, so while it has plenty of secrets and collectibles to tide you over, it doesn't provide as much value as it's fellow id Tech predecessors usually had.
Better than The New Colossus by far.

Would recommend squad any day.
What I like most about the game is that one person or squad can impact things heavily. This isn't your average run and gun fps, you will need to think carefully about where to go, which rout to take. Depending on what you have set out to do you will decide whether to open fire on the enemy or not and so on.
The game is based around squads (a group of up to 9 people) different kits will be available depending on how filled up the squad is, your squad leader will be the one giving orders and even macromanaging should they wish to, the leader can place strategic markers on the map and deploy spawn points for your squad and your whole team.
Communication is essential, you will constantly be telling your squadies, directions and amount of enemies present and so on. If you get the game with a friend you will have a blast, if not just join any squad.
Another great thing about squad is the community, everyone is pretty serious about playing the game right and 9/10 a squad that you join will be playing objectively and all have mics and good communication skills.
Now here is a way 2 people can make a big impact - big battle waging over the middle objective, several squads are fighting/defending/flanking and so on, both teams will have well places Rallies (squad spawn points) and FOBs (Forward operating base - team spawn point). Me and my friend sneak behind enemy lines, staying low and not firing a shot, find their FOB and get rid of it. Enemy team must now spawn at a further FOB or if none available their man base which means by the time reinforcements get there it will be too late.
Theoritically me and my friend can have a score of 0 and 0 kills, but this isnt a game about who got the highest killstreak and so on, its about the synergy between all the different things each squad is working to accomplish to win the round.
There are also constructables in the game that can be a lot of fun when fortifying positions or trying to get some cover on a random Afghani hilltop.
Did you mention that you will♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself when a machine gun opens fire on you? Not a single bullet has hit you yet but you will get a dose of andreline big enough to revive a dead rhino while you try to work out where the bullets are coming from, how far away he is and at the same time getting yourself to a position of safety.
I believe its worth mentioning that the company who makes this game are in constant talks with the community and release regular updates and are always working on new things and updating people on progress and so on.
There are plenty of different maps to play on and variations of each map present as well.
In squad you will always adapt and do new things depending on how each game is playing out, what your orders are, what went right and wrong and which kit you are using.
If anyone does get squad and you want someone to show you the ropes, explain how stuff works and be my human shield, feel free to add and message me.
If you read throught all of this, thank you ;)

my review of this game, with my opinion. ( note that this is my first review )
first i will talk about the cons of the game, ill save the pro's for later.
- the game uses the "genie engine" wich is a old engine, originaly used by the old age of empires.
the engine is weak and outdated, there are some big maps in this game wich the engine does not quite support.
i also get in some trouble when play with more than 3 friends with the population cap set to 500, probably because of the engine as well. i am using a gaming pc, and i still have this problem, so it can not be because i have potato specs.
- unit pathing is horrible, units will often get stuck or regroup in weird ways, this left me to lose a couple of battles.
- the isometric view of the game is iconic and comfortable but also gives fair amount of trouble because some things are unclear to see.
- maybe a bit hard to get into the multiplayer, but practice against bots easily customizable, and playing with friends gives you great benefits ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) in learning the game.
- 20 euro's is a bit expensive for a game that basicly is from 1999, even when remasterd, it is and stays the same game.
pros
- everlasting graphics style, the graphics stayed the same since 1999.
- random maps bring a constantly new experience to the game.
- a lot of different civilizations to choose from, with each unique units and every civilization can use unique tactics to win the game. this causes a unending stream of experience and replayabilty.
- multiplayer is fun, and had great modification options to optimize the game to everyone's needs.
- steam workshop, with nice and usefull content.
- single player campaigns with voice over.
- every unit has its counter, wich makes nice gameplay.
- co-op against bots, is a very nice way to learn the game and have fun, while still being challenging.
- improved unit cap over the old age of empires.
- new dlc's with nice content. ( civilzations, voiced campaigns, maps ) for decent pricing.
- the game is often on sale and easy to get.
- it is playable on older pc's/ laptops.
the final verdict.
in my opinion this game set a standard for rts games, the hd remaster give's a nice nostalgia feel, while still being refreshing.
i played the old age of empires when i was younger, and it is almost the same, but this new age of empires brings great improvements, personally i would never spend 20 euro's on a game like this. and i waited for one of the regular sales.
it is a nice game to play with friends ( if you have any that is ).
i personaly would give this game a 7,5/10
it is a good game, but has some mayor flaws, the biggest must be the outdated engine.

It has been 2 years and a half yet the game still suffers from many of the same basic problems, lack of progress and no innovation/ imagination.
The game is blurry/ pixelated which makes it hard to spot things more than 50m away. Post-processing is terrible and the developers either ignore this completely or choose to be oblivious to it.
The performance got a nice improvement in a recent patch, but city maps that look really bland anyway still run poorly. I can run it at about 90-110fps in open maps with drops to 40 in city maps with a 6700k@ 4.5Ghz and a 1080ti. If you complain about this, the fanboys claim they love the game at 30fps so we should be happy...
It's hard to believe this is a modern game, it only looks good in certain lightning conditions on certain maps. Most of the time it looks like a 2010 game. The vegetation is still the same and makes even forests look empty due to lack of undergrowth. The models that OWI made themselves look top notch though.
The gunplay is still very basic without a single feature to set it apart from a generic shooter game. All it does is add lots of recoil and sway. The infantry gameplay is very basic and very bland, all engagements end in a matter of seconds, there's no freedom to react or adapt during a firefight, it's kill or be killed. This largely takes away from the tactical perspective because in Squad the answer to: "Am I close enough, can I get the kill, can he spot me and kill me," is always yes. Shoot or be shot 1s later, far too little depth.
Recently the developers removed HMMVWs from the game due to what they call "licensing issues" but refuse to comment on it at all. We don't actually know why they were removed and they aren't being removed from other games either...

I was a planetside player all throughout PS1, and I was so unbelievably stoked when PS2 was announced. I was a founder, poured a few hundred into the game, and even though I never got super attached to it (I really just never got into a good outfit, my old outfit Azure Twilight moved from 1 to 2, but was vanu and I'd already invested heavily in NC) I still was very happy with the game from a gameplay standpoint.
The only gripes I have for PS2 are these:
I hate class systems. I miss the old way of having specific armor types with an inventory that dictated how much ammo, gear, and the variety you had.
There are a few too many "samey" guns. But there is no clear "best" gun, so the design balance is pretty effing outstanding.
I do dislike how your money invested into the game really does lock you into a faction a lot more than I'd like, unless you spend every penny on the cross faction weapons, which can be a bit bland.
Super weapons are just not as glorious as they were in PS1.
I do miss some of the supply utility runs of the old maps. And I do think the game shot itself in the foot by only releasing with basically one playable continent (when the original had nine)
The things I love
Graphically, this game is simply stunning and runs well on every machine.
Gunplay is satisfying, rewarding, skill based and the feeling of each weapon is impactful
Vehicles feel basically perfect
Game is very easy to play for free if you don't want to spend money
SERIOUSLY rewarding squad play. You can zerg, and have some fun, but the really rewarding meat of the game is in an outfit with friends. Something no other shooter manages.
Developers feel really invested in the game as something they want to succeed, rather than just a cash cow like call of duty (similar to warframe)
Untouchable variety of gameplay styles. Wanna heal? Sure. Wanna drive tanks around? totally. Want to scout on foot or on a quadbike? fantastic. Want to dogfight, bomb, fly the galaxy dropping platoons and be the lazy, yet loved pilot? no problem.
I just can't sing the praises of PS2 enough. My only gripes about PS2 are really just rooted in my love for PS1, so if you never played that ancient, archaic gem of a game before it was killed off, you're not going to miss out on anything I said.

First-up - the writing in this is awful and it's shoved into your face repeatedly in lengthy, unskippable (often repeated if you die) cutscenes in which cliched characters drone on and on about cliched nonsense - if it's trying to be ironic, it failed on me - it not, it's just awful.
The game - when you eventually get into it - isn't anything special either.  The earlier games were sharper - movement here is laboured, reloading/choosing weapons is clumsy and your bullet-time moves often don't quite work as planned.  You will get the hang-of-it but it's not a step forward imo
Every level is a sequence of set pieces with corridors inbetween for exposition - but the feeling the early games had of there being a 'solution' to each set-piece isn't so obvious here and there's no progression because you're still the same cliched and addled ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Over time enemies gain the ability to survive direct headshots/multiple shotgun blasts to the face and ammo becomes scarce because - well - let's assume they tried to make an action film in which you drive the 'shooty bits' but a game which also gets harder and those things don't mesh.
Watching an action movie, you don't want the hero to fail - you don't want them to stumble into stuff - you don't want bullet-sponge enemies who don't drop - you don't want the hero leaping gracefully into a wall/sign/fence, you don't want the hero shot to death over and over as they figure out what the developer intended (repeating the story in case you forgot it from 20 seconds earlier)
Progress here has not been useful.
tl;dr - Play the earlier ones first and then play them again

I was a planetside player all throughout PS1, and I was so unbelievably stoked when PS2 was announced. I was a founder, poured a few hundred into the game, and even though I never got super attached to it (I really just never got into a good outfit, my old outfit Azure Twilight moved from 1 to 2, but was vanu and I'd already invested heavily in NC) I still was very happy with the game from a gameplay standpoint.
The only gripes I have for PS2 are these:
I hate class systems. I miss the old way of having specific armor types with an inventory that dictated how much ammo, gear, and the variety you had.
There are a few too many "samey" guns. But there is no clear "best" gun, so the design balance is pretty effing outstanding.
I do dislike how your money invested into the game really does lock you into a faction a lot more than I'd like, unless you spend every penny on the cross faction weapons, which can be a bit bland.
Super weapons are just not as glorious as they were in PS1.
I do miss some of the supply utility runs of the old maps. And I do think the game shot itself in the foot by only releasing with basically one playable continent (when the original had nine)
The things I love
Graphically, this game is simply stunning and runs well on every machine.
Gunplay is satisfying, rewarding, skill based and the feeling of each weapon is impactful
Vehicles feel basically perfect
Game is very easy to play for free if you don't want to spend money
SERIOUSLY rewarding squad play. You can zerg, and have some fun, but the really rewarding meat of the game is in an outfit with friends. Something no other shooter manages.
Developers feel really invested in the game as something they want to succeed, rather than just a cash cow like call of duty (similar to warframe)
Untouchable variety of gameplay styles. Wanna heal? Sure. Wanna drive tanks around? totally. Want to scout on foot or on a quadbike? fantastic. Want to dogfight, bomb, fly the galaxy dropping platoons and be the lazy, yet loved pilot? no problem.
I just can't sing the praises of PS2 enough. My only gripes about PS2 are really just rooted in my love for PS1, so if you never played that ancient, archaic gem of a game before it was killed off, you're not going to miss out on anything I said.
Just buy it, you won't regret it.

The last instalment of the series, Max Payne 3 features a druken and shambling Max, wallowing in self-pity and bad poetry while in the employment of a Brazilian tycoon in Sao Paolo. The game features decent environment design and obviously, copious amounts of gung-ho action.
The story is quite action-packed and even in the highest difficulty, it does flow rapidly (apart from a few boss fights where one might want to hunker down and tread slowly) and there are several vehicle-based sequences, which were quite hilarious to go through. Bullet time still allows you to mow down an entire squad in 3 seconds in defiance of the laws of physics and in some cases where the scene allows, you may end up spinning rather great stunts. The locations are Sao Paolo, Panama and for a brief interval, New Jersey.
This brings up an odd dissonance - as the Max Payne series used to feature a heavy dose of film noir aesthetics, it is quite difficult to get the same feeling while flying in slow motion across a techno-pumping disco dance floor or while dressed in a garish Hawaii shirt, toting a (gold-coloured) M16 machine gun in a Brazilian favela roof top. The setting looks nice despite the -intentional, I guess- cheesy and self-mocking remarks by Max himself. Coupled with his later changes in apperance, it looks quite odd. Unlike the previous games, the third game features quite a lot of cutscenes instead of the graphic novel-style storytelling and quite annoyingly, the cutscene will leave you in the middle of a group of armed enemies, while you are barely in cover. One truly annoying mechanic is the Last Man Standing - if you have spare Painkillers (which pass for healing in here) and if you get a killing blow on yourself, you get into a greyed-out slow motion aview, where the only coloured thing is your shooter. If you can land a shot on him, you are resusciateted and your shooter gets shot down immediately. All fair and fine, until and unless you are in a messy background (behind foliage or maybe layers of different cover) and you suffera chance killing blow, which slows everything for nothing since you cannot always catch a sight of your shooter and watch in frustration.
The game is purposefully over the top, which is perhaps the only way to justify a fat, bald ex-cop to mow down 10% of Sao Paolo`s population as well as a good deal of New Jersey mob while high on painkillers and drinking like a bitter divorcee at Christmas. And that`s probably fine.
