What an amazing game! If you like roll playing and feeling immersed, this is the game for you. Long story incoming.
We crash on a habitable world. Scattered trees and deer. Our crew consists of Tanya the hunter, Navarro the doctor and Esper jack of all trades. We built a shelter, rather slowly as nobody has great carpentry skills. But it works. Tanya went out hunting and man is she good with that rifle. Nobody is a decent planter but we plant some crops(potatos, cotton and corn).
We encounter a passerby named Pyrra. She is extremely intelligent but does absolutely no work. Won't clean or haul anything. She has ner nose is books the entire time. Grant it, since she is borderline genius and she will be coming up with research projects left and right.
A single raider attacked up with nothing but a club. His name was Lynx. We put him down easily. His nose and arm were shot off, and we captured him and threw him into a makeshift cell. He wont be happy when he wakes up.
The next day, not only did blight strike our crops (100% of them were destroyed), but raiders attacked. Twice. This was a group of 3 tribesman armed with bows, pikes and other primitive weapons. We put that down easily as well killing all 3 attackers. We have technology on our side. The second group was looking for their friend, but we were not so lucky with them. They were armed.... well. Much better than us. They stormed us and we took heavy fire. Dr Navarro had a grenade go off next to her and she immediately fell into shock. We managed to kill two of the others and chase off the last guy. Esper caught up to him as he was already shot in the leg and beat him to death with the butt of her pistol.
This next day was even more of a nightmare. A heat wave set in, A raider snuck in behind us the day before and destroyed our generator, while we have our Dr laying in bed trying to recover from the grenade. Her wounds have turned into infection. Esper is bedridden from heatstroke. We are scrambling trying to fix this damage that has been done.
...Well our Dr didn't die of heatstroke. She went berserk in the middle of the night from all the damage our prisoner has brought upon us. She broke into his cell and attacked him. In self defense the cell mate beat her to death. We should have killed him when we had the chance. Immediately after this, more of his buddies showed up. They blew a hole in his wall and broke him free. Pyrra was injured in the blast and lost two of her fingers, but she will be fine. Esper recovered from heatstroke and tried to treat pyrra, but is not very skilled. We are running dangerously low on medical supplies.
Two days have passed since Dr Navarro was killed. Across our coms came a frantic voice searching for salvation. She(Emminent) has raiders on her tail. We agreed to help and I have no idea why. We were already in a desolate situation. Luckily it was tribes people again with low tech weapons. Tanya was hadling these invaders easily enough until one tribesman got close and cut out her eye. Our only soldier is now missing an eye and we have no doctor. As the tribe ran away, they set all of our crops and storehouse on fire. But we got lucky and it immediately rained!
We sifted through the debris and were able to salvage about 90% of our potatos 0% of corn or cloth.
The rain continues. We worked through it. Tanyas eye healed the best it could. Esper and Emminent rebuilt the store house and Pyrra researched some more technologies to possibly help us with our endless raider problem. We are starting to run into a food problem. This is my favorite FPS and I believe it is criminally underplayed right now.
Pros:
-Good amount of depth when it comes to vehicle and class customization. There's a weapon or vehicle for every situation.
-The large size of the game (4 continents and 3 factions) allows you a lot of freedom when it comes to picking your battles. You don't have to suffer through a fight you can't win or a spawn camp, just redeploy.
-No P2W features besides implants, but there impact on the game is not very profound anyways.
-Relatively new construction system. There's a lot of potential around base building and the features that are already there are solid.
-Devs that actually update the game. Daybreak has been releasing some good content on a regular basis since acquring the reins to this game.
Cons:
-Very steep learning curve. You'll die kind of often until you get a handle on the gunplay and general flow of battle. Find an outfit and join public platoons to make your learning experience far less painful.
-The grind is real. If you're just starting out it's going to be hard for you to earn the in-game cash(certs) you need to buy more weapons and upgrades. There are several ways to boost your cert gain but the better ones cost real money. Daybreak had to earn their money somehow and premium cosmetics and Paying-to-not-grind is how they chose to do it.
-Beefy system requirements. If you're playing on a toaster you're not going to get any enjoyment out of this game.

If you're looking for a game to be able to work as a team and not be the sniper sitting back by yourself, accomplishing nothing, then Squad is for you.
I've grown up playing CS 1.6 competitively and transitioned to playing almost every type of game there is. Now I've recently found myself bored of the small, close quarter maps that come down to who has the quickest reaction time or plays the most un-godly amount of hours to get an unlock. Squad has given me the casual mil-sim style combat that I've been looking for. I've found a strong, great group of people to play with in a clan and take part in weekly competitive multi-clan events to keep my enjoyment high. The nice thing about the game in its current stage, is the community is a smaller but strong one with a lot of communication between one another on Discord and on Reddit. There's always people I meet day-to-day that are encouraging, skilled, and great team players.
This is not a heavy game like ArmA by any means. It stands alone and with all of the great support from the developers and the monthly communication they give out as well as the daily responses to concerns and requests on social media, they keep up with it all. You won't be disappointed.
The team is having to do all their own, manual coding with the Unreal Engine so it's been a learning curve for re-working the animations to ensure good FPS as well as problems with AMD based systems. With every release, they've greatly increased the quality and output of their game by making slight changes and improvements to the coding while adding major things to the game. Updates are fast but the game is still in Alpha. Jump on board now, you'll be heavily glad you did for the price it's at come final release!

The intersection of story-driven gameplay and puzzle mechanics too often results in clunky, confusing interruptions to the flow of otherwise excellent and immersive narrative experiences. Puzzles may be absurdly easy and seem entirely out of place (e.g.
), needlessly lengthening parts of the game, or their extreme difficulty may grind gameplay to a halt (e.g.
series). However, just as Valve so brilliantly defied this rule with the
series years ago, Croteam manage in
to seamlessly integrate an interesting plot, as well as a mystifying lore, with absolutely exceptional puzzles. And where
and its sequel excel in wit and ironic humour,
achieves profundity, treating meaningfully and thoughtfully the most fundamental questions of philosophy and ethics, without being pretentious. The texts and audio files found throughout the world constitute a fully realized and intriguing lore, and dialogue with the Milton character is fascinating and thought-provoking; however, the game never forces any philosophy, or even the discussion of philosophy at all, upon the player. It made my experience richer by a hundredfold, but if it's not quite your cup of tea, and you're playing simply for the joy of the puzzles, then you may ignore it and skip it all and still have a perfectly wonderful experience.
Everything about this game, from its user interface and its world design, is absolutely beautiful (the last world, the Land of Faith, is the most striking). However, encountering over and over again very similarly designed ruins can, after many hours in the same world, leave one with a dull impression. The mechanics are smooth and seamless, without any of the usual annoyances or hitches, such as slow movement and limited sprinting. The puzzles themselves are progressively and rewardingly challenging, and, unlike so many other puzzle games, non-linear. Some of the game's more complex puzzles actually have multiple possible solutions, even incorporating one's solutions to other puzzles in the same level, and, if one gets stuck, a puzzle may be skipped and saved for later (up to a point, of course). Finally, the conclusion quite perfectly wraps up the narrative and allows the player a glimpse behind the veil of the lore, as the developers offer their own answer to question underlying it all: "What does it mean to be human?"
To anyone who loves thoughtful puzzles and thoughtful narrative, I wholeheartedly recommend this masterpiece of design and concept.

First off, thank you Rock Star Vancouver and Rock Star London, and everyone else who was part of making this iteration of Max Payne.  This was a solid game.  A well crafted and detailed 3rd person shooter with heart.  Not overly dramaticized or over-the-top.  Which is surprising, since it is a Max Payne game.  A lot of hallmarks of Max Payne, from my memory, are dark-tones, over-all noir feeling, dialouge driven cut-scenes executed like a dime-store detective novel, and near constant action dependent on the player's style, execution, and skill.  (Well...and if they are using a contoller or mouse.)  These facets may sound like a cluster-cuss all together, but with a game-world like in Max Payne, all of them work together.  It takes effort and direction to take a character like Max Payne and not have your experience turn into pure action schlock or a bliazzard of white noise caused by perpetual gun fire and player actions.  I felt that I had an equal measure of continuing story and action/ player-agency in each chapter.  Though, I remember, probably inaccurately, that the first Max Payne was a happy result of developers tinkering with how they could fit "bullet-time" into an exciting shooter for players, especially when a huge selling point was players could potentially live out their Jon Woo fantasies.  Enough reminiscing, my point is that this series has been rooted in the action and the gritty story-verse of Max Payne.  Again, in other hands, this type of mixture would lend itself to be way over-the-top, an experience where the story elements only serve to get the player to the next action segment.  Which is not to say, that the Max Payne games are meant to be realistic, they seem to have a crazy rythym with their absurd action components and grounding emotional story elements.  Max Payne 3 has the same rythym but does not feel it's age, as much.  So in summation, Max Payne 3, I recommend it.  Not for children, adult audiences only.  Detailed and beautiful level and character design.   Game mechanics flowed and were intuitive, though that could just be because I'm a fan of this series.  In the end, if this is the last Max Payne game I'll see in my life time, I'd be happy with that.  It was enjoyable, it was able to play with my feels, and was not lacking in it's content and creativity.  Afterall, as it is alluded to in the game, Max can't do this forever and the same problems seem to plague him like a bad joke that he's the butt of.  As Max walks into the sunset, maybe the series does as well.  That's not so bad, is it?  Max has had enough Payne.  Sorry, I had to do the Payne pun, sorry.

Well over 1000 hours on this game, and played since Alpha 10 or so.
This is an interesting, in-depth game that will both keep you playing, and keep you restarting as you think of fun new things  you want to try.  A wonderful addition and take on the survival basebuilding genre that has whole new sets of challenges and features.
The good:
- in-depth, challenging survival, with several levels of difficulty
- freedom to play how you want to play - add what you want or impose restrictions however you want
- Every game is different
- The game can get you really attached to your characters and you may find yourself making up stories about them as you play
- Runs on a toaster
- New features added every new version, and no sign of that stopping any time soon
- Semi-sandbox style play...do what you want, but the AI will throw random challenges or boons at you as you go.
-Great replay value, especially with the scenarios
- AMAZING modding community
- Again, because it is such an immensely great aspect of this game...AMAZING modding community
The Bad:
- The "win condition" is a bit underwhelming....the game just...ends.  Its clearly there so that you CAN win, and to appeal to the people that like a goal, but if you're looking for a game with a hugely rewarding win screen or a new game+ mode, this isn't it.
-Graphics are simple and unassuming.  It fits the feel of the game and makes it run super smooth on the slowest machines, but for people who demand each character's individual eyelashes to be rendered...this isn't that game.
- The game can lose its luster, but it takes a long time to play out all the various ideas you might come up with, Certainly enough to justify the game value.  On top of it, the game creator has been adding new features that revive it every new version....you'll easily get more play out of this game than most out there....but it will probably eventually get old.
- RNG can be a cruel mistress.  Random events can unfortunately end your journey despite your best efforts...The best advice i can give here is to learn to love your game losses...death by manhunter squirrels can actually be terribly amusing!
- a bit on the pricier side for an indie game, which unfortunately may turn people off before they even give it a chance - but as stated above, the content and gameplay you'll get out of it easily EASILY justifies the cost.
If you like games that will take a little bit of figuring out - a little bit of delving into the mechanics, and this genre appeals to you AT ALL, then this game is worth a look.

I enjoy this game immensely, even though it is very difficult.  Let me repeat, it is very difficult.  There is no handholding here, no experience points, no perks, no unlocks, no kill cams, no 3rd person view, no spotting, and no Pavlovian gimmicks/bs.  Your skill and how well you can work in a group determines if you can defeat your opponent.  If you die a lot, it's because you suck.  This is a 'big boy' FPS.  The other team will not go easy on you.  If it feels easy, try playing against a clan(s), I bet that will change your mind. If COD and BF are too arcady for you and/or ARMA briefings are too long, then this is for you. This is a no frills FPS that finally scratches that itch that develops over years of FPS BS games pushed out by big publishers.  At the time of this writing, it is in v6.4 ALPHA, and it is still very good.  For a small group of DEVs, they are pushing out a lot at a respectable pace.  Plus the SDK is already out, and seeing as this is the successor to Project Reality, the longevity of this game looks promising.
TL;DR: Easy to learn, hard to master and a lot of fun.

The intersection of story-driven gameplay and puzzle mechanics too often results in clunky, confusing interruptions to the flow of otherwise excellent and immersive narrative experiences. Puzzles may be absurdly easy and seem entirely out of place (e.g.
), needlessly lengthening parts of the game, or their extreme difficulty may grind gameplay to a halt (e.g.
series). However, just as Valve so brilliantly defied this rule with the
series years ago, Croteam manage in
to seamlessly integrate an interesting plot, as well as a mystifying lore, with absolutely exceptional puzzles. And where
and its sequel excel in wit and ironic humour,
achieves profundity, treating meaningfully and thoughtfully the most fundamental questions of philosophy and ethics, without being pretentious. The texts and audio files found throughout the world constitute a fully realized and intriguing lore, and dialogue with the Milton character is fascinating and thought-provoking; however, the game never forces any philosophy, or even the discussion of philosophy at all, upon the player. It made my experience richer by a hundredfold, but if it's not quite your cup of tea, and you're playing simply for the joy of the puzzles, then you may ignore it and skip it all and still have a perfectly wonderful experience.
Everything about this game, from its user interface and its world design, is absolutely beautiful (the last world, the Land of Faith, is the most striking). However, encountering over and over again very similarly designed ruins can, after many hours in the same world, leave one with a dull impression. The mechanics are smooth and seamless, without any of the usual annoyances or hitches, such as slow movement and limited sprinting. The puzzles themselves are progressively and rewardingly challenging, and, unlike so many other puzzle games, non-linear. Some of the game's more complex puzzles actually have multiple possible solutions, even incorporating one's solutions to other puzzles in the same level, and, if one gets stuck, a puzzle may be skipped and saved for later (up to a point, of course). Finally, the conclusion quite perfectly wraps up the narrative and allows the player a glimpse behind the veil of the lore, as the developers offer their own answer to question underlying it all: "What does it mean to be human?"
To anyone who loves thoughtful puzzles and thoughtful narrative, I wholeheartedly recommend this masterpiece of design and concept.

Greater than the sum of its parts, The Talos Principle is an excellent addition to the puzzle genre, one that's challenging but always fair, easy to play but always mysterious. The visuals are super clean and colorful. The quantity of puzzles is staggering. Weird as it may seem in a game like this, the story is actually the thing I remember the most. Specifically, the conversations with the Milton Library Assistant are engaging and sometimes unpleasant. You just have to experience it for yourself.
This is still a puzzle game through and through, and solving these puzzles is what you'll spend 90% of your time doing. Every puzzle mechanic is used with each other in every combination quite nicely, and the game allows for a lot of freedom when it comes to which puzzle you want to attempt next. The only downside to The Talos Principle is the overused puzzle involving tetris pieces. When tackled sporadically they aren't too bad, but they could've used a bit more variety. This is an excellent puzzle game that will challenge you with its puzzles and please you with its graphics and atmosphere. Highly recommend.

I enjoy this game immensely, even though it is very difficult.  Let me repeat, it is very difficult.  There is no handholding here, no experience points, no perks, no unlocks, no kill cams, no 3rd person view, no spotting, and no Pavlovian gimmicks/bs.  Your skill and how well you can work in a group determines if you can defeat your opponent.  If you die a lot, it's because you suck.  This is a 'big boy' FPS.  The other team will not go easy on you.  If it feels easy, try playing against a clan(s), I bet that will change your mind. If COD and BF are too arcady for you and/or ARMA briefings are too long, then this is for you. This is a no frills FPS that finally scratches that itch that develops over years of FPS BS games pushed out by big publishers.  At the time of this writing, it is in v6.4 ALPHA, and it is still very good.  For a small group of DEVs, they are pushing out a lot at a respectable pace.  Plus the SDK is already out, and seeing as this is the successor to Project Reality, the longevity of this game looks promising.
TL;DR: Easy to learn, hard to master and a lot of fun.

The story is better than any CoD game and the gameplay is ten times more exciting, although I think it would do without the spontaneous sex scenes that come from nowhere. There's also a difficulty unlike any modern FPS since you have armor and health that doesn't regenerate and enemies that take your health out almost instantly with lots of mechs that you have to take down with limited ammo and seemingly underpowered weapons, and I think that is what ultimately made me stop playing. If I didn't have a list of other games I want to try I would like nothing more than to sit down and figure out the easy ways of getting through, but it just didn't become fun dying to the same super tough Nazi while being swarmed by other Nazis after you had already killed two waves of Nazis.
Maybe modern FPS made me soft, but I don't think I'm bad at games or even this one. With most things it's just a matter of time before you figure out the easy strategy, and Wolfenstein made me do that so often fights became stressful rather than fun and the story just wasn't enough to make me power through it. Since I couldn't even beat it I can't recommend it.

This is one of the best puzzle games I've played in a while, which is weird considering it came from the makers of Serious Sam. Generally it's a mix of Portal and Myst with a dark and interesting story tying everything together. The atmosphere and music are wonderful and the mystery of the setting really pushes you to explore the world and solve its puzzles, if only so you can find another info terminal that will give you a few more clues on the plot.
The puzzles themselves start off very simple, but later on will become more challenging and can feel pretty clever sometimes. I know its been used in a few other games, but the sections where you need to interact with a recording of yourself are particularly interesting, especially when you unlock an item that lets the recording carry both yourself and tools around.
As for downsides, the game is bad at explaining certain mechanics. For instance, you can place boxes on top of the floating mines. Sure, I eventually worked this kind of thing out through trial and error but I can't help but feel the mechanics could have done with better introductions or some kind of tutorial.
The game is also a bit too long for what it is, with several puzzles being repeated at later stages as advanced versions. This wouldn't be too bad but there are only a handful of mechanics, so things can get a bit repetitive after a while, and it can be a bit annoying when you'd rather learn more about the setting than solve yet another laser redirection problem.
If you can look past these flaws and are a fan of puzzle games then I'd strongly recommend The Talos Principle, especially if its on sale.

I love the art style. its very similar to prison architect in art style which is also a great game. One of my favorite moments was when one of my colonists leg was shot off after a raid.  He was stuck and injured so i brought him to a medical bed. I then order a surgury so we could install a peg leg. My Doctor at the time had a skill of 15 which is pretty good. I started watching hi  preform the sugury but i got bored and started designing some other part of my colony. A little message pops up say *the surgury went slightly wrong* so i was thinking oh maybe he messed up and needs to try again. I move back over to the medical bed where my colonist was on and i see him bleeding out on the bed. Very confused i click on him and check on health. The first thing i see is *stomach removed* "what, excuse me" how the ♥♥♥♥ while trying to install a peg leg did you miss and cut his stomach out. And then i see *severe heart bleeding* and again i like "what the ♥♥♥♥ happened" how is it that while doing surgury on someones leg did you *slip* while cutting and cut a mans entire stomach out with one swoop and slice is heart open. AND THEN, i see the docter, WALKING AWAY TO EAT. Like Oh boy after that surgical mishap it would be a great time for a lunch break. While the colonist is still bleeding out on the damn medical bed.

I laughed for a good 10 minutes about it, and shared the story with all my friends who thought it also hilarious and all found an interest in the game!
I would Reccomend this game 10/10 if someone is looking for a Crash landing survival simulator with a prison architect kindof feel. It is worth the purchase as it can be replayed many times and has hours and hours and hours of content

Overall this is a proper clouser to one of the greatest triologys in gaming.

I had the chance to play this game first on my PS3 when it came out. I lasted 2 hours and got bored by it. When I saw it here on steam on sale I thought I give it a chance and it did get me into it but after a while again it got boring. My biggest problem with it is the stupid missions where you have to find some stuff for the NPC characters at your rebel base. This games brags about killing nazis but 20% of the game you will be looking for stupid things and play just with your knife stealth missions - really annoying. The missions are quite short and the enemies are easy and stupid, no challenge at all. I remember the Uber Soldiers from RTCW, I was scared to♥♥♥♥♥♥ they could easily kill you, here you just blast them with your laser and grenade launcher a few times and youre good. And the story is just stupid. I didnt care about BJ's love story and all the other resistance fighters. I mean  I dont expect a great story from Wolfenstein but this game tries to take itself too serious on some points and be moral and play on your emotions but it fails at that. I expected from this game some more nazi paranormal mysteries which keeps you interested to explore and fight against as in the old games. This game is just a modern FPS as any other, nothing special about it. Dont trust the ones who tell you this is an old school FPS, its not. Its not automatically old school if you do not have regenerating health. Besides this you have all the mixtures of modern FPS games, a "special abilities" weapon which you need to use from time to time to proceed, a cover system, which I was not using much, some missions can be done stealth (some need to be done only stealth), npc characters which ask you for favors or to get and find some stuff for them etc.
So to sum it up:
Pros:
- core shooting gameplay is ok and feels good
- the settings look nice and well crafted
- the nazis and their machines look cool
- voice acting and music is top notch
Cons:
- lacks any real challenges, Uber Soldiers easy to kill
- it lacks the mysterious and paranormal feels of its predecessors
- bad story
- some boring non-shooting and stealth only missions
- weapons feel kind of same, I was mostly using the assault rifle
I would recommend this game if its at a discount but else I would not. It just doesnt feel as an old school shooter and compared to modern ones is quite average. I would give it a 6,5 out of 10.

The game also contains hidden stars. This is where the game is really at, where the challenge is. You just can't beat the feeling you get by discovering 'how' to get and solve some of those harder stars. They are also dozens of easter eggs everywhere and those are all about exploration of the world, getting out of boundaries, being clever, taking a leap, being innovative and you get rewarded really good sometimes.
Most puzzle games have little story or not at all. But yet, Talos got me into it's story more than RPG games such as Dark Souls. You have those metaphysical conversations with a terminal. They get really deep. You end up questioning yourself about your actions, choices, who you are and what you believe, humanity in general, so much more too.
The music is quite relaxing and really amazing. It fits the theme really well and it didn't took me long to realize I might have to buy the soundtrack too.
I just bought the DLC Road To Gehenna to get me some more puzzles.
Talos also just made me buy Portal 1 and 2.

The first thing I have to say is that I'm a proud and happy contributor to this Early Access Game. Compare to other early access games, the developers are super active in their forums and Reddit. Every month they release an update and provide information about their progress.
Before purchasing this early access game, I strongly advise people to research a Battlefield 2 mod called Project Reality because this game mostly based on that mod. In fact, most of the developers who developed the Project Reality mod is working on Squad.
When people think of military simulator, they think of overly complex controls and lots of waiting before combat. I don't blame people for comparing Squad to Arma at first glance, but in reality, the game plays nothing like Arma. There are some downtime and waiting in between engagements, but they're in the short burst. The developers mentioned numerous time that they won't sacrifice gameplay over realism, so don't go in expecting a simulator.
Although the game might not be 100% ultra-realistic, that doesn't mean the gunplay and atmosphere don't feel authentic. The firefight engagements are super intense in this game. One moment you're just chatting with your squad while walking to the next objective, the next, you're on the ground with bullets blazing everywhere. It is adrenaline pumping, and I've never felt anything like it since my early days in Dayz. In Squad, multiply that feeling by 10. Every enemy encounter feels fresh and new. Its gunplay is all about flanking, positioning, and situational awareness.
This game, for the most part, is easier to learn and have less complex controls compared to Arma. If you play any military shooters for the past decade like Battlefield or Call of Duty, then you'll feel right at home. There's no navigation through scroll menus and a million keys to remember. The interface is easier to understand compare to games like Arma. The simple controls, however, doesn't exclude the fact that this game has a deeper learning curve than your average shooter. Although it is not as deep as Arma, you won't master and know everything in your first match unless you've done research on the game prior to playing.
The game also puts a huge emphasis on communication. If you're shy on the mic, I can almost guarantee you, if you're not talking to your teammates, your teammates will most likely be talking to you. Teamwork and sticking with your squad is a must in this game. If you're thinking of going lone wolf and Rambo, you won't have a good time. I mean you can try to do that in the game, but the game makes it really hard for you to enjoy it.
Now for the bad news. As of right now 06/21/2016, the game is unoptimized for AMD CPU. The developers said this is because of the Unreal 4 engine and sound optimizations. My rig is a GTX770 with FX8350 playing at 1080p. Right now I get around 30-40fps, and the frame rate drops to the high to mid-20s depending on the player count. This, of course, isn't only exclusive to AMD builds. There have also been reports of people with i5 or i7 getting low frames. The game is still enjoyable and playable, but I hope in future updates the game will be more stable.

This game is, and will always be, limited to a specific group of players who enjoy milsims like Project Reality and Arma. While it is less sophisticated than Arma, and in some aspects more fluid - you will never, ever get satisfied by this gaming experience if you think that jumping down a building will result in no injuries, or if you think that venturing alone in the battlefield, killing 50 enemies, will actually make any difference. There is no ranking system, no perks to buy ,no special abilities to unlock. The objective of the game is to secure / defend districts or find and destroy weapon caches. Anything you do, other than that, is totally useless. Nobody actually cares if you killed 20 enemies and died only once - a guy who died 6 times, but actively contributed to capture 2-3 objectives, is indeed more useful and considered valuable than any lone wolf sniper in the middle of nowhere.
Squad is about teamwork. Not necessarily about shooting at everything you see on the map. It requires basic infantry tactics and decent knowledge of what purpose each role is meant to observe. An Automatic Rifleman is supposed to provide cover or suppressing fire. A medic is supposed to stay in the back, while the Marskman is supposed to provide eyes for the team proceeding down a valley, or in a small settlement, while riflemen should advance, while all the elements of the squad cooperate for the capture of the next objective.
If you think this game is like Battlefield or Call of Duty, then don't buy it. If you are looking for a mature gaming experience, then this is the game you are looking for.

RimWorld is a colony-builder/survival simulation game from one man dev team, Ludeon Studios. In RimWorld you're presented with a scenario and using the group of people and resources you get, your aim is to survive on a randomly generated rim world. There are three basic scenarios but the game has its own scenario editor as well as workshop support which helps contribute to the game's huge replay value. Your main goal in the game to research and build a spaceship capable of getting you off what is usually a very dangerous world.

One of the key parts of RimWorld's gameplay is its AI Storyteller feature, effectively one of two difficulty levels. Your choice of Storyteller dictates what kind of events you'll see in the game while a second, traditional difficulty level, decides how tough these events will be on your colony. The most common events include the Mad Animal event (an animal will become very aggressive and target your colonists) a Raid event where a local pirate faction will attack you as well as positive events such as Cargo Pod drops or Escape Pod drops. There are also several different environmental events which add a new level of challenge to the game. They range from Solar Flares which temporarily disable all of your colony's electronics to Toxic Fallouts which will cause a Toxic buildup in a colonist (which can be fatal) if they aren't indoors. You also have colonist mental break events which occur when a colonist's mood becomes very low and stays that way for a long period of time. Sometimes a colonist will simply lock themselves in a room but serious mental breaks can lead to going berserk in which case the colonist will become hostile. Your colonists can also randomly get serious diseases such as malaria or the plague as well as common illnesses which are usually caused by combat-inflicted injuries.

Depending on your Storyteller and difficulty level these events can be very difficult, and will often be the downfall of your colony. Surprisingly, this isn't at all frustrating, in fact what I enjoy the most about RimWorld is the stories you get from your playthroughs and the most interesting stories come from the death of your colony. In my second attempt at the game, one of four colonists and the pet dog were killed during a pirate raid. The colonist who had developed a bond with the dog became incredibly unhappy and went beserk. He was equipped with a rifle and easily took out the two remaining colonists while the pirates worked on destroying my power supply. When my beserk colonists finally went outside, the pirates turned their attention to the poor sod, they peppered him with bullets and carried him back to their base. With that my colony was destroyed.

Generally when I'm utterly destroyed in a game I get frustrated and take a break from it, not RimWorld. Each time I've lost a colony I've restarted instantly and the reason behind this is the replay value the game has. Even if you're playing the same scenario, the colonists you 'choose' (you have no customisation options but you can randomise to get a group of colonists you'd prefer) have a huge impact on how your game turns out and how you manage your colony, even if you build similar structures. Your colonists will have varying skill levels for the different types of work in the game. To some extent these are random but they're also dependent upon the colonist's background (type of childhood and profession) and the character's traits. A doctor or vet will always have a high medical skill level while a torturer or hunter will have a good melee skill level. Traits often have more of an indirect impact on the colonist's ability. A beautiful character will be better in social situations and a psychopath is incapable of social interaction and only cares about things that directly impact them.

Colonist traits also influences how characters interact with each other and what consequences those interactions will have. If a character with the beautiful or pretty trait attempts to romance another character it's far more likely that the character will be successful. This might not seem like an important gameplay feature but interaction with other characters is one of the main happiness modifiers. Anything from having a nice chat to making love with another colonist gives a bonus to happiness but getting rejected or being insulted will make the colonist unhappy for quite some time. There are of course plenty of other happiness modifiers. Taking part in social or recreational activities gives large boosts while executing an innocent prisoner or eating human flesh give massive negative modifiers. The severity of the modifier dictates the length of the modifier. Having a rough night's sleep on lasts until the next night while getting rejected can last for an in-game week. There is some balancing that needs to be done for some of the modifiers, the modifier for getting rejected is particularly lengthy.

Being a colony survival sim, building is obviously a very important part of the game. If you're familiar with Prison Architect then the building mechanics will be fairly easy to grasp. You'll be designing and ordering your colonists to build different structures as well as furniture for your colonists to use and enjoy as well as production items such as butcher tables, cooking tables and research benches. You'll also have zones at your disposal to help run your colony. You can set up stockpile zones (and choose what's stored in any given stockpile) for storing resources, growing zones to grow food and other useful crops such as a plants for herbal medicine and cotton to use in the production of clothes. One of the things that RimWorld is missing compared to similar games such as Gnomoria is RimWorld doesn't have Z Levels, I.e. the ability to build up or down, you're stuck on the ground floor. This isn't a huge issue as the maps are very large (depending on what size you pick) but it's still worth mentioning. Tynan Sylvester hasn't ruled out Z Levels being added in the future but it requires a lot of work and so if we do see it in RimWorld it’s a long way off.


RimWorld is not only an excellent, highly entertaining colony sim, it's also one of the most polished and content rich Early Access games I've had the pleasure of playing. It may seem like its priced a little high but RimWorld is absolutely worth every penny.

By far one of the deepest, most interesting games I've played in some time, both in terms or story and in gameplay. On the surface, the story isn't exactly subtle, drawing obvious parallels between God, Adam/Eve, and Satan, with the God figure promising eternal life, Satan tempting you with knowledge of the world, and a large towering structure that is strictly "off-limits". As you go on, however, the true story is slowly revealed by means of found messages and journal entries as you debate morality and existence with the computer. Where are you? What is real? What isn't? What is a person? If Reality is a lie, does that really matter? I don't want to give away too much, but it really has changed the way I view the world in some way...perhaps not in a "good" way, though.
The story is held up by some truly fantastic puzzles using a multitude of different mechanics that are introduced to you slowly over time. There are no tutorials, all gameplay is left for you to figure out on your own, which is something I'm particularly fond of in a game. Some of them are truly mind-bending, and require some serious logic to get through. There are also a large number of stars to collect as optional items requiring further puzzles within the puzzle rooms, sometimes linking multiple puzzle rooms together to get to. Quite challenging.

[Edit 23/07/2017: A huge fan of the game who goes by the name Russian Doggo has been commenting on my review of Dirty Bomb seemingly taking exception to my observation that the matchmaking in this game is pretty poor, but he inadvertadly desribes the matchmaking and gameplay better than I could and in fewer words than my own review, he says: 'Dirty Bomb is one of those games that is going to abuse you (kinda like Rust) and once you get good you become the abuser (kinda like Rust)'.
There you have it folks, does that sound like a fairly balanced game to you? Where you are abused by higher level players only to perpetuate the cycle yourself when you reach high level? The matchmaking needs work, I rest my case.
I'd like to give Dirty Bomb a possitive review but as it stands at the moment matchmaking is quite broken. When you start you're put into games that are locked to players of levels 1-7, but after that matches are quite frequently full with far higher players, I'm talking 40+ sometimes even 100+ and the game does not balance teams before the game starts resulting in very lop sided matches. I'm level 8 and in the space of 7-8 I have had nearly every game turn out to be one sided with 30-40+ level players on one team and nothing but 6-20s on mine, more oftern than not resulting in the enemy team pushing a team of inexperienced players back to their spawn and then spawn killing relentlessly.
Unranked servers can be joint freely by anyone, spawn points are not protected and the game sufferes from the same draw backs as Overwatch where there are no limits to how many characters can be active on each team at any time which means in maps which have tight spaces it's incredibly common for the defending team to just grenade spam (happens alot with high level players who have unlocked Nader, who has a 5 shot gredade launcher, sure each gredade as about a 15 second reload time but when you have 4+ players playing as her, that cooldown goes out the window).
There is also a severe lag problem, game will stutter frequently but not for everyone, resulting in free kills on both sides until the issue resolves itself.
I haven't played ranked yet, because it takes over 10 mins to get into a game despite ranked games being locked to 5v5 instead of unranked rank of 7v7 or 8v8.
Good points are that the gunplay is pretty solid, characters are quite diverse in their specialised roles so you'll find one that suits your play style and the maps are designed with multiple routes, some of which need to be accessed by completeling secondary objectives, which also be repaired by the opposing team.
Overall the game is an avaerage fast paced FPS romp, with some severe balancing and stability issues that need to be ironed out.

Original Review -
First thing's first: if you have a high end rig that you are confident can run this game no problem, this is a solid shooter with stealth elements, judging by the little of the game that I played.
However, if you have a low end or even medium range computer (like me), be aware that many people have had severe performance issues. Running at 1280x720 with all setting at minimum, I got 25 FPS or lower most of the time, 40 FPS at best for 2 or 3 minutes occasionally. I found this unacceptable and a constant barrier to my enjoyment of the game. I did a lot of googling and tweaking, and none of them improved my framerate. Overall, I'm going to have to not recommend this game, as I met the minimum requirements and still could not reach 60 frames per second even at minimum settings, reduced resolution, and with a few tweaks that lowered the visual quality even lower.
I ended up getting a refund, but I do intend to repurchase the game once I upgrade my computer. I may or may not change this review once that happens, because while the game is enjoyable to most, many will not be able to due to not owning high end systems.

Squad has been a ton of fun. It is immersive, exciting and realistic (compared to other shooters). If played well, with teamwork, you won't regret buying it.
Note that this isn't COD and that it takes a certain amount of time until you get the vibe. In the beginning you can expect to get shot by enemies that you are unable to see. You will do and think very dumb things, like respawning over and over on a FOB camped by enemies, stand behind someone who is about to fire their rpg, walk on the hilltops, smoke your own position, and so forth.
Note that this game is alpha. Vehicles aren't implemented yet, but will be soon. The performance isn't great yet either, yet, so don't expect your potato to run it smoothly, do some research before buying it.
Here in the review section you may read alot about the devs being like the dayz devs. They're not. They've just been a little more quiet because they had to rewrite the entire vehicle netcode.  Note that these devs are from the PR community and have contributed to PR for years.
To all the people complaining; if you expected to play COD, suck at the game, or get bad performance; you should have done some research before blindly buying this game. If you give it some time, watch some videos perhaps, you will definitely get better at it and you'll enjoy it a lot. Cheers.

While Squad may show a lot of promise, I cannot possibly recommend this game in its current state. Progress has been painfully slow and performance is awful. This game is rarely updated, only getting a patch every couple months and they never add anything big or useful, just token bug fixes and maybe another half finished map. The developers are still struggling to pull acceptable performance out of UE4, often making performance worse with updates while failing to release promised content in a timely manner. Vehicles were supposed to be out a couple months after launch, which then turned into late May, which is now supposed to be late July or early August. Having seen the pace of development I hold little hope.
As it stands now most of your time in game is spent walking from point to point while the game chugs at an unacceptable framerate despite not being a terribly pretty game to begin with. Users with anything short of a high end Intel/Nvidia rig will be disappointed and users with AMD processors will likely find the game unplayable, an issue the devs have been unable to pin down or fix despite it having been a known issue for over six months now. While the gunplay is tight and frantic, it is rarely worth the effort of trudging around gigantic maps for minutes between engagements.
In short, do not buy this game. The team developing it is, while noble in their intentions and sound in their vision, seemingly incapable of delivering on said vision in a reasonable timeframe. While there may come a time when needed content has been delivered and performance improved to an acceptable degree those who look at the game objectively will note that the light at the end of the tunnel is nowhere to be seen. Your money is better spent elsewhere.

(This review contains spoilers. No multiplayer assessment.)
Max Payne 3, the third and thus far last instalment of the Max Payne series is a third person shooter, in which you are being put in the situation of Max Payne, an ex-cop and regular bar occupant, coping with his troublesome past and the losses which resulted from it.
This time our journey takes us from the cold and ruthless climate of New York City, to the hot and tropic São Paulo in the middle of Brazil. Here our hero is hired as a bodyguard for the rich Branco family, which own large parts of industrial Brazil and are well known family throughout the country. Payne, who was certain to have outrun his haunting record of suffered casualties, awakens in yet another hell which he was desperately trying to flee from.
As the rich and famous of Brazil throw parties on rooftops and celebrate their invincibility and pompous lifestyles, they are constantly and violently reminded that Brazil isn't the safest country on earth. Payne's mental state goes from bad to worse as the conflicts between the favela gangs and the rich Branco family intensify and the wife of his new employer gets kidnapped by the perpetrators. Far from an 'easy gig', as his friend and colleague Raul Passos said about the time he hooked the drunk up with this job.
From there on out, our hero goes on a suicide mission to rescue the woman, uncovering an even uglier truth at every step in this multi-faceted country. The insanity of it all unfolds as Max goes from tactical to an all-out open approach as he dives right into hordes of bad guys, hoping to die while desperately shooting everything in sight and living to fight another day.
With the all new RAGE engine first prominently used in the Rockstar game "Grand Theft Auto IV", the controlability went from the blocky and instantly responding Max Payne to an aged, clunkier and more realistically moving human.
The shootdodge which persisted throughout the whole series, in which your character dives into a given direction and where everything moves in slow motion giving you perfect time and a near invincibility as you blast your enemies in a near epic fashion, sometimes even followed by a close up or a bullet cam, following the projectile fired into the opponent's face, causing massive damage, has turned out to be just perfect and spot on, well done Rockstar.
With the new akimbo system in Max Payne 3, you can combine any picked up single handed firearm together and use both at the same time. A wide variety of assault rifles, shotguns, pistols, machine guns and more can be found throughout the stages. Also scattered throughout the different areas of maps are golden weapon parts for certain weapons, which can be collected and once all three parts for a firearm are gathered any future pickup of said weapon will get a stat boost and also have a golden paintjob on it.
I could go on all day talking about how well done this game was, even though it took a completely different approach compared to its predecessors in the series. The game sets a finishing point to an epic triology of Max Payne's mindblowing life and hunt for the truth. Whether or not Rockstar will consider making a sequel or prequel to the series is up to them.
In my mind this was a perfect last instalment of the series and if you played Max Payne 1 and 2, you will not be disappointed and if you consider buying this game as your first entry to the Max Payne series and you liked it, you should definitely give the first two games a go to understand some of the plot points which molded Max Payne to be the guy he is in this game.
Definitely worth a shot (especially if it goes on sale)

This is a story about Chad.
Chad was on the run from bandits when our tribe rescued him and welcomed him in with open arms. He was quickly put to work building and tending the gardens of our community, where he was clothed, fed and treated well.
What the tribe didn't know was that Chad was psychotic.
Because 'his room wasn't extravagant enough' he went on a crazy rampage. He took on the other six members of the tribe with only his fists and got his head bashed in. The other members of the tribe kindly picked up his broken body and took him to a medical bed where he was fed and given medicine until he was back to health.
However, Chad became angry again the next day 'because his clothes were in tatters' and this cycle repeated on a daily basis for 10 days in a row.
The rest of the tribe became uneasy with Chad around and were looking for ways to unburden themselves of him when by chance, during winter, Chad caught a nasty infection and the tribe ran out of medicine.
When his infection became serious, they rejoiced, and when Chad died from his infection, everyone was happy.
When our tribe member Camarro died, we built a lovely extravagant memorial to him with sculptures, flowers, and artifacts from our time spent on the planet.
But for Chad? Well his body was stripped and left to rot out the front gate with the remains of bandits in a makeshift graveyard built to deter future invasions. The tribe considered eating his remains as a further insult, but they had enough potatoes to last for a very long time, so this idea was quickly shelved.
With Chad gone, the tribal community was peaceful again and went back to how it was before his arrival.
10/10 would recommend to anyone who likes to see interesting stories and situations play out with every gameplay

I may not have many hours at the time of writing this review, but that's because I was a console casual when I first got it, therefore my hours were spent there.
Anyway, Castle Crashers, Like most Behemoth games, controllers are highly reccomended.
Unlike BBT where I felt keyboard controls were near impossible to play quickly and precisely with, this game has manageable controls as long as you mess with them so they're more user friendly.
Gameplay wise, this game is absolutely amazing if you're into Beat-Em Ups. It's good for casual players, and more experienced and focused players. It also has a very memorable soundtrack, I often find myself listen to many of the songs in the game.
While the normal story mode is rather easy, there's an enormous difficulty spike in insane mode. Because in insane mode, enemies have 10x damage, and 10x health. Essentially giving average enemies the health of a minor boss. And bosses get End boss HP.
The character variety is amazing, you can play as almost every enemy in the game once you set your mind to unlocking them, and because of the variety, you get some replayabillity as you wanna see how this character plays different from the others. Even if there isn't much difference. But the thing that changes the most is Magic, magic changes between each character, So it's always fun to try out a new character and his/her magic.
Something to note is, there are DLC, which totally not needed, however I will say what I know about them.
The Pink Knight DLC is esentially the character which has the strongest magic in the game, I'll be honest, it sounds Pay2Win, but it's not that strong, there are other magic characters who are just slightly worse.
The Purple Knight/Blacksmith DLC I do not own, and I have not played much with, but from experience is kinda just another character.
Anyway, in conclusion, Castle Crashers is a very fun game to play casually, and also fun to play in a more intense sense. In my opinion, it's a must get for those who like beat em' ups.

Note: I have not played Dwarf Fortress, but have played Prison Architect(Completely different, but I expected it to be that way, and it was).
When I landed on my first planet the number one thing you realize is that there's no tutorial. Okay, easy enough. I went on to YouTube and got the general idea of how to play.  But this was only the beginning.
THE CONTENT: On the surface there's a deep illusion of plenty of content to play with.The issue is when you need to start a new game eventually that things get repetitive. It has a "been here, done that" feel to it as you plant your first crops again and again. It's not hard to have a realatively comfy base, because everything is pretty low level and easy to get. You can "research" some items, but beyond the auto-turrent, the truly game-changing auto doors and colored lights have little impact on gameplay. The spaceship to get off the planet, which I guess is the end game, is pretty much a resource hole that doesn't accomplish much except make the player think they may survive for a while. Most players don't even bother.
THE ART: "Gets the job done" Not great, and certainly not polished. Apparently the devs got their graphics from the Prison Architect team (legally). The issue I have with this is that even though the graphics will certainly be polished later on, the game feels like it's too attatched to this style of art that's clearly not it's own. Could you imagine the same core gameplay in a decent looking 3D world while having a Z axis later on? Polish will help, but the issue needs to be adressed.
The main issue is the AI. The job system is down right nasty. You have the option of setting prioities yourself, but even then the system is broken. For example, I could order the command to mine something halfway across the map, but as soon as something higher priority comes on, they drop everything and run across the map to do a task that may take a half second, only to run across the map again to continue for fifteen seconds until they do it again. Great for events like fires, horrible for short, low impact jobs like harvesting a single plant or cooking a simple meal because you only have 9/10 left. The huge bases you see in the trailer really have no purpose. Having so many people is impossible to manage and has no real benefits other than defense for the overpowered raids. Be prepared for massive idle crowds if you plan to go that route.
In addition, colonists have moods that can be impacted by negative and possitive events. The only reason to keep moods high is that, simply put, colonists that have poor enough mood go on a homicidal rampage. The reason devs made it that way is because it gives reason for the player to do things like build pool tables and plant pretty flowers and have a shallow marriage system (They just sleep in the same bed) that otherwise have no meaning. Apparently this is the best way to do this. As you can imagine, the system is completely unbalanced.  Didn't get to eat at a table tonight? Stab someone. Food wasn't cooked? Stab someone. Room isn't pretty? Stab someone. Completely random and common event that lowers mood?  Stab someone.  Someone in my colony that I disagree with constantly? Stab them too. Have wedding proposal turned down? Stab fest for the whole year.
The COMBAT IS AWFUL. Colonists couldn't shoot a downed animal if they were a foot away, literally.  They have the accuracy of a drunk stormtrooper. Also, nothing is more satisfying than having a colonist die in friendly fire. A colonist could be standing in front of a raider, and while neither of them are moving,  colonists seem to have no issues unloading clip after clip into the same direction no matter who is in the way or how fast they are moving, making close/melee combat pretty much useless. Colonists need to be manually instructed on where to go because they like to shoot until they get melee attacked by an approaching enemy where they can't use their gun. They don't keep their distance like they should. Raids scale up so fast that you couldn't make enough guns in time if you tried, and you couldn't buy enough even if you had unlimited money due to a bad trading system. Most battles boil down to a boring grind of who has the most people with guns. Some people have noted how detailed the damage system is,  it is excellent, and is the most detailed aspect of the game. For example a colonist can have their arm shot off and have their aim worsened (if that's even possible). But events like this that affect the colonist rarely happen, and prompt medical care solves most problems. A cracked spine can be fixed with a little herbs and a good nights sleep.
The game is planned for your demise and feels like a tower defense with a battle decided. "Oh, well, you don't need those useful goals because you shouldn't survive that long anyway." is the general feel of the game.
"BUH ITZ RIMERLD AND THE EXPERIUNCE IS IN TEH STORY YOU MAKE ALONG TEH WAY"  and "ITS GREAT FOR MODS BRUH" are a terrible excuse for why a game is good. I shouldn't need to invent content for myself in a game that has none. At the moment, this game is worth about $10 max.
Most of the positive reviews are from the community pre-steam that got the game on steam and flooded the reviews(no bad intentions, but the reviews certainly aren't from a "new player" perspective)
-Fix AI
-Fix Combat
-Fix mood system
-Add real content
-Lower price
-Rip out and redo all art It's still a mashup of Firefly and Prison Architect
UPDATE 11/5/16-
I've been playing this game for a little while, and while it's improved there's still major issues.
-Job AI seems to have improved a little, but issues still arise with larger colonies and the automated job system (4+ colonists). Makes the game almost unplayable.
-Shooting/combat is still bad/buggy (Harder to hit a downed/dying animal than a healthy moving one, and colonists will still walk/shoot in friendly crossfire situations)
-Mood system shows the greatest improvement, colonists are way more mentally stable.
-Content hasn't changed, I still shouldn't have to rely on mods.
-Art is as unoriginal as ever.
OVERALL: While the game has made slight improvements, it still isn't worth $30, and seems like it won't ever really change/grow beyond bug squashing despite being an EA title.
On the other hand the developer is embroiled in an SJW fight about how gay and lesbian colonists were programmed, so some sparks are currently flying(he's currently paying the price for adding gay characters in the first place, because now people are complaining about not adding the other "genders" too). I wouldn't be surprised if developement is slowed until everything calms down.

This is the story of how "M" murdered "Engie."
-M joined the colony early on.
-M and Engie started a friendship, as they worked tirelessly getting the colony up and running.
-However, all good things come to an end.
-Raiders, jealous of my town of "Freedonia," initiated a raid against us.  It was not uncommon, but, in a sick twist of fate,  M's brother was one of the raiders.  Engie had no choice but to gun down M's brother as he charged her with a club.
This broke something inside of M.
For weeks later M would have nervous and mental breakdowns.  The colony always nursed him back to health, and with the introduction of beer, we thought all would be well.
But M always held a grudge against Engie.
The emergency sirens go off.  Another attack is underway.  A mad elephant has grown a taste for human blood.  Engie and M go to defend the colony at the sandbags.  Engie takes aim, and fires the killing blow against the rabid elephant.  M took aim as well....but he was not targeting the elephant.  In a single shot that resounded from my speakers, M shot Engie once in the back of the head.  I looked on in horror as Engie, my best colonist and leader, lie dead next to the elephant.
I knew M did it on purpose, but I couldn't prove it to the other colonists as they hid inside the base during the attack.  Fortunately, a new colonist named Timo joined up and I knew what must be done.  I told M to go hunting for food, but little did he know that he was hunting a Warg.  I made sure he didn't take his gun, as he thought he was going to hunt rabbits.  The warg vicisiouly attacked M, but did not kill him.  As he lay unconscious, Nemo, our doctor,  wanted to rush to the rescue.  I told her "no. Timo will go get him."  I gave Timo Engie's old pulse rifle, and sent him to "take care of M."
As M lay dying with hands outstretched for help from our new colonist, Timo raised his rifle.  "For Engie."  Those were the last words heard by M before the sound of a discharging pulse rifle resounded through the air.
***10/10.  If only TV writers would play this game, we would have no end to outstanding drama on television!***

I bought this game because it was supposed to have a good story with a focus on philosophy. Fun puzzles couldn't hurt either. Well, I got fun puzzles, but the story is not as good as I hoped.
The first issue with the story is the philosophical themes. They're not unique or interesting. If you've ever taken a philosophy course and are vaguely familiar with the basics of Christian theology then there's nothing new or thought-provoking for you here. The game focuses on what makes a person a person, whether AI are people, creating a legacy to overcome death, etc. These themes are not explored in more depth than a Philosophy 101 class, and pretty much every sci-fi story with AI in it uses some or all of these concepts, even Hollywood movies like I, Robot. As far as the religious references go, the Garden of Eden, Tower of Babel, and Paradise Lost plot elements are also pretty cliche and make the plot predictable if you know anything about what's being referenced, as the game's plot borrows heavily from them, especially the Garden of Eden. The writing is good in execution, but the content of the story is not interesting.
Cliched, predictable stories can still be good so long as they provide a unique experience in some way, like with their own interesting characters. Unfortunately, Elohim and Milton don't get that much screentime, saying something maybe once every two or three areas. This limits the amount of development they can get. The fact that they fall pretty neatly into the obvious archetypes from the story of the Garden of Eden also means that they're not particularly unique or surprising either.
Another problem is that the pacing of the plot is slow. The puzzles are fun, but there are so many of them in between things happening in the story that they feel like padding. The slow pace of the plot also means that aren't really many plot twists or things happening in the plot in general, especially in the middle section of the game.
Overall, the game's story felt like it stuck a little too close its premise and didn't explore its philosophical themes deeply enough or have plot/characters that would surprise you. Everything in this story has been done to death elsewhere.

Rimworld is a strategy game masked as a top down colony sim with a unique aesthetic and an emergent, complex AI system. Yes, you have to build and manage a base like most sim, sandbox games. However in Rimworld there are complex factors that are super important to the success of your colony.
Stories are generated by "simulating psychology, ecology, gunplay, melee combat, climate, biomes, diplomacy, interpersonal relationships, art, medicine, trade, and more". Key word "and more". Your sims can go insane and it will completely ruin your entire colony when Bert decides to strip and run out into the tundra and pace around in an unresponsive daze! Factions can attack but when taken prisoner can potentially become part of your colony, but only if you have someone with social skills that can chat em up.
This is what makes Rimworld so fun and addictive. I have started over about 6 times, sometimes because of updates but also because I am super curious about how colonies will end up in tundras, or jungles, or if I choose 3 men or 3 women, or 5 tribal members or 1 rich loner. No two stories are ever alike! It's hard to tell that this is even an Early Access game. It could be balanced a bit more, especially in Cassandra Classic mode, however it is very enjoyable.
I would highly recommend this game if you love simulation, strategy, humor, survival aspects, and if you enjoy replayability. 10/10 I'm totally obsessed and can't stop playing. It's summer and I'm always inside playing this game, dammit! Look what you've done to me, Ludeon Studios!!

The Talos Principle is a unique first person puzzle game that involves a large set of worlds with many different levels within them.  You collect puzzle pieces from each level to unlock other items and levels which give access to more of the story and extras.  The story is rather intriguing and will challenge your thoughts on philisophical concepts that you take for granted or as set in stone.  Reading everything and doing everything is my most recommended approach as you will get much more out of the game.
The puzzles themselves in the original portion of the game are difficult but not to the point of pure madness.  Some will take longer than others and obtaining the stars for each world definitely takes a little more brain power but is required for different endings and the best ending.  If you also have the Road to Gehenna, please play the original portion of the game first as the puzzles are much more difficult and will take more time.  The expansion is basically a prelude to the original game.
The sound track, graphics, controls, and story are all well designed.  Nothing is out of place and there are plenty of easter eggs to find.  Most puzzles have one primary approach but some share different methods to solving the puzzle.  The game has hours upon hours of content and I don't see how you could finish it in less than 7 hours unless you are already familiar with the game.
Overall, the game is fantastically done from the creators of Serious Sam.  If I had to point out one flaw in the game I would have to say I would have hoped for more puzzle concepts.  Once you complete World A and some of World B you already have a general idea of how to solve the puzzles.  Yes, they are still challenging but more variety in interactable objects would have been nice.
Still, with everything being said, the game gets a solid 9/10 in my opinion.  Everything was executed well its just that puzzles seemed to become standard situations towards the end.

Fully playable. Fascinating. It's basically an ant colony where you have to work to establish a base colony, expand it slowly over time as you gather and create resources, and then complete one gargantuan task (such as building a spaceship to escape the planet you crashlanded on) in order to win.
It gets into what it means to be human (you have to balance the moods of your crew) and what it means to be suddenly separated from the modern world. Research is essential, but you can't get to it until you handle the essentials like food and shelter.  You also need to repel attacks from invaders and beasts -- which are often very tricky as you can lose sight of your enemies if you get distracted by the day-to-day grind of feeding and clothing your people.
I really like it a lot. It's a next-level Sims experience with the noble goal of illustrating what it means to build yourself up from nothing.

With Robocraft finally in 1.0, I decided to update my review.
Quick note: this game is NOT Pay 2 Win. All parts can be obtained from crates and/or purchased with Robits. Also, bigger weapons does not equal superiority.
Pros:
-Highly creative game; many different parts to choose from.
-The maps look fantastic, especially now that their graphics have been enhanced and sizes increased.
-Sound and music are great; seriously, whoever did the soundwork deserves a medal.
-Free to play, and not Pay 2 Win.
Cons:
-Some bugs are still present.
-Certain weapons and movement parts are still better than others. However, the devs are working on balance, among other things.
-Matchmaker has some kinks. That said, I think this will improve as the devs update the game and the matchmaker balances out (hopefully).
-Crate contents are sometimes pretty meh, but at least you can scrap any unwanted parts you get if you don't want them.
Overall, despite the (sometimes justified) salt I see on Steam and the official forums, I still love this game over three years later and 800 hours in, and I encourage anyone who hasn't already played Robocraft yet to give it a shot; it is free to play, after all.
On a final note, here are some tips once you start up the game:
-Robots can now get damage, speed, and health boosts. However, going strictly for damage and/or speed means you need a lot of skill to avoid taking hits. Thus, until you're comfortable with the game mechanics, I recommend building your starter bots so that they have a big health boost.
-join a clan; as long as you play matches, you can get a nice amount of currency for more parts!
-If your bot ever flips over, press the "F" key to flip. Be careful, though, as you won't be able to defend yourself until the 3-second animation finishes.
-Your bot automatically spots enemies within a certain radius; make sure you keep an eye on that radar!
-In the hanger, press "X" to enable mirror mode.
-You can ping the map by holding down the left "control" key, and scrolling over one of the three commands (go here, on my way, and alert).
-Check out Youtube: while Robocraft's tutorial is still bare-bones as of writing this, some players have helpful guides and build tutorials to help you get started.

Talos Principle is legitimately one of the best games I’ve ever played. Certain games give me motion sickness to play and Talos did it to me worse than any other game. I still finished it by chugging ginger tea nonstop so I wouldn’t have to lie down and not move and it was 100% worth it. It’s that good.
It’s a 3D puzzle game with a well told story. I don’t want to spoil anything but it’s an old story so it’s even more amazing that they could retell it so well. It has one of my favourite depictions of a character damn near ubiquitous.
Though if you’ve had motion sickness problems like me in the past, watch a video of one of the puzzles being done on YouTube or something fullscreen and see if it does it to you, in case you’re not as willing to suffer through it. Just watching a puzzle shouldn’t spoil anything as long as it's not one of the final ones. There are suggestions out there to reduce this effect (it seems this game commonly triggers motion sickness in those susceptible) and I did try them all but they didn’t do much to help; so don’t bank your hopes on those.
10/10 will probably make myself want to die over several sessions again to 100% it.

(Full review follows below)
is an outstanding action-shooter that offers a strong narrative and a highly cinematic experience.  If you are someone who wants raw action, and doesn’t want to see a lot of cutscenes or kill-cams: then you may not enjoy this. However, if you are someone who enjoys games that play like movies, this is something you must play.  In my opinion,
is one of the best cinematographic-action games ever made and likely will be for a long time.
The first aspect I will highlight in defense of my opinion is the writing and dialogue.
easily has some of the best writing I have ever encountered in a video game.  The overall narrative is interesting and entertaining, but the real beauty of the writing shines through in the dialogue.  There are several lines throughout the game that will evoke that inner-thought of: “that was a good one.”  And the excellent voice acting ices the cake to ensure the cutscenes have an A-one quality that rivals Hollywood movies.
Besides the main cutscenes that give life to the actual narrative, there are also many other cinematic features woven deep into the gameplay mechanics.  You can activate
® and
™ as you play through the fight scenes in each level; doing so will slow time and allow you to perform elaborate kill sequences.   Further, bullet-cams and kill-cams will pop up periodically to show some nasty kills.  There are also level-specific “special” kills that will slow time and create cinematic opportunities.
The fight scenes encompass the vast majority of the actual gameplay of
.  The game is very linear and generally ushers you from one shootout to the next, with a cutscene in between to show more plot development.  There are some secret areas and collectibles, but generally the areas where you are in control are rather small and undeviating.  However, this is perfectly aligned with the movielike feel of the game; and the levels are well-designed and diverse, so they never feel boring or plain.
The whole experience is brought together nicely by solid graphics and animations, a high level of attention to detail, and advanced physics and particle effects.
Now,
is the third installment in the franchise.  It is technically a direct sequel, although it feels a bit more like a spiritual successor.  You can easily enjoy this game without having played the first two.  (Of course, it is still best to learn what happened in the story during the previous games).  Also the first two installments in the
franchise were created by different people than this one.  This game does go in a bit of a different direction compared to the earlier installments.  For example, it isn’t quite as dark and noir; and also eases a bit on the deep, psychological inner-war concept.  These, and other differences, upset some fans of the franchise (as seems to be a common theme in new installments of long-standing franchises). So be aware of this. I personally feel that all three games can be appreciated for what they are.
Arcade-mode, timed-mode, higher difficulties, and achievements all contribute to the possibility of many gameplay hours.  There is also a multiplayer mode that is pretty fun.  During the time I played, there was a decent amount of people who played regularly; although there were times I couldn’t find a game.  I actually liked the multiplayer a lot and played it for dozens of hours, but I will admit that most people will probably find it lackluster.
In summary, I highly recommend
to anyone who would enjoy a heavily cinematic action-shooter and who would appreciate the amazing writing.  It is one of the best “plays-like-a-movie” games ever made.  Having said that, I can understand some of you just want action.  If you want pure gameplay and/or generally skip cutscenes in games, you definitely should look elsewhere for your next shooter.
