I wish there was more to Steam ratings than just a thumbs up or down.  I'd say I'm neutral about this game but depending on your comfort in an FPS, you might sway one way or the other.
The gameplay itself is pretty fun, it features small squad combat (that has become pretty popular since MOBAs have) with a variety of classes and unlocks to modify your play.  Loadout cards give your classes potentially slightly different weapons (though all within the same theme, shotgun classes tend to stay in the shotgun family) as well as passive bonuses (reload while sprinting, ability recharge faster, etc).
The best way I can describe how it feels is Counter-Strike with a little bit of Overwatch and TF2 sprinkled in.  It's fun, I like it.
But the progress in the game is painfully slow.  If you happen to be amazing at FPSs, your progress will be faster.  The equipment cases, which give you new loadout cards, trickle in at a horribly slow pace and their rewards are largely boring.  You can melt those cards down for scrap and build a specific rarity for a specific class.  But I had to spend most of my gold to buy equipment cases to afford building a decent rarity card.  Then find out I need about as much gold as I had already spent on cases to craft the single card :(
It's a fun game that dies out from such a slow drip feed.

150-250 meters away is a small compound.  3 buildings.  My squad is on top of a mountain.  While squads 1 and 2 move in to try and take the objective, we are raining down M230 grenades and rockets into the enemy position.  At this distance we can barely see the moving specs, so it is up to our squad leader to adjust our aim as he looks down with his binoculars.  I launch another grenade, after up, up, left, and I hear "nice got one". One kill, but damn does it feel good.  Run back to the ammo can we set up to get a few more grenades.
It’s nighttime.  The enemy is searching for our weapons cache.  We had created a defensive line, and been knocked back to the village. Squad leader sends me back to the mountain to provide overwatch and sniper cover.  I watch the intersection, calling out targets and directions for my squad, while providing the occasion cover fire or kill.  “Hey” I call out to two members heading towards the enemy.  “ Be prepared for contact”.
Both of those are just two of the epic stories that I have experienced and created in Squad.  To provide the full truth however, those tales were followed with periods of waiting, running, or just getting killed often.
Whether or not you like this game is going to depend on you.  But I have fallen for its magic, and am a firm convert.  It is slow paced, methodical and very tactical, followed with short (or longer) bursts of intense action and furious firefights.  It is the most realistic shooter I have ever played, in that real infantry tactics work, where CoD style gameplay gets you and your team killed.
The visuals and sound design are nice, but even more so in how they allow you to move and play.  Cover and concealment are real, one hides you, the other protects you and both are useful.  Weapons feel real, and it will take several shots to down someone, because you need to hit them!
It is a team game, and when played together you have tremendous experiences, but a bad squad or a poor game can be rough.  I have enjoyed about 75% of the games I have played, and I will continue to sink time into this game.
As an alpha game it is superb, and even more so because of the great things that seemed planned.  I for one hope they succeed, because I am excited to see where this game can go.
TL;DR - Super realistic, epic firefights, with some tedium.  (Like a real patrol) Game quality depends on squad quality.  Alpha game heading in the right direction.

Year 12.  While hunting a wild boar, Sabine is gored in the torso.  This becomes infected.  After weeks of struggle and being a burden to the team, she dies.  Later, a starving crewmember gnaws on her frozen body, then goes on a berzerk rampage in which he kills the third crewmember in her sleep.
His toes are infected and he has frostbite.  In the midst of his starving madness he's attacked by three bandits.  In desperation he blows a hole in the wall of an ancient building and giant insects come pouring out, killing the bandits.
He later succumbs to his infection, and dies face down in the snow.
The base, now abandoned starts to deteriorate.  Raiders and vandals come, fires break out.  There is little left but a shell, metal debris and bones.  The walls and floors are spattered with blood.
Some time later, a lone spacer running from pirates finds the place and takes refuse.  Laying on the floor she finds the grenade satchel left by the murdered engineer.  She runs to the door and waits - and when the pirates arrive she throws the grenade at the door - blowing it open and killing two of them.  The third runs off in a panic.
She strips the pirates looking for anything valuable, and heads to the back of the abandoned outpost.  Claiming one small storage room as her own, she sets up a desk, bed and candle - cleans the floors and repairs the door.
Fast forward 6 months.  She sports a peg leg from where her leg was shot off by friendly fire.   Her two main fighters are both snipers.  One of them got his ear shot off, the other one has a facial scar from a fight with a raging elephant, incredible as that might sound.
The doctor just finished cutting off the cook's toes to stop an infection from frostbite.   His wife has a shattered jaw, and can no longer speak.
Solar panels are up and working, and the radio is online.  Time to find out who else is out there, and what their angle is.
10/10 - Would desperately hang on for my dear life again.

150-250 meters away is a small compound.  3 buildings.  My squad is on top of a mountain.  While squads 1 and 2 move in to try and take the objective, we are raining down M230 grenades and rockets into the enemy position.  At this distance we can barely see the moving specs, so it is up to our squad leader to adjust our aim as he looks down with his binoculars.  I launch another grenade, after up, up, left, and I hear "nice got one". One kill, but damn does it feel good.  Run back to the ammo can we set up to get a few more grenades.
It’s nighttime.  The enemy is searching for our weapons cache.  We had created a defensive line, and been knocked back to the village. Squad leader sends me back to the mountain to provide overwatch and sniper cover.  I watch the intersection, calling out targets and directions for my squad, while providing the occasion cover fire or kill.  “Hey” I call out to two members heading towards the enemy.  “ Be prepared for contact”.
Both of those are just two of the epic stories that I have experienced and created in Squad.  To provide the full truth however, those tales were followed with periods of waiting, running, or just getting killed often.
Whether or not you like this game is going to depend on you.  But I have fallen for its magic, and am a firm convert.  It is slow paced, methodical and very tactical, followed with short (or longer) bursts of intense action and furious firefights.  It is the most realistic shooter I have ever played, in that real infantry tactics work, where CoD style gameplay gets you and your team killed.
The visuals and sound design are nice, but even more so in how they allow you to move and play.  Cover and concealment are real, one hides you, the other protects you and both are useful.  Weapons feel real, and it will take several shots to down someone, because you need to hit them!
It is a team game, and when played together you have tremendous experiences, but a bad squad or a poor game can be rough.  I have enjoyed about 75% of the games I have played, and I will continue to sink time into this game.
As an alpha game it is superb, and even more so because of the great things that seemed planned.  I for one hope they succeed, because I am excited to see where this game can go.
TL;DR - Super realistic, epic firefights, with some tedium.  (Like a real patrol) Game quality depends on squad quality.  Alpha game heading in the right direction.

Let's see... Wolf-3D in 1992 basically launched the FPS genre. Then we had RTCW and 2009's Wolfenstein, both good but not-that-memorable games. Then Call of Duty, Brothers in Arms, and other games eventually made WW2 and Nazis feel overused and tired.
Until Wolfenstein The New Order, that is.
Once again you play as BJ Blazkowicz, aka BJ or just Blazko, saving the world from Nazi scum. However, things are different. Adolf Hitler is not in charge. D-Day was a colossal failure. A last ditch attempt in 1946 to find and eliminate General Deathshead, the supreme Nazi leader, also ends in a heart-wrenching failure that sees one of Blazko's close friends horribly murdered before his eyes. Blazko and his remaining friends escape, but in the process Blazko gets knocked into a coma thanks to shrapnel hitting his brain.
He awakens 14 years later in a Polish mental hospital, into a 1960 where the Nazis have won WW2, controlling the entire world including the USA which surrendered after the atomic bomb fell on New York City. Heck, the Nazis even have a base on the moon! It's a truly dark world out there, and it's uncertain if even someone as badass as Blazko can save it. Especially when General Deathshead's Nazis command superior technology decades ahead of its time (hence their ability to win the war).
Playing as Blazko is wicked fun, bringing back many fond memories of old-school FPS games, without feeling too old-school itself. You have partially recharging health, aim-down-sight mechanics, and a cover system, just like many modern shooters. However, you can also fire from the hip without accuracy penalties, your health only recharges to the next highest multiple of 20 (making it necessary to scavenge for health packs), you have to watch armour levels too (which don't recharge), you can carry every single weapon in the game at once, and even dual-wield assault rifles and shotguns. Like I said, a very effective blend of old-school and modern mechanics.
The levels are well-designed, many offering the option to take a stealthy approach, with multiple paths to the objective. You can sneak up on unsuspecting Nazis, slashing their throats or throwing reusable knives into their chests, like Splinter Cell, while hoping no one manages to raise the alarm. Of course, this being a Wolfenstein game, letting the s**t hit the fan is just as fun! The weapons feel powerful and sound great, especially when dual-wielded. The gore system is one of the best I've ever seen, with hilarious dismemberment mechanics especially when using shotguns, explosives, or the Lazerkraftwerk, the BFG of the game. It just feels so right to blast off a Nazi's arm at the shoulder and see his blood spurt everywhere as he screams in agony, or to burn a laser hole right through his guts and see his intestines spill out. These scum deserve no less.
As for weapons, all of them can be upgraded by performing a certain number of kills in a particular manner (e.g. 10 headshots), or by acquiring parts hidden through the game. Better yet, any upgrades you get will be carried over when you start a new game, so you have incentive to replay the game in order to find any upgrades you previously missed (I certainly did). Keep an eye out for Lazerkraftwerk upgrades - this has to be one of the best FPS weapons in existence, period.
The story plays a bigger role in the gameplay than ever before, and it's a damned good story if you ask me. The characters including Blazko are well written and you really do feel the emotional connection with each and every one of your buddies. The villains themselves also come off as truly menacing psychopaths rather than cartoonishly evil. There is also one important decision you need to make at the beginning of the game, which will have an impact on the plot, encouraging at least one more playthrough.
On the technical side, the game looks superb and runs even better. I initially ran it at 1920x1080 at high settings with over 50 fps on a 1GB GTX560 non-Ti. On my new 4GB GTX760 Superclocked, I easily nail it at max settings.
If you like first-person-shooters with good plotlines, this is the game for you. If any FPS deserves a sequel, it's Wolfenstein: The New Order.
Now go blast some Nazi scum.

TL;DR: I am a veteran who has seen Robocraft go from glory to ****. I have been playing for over 1000 hours, and believe me, this is terrible. Here's how it all started:
(Full review)
One day, my friend and I got on Robocraft. Next thing you know, we were staring at tons of crappy changes, such as: tiers, TP, GC, RP, etc., taken away. Then we go in to the main game. Here is how it went: We spawn. We start our attack. Next thing I see is either an SMG bleacher column or a plasma bomber blimp floating above the map. Once we got back to our garage bay, we notice that there is a paywall that is forcing us to pay to color our robot. WHY THE **** WOULD WE HAVE TO FRIKIN PAY TO COLOR OUR BOT?????!!!!! What also bothers me is that now, the worst thing yet is here: crates. They ruin the challenge on selecting what you want to buy. With crates, you can either get: 5-10 robits, or a dinky shield that you could've got with premium. My worst problem is, is that I have seen it all: the first offense. 2 years ago, everything changed. I have witnessed it all. I am haunted by what I have seen. And this is the reason why I will not play Robocrap again, FailJam.
A few facts of present day Robocrap:

If you're here to check reviews you are either justifying your purchase or genuinely concerned about spend $40 on another Early Access game. Well this review will strike both of them with my honest and brutal opinion from either standpoint.

Yes, this game is definitely worth it if your a fan of the Arma series or a Battlefield fan looking for something more intense and MilSim-(Military simulator)-like. If you want something fast-paced, close spawns or anything that requires little patience and thought,
. But as I said, if you play Airsoft/Paintball, or just want a more realistic approach thats easier to learn than the rather confusing Arma tactics and keybindings, this is right on spot and for you. I'm not saying this isnt fast-paced either, it just takes some walking from Point-A to Point-B. The firefights you get with you and other squads are absolutely amazing and intense. I have gotten expierences with this than no other game than before. Now for some short reasons why this game is worth it in my opinion:
Only negatives I can really see from playing so far is the decently high price point for an EA game, and the FPS issues and stuttering with AMD systems.
With the current situation, I would avoid buying this game with AMD equipment. Its still pretty bad on nVidia systems as well, but fairs much better than the AMD side. For example I get around 50-60 on a 40 man server on a GTX 970 OC and i5 4690K. Most servers are populated towards 70 man, around that I get 30-40 frames.
P.S. - I will update this review as the game evolves and possibly fixes some of the issues above or creates some new problems. Cheers.

Thought provoking puzzles, beautiful physics engine, co-operative (or counter-operative, depending on your playstyle!) gameplay, and Sass Master Glados. What more could you ask?
Graphically the game is presented exactly as advertised: You're a robotic test subject in a test lab, testing things. Which would normally lend itself to some stark and boring visuals, and at times they do have a bit of chronic same-face, but it fits well. Right up until the point where you're thrown a massive curveball and suddenly all the sterile white surfaces become a thing of the past.
Audio? Who doesn't like a little friendly (or unfriendly) spurring from the robotic overlord insighting a bit of friendly competition between you and your co-op partner? The dialogue is as funny as you'd expect and no matter how good of friends you are (my co-op partner and I have been friends for twenty years now), Glados seems to find just the right buttons to push to inspire a few rib-jabs between you.
The storyline leaves a bit to be desired thus far, but then again we haven't actually finished the game yet - so I'll reserve my thoughts on that for another day.
If you haven't played it yet, you should! Find a friend though. It'll make it that much more rewarding :D

Pros:
High movement speed and wall jumping for excellent mobility. The crouching and jumping mechanism is very crisp and with a nice monitor and enough frames (cough 144) can pretty accurately display them.
Good ttk.
Good teamwork concept with reviving, ammo, and brute force.
Nice visuals once you get them dialed in for your tastes. In my experience with trying to be a god at this game I found that absolute lowest settings made it easier to aim.
Decent crosshair system finally, like that took a long ♥♥♥♥ing time, and even when it was first added you could only do it in between games.
Healthy playerbase in us east allows constant matches.
Cons:  keep in mind these opinions might be considered controversial.
Aimcone: The amount of spread you get while strafing left and right is almost enough to make the game feel like it should be slower paced than it is. Hitting headshots consistently should be obtainable as long as your crosshair is placed over the victims head (except perhaps mid air, but definitely not accurate for jump sniping)
Aimpunch: Aimpunch in its current state allows people who re peek faster to gain an advantage on an otherwise superior aiming player, however once the shots stop hitting you you are free to aim steadily again. Aimpunch from guns onto enemies isn't that bad overall imo, and possibly adds strategical depth to this game. Aimpunch from explosives on the other hand, LOOKING AT YOU FLETCHER AND NADER is ♥♥♥♥ing cancererous to this game. They already have effective aoe damage, why do they have to punish you further than that?
Card system: I don't really care about the loadout system, even though I have 260k extra credits. And thats low compared to other players, believe me. If you don't have value in cobalts and golds, you can't craft more end game cards. Its simply not mentally stimulating enough to make people grind for it in itself.
Good game, could possibly benefit from testing out new ideas or even just temporarily tweaking things with a clear devblog and forum to allow people to give feedback.

This game is quite an achievement-a real piece of art. It has an engrossing sci-fi story with heavy philosophical underpinnings, challenging puzzles, stunning visuals, and a great soundtrack. It's easy to make comparisons with the Portal games if you want to get an idea of how this game plays, but besides the first person perspective puzzles (complete with cubes that you need to put on pressure plates to open doors) they are very different experiences. This game demands much more of the player with "meaning of life" questions-what does it mean to be a person? Etc. This game also really rewards exploration with all kinds of hidden rooms and easter eggs, as well as multiple endings. My only real complaint is that half way though, I began to tire of the number of puzzles I had to grind through just to advance the story. At some point, I just wanted it to be over. Overall, though, I highly recommend this game.

Dirty bomb is a neat idea of a game. But it fails in so many ways.
Is it fun? Hell yes. Is it worth it? Hell no.
Why?
It's poorly optimized,small maps,and gets stale.
The gunplay is ruined by the constant ping issues. You could have NASA net and you'd still get issues and constant ping or packet loss.
Guns are OK. Most feel the same. Most SMGs and ARs are basically the same thing,just one will get more ammo per mag,while one will get more ammo in general. Snipers are bleh,but if they hit,they'll one or two shot you so thats good. Shotguns only work at point blank,or sniper range,there's no inbetween. Pistols are all over the board and melee is wonky as Willie Wonkas Chocolate factory.
Also,just spray and pray,or use a shotgun in the bum.
But it's the cards that ruin the gun play. I could see perk cards. But not with primary/secondary/melee weapons. It just doesn't work. You'll know it when you see it when you fight a team of high end cards and nobody on your team has anyhting of note.
Oh wait,matchmaking. It's awful. It doesn't work. It's frustrating because both players don't play the objective,and the MM often doens't do a good job mixing and matching high and low ends of the player skill spectrum.
The maps often cause snowballing. Once a certain point is reached in the map,you really are powerless to stop it,due to the spawn system using 20 seconds unless you get lucky on the spawn timer and catch it on it's last few.
The classes and mercs. There's simply too much overlap and you often have a few good gems,and some real turds. Good luck figuring that out when you're new.
The grind is way too long,and you don't get many good,or decent cards. Expect a lot of the basic garbage ones that are only good for recycling to try to make new better ones. And good luck on that.
I want to like it. I really do. I like the concept,I like the mix of parkour and speedy games,but I can't like it because of the above issues.

I considered the trailer for this game to be one of the best ever made, due to this perhaps I expected too much as a result, but in all honesty, I am disappointed.
It isn't in regards to the combat however, I throughly enjoyed the guns and the enemies were rather a pleasure to fight, if not overwhelming in some scenarios.
The main issue I have with this game is the lack of direction. I spent half the game just looking around trying to move onwards or find something with pretty much zero hints whatsoever. It's one of those games were you just get stuck over and over and feel like looking up a walkthrough on how to solve the issue as it gets so frustrating. The map is quite awful and as the game has no minimap it is hard to get around. I don't complain at hard games, but this isn't hard, it's just frustrating due to lack of direction, not a challenge or puzzle.
The game features disturbing scenes but no where near enough considering the enemy we are supposed to be facing, which is another disappointment. The story also just doesn't even seem plausible, I mean obviously this is alternative history, but it just seems like blatant fiction considering how ridiculous it is. I like the characters, but the game barely even develops them and it felt like it ended far sooner than it should've- plus the ending was crap to put it bluntly. For the price of the game, it's a absolute letdown I completed this in under 9 hours.
There are also some technical difficulties you may face. Despite me owning an Nvidia card and the majority of issues being reported on AMD hardware, I still have odd stutters when I start the game, plus the abysmal fps in some cutscenes.
I bought this game thinking I'd walk away knowing I had made a good purchase, unlike most people who seemed not to expect much then report it to be great, sadly with me it is the opposite. I expected much more and  though it pains me to say, I would not recommend buying this unless on sale. To all those calling this a masterpiece, you've forgot the meaning of the term.

Having now played both the base game and the DLC "Road to Gehenna" I can definitely say:
If you like puzzle games in any way then buy this game!
The Talos Principle is highly addicting with its amazingly hard puzzles. If you were dissapointed with Portal 2's difficulty like me this game will finally satisfy that craving for a properly engaging puzzle game.
The gameplay at first reminds of the Portal series with levels based around solving logic puzzles, each in their "separate" area, with the help of a selection of gadgets and while carefully considering the attributes of all the elements in the level.
But while Portal only equips you with the Portal gun and maybe the companion cube, this game introduces you to several different gizmos.
Another difference is that Talos Principle very rarely depends on your reflexes and ability to quickly solve puzzles while sailing through midair, although some do depend on a bit of timing.
The various level elments provide a great variety to the puzzles.
The game also offers tons of extra gameplay beyond the normal story playthrough by the means of bonus content.
All the various worlds contain stars that you can collect. Those are another step beyond the difficulty of the normal levels. Sometimes they are clearly presented to you as if to taunt you: "Here I am! Now how the hell do you get here to get me?" and sometimes they are hidden away somewhere in the world.
You will often find that getting the stars requires you to think outside the box and often outside the regular levels. You will regularly need to combine several of the seemingly separate levels and try to bend the rules to get to the stars.
Beyond that the game has to offer tons of easter eggs and hidden areas to find.
Besides the gameplay there is also the story which will probably make you think you know what is going on at first. "Pretty generic idea huh, kinda similar to Portal in its pretense. Well I don't really need there to be a strong story anyway. It is all about the puzzles."
Well think again because this game very quickly makes it clear to you that this is not your generic story to "somehow" justify you doing all those puzzles.
And where Portal went for a wacky adventure through Wonderland this game will take you through an intimate journey through your own mind and those of a few philosophers (metaphorically of course).
It will quickly suck you in and you will be craving for every single line of text more that you can get from the terminals. At the same time it will seriously make you think about some quite fundamental philosophical ideas, nag you for your own standpoint on them, lead you around a maze of thoughts all the while asking you more stuff, then point out how you ended up back at the entrance of your thought labyrinth and how you probably contradicted yourself in the process.
So finally 10/10. It is worth every cent unless you really hate puzzles.

I have always questioned myself, what if the Nazis had won WWII and took over the world, well, one version is that of Wolfenstein: The New Order which is a spriritual successor to the classic id Software game Wolfenstein
The game makes part of the Wolfenstein series but seems to ignore all of the past Wolfenstein games and make new with The New Order
The story basically continues and answers one version of what if the Nazis had won World War II back in the 1940s. The Nazis win the war, take over all the world, advance in technology and build war machines that will tear every innocent civilian to shreds
Captain William "B.J." Blazkowicz is your typical, strong American soilder and honestly, I did feel that he was the stereotypical American guy that we have all seen in movies, but I did feel happy that Machine Games did flesh out his character, but not so much, just in some cutscenes here and there
The environments are absolutely stunning, to see Nazis taking over well known landmarks such as London, Gibraltar and the Moon is really cool! However, the ugly textures did ruin it a bit, even on the highest of settings, the textures were really badly done and I have the latest graphic card and everything that can run this on a solid 60 FPS. Also, I cannot understand why this game is almost 45 GB big, where the graphics aren't the best...
Talking about game performance, this game does suffer with poor game performance. All cutscenes jerk around and freeze sometimes. Sometimes the game freezes monetarily even in heavy combat areas, the game just freezes...
The A.I., although I appreciate the different difficulty options in the beginning, very true to the old Wolfenstein games, and that you can change the difficulty anytime while playing, the game's difficulty changes drastically, played first in Normal difficulty, it was so annoying that I died so many times that I had to lower it to the Casual difficulty which lowered the amount of times I died, but made the A.I. dumb as ever, the Nazi soilders walk past you, notice you by saying "Huh?" or something along the lines and just walk on by, then sometimes if you are hidden, they notice you immediately!
Plus, I'm sure that during the real World Wars, the Nazi soilders did not have precision aim shooting, but in Wolfenstein: The New Order they have precision aim shooting, even if you are hidden in smoke! Very realistic!
The music and sound effects, although the music was really cool and very heavy, there were some instances that sometimes the sound effects didn't play or were just missing which ruined the experience. The cutscenes, they were very well done, lip syncing was really good, but why on earth from one cutscene it jumps you straight back into the game without any proper transition, this may be my OCD kicking in, but it did ruin the presentation of the game. Also, whenever you were killed, it just sent you to a loading screen without something saying like, "You are Dead" or something along those lines. It may be my OCD, but AAA companies should present their games in better presentation
Like previously said, you will die, a lot, thankfully there is a fair checkpoint system in the game. The voice acting was really well done and the characters were really well presented which made me happy and made it very realistic with its different langauges such as German and Polish as well as English, however, the game did not really focus on each and every character like Frau Irene Engel and Deathshead which were my two favourite villians in Wolfenstein. As usual, the main character HAS to fall in love with someone, and this someone is Anya, which I can understand, but why did they add two sex scenes out of the blue, they felt really awkward and out of place in my opinion
The gunplay is fantastic and then there is the stealth, which for me was the weakest in the game and made me question myself why on earth did they add stealth in the first place. I wish Machine Games could of added a better stealth system if they wanted to make Wolfenstein an action/stealth game, but for me, I don't think Wolfenstein: The New Order should of had stealth in the first place
The New Order is nothing like its predecessors, and made me cringe at some of the scenes offered. The excessive gore and torture scenes in particular made me cringe the most
I'm surprised why Wolfenstein: The New Order has no multiplayer, but I can sense that Machine Games really worked hard on making The New Order as true to the Wolfenstein series as possible, hell, even recreating the first level from Wolfenstein 3D as an easter egg really made me happy
I had fun playing The New Order, even though it did have its fair share of problems here and there, but on the whole, it was a really good action game. If you like history (like me) with a mix of alternate history and heavy gory action, without thinking about the Nazis, then Wolfenstein: The New Order is the game for you!

I was a huge fan of Max Payne 1/2, and it took me a while to get Max Payne 3 for whatever reason. The first thing I am confronted with is Social Club. I register, and surprise surprise, It won't let me log in. Finally after 20 minutes of finagling I get in.
Gone are the charming and novel cutscenes of the original, (the comic-book format), which graced the screen with good illustrations, bad♥♥♥♥♥voiceovers, and the ability to read at your own pace; instead these are replaced with in-game cutscenes (which seem to try to emulate the comic format somewhat, but fail quite miserably), so  right off the bat, part of what made the original great is gone.
The setting is quite novel, the nightlife of Sao Paolo, Brazil, and they drop you right in a firefight which is promising enough, but you quickly realize one of the first major problems of this game- the cutscenes are way too long. I don't want to skip them and not know what's going, so I stay through. Most of them are of something stupid, like Max drinking over and over until you yourself want to get drunk, or pulling himself up and taking a year or so to recover. Some of them are skipable, but most of the checkpoint transition cutscenes aren't, so I would end up watching the same clip of Max slowly creeping through a door, looking over the enemies. What makes it even worse is that the shooting is frequently interrupted by a long♥♥♥♥♥cutscene that could be easily have been done with scripting, like in the earlier games. It's not fun being stopped from having fun over and over. Thankfully it lets off a bit later in the game.
You quickly catch on that the gameplay isn't very good. The original two games were fast-paced and engaging, but MP3 is a cover shooter. I ended up just getting behind the first box/wall I would see at the start of an area, and all the enemies would run to me, as I pressed Q over and over to get in/out of cover until everyone was dead. What gives? Was anything that wrong with the first game's run and gun gameplay?
The game gets worse from there.
I soon found out that this game is also a collectathon! There are "Gun Parts" scattered around the map. If you get all 3, you get the golden gun version of it, as well as "Clues" to find that give a bit of backstory/narration.
There's nothing really wrong with that, except that every door locks behind you as soon as you enter a new area, meaning you're fresh out of luck if you happen to wander into a door that triggered a cutscene transition. And Max JUST WON'T SHUT UP. I'm looking for parts and stuff, and he's telling me over and over that "I had to get a move on, she doesn't have much time". If you want me to look for collectables, why do you have to have Max nag me all the time?
Speaking of unrealistic things, the enemies in this game seem to come out of nowhere. While the first game had you infiltrating the baddie's dens, one level had you in a bar, ambushed by a small group with guns. You take them out, only to discover that they have dozens of people outside the bar as well, and then 50 more people in the alley, and 20 more on the roof, and 20 more in the closet, and 30 more in the hall. I thought this was a small party that I insulted, not an army. The game is conspicuously missing any weapon/ammo caches that the previous games had, which I find a bit odd. Finding hidden weapons was a fun and rewarding part of the first few games, and keeping it in would have had no downside.
The game is somewhat poorly tutorialised, as they don't mention that you press "E" to vault over walls and boxes, which led me to try and use the lunge to get over short walls, draining my Bullet Time Meter, as well as the mechanics for dual-wielding, using a rifle/two handed weapon, cover, and some other things being obtuse.
What happened to the melee weapons anyways? Not that you would ever get close enough to melee an enemy, and you have some sort of takedown move anyways.
More technically, the options menu is good, and all the keys are rebindable. However, the game is plagued by horrendous pop-in, which is extremely noticable in jungle sections. Haven't the developers heard of fade in, or at least making the pop-in not right beside me?
Basically, the game isn't really a true sequel to the Max Payne franchise. The story isn't hardly as interesting, and I could really care less about who I'm saving or stopping.  The gameplay is wildly different, and it's pretty dull in general. If you really want to finish the Max Payne series, get it I guess, but otherwise skip this stinker.
Edit: I just noticed that the game does the same quit screen gimmick as the first game. Except that the tone of the game is completely different, and it doesn't fit at all. Nice try, but at least make something original if the theme doesn't work.

This game is pretty great! For starters, it's free, and also, it's just pretty good.
Pros:
-Fun gameplay

-High skill potential

Cons:
-Microtransactions (I'll get more details later in the review
-No proper team system (for standard matches)

Notes:
-While the game does have microtrasactions, they don't give TOO much of a major advantage, but are also quite expensive, take this how you may.
-It can be hard to get the loadout you want, but you can buy it if you have the money, either in game, or out.
-The loadout cards stop giving you the in-game advantage at Bronze, Bronze loadout cards can be found in cases, crafted, or bought, Bronze is the only type of loadout card in the store.
-Cases can be bought from the store for 1,000 credits, or found randomly after games. You can also get better cases for real money.
-You can craft loadout cards at varying rarities for various amounts of stuff, you need the crafting points, which you can get by breaking down loadout cards, and then you can use in-game currency, or crafting kits you buy with real money, to make the cards, then you get a random card of that rarity. For Silver and higher level cards, you can choose the primary weapon, but you have to find weapon kits in cases, and they are quite rare.
-There is a character rotation that rotates every once and a while, giving you free access to three characters. Usually one is a medic, one is an objective specialist, and another is an attack type.
All in all this is a pretty good game, it's free with some microtransactions, but spending real money dosen't get you too far.

Gameplay
Max Payne 3 differs a lot from the earlier entries. It feels a little faster paced, which does not make it worse or better. Of course bullet time has returned and it's better than ever before! Seeing bullets go through your foe's head slowly is very enjoyable! The main story is interesting enough to make you want to proceed and this game desperately needed that. The game is nothing more then shooting enemies and proceeding to the next area. The shooting part is great and there are many different ways to execute parts so that makes the game still fun to play. And to be honest, I didn't feel like it was as repetitive as it may sound. The cutscenes are very interesting and fun to watch with top-notch voice acting. After you complete the main story, which is around 10 hours. You have arcade mode and a great multiplayer mode to mess around with. Nothing too special but it does make the game last quite a bit longer!
Graphics
This game looks amazing! even on the lowest settings most things still look very crisp and clean... well until you make another bloodbath of course Wink. Graphical wise this game amazed me. The only game I can think of with better looking graphics is L.A. Noire!
Multiplayer
The multiplayer didn't do a lot for me, but it's solid. There are not that many maps, but the ones that are there are great. The way bullet time is implemented is great and works. Kudos for that. But all in all the multiplayer is just a solid experience, nothing that really blows your mind.
Story
The story, just like the earlier entries, is told in an unique way which I personally really enjoy. The story really makes you care for Max and yes, it is definitely depressing. And the ending is also worth it. While all of this sounds like I'm amazed by it, I am not really, It's great, don't get me wrong. But the story falls short at some points. I had a few moments which I found a little cliché. But other than that the story is interesting enough to keep you playing.
Addons
There is quite some dlc for the game. some DLC whilst being very cool, Is pretty expensive and you don't really get much in return in comparison. And I am very disappointed in one of the DLC's. Quote: " higher damage bullets in Max Payne 3 multiplayer". This makes purchasing DLC make you have an advantage in multiplayer which is not a good thing!
Value
The price tag has dropped to roughly $35 for the complete pack on pc. The game is worth it. I have played it for aroun 65 hours and I don't think about playing it again anytime soon. So it's definitely worth the money!
Verdict
Rockstar once again drops a solid game on the market. Though it has a few weak points nothing really makes the game unenjoyable or unplayable. It's even better if you play the first 2 entries in the series first just for the story's sake! I'd recommend this game to most people!

"In the beginning were the words, and the words made the world. I am the words. The words are everything. Where the words end, the world ends."
The Talos Principle fills an insatiable hunger for puzzle/problem solving after finishing a different game.
At the time i've posted this, i've logged about 8 hours.
To help understand how this works, this game plays very similar to the Portal games.
The theme and feel of the game is much more serious but I am still having a great time with some of the more challenging areas solving the puzzles all the same.  You are introduced to the tools to solve puzzles slowly, and not every puzzle uses every tool. The tools are within the puzzles themselves as opposed to carrying them with you.
It has much less spoken dialogue of Portal 2, it won't be humorous, witty or as narrative to guide you along.  While Portal is basically puzzles on rails, The Talos Principle has zones with many puzzles inside.  As long as you collect enough keys to unlock a new zone, you won't have to complete all the puzzles in a given zone to move forward and you can do them in any order you wish.  If one is too difficult, you can try another then go back later.
The story is largely theological, and relayed through sessions at various terminals reading half decrypted files, communications, documents, a few found recordings and a mystery entity that eventually reaches out to you through terminal to communicate.  The ambient score is very pleasant as well.
Expect puzzles that are similar in challenge and reward, but without quite so much story compelling you along from one puzzle to the next.

My latest colony was using the rich colonist scenario on RR Rough difficulty. Evie a 55 year old female bounty hunter landed with a 12 year old warg, Buzz, who suffered from asthma and was destined to die sometime during the colony's lifespan. Eventually I gained a second colonist named Pyrrha. She mostly stayed in her room researching all night long coming out only to eat and build entire buildings while Evie was asleep. A little while later and I have a nice fully functional two person village going with a full stockpile of food in the freezer and another fridge with some corn stockpiled and chilled. I'm good. Things are going slow, but good.
Then I see the warning. A manhunter pack of six boomrats are approaching from the Southwest. No big deal I think. I can lure them in to my stone buildings and then get them to blow up and kill each other. If I'm lucky I'll even get the meat! Well... Evie got caught trying to get in the front door barely making it inside. Unfortunately the six boomrats had no problem following her as she limped slowly in to the dining area. Pyrrha quickly ran in to the room to assist and began firing her charge rifle from cover around the corner. She managed to take out one of the rats, but not before they took down the injured Evie in a flurry of hits and turned their sights for Pyrrha next.
They quickly descended on her with no place to run in the small room. She took out another rat, which exploded in her face and knocked her unconcious. Now Evie is bleeding out on one end of the room and Pyrrha is doubled over in pain on the other. She's not hurt too bad though and should recover naturally from her wounds, or would have until another boomrat gave in to his own injuries from the explosion and he too exploded, setting Pyrrha on fire in the process. She burned to death at the dinner table leaving nothing behind to show for her existence except an empty bedroom.
Over the next couple nights Evie slowly began to starve to death and her wounds continued to drain to the floor under her. Heat stroke set in as the open front door let the hot desert air in raising the temperature inside to 100 degrees during the day. Finally, Evie succumbed. Buzz, the eldery asthmatic warg was now the sole survivor of the colony. Now she is left to eat her owner  and wait for her own passing.

"In the beginning were the words, and the words made the world. I am the words. The words are everything. Where the words end, the world ends."
The Talos Principle fills an insatiable hunger for puzzle/problem solving after finishing a different game.
At the time i've posted this, i've logged about 8 hours.
To help understand how this works, this game plays very similar to the Portal games.
The theme and feel of the game is much more serious but I am still having a great time with some of the more challenging areas solving the puzzles all the same.  You are introduced to the tools to solve puzzles slowly, and not every puzzle uses every tool. The tools are within the puzzles themselves as opposed to carrying them with you.
It has much less spoken dialogue of Portal 2, it won't be humorous, witty or as narrative to guide you along.  While Portal is basically puzzles on rails, The Talos Principle has zones with many puzzles inside.  As long as you collect enough keys to unlock a new zone, you won't have to complete all the puzzles in a given zone to move forward and you can do them in any order you wish.  If one is too difficult, you can try another then go back later.
The story is largely theological, and relayed through sessions at various terminals reading half decrypted files, communications, documents, a few found recordings and a mystery entity that eventually reaches out to you through terminal to communicate.  The ambient score is very pleasant as well.
Expect puzzles that are similar in challenge and reward, but without quite so much story compelling you along from one puzzle to the next.

This is a must have for any RTS gamer since it's really the one that brought the genre to the forefront. If you already own the game, then getting this is also recommended since it's optimized for modern systems and supports steam online play. The HD remake was unfortunately riddled with bugs at release but most of these seem to have been fixed.  However even though online "works" and there is a sizeable population, the HD remake still is plagued with many of the problems that affected the original AoE2 such as random out of syncs, atrocious lag every other game, and players dropping randomly. These are problems more to do with AoE2 itself and are not unique to the HD remake.
As for the expansions, thankfully you can filter multiplayer games according to which DLC is required. I would say that The Forgotten is easily forgotten (no pun intended) since the campaign scenarios lack any narration and really although the civs have new art styles, the only one that people seem to use are the Incas. The African Kingdoms on the other hand is a true solid expansion pack. The campaigns are very well polished and are narrated. It's also a blast to play as the Berbers, Portuguese and the Ethiopians. I just wish that both xpacks got the same treatment but apparently The Forgotten was already a fan made modification that was just modified further for commercial release whereas the African Kingdoms was a fresh new xpack. All in all though the online community for this game is still fairly active suprisingly after all these years and it's welcoming to all skill levels.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a game with a story that begins in 1946, then fast-forwards to 1960. The Nazis won the war in 1946, the Allies lost, so that Nazis have taken over the world. The introduction to the narrative is long enough that it takes a long time for B.J. Blazkowicz, the main protagonist of the Wolfenstein series, to carry firearms. Mr. Blazkowicz fought in the war for the U.S., but was wounded and spends time in a Polish mental institution in a vegetative state until 1960.
This game is a continuation of the famous Wolfenstein series that has no shame in allowing you to kill as many Nazis as possible. Cities like Berlin and London are now occupied by Nazis as technological terrors such as large mechs and robotic dogs patrol the streets. There are many propaganda posters strewn throughout Germany and London, England making it clear that the Nazis are ruling and that citizens who violate their laws will be severely punished. Mr. Blazkowicz is the man who will take on the Nazis with some help from NPCs who will advise him on where to go and what objectives to complete. Killing Nazis is in his DNA.
The narrative requires you to choose one of two paths that will be slightly different from each other based on which two comrades will die at the hands of evil General Deathshead, the leader of the Nazis. Deathshead kills one of the two comrades you choose for death so that he can use him in an evil experiment that he says will change the world for the better. You will then have to play the game based on the survivor’s timeline. This ability to choose may be cruel, but it adds replayability to the game by encouraging you to play the game twice so that you can experiences both timelines that result in slightly different versions of the narrative.
The gameplay is pretty much an old school FPS. The weapons in the game are not innovative, but they still feel very satisfying and have alternate modes. The run –of-the-mill weapons include handguns, assault rifles, shotguns, and sniper rifles. Each aforementioned weapon can be upgraded and the upgrades will be necessary to take on the bigger and more powerful Nazis. Assault rifles feel powerful when dual wielding them and can be upgraded by acquiring the rocket upgrade. There are perks in the game that you can keep track of that Mr. Blazkowicz can acquire throughout the game to improve the stealth, tactical, assault, and demolition aspects of combat. These perks add a role-playing like feel to the game. The ability to pick up ammo, weapons, health, and armor feels a like old school FPS.
There are certain locales that seem to encourage stealth. This is when the knife comes in handy, allowing you to slash unsuspecting Nazis from behind. The slashings are truly gory and horrific, but satisfying since it feels like they deserve to be slashed by your blade. Some locales can overwhelm you to death if you don’t use stealth, especially if there are officers stationed there. You can detect signals that alert you to the presence of officers. Officers are capable of calling in reinforcements to overwhelm. Stealthily taking down officers is rewarding as the game’s map will open up and reveals secret items such as enigma codes, letters, and gold items. There are other locales that seem to encourage a shootout with Nazis of different sizes and abilities. Nazis are varied enough in terms of clothing and weapons. Some Nazis are powerful rocket wielding and shotgun wielding foes that will seriously test your FPS skills such as the ability to take cover. The levels are varied enough as they include a prison that you must infiltrate, a lunar base run by Nazis, the city of London filled with swastikas to indicate Nazi dominance, and a base occupied by Mr. Blazkowicz’s friends where he receive objectives. It is interesting to see an alternate perspective of World War II with the Nazis winning the war and dominating the world. They actually landed on the moon before the U.S. could ever land one of its own citizens on the moon.
I have always been of the opinion that characters in games should speak their native language. This game nails it by having Nazis speak German when engaged in combat. It makes the game feel more immersive than if they all spoke the English language in a setting that is German. Some of Blazkowicz’s friends speak German and say a few words in German. I felt like I was truly in Germany when the Nazis spoke German during combat. The A.I. is not always perfect, but it is good enough to test your FPS abilities in the spur of the moment.
One new weapon in the game is the laser cutter known as the laserkraftwerk (LKW). When you first acquire this weapon, it is a utility that can be used to cut holes in metal gratings that block your progress. There are other metal gratings that can be cut for the purpose of finding secret items. Once it is upgraded the LKW becomes more than a utility item: it then contains an alternate mode which is a weapon that is very effective against mechanical enemies. They don’t require ammo since they run on batteries that can be recharged at the various recharge stations.
The graphics look very modern and make the 1992 version of Wolfenstein seem pale in comparison. The cutscenes look polished. The levels look picturesque and very realistic, whether they are in Berlin, Germany or London, England.
I think this 2014 entry into the Wolfenstein franchise is breath of fresh air. The narrative is always interesting, although it felt like it took a little too long to carry a weapon, let alone engage in intense combat. This game provides an interesting perspective on what it would be like if the Nazis had controlled the world after World War II. The gameplay is challenging enough that it forces you to think about how to approach dangerous combat situations. The acting performances are convincing, especially from the evil Deathshead to the courageous Caroline Becker, who is an important guide for Mr. Blazkowicz. This FPS is definitely worth playing.
My Score: 9/10

I started off in the desert to see how it was as a change. We had 3 survivors, Bellerose, Roman, and Ramyn. AKA Noodles.
Noodles was the greatest doctor in the game. He could patch up anybody, with a stick and a block of ice, probably. Sadly, we had few resources. The only steel we got was from steel walls all over the world and wood was not to be seen. We managed to build our homes shotgun style (one corridor with rooms on the left and right) and hoped for the best.
We found an "ancient danger" which was a large limestone room, covered in darkness. We needed supplies, so we broke it down to see what was in there. It was cyrptosleep chambers. 4 of them. Despite warnings I had read from guides, I opened them.
3 guys and 1 female popped out of the chambers, 3 of them in shock. The other one had an SMG. He opened fire at Bellerose, who fled the scene. Due to cyrptosleep sickness, the man started to spew his lunch all over the limestone floor. Noodles, being a brawler, rushed at him with a knife. He managed to kill the man, and we gave Bellerose his SMG since she was the only one who wasn't a brawler. However, during the fight, Noodles got his left foot shot.
Since he was the only certified doctor in the colony, we had to put him through amateur care. Meanwhile, a mad animal was running around (Iguana) and was closing in our home. I sent Bellerose out with her Tec-9 and she shot the Iguana, but she got injured as well.
While Bellerose was in bed, resting away her pain, Noodles, who got shot in his foot, crawled out of bed to get a medic kit and heal Bellerose. This hero. Sadly, he got a major infection in his left foot. Due to the lack of medical knowledge from anyone, we had to amputate it.
When he recovered, we gave him a wooden peg leg. He was fine with it, even though he moved slower. When he woke up, everyone went back to sleep. He continued the freezer we were building at the time for around 4 hours before going to sleep. Around this time, a woman named Minla joined our colony.
This man has done so much. But sadly, he couldn't help our food problem. We were running low on food. We had to grab the bodies from the cyrosleep chambers (they were still fresh) and poor Noodles was so hungry, he had to eat the corpses. Raw. Before they were bucthered.
This obviously took a toll on his mental health. He asked Bellerose out, and got rejected. This was the breaking point. He stabbed his cat, and chased after Roman, who got cut up. We needed Noodles. He was a great doctor. I decided to make Bellerose melee attack Noodles. This didn't work out well. He chased after a rat, stabbed it, and finally stabbed Minla. He got over his mental breakdown, and rescued Minla. Due to his peg leg and his wounds over his torso, he walked at a snail's pace. This resulted in Roman and Bellerose slowly bleeding to death in the middle of a desert.
Minla and Noodles rested. The wounds over Noodles chest got too much, and he got a major infection. Then, Minla woke up, grabbed a knife, and went berserk. She tried to stab Noodles for killing everyone else. Noodles was quick to take her down of course, and went back to sleep with a corpse in his room. When he woke up, he truly snapped. He wandered around the corridor, completely nude, and dropped his knife.
Raiders attacked. They smashed the cooler, the solar panels, stole gold and a bunch of clothes, and lit one of the wooden walls on fire before running off. Noodles didn't notice this. He wandered around still, until he got downed from a heat stroke. He couldn't escape.
The fire burned everything inside the entire house, except for a couple of human meat for some reason. Including Noodles.
Rest in peace Noodles. You may not be thinking right, but you'll still be a hero.

One of the better first person shooters of recent years, Wolfenstein the New Order managed to surprise and entertain me on so many levels. Not only is the shooting extremely satisfying, with the ability to dual wield a multitide of guns with a variety of firing modes, but there are some also fairly robust stealth sections in there - of course they can be bypassed with regular shoot em up action, but its nice to see how far you can get before sounding any alarms.
Unlike most shooters, I actually cared about the story and its characters. While the large majority of the game is bombastic violence, the pace constantly changes with downtime in a safehouse to interact with the multiple characters. You never get bored because the game mixes things up so frequently, nothing seems to drag on too long.
The art and sound direction is also brilliant. The new world under the nazi regime has been (dare I say) beautifully realized with nothing ever seeming out of place. The sound design of the guns is amazing - each one has its own unique firing noise with real weight to them, and, for want of a better description, they just feel plain badass. The level design is fantastic, and the game really does take you places with a multitude of settings. You might be in an underground base, a towering skyscraper, a submarine, or maybe even another planet.
So ultimately, pretty much everything they could have done right, the developers got right. And it all comes together in one badass, well crafted package.

I first heard about this game via RPS, which touted it as being 'more than just a mindless FPS,' repeatedly referencing the humanity of the story. I can definitely see that a lot of effort went into character building and making you interested in the predicament of the main cast. However, if you're looking for a game that's more story than gory, you're looking in the wrong place. At it's core, Wolfenstein: The New Order is about dismembering Nazi soliders while duel-weilding automatic machine guns. It's about mechanical dogs, mechs as tall as skyscrapers and disfigured villains plotting to steal your brain.
With that said, I heartily recommend it to anyone who is looking for a fun, but not ENTIRELY shallow FPS. This sits nicely somewhere between Serious Sam/Painkiller and games like Half Life 2 (which the art direction is obviously heavily inspired by) or Bioshock. Definitely worth a look!

Who are these other colonies and towns and bandits, raiders... or if your really eccentric with your mods... these lovecraftian cults, vampires, werewolves, xenomorphs and heretical tribals and mutant aliens?  Ask yourself, what are you really trying to do here?
An offworld prison colony, a vegas-like casino strip and lodging for travellers, a bar, cantina, trading post... fight pits?   Maybe you just want to bring civilization to the rimworld you've found yourself on and seek to create a few more colonies than just one and mobilize some trade caravans or fashion some uniformed soldiers to euthanize the xenos, mutants and bandits that roam the region.
Or... you could open up the easy-to-use devtool menu, hollow out a mountain and seal your colonists inside for Fallout styled Shelter expirements.  Raise an army, build a town, industrialize the morbid, cultivate society, etc
Its all really open ended with plenty of late game opportunities that arent openly displayed to you, but moreso require you to decide on it.
TL;DR
Plays, manages, builds quite like Prison Architect,  with the status screens and description statistics akin to that of NEO Scavenger/Project Zomboid.  Base game is about surviving a crash on the planet long enough to research required structures for building a ship, aquiring those materials, and building the ship.
If you're avid about "base building" and colonizing, and have a great taste for avant garde variety with permadeath roguelike elements - the best selling point of the game is its easy and large modding community and that escaping the planet is =only= an idea.

The Talos Principle is amazing, it's a first-person puzzler, if you've played Portal or its sequel then it's quite familiar. The puzzles are fantastic and the difficulty curve is good, though you might have to look at some hints (I'd advise against full-on guides, it spoils the fun) to find absolutely all the collectibles.
The graphics are more than sufficient, yet won't require a beast of a PC to play.
The sound is very well done, ambient music which sets the scene well and the voice acting is good.
The gameplay is where this game really shines, though. If you like lateral-thinking based puzzles then this is for you. The feeling of solving the complex mind-bending puzzles is fantastic and really gets you thinking out of the box later on in the game.
The story / premise is very good, too. It's relatively serious and philosophical.
There are regular auto-saves (and a list of them, so you can return to any of the previous ones, not just the most recent one) and if you "die" then you're resurrected and the puzzle is reset, so there's little pressure to get it right first time.
The only downside I can think of is there's little replayability, but that's inherent with all puzzle games. If you leave it a few years then you might forget the solutions, but I think it's most fulfilling the first time you play through the game. There's plenty of secrets and optional things to collect, so once you've finished the basic ending, go nuts and get everything.

This is a must have for any RTS gamer since it's really the one that brought the genre to the forefront. If you already own the game, then getting this is also recommended since it's optimized for modern systems and supports steam online play. The HD remake was unfortunately riddled with bugs at release but most of these seem to have been fixed.  However even though online "works" and there is a sizeable population, the HD remake still is plagued with many of the problems that affected the original AoE2 such as random out of syncs, atrocious lag every other game, and players dropping randomly. These are problems more to do with AoE2 itself and are not unique to the HD remake.
As for the expansions, thankfully you can filter multiplayer games according to which DLC is required. I would say that The Forgotten is easily forgotten (no pun intended) since the campaign scenarios lack any narration and really although the civs have new art styles, the only one that people seem to use are the Incas. The African Kingdoms on the other hand is a true solid expansion pack. The campaigns are very well polished and are narrated. It's also a blast to play as the Berbers, Portuguese and the Ethiopians. I just wish that both xpacks got the same treatment but apparently The Forgotten was already a fan made modification that was just modified further for commercial release whereas the African Kingdoms was a fresh new xpack. All in all though the online community for this game is still fairly active suprisingly after all these years and it's welcoming to all skill levels.

So, I recently completed Portal, and that was one amazing ride. This game takes what we learned about Portal and Apeture Science and rips it apart, letting us see the true innerworkings of the lab. We're introduced into more characters, and the story is stronger than ever before, and there's not a single point where you don't have a goal in mind.
So a short review, here's this. Portal 2 takes everything you experienced in Portal and adds so much more on top of it, including new mechanics, newly themed areas, a new, bigger story, and even a new main character. This game is an amazing treat for any Portal fan, and I'd highly recommend it.
Now, for the full review. And quick note, there
. This game is constantly revealing more as you go, and it's very, very hard to talk about this game without bringing up those plot points.
Now, I'll begin with the simple story that is the beginning. You wake up in a containment room, where you've been held since the ending of the first game. You do some basic exercises, then you're put back to sleep, where you're not woken up for a large amount of time. A small robot appears at your door, who we eventually learn is named Wheatly. He is trying to help you get out of the crumbling facility. From there, you and Wheatly make your way through, and eventually reach GLaDOS, which Wheatly accidentally activates. She throws Wheatly to the side, and says it's time to begin testing again.
So you're thrown into a brand new set of tests. The enhanced visuals and the beatiful art style of the worn out facility is great, and I can't help but really enjoy it. You get through most of the puzzles before Wheatly finally pulls you away so you can escape, and you're on to an escape portion, which interesting puzzles.
I'm not explaining exactly what happens, but let's just say that Wheatly turns GLaDOS into a potatoe, and Wheatly goes power crazy and smashes the escape pod you and GLaDOS are in, and fall to the very bottom, where the original labs were.
As you fall down, GLaDOS gets taken away by a hungry bird, but we'll catch up to her later on. You go through and explore the area, and you learn that this was the original Apeture Labs where Cave Johnson took in test subjects to test the new major mechanic of this game: Gel. This section of the game is crazy fun. You meet up with GLaDOS and mess with blue gel, which makes you jump higher, orange gel, which makes you run insanely fast, and white gel, which allows you to place portals on it.
All the while, GLaDOS is making connection to Cave Johnson's assistant (who is heard on the speakers), Carol. She then decides that you and her should work together, and if you can get GLaDOS back in control, she'll let you leave the lab. You and GLaDOS then escape the old laboratory, and confront Wheatly, who puts you through a series of new chambers (that were created by GLaDOS a long time ago). Even these chambers have new mechanics, which is great. At this point in the game, you're about half way through, and they're still giving you new things to play with. And note, these puzzles are far more difficult than the ones from before. From that point, you go onto defeat Wheatly (who has no idea how to maintain the facility) in the opposite way you defeated GLaDOS. I'm not spoiling the very end, but I'll leave you with that.
So, I guess it's time to give my complete thoughts on this game. For starters, I love the difficulty curve. Whereas in the last game, some of the later chambers were easier than some of the early chambers, this game gradually gets more difficult. On the other hand, there were points where I was stumped for a good 15-20 minutes, just experimenting. That's a good and a bad thing. I still enjoy the fact that you can get through the game just by experimenting, but it does eventually take a long time to get through a single chamber, and while it's fun, it's also boring at the same time. In Portal, I never was bored. Never a dull moment.
That's not the case with this game.
I frequently found myself progressing just for the sake of progessing. This problem really only happened in the gel sections, but it still taught me new mechanics, so... I can't complain new mechanics. I guess I'm just in different about this game. Everything was super fun and exciting, and I loved the story, yet, at the same time, it got boring more often than I'd like it to. But, the good moments very much so outweigh the bad ones.
The updated visuals are beautiful. This game looks crisp and clean, and I absolutely love it. I especially love it when GLaDOS cleans up the facility, and for a little bit, it's the updated visuals but with the style of the original game. It's honestly really pleasing to look at.
Now, if the long campaign is not enough, there's also the rather lengthy multiplayer campaign, where you can grab a friend locally, or play online. This mode is where most of my time in this game prior to this review came from. This mode is so much fun with a friend, and the puzzles are hard, but rewarding.
And if that's still not enough, there's Community Chambers, where you can create your own chambers, and play through Community made ones. This is fun, and with the thousands of Community Chambers there are, you could easily get lost in this one if you want a new, difficult challenge. Believe me, these ones are not easy.
Now, if the hundreds of hours the base game can provide is still not enough, there's mods as well, which add a lot to the game, and there's some that I personally will be playing soon.
The base story itself is great, and there's so much this game has to offer, it's hard to get tired of this game. So, in conclusion, I did enjoy this game. Maybe not as much as the first one, but there is so much more here to do, that is makes up for it. I do plan on playing this more. This game is perfect for anyone that is a fan of the first game.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a game with a story that begins in 1946, then fast-forwards to 1960. The Nazis won the war in 1946, the Allies lost, so that Nazis have taken over the world. The introduction to the narrative is long enough that it takes a long time for B.J. Blazkowicz, the main protagonist of the Wolfenstein series, to carry firearms. Mr. Blazkowicz fought in the war for the U.S., but was wounded and spends time in a Polish mental institution in a vegetative state until 1960.
This game is a continuation of the famous Wolfenstein series that has no shame in allowing you to kill as many Nazis as possible. Cities like Berlin and London are now occupied by Nazis as technological terrors such as large mechs and robotic dogs patrol the streets. There are many propaganda posters strewn throughout Germany and London, England making it clear that the Nazis are ruling and that citizens who violate their laws will be severely punished. Mr. Blazkowicz is the man who will take on the Nazis with some help from NPCs who will advise him on where to go and what objectives to complete. Killing Nazis is in his DNA.
The narrative requires you to choose one of two paths that will be slightly different from each other based on which two comrades will die at the hands of evil General Deathshead, the leader of the Nazis. Deathshead kills one of the two comrades you choose for death so that he can use him in an evil experiment that he says will change the world for the better. You will then have to play the game based on the survivor’s timeline. This ability to choose may be cruel, but it adds replayability to the game by encouraging you to play the game twice so that you can experiences both timelines that result in slightly different versions of the narrative.
The gameplay is pretty much an old school FPS. The weapons in the game are not innovative, but they still feel very satisfying and have alternate modes. The run –of-the-mill weapons include handguns, assault rifles, shotguns, and sniper rifles. Each aforementioned weapon can be upgraded and the upgrades will be necessary to take on the bigger and more powerful Nazis. Assault rifles feel powerful when dual wielding them and can be upgraded by acquiring the rocket upgrade. There are perks in the game that you can keep track of that Mr. Blazkowicz can acquire throughout the game to improve the stealth, tactical, assault, and demolition aspects of combat. These perks add a role-playing like feel to the game. The ability to pick up ammo, weapons, health, and armor feels a like old school FPS.
There are certain locales that seem to encourage stealth. This is when the knife comes in handy, allowing you to slash unsuspecting Nazis from behind. The slashings are truly gory and horrific, but satisfying since it feels like they deserve to be slashed by your blade. Some locales can overwhelm you to death if you don’t use stealth, especially if there are officers stationed there. You can detect signals that alert you to the presence of officers. Officers are capable of calling in reinforcements to overwhelm. Stealthily taking down officers is rewarding as the game’s map will open up and reveals secret items such as enigma codes, letters, and gold items. There are other locales that seem to encourage a shootout with Nazis of different sizes and abilities. Nazis are varied enough in terms of clothing and weapons. Some Nazis are powerful rocket wielding and shotgun wielding foes that will seriously test your FPS skills such as the ability to take cover. The levels are varied enough as they include a prison that you must infiltrate, a lunar base run by Nazis, the city of London filled with swastikas to indicate Nazi dominance, and a base occupied by Mr. Blazkowicz’s friends where he receive objectives. It is interesting to see an alternate perspective of World War II with the Nazis winning the war and dominating the world. They actually landed on the moon before the U.S. could ever land one of its own citizens on the moon.
I have always been of the opinion that characters in games should speak their native language. This game nails it by having Nazis speak German when engaged in combat. It makes the game feel more immersive than if they all spoke the English language in a setting that is German. Some of Blazkowicz’s friends speak German and say a few words in German. I felt like I was truly in Germany when the Nazis spoke German during combat. The A.I. is not always perfect, but it is good enough to test your FPS abilities in the spur of the moment.
One new weapon in the game is the laser cutter known as the laserkraftwerk (LKW). When you first acquire this weapon, it is a utility that can be used to cut holes in metal gratings that block your progress. There are other metal gratings that can be cut for the purpose of finding secret items. Once it is upgraded the LKW becomes more than a utility item: it then contains an alternate mode which is a weapon that is very effective against mechanical enemies. They don’t require ammo since they run on batteries that can be recharged at the various recharge stations.
The graphics look very modern and make the 1992 version of Wolfenstein seem pale in comparison. The cutscenes look polished. The levels look picturesque and very realistic, whether they are in Berlin, Germany or London, England.
I think this 2014 entry into the Wolfenstein franchise is breath of fresh air. The narrative is always interesting, although it felt like it took a little too long to carry a weapon, let alone engage in intense combat. This game provides an interesting perspective on what it would be like if the Nazis had controlled the world after World War II. The gameplay is challenging enough that it forces you to think about how to approach dangerous combat situations. The acting performances are convincing, especially from the evil Deathshead to the courageous Caroline Becker, who is an important guide for Mr. Blazkowicz. This FPS is definitely worth playing.

Amazing coop game, a definite must buy for 2+ players game sessions.
Just some small tips:
-Experience is gained each time you hit (including magic multihits)
-Gold is NOT SHARED, not even in local coop, each character has their own gold stash
-Weapons are only shared in local coop, but multiplayer friends can trade weapons by picking up drops and switching
-Same as above for pets
-Potions function like lives ONLY with 2+ players, so if a solo player dies with 5 potions he WILL DIE, but if a player in a 3 person team dies he will lose a potion and be returned to full health.
What all of this means is that you gain less experience and money with more players. Which isn't all bad by any means, since with more people there is more damage to be dealt to enemies, and the number of enemies is always the same.
As the number of player increases its also easier to lose yourself in the heat of battle and take unecessary damage as things will get very chaotic.
So, my point is, the optimal number of player is about 2-3 since things won't get too messy fighting enemies/each other for money.
But please don't take this as me saying "Don't play single player/4-person coop", the game is really fun either way, just more challenging with 1 or 4 people.

If you know what Age of Empires 2 is: get it. The HD version is a delight and they also added multiplayer support and decently-priced DLC. The remake is among the best i’ve played.
If you don’t know what AoE2 is, you are in for a sweet treat, a blast from the past, a game of… much fame? Alright I’ll stop.
AoE2 is a RTS in which you play one of many olden civilizations, starting in the Dark Ages, and progress all the way to the Imperial Age, all while expanding, building an army, creating defences, researching military/industrial/agricultural improvements, leading your forces to battle, creating trade routes, protecting wonders, finding relics, gathering all seven Dragon Balls et cetera et cetera.
The “to do” list might intimidate new players, but AoE2 plays as smooth as butter, with easy controls and button layouts. After a few sessions and looking up a guide, you too will have a strong starting economy and empire in 15 minutes during skirmishes (campaign can be a different beast altogether).
The economy is based on 5 resources: food, wood, stone, gold and population (from houses). There are multiple ways to get each resource, albeit stone and wood trading is a bit difficult with the AI since this isn’t really a game about diplomacy. Gold however can be taken from “trading” easily among two of your marketplace buildings: the further they are, the more you get.
Be prepared to spew out villagers left and right and grab any rock and log you can get, since you will need them to build an army. Besides the regular soldiers, each civ has it’s own perks and a castle with a unique soldier. Some have restrictions to certain troops or upgrades, making sure each one feels and plays slightly different.
All of these can be inspected neatly in the Tech Tree, available both in and out of game. You will also find an encyclopaedia about medieval battles, units, buildings, kingdoms; all sorts of neat things that old farts like myself wish were still around in modern games. It’s also worth mentioning that AoE2 HD, without any DLC, has 9 historical campaigns that are both entertaining, educational and, at times, hard as nails.
If you like “easy to learn difficult to master” RTS games, absolutely get it.
