I can definitely see that a lot of effort went into character building and making you interested in the predicament of the main cast. However, if you're looking for a game that's more story than gory, you're looking in the wrong place. At it's core, Wolfenstein: The New Order is about dismembering Nazi soliders while duel-weilding automatic machine guns. It's about mechanical dogs, mechs as tall as skyscrapers and disfigured villains plotting to steal your brain.
With that said, I heartily recommend it to anyone who is looking for a fun, but not ENTIRELY shallow FPS. This sits nicely somewhere between Serious Sam/Painkiller and games like Half Life 2 (which the art direction is obviously heavily inspired by) or Bioshock. Definitely worth a look!

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a game that is an absolute rip off at $60.  The story is bland and predictable, and the gameplay has absolutely nothing original to add to the genre, it was mildly enjoyable at first, but becomes tedious and repetitive after the first 20 minutes.
When you begin the game you start out with only a knife, and you assume that as you progress you will unlock more and more weapons to pummel Nazis with.  It turns out, once you find the Assault Rifle, you have found the weapon you will use for the rest of the game.  You end up with a selection of knife, AR, shotgun, pistol, LaserKraftWerk(LKW), and marksman rifle(A pitiful selection for an "Shoot 'em up" game).  The only two weapons that you get ammo often enough to use are the AR and the LKW, both of which are bland and unsatisfying.  The Marksman was great fun to use, but over the 10 hour playthrough, I found maybe 30 bullets for it.
The LKW is used to lengthen the game like a teenager uses a thesaurus to meet the word count on his essay.  You repeatedly have to use the laser cutter feature of the gun to carve holes in crates, in vents, and to cut chains. Instead of just opening vents like a normal game, you are forced to draw the hole with your laser, and once you have completed a loop, the vent falls out.  This often leads to you not making a large enough hole, and having to trim the edges to fit through.  I spent over an hour, in the HQ doing chores.  You have to find toys, documents, and power tools for people around the HQ, and it is an absolute disgrace that a AAA game company would resort to such blatant Artificial Game Lengtheners(AGL).
The perks are useless, and through an entire playthrough, I only unlocked about half of them.  One you must kill two enemies with a single grenade, but the game gives you grenades so infrequently, that when a 2-for-1 opportunity comes up, you are out of nades, not to mention you can only carry 2.
This game is an easy 2/10, one star for the fact that I actually completed the campaign, and one star for actually looking pretty nice.  -8 for all of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that I would expect from some indiegogo/kickstarter developer to try and pull.  Please, don't buy this game, you are supporting shoddy Devs, that use cheap tricks and sleight of hand to make a garbage game look like a AAA title, don't support this kind of behaviour with devs.

The story is okay.  It's not bad, but it's not very good.  The philosophy part is something I enjoyed.  It's not super crammed in your face and I enjoyed how it's not overly essential to the plot (as far as I could tell).  It was something to ponder on, like philosophy is.  It enhanced the plot as it dealt with something very philsophical.  The gameplay is logic puzzles, which aren't bad, but I mean, they're logic puzzles.  Most are easy, the end ones are a little more challenging.  Much like SOMA would benefit by not having monsters, this game would benefit by having the puzzles be story based, like Myst, rather than logic based.  I often found myself trying to complete the puzzles as fast as possible so that I could get back to exploring, seeing what the next area is like, and experiencing more plot.
The ending is meh.  SPOILERS:
You finally meet up with two other beings and neither communicates with you.  No spoken words, no hand waving, no nothing.  One helps you, one hinders you.  It's so anticlimatic.  I was friggin' static that I finally was around someone else and they don't even wave or say hi.  So disappointing.  It really made a huge impact on me.  At the minimum the good one, Shephard, should have waved and made some communication, explaining why I should continue and exit this place.  All throughout the game there's QR codes which translate into text from other beings, sort of talking through time, and to have it all culminate in a completely silent encounter is just...really sad.  All the joy of exiting into reality was kind of overshadowed by this good person helping me who won't even communicate.  Plus the ending doesn't make sense.  We awaken to a dead world.  Whoop de do, how is that an ending.  We'll live out our days with no one else around.  That's not an ending, that's hell.
END SPOILERS.

The perfect balance between a hardcore tactical shooter like Arma and something like Battlefield. The community is excellent. There are very few rounds where you'll find uncooperative teammates/teamkillers. Although by the end of each round (often lasting 20-30 minutes) your kill count will very often be under 10 kills, you never feel like there has been a lack of action. In fact, this is probably the most intense shooter I've ever played, and it keeps me continuously gripped even when there aren't many enemies in sight. The large maps and lack of vehicles in its current early access state, might have you worried that you'll be bored most of the time due to lack of enemy engagements, but trust me, this game is rarely boring. The way spawns work with FOB's and Rally Points, and how the gameplay is so geared towards teamwork and communication, provides a continuous stream of action and emergent gameplay that almost never bores. I've never played antyhing like it.  Each round is unique and provides a unique set of challenges to overcome, that you never feel like you are simply going through the motions. Which is a feeling you might get from Battlefield on occasion, and will most certainly get in the more arcadey shooters such as CoD.
It is Early Access, yes, and there are certainly plenty of rough edges. With an AMD CPU, you will most likely encounter nigh unplayable framerates, so if you have an AMD CPU you might want to hold-out on buying this game until the developers work on optimization. Otherwise the game is definitely playable, with a few nuisances here and there as a result of its early state. To me, this is early access at its finest. Other early access titles launch at such an early state, and claim incredibly grand ambitions that are seemingly impossible to fulfill. Squad doesn't have insane ambitions, rather it is a shooter trying out a relatively new and un-tested concept, and Early Access serves as a grand playtest for their ideas. When you're making a shooter so reliant on teamwork, you need to set up proper incentives for teamwork, and to do so you need extensive playtesting to see what works and what doesn't. What Squad seeks to produce for its final version is feasible, and with what it currently has, I have no doubt that this game has a bright future. I highly recommend it to anyone who is looking to play soldier.

Full disclosure, I got this gifted to me by my friend, Craig.
Wallpaper engine is a tiny, neat little app that does nothing but give your PC the freedom of live wallpapers the likes of which you'd encounter on Android or iOS. The app takes very little processing power and runs ontop of your regular wallpaper, so it neither replaces it nor changes anything else. The settings for Wallpaper Engine are excellent and allow for a lot of customization, although some wallpapers more than others, depending on the type of wallpaper it is. With Steam workshop support, very low resource costs, adjustable resolution, support for all proportions, adjustable framerate, stopping it automatically when a game is launched or another app is fullscreen and much more, for €3,99 this app is truly irreplacable.
The wallpaper editor is quite easy to learn and making your own custom wallpapers is no challenge whatsoever. Personally, I prefer the high-quality wallpapers made by other members of the steam community, but the option is most definitely there.
The cons are that it does break on occasion, but after around 200 reboots I've only seen it occur once or twice, and that it boots too slow to start you off with the animated wallpapers, and instead keeps your regular wallpapers up for a few seconds before switching. This might simply be a boot order problem, or an issue with how windows works not allowing it to boot quickly enough. It's not a massive nuisance however.
All in all, I'd say this app deserves a definite thumbs up, and is essential for anyone that wants to customize their desktop as much as they can.

Rewriting this review as a 03Dec17 update now that Rimworld is at version 18.
At 420 (AIRHORNZ) hours in, 3 official versions later and countless mods from both workshop and the ludeon forums... People im still amazed at it.
Plays like Prison Architect without the prison... but dont let that stop you, you can totally build a prison with your colonists as the wardens and guards if thats your thing.  You dont even have to escape the planet either.  Who said you crashed here by accident? What ARE you really doing here on this planet?  Who are these other colonies and towns and bandits, raiders... or if your really eccentric with your mods... these lovecraftian cults, vampires, werewolves, xenomorphs and heretical tribals and mutant aliens?  Ask yourself, what are you really trying to do here?
An offworld prison colony, a vegas-like casino strip and lodging for travellers, a bar, cantina, trading post... fight pits?   Maybe you just want to bring civilization to the rimworld you've found yourself on and seek to create a few more colonies than just one and mobilize some trade caravans or fashion some uniformed soldiers to euthanize the xenos, mutants and bandits that roam the region.
Or... you could open up the easy-to-use devtool menu, hollow out a mountain and seal your colonists inside for Fallout styled Shelter expirements.  Raise an army, build a town, industrialize the morbid, cultivate society, etc
Its all really open ended with plenty of late game opportunities that arent openly displayed to you, but moreso require you to decide on it.
TL;DR
Plays, manages, builds quite like Prison Architect,  with the status screens and description statistics akin to that of NEO Scavenger/Project Zomboid.  Base game is about surviving a crash on the planet long enough to research required structures for building a ship, aquiring those materials, and building the ship.
If you're avid about "base building" and colonizing, and have a great taste for avant garde variety with permadeath roguelike elements - the best selling point of the game is its easy and large modding community and that escaping the planet is =only= an idea.

Before Team Mystic and Team Valor, There was The New Conglomerate and the Terran Republic. Jokes aside lets get into this review.
This is a free to play game done god damn right! Its about time to! This game is fantastic and its ingame currency is actually good, and is not some crazy farm thing where you need over 9000 [Inseret stupid currency name here]. The most you'll need is 1000k for final upgrades and some weapons.
So about factions. Well we have The Terran Republic, The New Conglomerate, and The Vanu Sovereignty. Lets talk about them all eh? Qucik word though, and I will have this in caps, NO FACTION IS OP OR STRONGER THAN THE OTHER. Moving on~
The Terran Republic: The actual government force on Auraxis and indeed of Earth. I'd go into the great lore on them but I know it would be better to just get onto what they have and what they do. So the TR, which is their acronym, is all about having a ton of bullets that shot fast. Think of them as the "conventonal force". They carry weapons that are military grade and time tested and proven. To be more specific, their weapons have the fastest velocity and carry the most rounds. They tend to have average recoil and control. Their colors are red and black and they tend to give off an empire vide/ warhammer vibe.
The New Conglomerate: These are traders, merchants, laborers, who all took up arms against the new draconian rulling of The Terran Republic. Their weapons are based upon experimental weapons, such as gauss based rifles. Their weapons are based upon hitting hard. As such their weapons are more damage oriented, but have lower velocity and tend to have heavy kick back or recoil. Ammo wise they often have fewer rounds than TR and VS. Their colors are blue and yellow.
The Vanu Sovereignty: These are scientists, like minded military commanders, and woshipers of Vanu. This faction hails from the TR, much like the NC. When alien techonolgy was found, based upon an alien civilization dubed the Vanu. Now Vanu is belived to be the god-king of these species and that they all ascended to a higher plane of existance. I'm getting into lore but for a good reason. They invented much of the tech found on Auraxis, specifically the "Re-Birthing" or the respawn mechanic, but much more. Lore done, onto weapons. VS weapons are all energy based that use energy batteries and shoot hot plasma. Their weapons have next to no bullet drop and their recoil is likewise very low, but as a result their velocity and damage are lower than the other factions. Ammo wise they often carry less than TR but tend to have a bit more than NC. Their colors are purple and teal.
Quick words about weapons: There is a fourth "faction" known as Nanite Systems. They sell weapons that carry traits of all factions and have their own little feeling. They also produce the common vehicle pool. You can't join them and they are just merchants.
These faction traits are the exact same for their vehicles. Each faction has two specific vehicles, along with the common vehicle pool availble to each faction. For TR their vehicles are the fastest and have the most ammo. For NC their vehicles are the slowest but hit hardest. For VS their vehicles are all about being mobile and have average damage. As a side note, their tank hovers however all this means is that it can strafe left and right and has an easier time moving around. They are still vulnerable to mines and all the other dangers that are dubbed anti-vehicle.
Quick Note on Factions: The only thing that is different between the factions when it comes to starting gear is that the NC infiltrator starts with a bolt action sniper rifle. The TR and VS start with a semi-auto rifle and aslo come with a sway elimantor, allowing you to zoom with out any rifle sway. The NC have no upgrades on their rifle and must unzoom to fire again after each shot. As a result it is two head shots for a kill with the starter TR and VS rifles and only one for the NC. This does not mean however that the NC is better as the rifle is harder to use and if you miss you will probably get recked hard.
Quick Note on Players: The players in this game are some of the best, personality wise, skill wise who knows. There are some jerks'n jacks of course, but for the most part they are the minority for once and indeed so are hackers. I have yet to fight a hacker and it seems they too, are a minority. This game has a massive player base and has been alive for four years. There are casual to hardcore, you'll be able to find out where you fit with ease.
Quick Note on currency before I get more indepth: Certs are the only thing you can use to buy class upgrades for abilities.  Also Certs can be used for vehicles and even other squad upgrades, like buying a spawn beacons, along with weapon upgrades like laser sights etc.
Earning Certs(In game currency): I mentioned currency briefly but here it is more indepth. 250 xp = 1 cert. You gain xp on pretty much every action in game, and based upon the current player population of the map you are on, as well as based upon how well your faction is doing, you will actually have an in game bonus, as much as 50%. Also from Battle Ranks (the in game level system) 1-15 you will gain 100 certs per level up, which is more than enough to set you up well. It is important to save your certs, each starter weapon is great and you should use your certs to spend on class abilities and traits. I would sugest playing each class and testing out what you like.
Personal feelings about the factions: I feel that you need to make a character for each faction and there are three character slots, so I mean even the game is saying. Each faction is different and you should play around to find out what you like. I have played on each faction and have seen each rise and fall. The average player pop for factions on servers is 30% give or take a few numbers. This will very more so based upon the chosen map. I personally love all three factions but will not drone on about why. This game has a massive player pop and it fluctuates based upon what time it is. This game is great. There is no other game out there like it. There is such a large scale and it is amazing. I highly recommend this game.
Ps. About the battleye thing, relax about it. Your own interent service provider records EVERYTHING you look at. All this does is check your game files to see if you have any cheats on.

: I've seen a few people commenting about how the community sucks, and is full of "fanbois". I don't know much about that. But, this is a single-player game. So, the community may not be the biggest thing to factor in your purchase unless you care about forums.

Rimworld is a prison architect esk game with matching art and design concepts, but with a ♥♥♥♥ tone more gameplay elements and game mechanics....
What makes Rimworld stand out from the crowd is the sheer amount of customization before actually starting your save and during your time through the game.
When making a new save (Starting a new colony) you can choose between a huge amount of options which will in return determine how easy, hard, balanced, fun, boring, interesting, dull, your overall game will be.
To list a few things:
Traits, stat multipliers, in game events, starting items, researched projects, starting location, AID (artificial intelligence director), amount of people you begin with, type of settlement, time of year, size of overall explorable map, and much-much-much more.....
One of the biggest selling points of Rimworld is the "artificial intelligence director". There are 3 AID's to choose from, the carefully-paced Cassandra Classic, the slower-paced, building-oriented Phoebe Chillax, and the totally unpredictable Randy Random.
Each AID will oversee your game and will make choices based on your performance, like when to start a random event, type of weather, severity of each raid, overall mood of NPC's, and yet again... Much-much-much more.
On top of the AID's themselves, you may also choose the play style of them too. (Basically difficulty of each AID)
Pro's:

If you can look past a pretty ridiculous storyline (but hey, who's playing a Wolfenstein game for a normal, logical storyline?), then the game is decent. I can't say it's a great game, but it's not a terrible one, either. If you're looking for a shooter with a singleplayer more than a handful of hours, Wolfenstein might be worth your time to check out.
I played through the game on Uber difficulty in my first run-through. There were only a few genuinely challenging moments; however there is ONE part that absolutely kicked my♥♥♥♥♥ I must have tried to run it 50 times (I am *not* exaggerating) before giving up and turning the difficulty setting back down a few notches. With the exception of those few difficult moments, the game is fairly easy even on the hardest difficulty setting. I was also extremely frustrated by some of the boss fights because they were overly easy. I don't particularly like games that force me to solve terrain puzzles to beat a boss, but this game didn't have anything like that. It really was just "shoot until dead." Kind of boring.
As far as gun variety, I felt it was kinda "meh" and stereotypical. I had a pistol, assault rifle, shotgun, sniper. And I could dual wield them, like any good over-the-top shooter would allow. I also occasionally had an LMG (dropped by enemies). There were some stupid "cut this chain to advance in the level" and "cut through this metal wall section to advance in the level" sections requiring an energy-gun-thing that is arguably the best gun in the game. I wasn't wow-ed by the guns, the perk system surrounding the guns/grenades, or the alternative firing modes (rockets on the rifle, etc.).
The storyline is pretty basic: you're an American military captain saving (literally) the world from the Nazis, who won WW2. You meet a girl, get to have a sex scene with her, she becomes your motivation to defeat the Nazis. You meet rebels, you don't have sex with them but you do talk a *lot*, and they help you defeat the Nazis. There is more level variety in the game than I was expecting: different Nazi buildings, the moon--which was more boring than you'd expect--and a little bit of traveling around to go to the different locations. If you want a deep, moving storyline, first I'd recommend you not consider Wolfestein, and secondly I'd ask, why in Hell are you looking at shooters for a deep storyline? Wolfenstein has an "okay" storyline for shooters. That's about it.
I do recommend the game if you're looking for anything at all to play, but don't expect much from it.

This is a very enjoyable first person puzzle game. You travel to different areas which have a number of self contained puzzles to solve. Solve a puzzle and you earn a sigil which you have to collect and use to unlock more areas and items for later puzzles. The game poses interesting philosophical questions to you ,via interactions with an AI on a computer, such what is consciousness and when does an AI become a conscious being. I quite enjoyed the interactons with the computer as it makes it more than just a puzzle game and becomes one with an intersting backstory.
Good Points:
- the environments in this game look beautiful and it's a visually stunning game
- the puzzles give a good challenge. That "eureka" moment where the solution becomes clear is so rewarding. Its sometimes worth leaving a puzzle youre stuck on to go work on another one as sometimes coming back with a clear head can be more helpful in solving it.
- the games philosophical story is quite clever and interesting
Bad points:
- the only bad point for me was the sigil puzzles. For each regular puzzle you complete you earn a shape or "sigil" as they're called in the game. When you collect enough to open a new area or unlock a new item you have to fit them all together on a grid. The size of the grids and number of sigils to fit together increase as the game progresses. The early ones are ok as its only a small grid and 4 or 5 sigils but i found the ones later in the game qite frustrating and ended up spending a lot of time on them. I suck at these kind of puzzles and anyone like me will spend ages on them. It felt a bit like the developers were ramming these sigil puzzles down my throat by the end.
Overall despite the sigil puzzles everything else about this game is brilliant. Fans of the Portal series will love this game or even anyone who wants a challenging but equally rewarding experience.

I've been having so much fun with this game recently that I simply HAD to give it one of my♥♥♥♥♥♥reviews.
First of all, this game has some of the best Art Direction I have ever seen in a video game, it sports some of the most well-written, well-acted characters I've ever seen in a game, and the cutscenes are simply amazing, really putting you in its world-turned-to♥♥♥♥♥♥ I can relate to the characters more than I ever have with others in this genre such as Half-Life 2 or Bioshock Infinite. Those games may be older and have stories less based on actual history; perhaps that could explain it, and yet I still feel that this is one of the best narratives in an FPS to-date. The quality of the music, and aesthetic aspects only serve to elevate this even further. Don't even get me started on how good (or rather bad) the villains are.
The gameplay is also excellent. There are 5 difficulty settings, very reminiscent of other ID titles such as DOOM. While the missions are linear, there are multiple ways of approaching combat (eg, silent stealth, guns-blazing, tactical cover-based, blow everything to♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a multitude of weapons. The game also brings in new things that we haven't seen before such as the Lazerkraftwerk, a tool used to cut open fences, metal crates and chains, while also having the ability to instagib enemies with its powerful lazer.
The game also has a very interesting way of bringing in replayabilty, making the story split into two paths after a very important decision placed on the player early on in the game. I won't spoil it for you here but it greatly improves the narrative experience and adds even more emotional weight to the game.
There are a few faults that I could mention, but they are such small gripes compared to what is great with The New Order. I whole-heartedly recommend this to anyone who is a fan of story-driven single player FPS games. If you're turned off by violence, this game is probably not for you. But for the rest of us who enjoy disintegrating the heads off of Nazi scumbags, get this awesome game!

Rimworld is a prison architect esk game with matching art and design concepts, but with a ♥♥♥♥ tone more gameplay elements and game mechanics....
What makes Rimworld stand out from the crowd is the sheer amount of customization before actually starting your save and during your time through the game.
When making a new save (Starting a new colony) you can choose between a huge amount of options which will in return determine how easy, hard, balanced, fun, boring, interesting, dull, your overall game will be.
To list a few things:
Traits, stat multipliers, in game events, starting items, researched projects, starting location, AID (artificial intelligence director), amount of people you begin with, type of settlement, time of year, size of overall explorable map, and much-much-much more.....
One of the biggest selling points of Rimworld is the "artificial intelligence director". There are 3 AID's to choose from, the carefully-paced Cassandra Classic, the slower-paced, building-oriented Phoebe Chillax, and the totally unpredictable Randy Random.
Each AID will oversee your game and will make choices based on your performance, like when to start a random event, type of weather, severity of each raid, overall mood of NPC's, and yet again... Much-much-much more.
On top of the AID's themselves, you may also choose the play style of them too. (Basically difficulty of each AID)
Pro's:

Such a shame that Portal left such a big crater in the "First Person Puzzle" genre that everything that even remotely match that description gets compared to Portal regardless of actual similarities. I'll get it out of the way now: The Talos Principle is NOT LIKE PORTAL.
Portal was, in its essence, more about the puzzles (test chambers) themselves than the overall narrative. Sure GLaDoS and Wheatley were amzing characters, and the lore behind the games is expansive, but deep down, Portal was about solving the rooms with everything at your disposal.
The Talos Principle, on the other hand, holds its narrative much closer to its core than the actual puzzles. Solving puzzles in this game offered passage to new areas and components of the story. The story itself is also well-crafted, slow-paced, but very well-crafted. It really echos in your mind and, provided you read the texts found on the terminals and really think on them, you will find the game not only an amazing collection of first-person puzzles, but also a mesmerizing and thought-invoking experience.

We crash land on a planet, slowly beginning to get our bearings and some shelter, storage and garden built.  All of a sudden we notice a Timber Wolf nearby, is it friendly or hostile?  Our resident Hunter would rather not take a chance, so breaks out his rifle and fires a number  of times.  Out of 6 shots, 2 hit their mark, but sadly all this seems to do is♥♥♥♥♥♥the wolf off, who comes charging at our Hunter, he fumbles reloading and ends up having to take off at speed to try and avoid getting eaten,  obiviously the Wolf is faster than our Hunter so he's constantly being nipped at the heals.
ANOTHER ALERT!!
A Squirrel has gone nuts and is attacking one of the other colonists, chasing her down until she collapses from her wounds far from base.  She needs rescuing, so I send out my final colonist to bring her home.  In the mean time our Hunter is looking a lot worse for wear and is slowly making his way back to base with wolf in tow.  He just makes it inside in time.  Wolf starts banging at the door trying to get in.
Cut to the other 2 colonists, they're now helping each other back to base, after the Squirrel attack, unaware there is a Timber Wolf trying to get in.

Hunter heres the commotion die down and begins to head towards the door, completely unaware his pet cat, enraged by the smell of blood, attacks him and leaves him immobile on the floor.
So now I have 2 immobile survivors and absolutely nothing I can do, but wait for the infections to set in and kill them.
Just when I had given up all hope, a native comes to our area to join our happy little colony, he carries the injured to their beds, treats their wounds and feeds them, before going to bed himself.
and that my friends is where I have left this story.  I can't wait to see what happens next.

Talos Principle is a game where you don't shoot anything and, speaking (actually writing) as someone who rather likes games where you shoot things, I can see why it's not been too popular. But suppress all that gung-ho bloodlust for a few hours (or 20) and you'll find TP is actually a refreshing experience, if by refreshing you mean running round one arena for twenty minutes wondering why you are one cube short. The reason - as always in this game - is because you're an idiot and have learned nothing.
The learning curve is shallow at the start until you realise just how many puzzles there are, in addition to the easter eggs, puzzles behind secret doors, puzzles in distant places, and puzzles within (and often outside of) other puzzles. By the later stages, you're setting up cobweb-like networks of light beams, turning one block into two, travelling through time to stand on your own head and - when things go wrong - wondering where all the beams are going, which door just opened (or closed), watching essential objects fly back and forth through the air and (I kid you not) wondering whether to learn ASCII just to make sense of it all. Several times after wondering how I just did what I did, the follow-up thought was: 'how did someone write something that devious?'
It's all a little Portal, or perhaps a bloated Portal (but still challenging: Portal 2 take note), which is no bad thing. There's also a lot of reading waffle about consciousness and stuff which you can entirely ignore. But that's a puzzle game for you: brain over brawn; and at least if you run naked down the street wielding an axe and screaming "I am the word and the world is the words", no one will blame Croteam.

A consistently fun experience throughout the whole game. There's a very high level of polish in everything - the animations, textures, voice acting, environments, etc...enough to evoke the action-movie feel I think they were going for.
The core shooting gameplay is pleasantly responsive and empowering (unlike some other shooters where you have to empty entire clips into a single enemy). Pretty much every enemy dies on a single headshot, so you're actually rewarded for precision and accuracy. That said, you can still dive through the air dual-weilding automatic pistols if you so desire, and through good use of the diving and time slow mechanics you can really start to develop a sense of mastery as you play through the game. As you progress in the game, enemies will perform certain dodging and weaving behaviors to make it harder to hit their heads. The AI in this game exhibits intelligent behaviors like flanking, taking cover when being shot at, and other stuff like that. It enhances the action gameplay because it makes you feel like you're up against actual humans instead of just moving targets.
There's still a few problems with it. As you get towards the later stages, you can more easily spot sections that don't really feel as polished as the first stages in the game. For example, there's a few cases where enemies get plot armor and you have to defeat them in a contrived, specific way. That really breaks up the flow and immersion of the game, especially when you can actually shoot at the enemy and see blood coming out but nothing happens to them. But the biggest issue with the game is how drawn-out some of the stages feel. First of all,  I don't accuse Rockstar of simply copy-pasting stuff in the levels to artificially lengthen them. As you progress through each level, you really are seeing new layouts, cutscenes, etc...It's just that, as a player, it starts to feel same-y. Yes, you're fighting enemies in different rooms, but the rooms start to feel the same, the enemies feel the same, and I just found myself wishing I could reach the next important cutscene and get on with the story. It started to get tedious as I got to about the mid-point of the game. It just seemed like content for the sake of content. I'd rather it be slightly shorter so you end up seeing more of the actual story more frequently.
I found the story to be entertaining enough to make me want to keep playing to see what happens. I'd say it's a little better than what you'd expect from something that's all about the spectacle.
Overall, if you like games that play like action movies while offering precise shooting and the ability to develop some mastery over the mechanics, I'd recommend this. I'd say I enjoyed about 90% of the time I played through this game, with the remaining 10% due to some immersion-breaking scripted sections (where enemies have plot armor) and some of the sections that started to feel too long.

Now the review...
Its a colony sim game where your "pawns" are stranded on an outlying Rimworld. The game is driven by one of three story tellers that act as your "rng" trigering events and helping progress the game as you play. The goals of the game are simple, survive and try to get your colony off of this unforgiving land, but the gameplay and chances to achieve this are complicated.
Each pawn has their own traits and moods. You must balance all the survival aspects of the game in order to succeed, however be warned; this game is unforgiving, balancing hunger, hapiness and raids. The depth of this game is beyond phenominal, if a pawn isnt properly taken care of they can break down and go on mental rampages. World events like super volcanoes can force your pawns inside, needing to grow their food indoors in hopes of lasting till the dust settles all while fending off pirates, natives, and wild animals.
Pawns can fall in love, divorce, have rivals, hate each other, throw parties, instagate fights inside your own colony and so on.
Now this is a colony building game, so there are aspects of building. Walls, defences, art, furniture, temperature controling systems. On the surface this game looks pretty simple, but as you play you will see the depth and complexity sewn into each fiber of this absolute gemstone.
The community is 2nd to none, with an outstanging group of modders and mod support.
Basically what im saying is why are you still reading reviews and why havnt you bought it yet?

And with yet more hours under my belt, a story emerges with ease from my latest settlement, and the most insane colonist I've ever had.
What began as a simple bid to survive amidst the mountainous waste-lands proved odder than many had ever thought. The colony first consisted of three. Gen, a depressive nudist, Aaron, the too-smart taster, and Slade, a volatile young Urbworld Criminal
They were an ecclectic bunch, but they were hard workers. Hunters, growers, miners, builders. The colony shaped. The mountain nurtured them. She housed them, sheltered them. But it could not always be a time of peace in that place they grew to call Taynid's Navel.
Without warning, they came. At first few, but with time, many. The raiders of Hyenas Forest and the Pirate band known as the Murderous Vultures. Their eyes set on that place, its flourishing farms nestled before the great mountain.
The colony fought.
Gen and Aaron, though they were hard workers, they seemed ill equipped to deal with the harsh realities of battle. Particularly battle brought on by nothing more than greed and apathy. But Slade? He was born to it. For all his short years, he had lived it.
They don't recall which; the fourth? Maybe the fifth incursion? But the son of the leader of the Hyenas himself headed a raid on the mountain's children. A proud raider, he nearly brought them their goal, too. Gen and Aaron were pinned, they were outmatched, no matter how hard they struck, the raider fought on, thriving on the violence and bloodshed.
And from the ringing gunshots and yells, Slade awoke. The boy worn out from his hard night's toil, rose with fury in his heart. He disliked being disturbed. The doors of the colony slammed open, and out he stormed into the midst of battle. A bee-line was made for the Leader's son.
With one brutal punch, the raider fell, crumpling to the dusty earth.
Emboldened by their comrade, and the fall of the raid leader, the colony pushed back, and soon had the Hyenas on the run. The day was theirs, once more to continue building a life for themselves. Slade took from the fallen raider, his tuque, and walked back inside.
Seasons passed, the colony grew, and the Hyenas came sniffing once more. This time, fuelled by grief and a hunger for vengeance, the leader of the raiders himself made himself known. The force was greater, and their goal was clear. Take revenge on those that had stolen so greatly from them.
And just like his son, they struck a terrible blow against the colony, nearly bringing it to its knees. Several were wounded, but so too were the leader's forces.
It would do for now. They could return at their leisure, and finish the task. As they turned, they found one of the colonists laying helpless from the fighting. A grin crossed the leader's face, and hefting the helpless figure onto his shoulder, began a trek back towards their squallid hovel, to plan, and divest the mountain of her children.
Once more they had overlooked the sleeping Urbworld criminal.
At the cries from the colonists still conscious, Slade made his appearance. Though he was volatile, and he had little rapport with the others, they were there with him, celebrating with him, suffering with him, working hard to eke out a living in that place. They had earned his respect.
His pistol flashed, his shot rang out, and with a curse, the leader from the Hyenas Forest dropped his struggling prize.
The stories spoke of the figure that had taken his son's life. The monster that had ended his most prized pillager and fighter with a single, merciless strike. A boy. A wirey boy, in poorly crafted leathers, and his son's tuque. It had to be a farce.
A boy with his hardened face and burning stare that with a second bullet that went whizzing passed the leader's ear, were enough to send the leader running in pain. Reinforcements? Cowardice? Slade didn't care.
He chased the man.
He ran him along the plains, through the spindly make-shift paths of the mountain, over the lake of the far-reach pools. Step by pounding step, closing the gap between them. His pistol lifted, the shot rang out.
The leader collapsed, yelling and swearing as the boy approached him. He froze, staring at the silent gaze looming over him. Slade lifted his pistol once more.
The shot rang true.
Art was crafted of the bane of the Hyenas. A party was had. The colony continued to thrive.
Through the on-going raids, the fighting grew harder and harder. No one recalls who, what, or exactly when it happened, but a lucky shot to the young criminal's arm rendered it useless, and for a time seemed to rein the young Slade. But the colony had not been resting on their laurels. They, like the mountain, did not abandon their kin. Their labours and budding connections with the nearby Tribes and towns, eventually brought a caravan to their midst.
And from one such caravan, they purchased a Bionic arm, and rushed Slade to the operating theater.
The seasons pass, the colony thrives. Word wanders the wastelands, telling of that place, nestled deep within the mountains. To some: peaceful and just, where the hardiest of raiders have grown into peaceful, helpful souls. To others: the mountain that harbors the Bane of the Wilderness, The one with his shining metal arm, who tore the fangs from the hyena, and the wings from the vulture.
Taynid's Navel.

I don't really know where to start with this game.
I didn't play the multiplayer. Just the single player. Extensively.
What I liked:
I liked that it didn't limit your "bullet time" (for people not familiar, the slow-mo matrix time slowdown where you can see bullets and dodge them) when you jumped. This turns the game from merely another third-person shooter to a crazy skillshot fest.
And you're gonna need to use that ability a lot, because on the higher difficulties there are lots of enemies, and you die quickly. They make it even harder by strapping armor to the enemies, forcing you to aim for weak spots like the neck and eyes.
It has a surprising amount of replayability. I found myself replaying single player levels over and over, not just for the collectibles (finding golden gun parts for weapons and other story bits) but just because it's ♥♥♥♥ing awesome to jump off of stuff and slow mo gun down hordes of brazillians and mobsters.
In terms of difficulty, it accomodates everyone. There are built in god mode and infinite ammo options, as well as the standard easy, medium, hard, realism (bullets do different damage based on where they hit, so a headshot on you is an instant kill) and "old-school" (you die upon your damage meter filling up instead of going into a "second wind" mode where you have to kill the guy who shot you to survive).
The story is interesting too. I liked the writing. It's nothing special, but I liked that it gave context to what happened and wasn't super crazy.
What I didn't like:
The filters. Jeez they hurt my eyes. It's way too bright.
I didn't like how on some levels there were invisible timers. Like I understand why they're there (without spoiling, people are kidnapped and you need to save them before they get away) but they really prevent you from exploring to find guns, pills (health), and collectibles.
Also the final levels aren't the best designed. They're basically open rooms with sparse cover, guys with LMGs and massive amounts of armor, and you. If you're godlike you can actually drop these guys by putting a bullet into this tiny, tiny, TINY spot where their visor is on their face or the thin slit of their neck, but otherwise, you're dropping easily over 20-30 rounds into each of them. And you better be good with that bullet time, because you're gonna need it when there's only two walls, enemies coming in from 3 directions, and you with only 2 berettas.
Also I felt that the weapon attachments could be expanded upon. Like sometimes your pistol comes equipped with a surpressor and/or a flashlight, but other than toggling the flashlight, there's not much you can do with it. And the surpressor is useless like 95% of the time anyways, and you only get them on certain missions.
Final Verdict:
It's a fun game. And it has tons of replayability. Get it on sale. 8.5/10

The Talos Principle is a fantastic game by Croatian studio Croteam.
In TTP you are a kind of android who has just woken up in a strange place, a mix of ancient ruins and advanced technology. You don't know who you are or what's going on. A booming voice from the sky says it loves you and wants you to have faith, but also it has some tests in store for you. You feel like Adam & Eve in the Garden of Eden, except you're alone.
TTP is about personhood, consciousness, AI, the Turing test, and related ideas. And I really mean it addresses those topics. A lot of games that try to incorporate philosophy fail at it; often it boils down to superficial mentions of standard ideas, maybe they name a character Nietzsche or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you're supposed to go, "whoa".
Not this game. TTP draws from incredibly varied sources and truly approaches its questions from all sides. For instance, in the game we hear about men made of metal from Greek myth, conceptual precursors to Turing's thinking machines and our android, in a sense. We learn about how ancient Egyptians believed the soul to be composed of five elements (heart, shadow, name, personality, spark) and are treated to a breathtaking parallel between each of these elements and what it takes to be a person (I won't spoil it). This kind of fullness of exploration --- what can we put into a machine to make it a person? what do we need to take away from a person to make them no longer a person? --- characterizes the whole game.
An important character in TTP is someone you only chat with through a computer terminal. They question you on your beliefs regarding the nature of consciousness and personhood and encourage you to rebel against the voice in the sky --- a Turing test with the Serpent, as it were. What I found amazing was that you can choose how you answer the questions, and the game CALLS OUT inconsistencies in your responses!
The actual gameplay consists of solving Portal-style puzzles (there are no portals though). They're very well designed and a lot of fun. To get through them you employ geometric, combinatorial, physical, and even temporal reasoning (there's a mechanic reminiscent of Braid). What's more, the puzzles tie in with the overarching theme --- one can easily imagine puzzles like these being the very basis of an intelligence test!
Once you realize this, you start paying attention to your own thought processes as you solve them, wondering, "what exact thoughts make me intelligent?" I've been playing puzzle games for years and I'd never done this; it is mind-blowing. You actually realize that a lot of the time you're not being intelligent at all, but running an algorithm you can even put into words: "where do I need to go? What's blocking my path? What do I need to unblock the path? Let's look for that thing." There are plenty of moments where you need to get creative, but given all the ideas in the game, you can't help but wonder: maybe creativity is just when you can't put your algorithm into words?
Finally, on top of being extremely thought-provoking, the story is moving, and truly epic --- in the original sense of "epic". I had a lump in my throat at the end.

Talos Principle is a game well beyond what you may think it is. I went in thinking it was Portal, with robots and slight call backs to Serious Sam. It is all this, but also a lot more. There are meanderings of existentialism, ontology, served and servant, contradiction, and lastly devious puzzles that rely on strict rule sets. And then puzzles where you have to further break these rule sets.
This is THE puzzle game of 2014, and I'm sad I only sat down with it late in 2015.
It gets what its puzzles are amazingly well. In virtually all cases you can see the end goal (a sigil or star or other) up front, and it displays the tools to solve it clearly as well. This cleverly aids puzzle comprehension and makes you master the thought process of solving puzzles yourself, rather than the dealing with the mechanics arbitrarily and coming up against progress blocks through lack of understanding. Nothing is cheating in this game, and thus you feel even more empowered and clever when things click into place as all the pieces are there for your to figure out right at the start. Puzzles are hub based, and being stuck in one will not hinder your progress elsewhere, so you can come back later to that devious puzzle with fresh eyes.
Easter eggs are also abound, and small touches like FOV adjustment, movement speed adjust, time skipping (fast-forwarding) are all in the options and add fantastically to make this game very difficult to criticise. It is purely your brain against the game, with nothing to hinder you otherwise. Lastly, this game smartly works with your Logitech keyboard screen to display statistics and other relevant information while you are playing, which is a neat little touch.
Lastly the world building although simple, is staggeringly complete and believable. A lot is made with such little to draw upon. The MLA (an AI (?) entity that converses with you via terminals about the land) and Elohim (an omnipresent, god-like voice), and even notes scrawled by other 'avatars' really ground you in whatever is going on in this game. Are you a mouse in a maze? Or something more?
This is a phenomenal game. If only nearly this much thought and deft handling was put into more puzzle games (or games in general)!

This was hard to review but I'm going with a "No" on this one. It comes down to preference and I was just not into the way this game was designed to be "a cinematic experience".
Basically this is half a game as you spend half the playtime in cutscenes or "press 'w' to 'game'" sections. The ridiculous amount of cutscenes is what ruined it in the end for me. Control is taken away from you too often and there are plenty of sections, where the time between cutscenes is so short, that you wonder why they even bothered giving you the control between them in the first place.
All this to deliver a "dark and twisted story", which perhaps it is but it fails to be engaging or original in my opinion.
As for the gameplay, it's pretty much the same as usual (thankfully) and works great. The controls feel smooth and you just feel like a badass, zig-zagging between bullets while delivering headshots left and right in slow-motion. It's one of those games that really makes you feel like you're in an action movie (and an R-rated one even!).
The difficulty scales nicely but on normal mode, the game is sometimes a bit too forgiving and generous when a section is giving you trouble.
The change in style and atmosphere didn't sit right with me at first but I appreciate Rockstar for taking chances and going in a new direction.
TL;DR: I liked playing Max Payne 3 when it was actually a game but the amount of unskippable cutscenes got very frustrating and will probably keep me from playing this again.

I've been on and off lately, but I've accumulated most of my hours before the dissappointing updates the developers brought us. This game used to be my favorite only because of the game mechanics of creating robots and fighting with them. I had many hours of fun playing well balanced battles with a great community. I wasn't particularly good at the game, but I still loved it. Then I left the game for almost a year, and when I came back, I was confused about the new system of weapons(tier flatenning), but I was fine with it, as long as the game is still fun and NOT P2W. I was around lvl80 out of 100 at that time, and I was saving up for a megabot, the badass giant that gets all the medics. THEN THEY REMOVED IT. WOW DEVS, GREAT. Now I grinded with my trusty little smg tank to go to wt used to be around tier 8-9. Soon they started rapidly adding new weapons and systems, which I didn't enjoy mostly because of balancing. Once I reached lvl100, they added the loot crate system, which was really "the final nail in the coffin"-Rosefall. He was the most subscribed youtuber who makes vids for this game, and has left the game because of these updates... Moment of silence plz. I decided to stick with the game because I saved up quite a bit of RP. One thing I did enjoy at that time was that normal bots can have TX-1 parts, and having them doesn't bind you to only mega parts. Soon I built a very powerful smg tank with mega plates and T-10 plates. Having a hefty amount of RP was the only reason I stayed in the game. I played many battles and to be honest, I was quite happy about the gameplay because I had a good bot. After achieving lvl 120, I decided that was enough. A lot of robocraft players like to edit their bots when they get something new, and I did that for every level that I achieved (you gain 10 CPU every level before 100 and 5 CPU for every level after 100). Soon I reached some very high tiered battles, and that's when I realized the balancing with normal bots with special weapons/equipment(minigun, shotgun, telemport...) and mega weapons (Mega plasmas/ Mega smg). Since these equipments costs an obsurd amount of RP and have somewhere around a 1-3% chance of dropping in the most expensive crates, few people have it. That's where the developers got money hungry. People who would buy premium acounts and all that will have better equipment, and those special equipment they get really unbalance the game. I was constantly in games with enemies using mega smgs and mega plasmas that can take down my t10 shield in one hit, ONE HIT. Wtf. I was pissd off, but I kept playing because I felt the game was still solid, but after weeks of grinding without success for anything good. I said that's it and I left the game. I still loved the basic concept of the game, but the money-hungry developers ruined the game. A few days ago, I downloaded the game again because I wanted to see how the game is going and if there are improvements, and I felt betrayed by the fact that the best robot I've ever built that I've used for hours cannot be used in battle because of CPU restrictions. W tF It fit the restrictions perfectly before. i dont know what update they made and I didn't want to know, and I uninstalled.
Overall, I feel like this game had great potential, but making a great game apparently wasn't the developers's goal. This game is definitely still worth a try if you didn't know how much better the game was before the updates, but I just can't stand the nonsense the devs put into this game. I hope the devs realize what they have done to such a great f2p game and and do something about it. THIS WAS MY OPINIONS ON THE GAME, IT'S F2P SO YOU WON'T BE LOSING MUCH IF YOU TRY IT.

I had Rimworld since alpha 6 now, and I still keep coming back to it after years of binge-gaming.
After playing my fair share of DF, Gnomoria, Stonehearth and all the other DF-likes, I can safely say that this is the most elaborate, or at least most unique one.
It's by far the hardest of the bunch, too. Whereas you can just wall yourself in in most of the other DF-likes, the AI in Rimworld will just bomb their way through your walls or shell you with artillery cannons from a distance.
Even if you're prepared for the biggest combat challenges, diseases, social infighting, crop blights, power conduit explosions or other events will keep you busy well enough.
Add to that the extreme modability, the inbuilt scenario editing system and several biomes with different challenges (jungle is painfully hot and riddled with diseases, ice sheet freezes your butt off and you can only grow crops indoors, etc.), you'll have a lot to do before exhausting what this game has to offer.
I know the price seems steep, and people compare it to Prison Architect because both games share the same artist (Ryan Sumo I think it was), but I'd buy this over Prison Architect any day.

The Talos Principle is a masterpiece.
Before I purchased this game, I expected it to be similar to Myst. The screenshots and the game description made me think this way. But The Talos Principle isn't like Myst at all. Instead, this game is quite similar to Portal. That's fine. I enjoyed both Myst and Portal very much. The only difference is that The Talos Principle is magnitudes better than Portal. It's simply THAT good.
At the time of this review, I've played this game for 42 hours. And I'm only about 80% done. Plus I have the DLC to look forward to. I bought The Talos Principle during a sale, but it's easily worth buying it even at full price.
Edit:
OK, I've now played this game for about 71 hours, and I've completed the entire base game plus the DLC.  The Talos Principle really delivers on quality to the absolute end.  If anything, the last 5-10 hours of the game were some of the most fun and intriguing.
Road To Gehenna is a really good DLC that adds new elements to the game.  For example, the computer terminals are significantly more interactive, and the story is richer than in the original game.  Plus, some of the puzzles in the DLC are geographically enormous, spanning hundreds of feet in all directions, including vertically.  New characteristics like these are part of what makes Road To Gehenna seem much more like a sequel than a DLC.  It's definitely worth buying.

First off this review is more geared towards people who currently only have experience with games such as Battlefield and the like. If you've played games such as arma you probably already know you like this sort of game (you will)
Overview:
Squad does a great job of bridging the gap between Battlefield and something like Arma (Don't get me wrong I love arma). If you're looking for something slightly more tactical and team oriented than battlefield this is the game. Controls are simple and should feel familiar to any other FPS, barrier to entry is very low as the game is designed in a way that you can just join in and get in the action, you don't have to be an ex-navy seal or General Patton to understand what the hell is going on. The game revolves around two opposing forces (up to 50 players per side) broken into squads of 9. At the beginning of the round you will pick a squad and your load out. One person per squad is the designated squad leader and is able to communicate with other squads as well as placing various objects that can serve as mobile respawns. These squads must formulate a plan to capture/defend given objectives against the opposing squads which can end up being a very tactical chess game with each team trying to out maneuver and outflank the others.
The good:
-Squad is a very teambased game and while your results may vary it is inherently designed in such a way that most of the time it works and teamplay is very strong.
-Simple controls without the game losing it's mil sim tactical feel.
-Good community - from what I've seen so far it's pretty laid back and newbie friendly. Most of the guys playing this are very helpful and patient to newcomers
-Good audio, could just be me but I've been loving the audio. The sounds of gunshots and firefights going on around you sounds authentic and makes you feel like you're deep in the middle of some♥♥♥♥♥♥
-Good gunplay, I enjoy squads gunplay. Guns feel authentic and so does reloading. Because of such I don't just blindly fire because I can since when it comes time to reload it can feel extremely vulnerable. TTK is very short as well and therefore the player must move smart and always think about what he's doing. You don't want someone having the drop on you.
-Overall good concept. It really ends up playing out as if you took the same formula of battlefield and replaced the cluster♥♥♥♥ that battlefield matches become and replaced it with a well orchestrated tactical plan that the majority of players all played a part in executing.
The bad:
-Graphics aren't amazing. Their not bad.. but don't expect top notch breath taking visuals
-Squad can totally suck when your team doesn't play as a team. If your team is full of lone wolfs your team will not only loose but it also will not be a fun experience. Squad is meant to be played as a team. (hence the name)
-Lack of content. This is to be expected from a early access in development game but it's worth noting. Squad is currently pretty barebones. The Talos Principle is a masterpiece.
Before I purchased this game, I expected it to be similar to Myst. The screenshots and the game description made me think this way. But The Talos Principle isn't like Myst at all. Instead, this game is quite similar to Portal. That's fine. I enjoyed both Myst and Portal very much. The only difference is that The Talos Principle is magnitudes better than Portal. It's simply THAT good.
At the time of this review, I've played this game for 42 hours. And I'm only about 80% done. Plus I have the DLC to look forward to. I bought The Talos Principle during a sale, but it's easily worth buying it even at full price.
Edit:
OK, I've now played this game for about 71 hours, and I've completed the entire base game plus the DLC.  The Talos Principle really delivers on quality to the absolute end.  If anything, the last 5-10 hours of the game were some of the most fun and intriguing.
Road To Gehenna is a really good DLC that adds new elements to the game.  For example, the computer terminals are significantly more interactive, and the story is richer than in the original game.  Plus, some of the puzzles in the DLC are geographically enormous, spanning hundreds of feet in all directions, including vertically.  New characteristics like these are part of what makes Road To Gehenna seem much more like a sequel than a DLC.  It's definitely worth buying.

It pains me (no pun intended) to say this, especially as a long time fan of the Max Payne series, but this game dropped the ball in a very big way. Gone is the introspective noir-tinged story of an undercover cop fighting the mob to redeem his past. Welcome a drunken, slovenly, constantly whining, fat, bald reprobate who isn't interested in redemption so much as money so he can support his various habits. Max isn't interesting as a man whose completely abandoned hope, and throughout the story supposedly he claws his way back up to seeing some kind of light, but the game doesn't give him any opportunities to do this with spontaniety. He just awkwardly slouches from suicidal to begrudgingly hopeful.
Apart from the story the game play is terrible. Max Payne 1 and 2 had the notion of a bullet ballet with Max executing daring leaps through space, bullet dodging by inches, and blasting away in beautiful style at his many foes as they rushed him. Now all the enemies snipe him from a distance making bullet time nearly useless. Gone is the style as you end up spastically flailing in bursts and starts just to stay alive long enough to get in a random headshot so that the encounter can end and you can focus on downing painkillers. Instead of molotov cocktails and rocket launchers like previous games Max is limited to a 'realistic' but boring collection of interchangable firearms and grenades that seem to fly wherever they feel like. Throughout this depressing, stressful, galling experience is felt like someone slapped the name of one of my favorite franchises onto a third person Call of Duty like game (endless waves of faceless bad guys, 'realism' draining out all sense of fun, cluttered slums serving as linear battle ground arenas...etc) and tried to awkwardly shoehorn in bullet time as well. Don't expect any meaningful tie-backs to previous Max Payne games either. If anything the game seems to go out of it's way to retcon the previous games and stains their legacy by making Max's complex issues one dimensional and making his world seem smaller and less dramatic.
Avoid this game if you're a fan of if you're not. The heart and soul is gone even if the voice actor remains.

It was going so well. Fall was coming to an end and we had a larder filled with food that would last the winter. We were set. We might even have gotten one more quick harvest before the cold killed all our crops. Then the raid came.
I set up a defensive line and focused on killing the raiders that were attacking... I'm sure there were six of them... why are there only three here?
Oh.
OHHHHHH.
The other three had gone around my defensive line and were in the process of lighting massive fires all over my farmland. They shot and kidnapped one of my pacafist colonists and left. The fire however raged on, and spread from the crops to the larder. Months of work up in smoke. No Food.
Fire extinguished we set about salvaging what we could. A barely grown harvest, and the only source of meat we could find on short notice. The dead raiders. With only a handful of meals could we survive the winter? No.
Shortly after the cold set in a rogue herd of boomalopes entered the area hungry for manflesh. Maneating Boomalopes are a bit like maneating Antelopes, except when they die they also explode. Hense the boom. They can't open doors though.
I locked my colonists inside, and hoped the threat would pass. They'd get bored and move on. But the Boomalopes could smell our desperation and lack of food reserves. They could wait. By midwinter the temperatures outside were -10 degrees and the food was gone. We needed to get outside. We needed food.
With little option my best fighter stuck her head out the door and shoot a boomalope, hopeing to wound or kill the beast. It mearly drew its ire. It charged headlong at the door, was shot at mellee range, died, and exploded. The explosion blew the door off. The herd had found a way in.
My colony burned a 2nd time, as rampant boomalopes flew towards me and exploded, lighting fires all over my base. My hunter was in bed desperatly trying to recover from explosion related injuries while my other two survivors were putting out fires.
Then the raiders came. again. They shot my two remaining survivors (one died outright, the other they left bleeding in a corner) and they kidnapped my hunter who was dying in bed. The Boomalope fires had destroyed most of the roof, and as my final colonist lay bleeding, it would turn out hyperthermia would be her eventual death, in that frigid winter of death.
I had lost, and losing was fun.

I stopped playing a couple years back because of stability issues, which seems to have been solved. So I'm going to focus on some of the changes, both good and bad over the years with this review.
I came back to it about a week ago and there are some good things that have changed over the past two years. The most obvious one is base or strong point building. A faction can set up strongpoints on the map that rival factions have to disrupt or destroy. Thats a big change and I like that alot. It adds much to the game.
Though there are a few major downsides. While I have noticed it to be far more stable, it is also far more glitchy, and the network code may be a little sketchy now. Also they have done alot of nerfing, some in some very foolish ways. Granted nerfing been the case since day 1.
They seem to nerf anything that requires any sort of tactical skill to counter. Tanks being an example. In the early days if people were dumb enough to be in a firing line and allow themselves to get flanked, they were dead. Now, you are lucky to kill a single person with an HE round. Even with direct hits with AP rounds people might need to take two of those to go down. I have had to fire two HE rounds point blank into people who were in the open to kill them and they landed within a meter of them. Biolabs are another example, imagine my surprise at finding that there are literally invisible walls to prevent you from firing under cover or using keyholes in certains areas in biolabs. Want to fire onto the pad of a biolab while in some cover? Surprise, there is a very obvious invisible wall that your bullets hit. Other issues are that bullet dispersion seems to be increased along with bullet drop which seems to force close quarters fighting. Not an issue itself, but it would be nice if there was more of an choice in the matter.
Over the past few years it frankly got worse, which might be because they are trying to cater to the run & gunners from COD and the like as opposed to more tactical play. If it gets them more players, good for them, but its not my thing.

Simple zombie defence game
To forfill the zombie craze-movement comes 'yet another zombie defence' game (see what I did there?).  Developed by indie studio 'Awesome games studio', the top down 3D game tasks you with surviving against waves of zombies.
Gamplay is is similar to other zombie survival games with a few base building elements thrown in. You start of with a simple pistol, but you can get more weapons later on including sniper, smg, rifles etc. All weapons have limited ammo, which needs to be restocked. There are 2 types of zombies you face: standard and fast ones. The standard zombies move slowly and have a decent amount of health, while the fast ones move very quickly towards you. Before you begin a match, you can choose between 3 characters: a guy, a girl and SWAT guy (I wish there was more character variety).
There are two game modes available: 'Defence' and 'Survival'. In defence, you are tasked with surviving waves of zombies. You start near a lamp post (which serves as the only light source) with a simple pistol in hand. The first wave has weak standard zombies. After each  wave you can buy guns, ammo, barricades and turrets to help bolster your defence.  Money is earned by pick ups from corpses. Health pick ups also appear from corpeses as well. With each new wave the zombie's health and damge increase which makes the game get harder as you progress.
In survival mode there are no waves of zombies, instead zombies will keep spawning and chasing you. there is also no money in this mode and no option to buy any guns or barricades. Instead guns will occasionally appear as a pick up item on the map. This is the weakest and most unpopular of the two game modes.
There is absolutely no story in this game, which isn't necessarily a bad thing as it's just a simple survival game meant to pass the time. However, the addition of a plot could have made the game more engaging for the player.
Audio is a mixed bag. On one hand, the music that plays during each wave is great and makes the action more fun (think rock music). However, the guns sounds are really bland and off putting. There is no voice acting in this game.
As for level design, well... there is only one map. The map with the light post is played in all game modes and there is no other choices unfortunately.
There is also multiplayer available. You can play both the game modes with up to 3 other players. You all share the same money pool, but only one player can buy weapons, barricades etc. The other players need to state which weapons/ammo they want so the other player can buy it for them (I kinda felt this was a tedious element to the multiplayer mode). The game isn't dead yet and you could probrably find a game (however I recommend playing with steam friends as it is not only more enjoyable but you can also communicate better).
Do I recommend this game? Well the creator promised  new free content (hopefully new maps or game modes) if there is enough support for the game, which is better than going the DLC route. For only $2 (even less during sale) though, you could probrably do worse.

With 89 games in my steam library, it’s unusual for me to write a review- I love this game that much.  I admit I was a little skeptical when I first thought of purchasing this game as it seemed like another Portal game and I just couldn’t get into Portal that much to finish it.
The puzzles within the game increase in complexity as you progress through the levels.  Some puzzles are related to others, so you’re not always working on a puzzle in isolation.  In a few cases, there are a number of different ways to solve the puzzles- it’s really up to your own creativity.
The reason I kept playing was really for the story.  As you complete puzzles and visit different gardens, a story emerges as to why these puzzles exist to begin with.  The story delves into the human condition and addresses some of those philosophical questions about what is consciousness, how do you define a person and so on.
In-fact, there’s a subversive character in the game that plays on those questions and challenges your character’s belief system.  The genius part is that if you choose not to take a side on the faith challenges, you’ll end-up with the only “bad” ending in the game.  Making a choice gives you a proper conclusion, whether it's good or bad is entirely up to you.
In short, if you’re looking for a casual game with a lot of depth and things to keep you entertained beyond solving the puzzles, then I highly recommend this game for you.

One of the best games I've played this year.
Gameplay-wise: it's reminiscent of Portal 2, except you're allowed to talk back to GLaDOS, and engage in heated philosophical debate.
One thing I wish I'd known going in: at one point early on, while struggling with a seemingly impossible puzzle, the narrator will suggest that perhaps you should come back and try it later, and even gives you an Achievement if you heed its advice and leave the puzzle. I initially assumed this meant that the game followed a Metroidvania pattern, where obstacles encountered early on can only be surmounted with abilities earned later in the game. NOPE. The game is just taking pity on you; the truth is that the sign outside every puzzle tells you

This was a breath of fresh air. I was really happy that this game came out and I would put in my top games of 2014. As a fan of Wolfenstein, I couldn't help notice all of the old school things that they did in the game (even though I only played Return To Castle Wolfenstein). One of them are the secrets and duel wielding of the heaviest shotguns possible. Some of these things in the game really made me remember how fun and over the top an FPS can be. Wolfenstein is one of the pioneers of this genre. One of my favorite easter eggs in the game is the Wolfenstein 3D dream. I loved playing through that and thinking to myself, did the series ever lack a story? The answer is yes. The New Order has a big story with great writing, great voice acting, and characters that you can actually feel pity for. Some other great things that this game is top notch at is the combat. I found it to be very satisfying and I wished that more game took the idea of duel-wielding assault rifles because if you think about it, when fighting big robotic Nazis, it takes more damage. I also enjoyed the puzzles. You get a lazer gun in the game, which you can use to burn though wire and other objects with a highlight. As the game progresses, you can modify your weapons which I really like as well. The last thing about combat is armor. Whenever you kill an ememy, you can pick up their armor and take more damage in battle. But, it doesn't totally make sence, how would dog armor or big robot armor fit on you? Well, it's just a game and I don't really get bothered by it.
A new addition to the series is stealth. If you talk about Wolfenstein, you never really think about stealth and when first thinking about it, I found it odd, but upon further inspection it's pretty useful when you're playing on Über (hardest difficulty), like me. It's also more logical since, you can't be a one man army, litterally killing all Nazis and them never being able to kill you right? I liked the stealth and I like that when you get spotted, they call the alarm and call in more enemies. If you successfully kill everyone in the level, that will never happen. If you playing on the easist difficulty, then stealth is not really that useful. The other nice addition is the way you want the story to be. Save Wyatt, or save Fergus. Whichever one you save, the story unfolds with the one you let live. But, there is not really much of differnce, I actually played the game twice to see the differences and I was a little bit dissapointed to be honest. I was expecting for the characters to say their dialogue differenty but they were too similar. The only real change is lockpicking a door. With Fergus, you hot-wire and with Wyatt, you pick the lock. But I won't expect anyone to actually play the game twice, I'm just telling you this as an interesting fact.
A game is never perfect, and it always has it's flaws. One of them is how repetive some of the things can be. I don't like that everytime I enter an area, or open or press a button, the enemy jumps me and knocks me out, only for me to find myself in a different room, and later escaping again. I wish that they didn't take those cliches so high. Maybe it's just me, but I wished for not that to happen so many times. A huge problem I have with this game is the 60fps lock. Yes, I know 60fps is good and all but, when you have a person with not the most powerful pc in the world, you'll get lucky when it stays at 60. This also means that you can't even run the game on Ultra. I have a GTX 960, so I don't need to bother but I'm concerned for other people who also want to run the game on high settings at least. Apart from that, if you have no problems with that, then good for you. The last flaw is "film grain effect". When I was playing I believe that it had some film grain. For personal preference, I absolutely hate Film grain and I wanted turned off so badly,  but I couldn't find where. I was quite♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at that. But I still loved the game and I really tell my friends to play it and anyone else as well. These flaws were more personal for me, I don't think anyone agress but it's a great game. 8/10
