I picked this up because I heard a lot of people raving about it.
The Talos Principle is a first-person puzzle game in the vein of Portal. It doesn't actually use portals but it has a similar format where you're going into rooms and moving things around to solve puzzles. It's more non-linear and much longer than the Portal games were.
The plot, such as it is, is generally delivered through finding text and audio logs. Personally I think this method of storytelling is only growing more stale as time goes on, but to the game's credit it doles everything out at a pace that keeps it from being overwhelming. The general theme of the game seems to be a rumination on whether sufficiently advanced robots could truly be considered conscious or not. I think the game spends too much time simply rephrasing that one idea and posing it to the player over and over again instead of putting it into practice, but I could see how there's room for disagreement.
The big thing that keeps me from recommending this game is its difficulty. Anyone who hopes to get anywhere in this game is going to need to possess two things: a fondness for puzzle games, and a lot of persistence. I think modern games, for better or worse, have conditioned players to accept a lot less challenge and tedium than in years gone by. It's become so easy to acquire games and switch between them that the player's sense of individual investment in any one particular game has lessened, and it must be harder than ever to make a game that players won't immediately turn off when they get stuck in favor of whatever else they have in their Steam library.
Unfortunately for the Talos Principle, there aren't any difficulty levels, and while there are some optional challenges, you can't see an ending without completing the overwhelming majority of the game's content, a lot of which is quite challenging. If there's one puzzle room driving you bonkers, your progress in the game will be halted until you can finally figure it out. There's a very limited in-game hint system where you can eventually get help on three puzzle rooms of your choosing, but since there are several dozen rooms in the game, it feels like such a scarce resource that you'd be a fool to even use it. You can also just get on Youtube to find the solution to any given puzzle room, but it feels really unsatisfying to do things that way. There's a ghost of a hint system in place in the form of an extremely basic player message system a la Dark Souls, but it's not robust or effective enough to be of any assistance.
If you don't see any problems with that notion, and indeed if you relish the notion of bashing your head against puzzles aplenty, then this is the game for you. But if that doesn't describe you then I don't think you'll get your money's worth out of this game. I try to make a good-faith effort to complete the games I purchase, but after making it through about 70% of the game I eventually gave up on it. It's not that it didn't feel satisfying to make progress in the game after solving some thorny puzzles, and the game tries to encourage you by saying that it's testing you to make you better, but unless you're predisposed to like games of this type then I think the frustration will eventually catch up with you.
It's a bummer to think that a lot of the plot is locked behind a very high level of difficulty. While I'm sympathetic to the argument that games baby their players too much these days, I feel like the game would be better overall if the denouement was accessible at a lower level of completion, and structure the game such that the harder parts were optional yet encouraged instead of mandatory. I can tell that a lot of love was poured into this game, but when you're stuck, you're really stuck, and we're no longer in the days where the simple act of purchasing a game was enough to compel you to finish it. I feel bad that I have to confine my recommendation to a yes/no rating, but if someone's reading this to determine whether they'll spend money on this game or not, I want them to know that they should be careful about their decision.

This game has depth. It makes you think, it rewards you for breaking the rules, and it screws with your head. It's wonderful, for both it's polished gameplay and exceptional story.

DISCLAIMER:
The game is in Alpha and it has multiple bugs and low overall graphical quality so this is the review of a concept and gameplay more than a finished polished product.
Pros:
-Very Tactical
-Positioning over rushing
-Tactic over reflexes
-Amazing sounds
-Very realistic locations
-Teamwork is the ONLY way to win
-No k/d ratio during the match on the scoreboard
Cons:
-Requires very good Squad leaders (one idle squad can lose a game for the whole team)
-Incredibly big maps with no vehicles (yet) make it very boring to walk around
-Animations (in particular jumping) are broken... getting stuck under fire behind a knee high wall because you can't jump it is very frustrating
-Graphically is definitely sub-par (I expect this to get way better with time)
-VoIP if used incorrectly can be extra annoying
-Hit registration is sometimes broken
-Firing is very challenging... way more than real life
Overall I love the experience this game gives me even if some times I hate it (can't jump over a small wall under fire).
The direction where this game is headed is definitely the right one: hated by COD/BF fanboys, only serious people need apply, tactic over reflexes, positioning over rushing, thinking over shooting.
It needs better graphics (textures, polygons and so on) and I would trade 10 players for it (64 people are enough on a server), better hit registration, less unrealistic shooting mechanics, vehicles (not too many... just transports and infantry support vehicles... no tanks, no helicopters, no jets), maybe an artillery/close air support (to be called by the artillery spotter role once every 10 minutes).
I definitely recommend this game to anyone who loved Project Reality or even enjoyed BF2 (life doesn't replenish itself, when you see many enemies/tank you hide, moving together is important) and to anyone who is looking for a realistic and intense combat experience videogame.

This game... I have a mixed opinion on this but in the end it's mostly negative:
If you want a list on pros and cons you can find it already in this page, what I feel about the game is that microtransaction are at the heart of this game, things normal player think as standard are not in this game, like for example reloading a bolt action rifle while aiming down the sight, or having an AA weapon, or a solid secondary gun... noone of that and much more are just absent from the start phase of the game which make it REALLY difficult to pass it while enjoying it, if you combine that with the fact that in order to acquire a single gun for a single class can take weeks of meaningless grinding you just got a tedious, boring FPS with some amazing moments sparkled here and there. The paying format I would say is more like a "Pay to be good" sistem, in which you either spend a fortune or just live as a F2P player untill you get bored and uninstall.
On the gameplay side it just boils down to spawnkilling, that's how you do the most ammount of points, no tactics are involved to play this game, just follow the horde untill you arrive at the spawn of the enemy and keep shooting from a safe location, plus if you bring with you a spawn vehicle near the enemy spawn you'll get even more points (btw "all this points" means 0.1 cost of a weapon for each night you spend doing this strategy). In the end it was fun for the first few days as it was a new experience but then you realize how much time you have to put in order to acquire a good equipment and you just skip to the next FPS. Plus all the times you just don't have the right equipment to deal with the situation which makes it more frustrating than else. So yes, for the first 10 hours good, then just decide if you want to spend 100 or more € or skip to the next game. Thanks for the experience and good bye PS2.

I picked this up because I heard a lot of people raving about it.
The Talos Principle is a first-person puzzle game in the vein of Portal. It doesn't actually use portals but it has a similar format where you're going into rooms and moving things around to solve puzzles. It's more non-linear and much longer than the Portal games were.
The plot, such as it is, is generally delivered through finding text and audio logs. Personally I think this method of storytelling is only growing more stale as time goes on, but to the game's credit it doles everything out at a pace that keeps it from being overwhelming. The general theme of the game seems to be a rumination on whether sufficiently advanced robots could truly be considered conscious or not. I think the game spends too much time simply rephrasing that one idea and posing it to the player over and over again instead of putting it into practice, but I could see how there's room for disagreement.
The big thing that keeps me from recommending this game is its difficulty. Anyone who hopes to get anywhere in this game is going to need to possess two things: a fondness for puzzle games, and a lot of persistence. I think modern games, for better or worse, have conditioned players to accept a lot less challenge and tedium than in years gone by. It's become so easy to acquire games and switch between them that the player's sense of individual investment in any one particular game has lessened, and it must be harder than ever to make a game that players won't immediately turn off when they get stuck in favor of whatever else they have in their Steam library.
Unfortunately for the Talos Principle, there aren't any difficulty levels, and while there are some optional challenges, you can't see an ending without completing the overwhelming majority of the game's content, a lot of which is quite challenging. If there's one puzzle room driving you bonkers, your progress in the game will be halted until you can finally figure it out. There's a very limited in-game hint system where you can eventually get help on three puzzle rooms of your choosing, but since there are several dozen rooms in the game, it feels like such a scarce resource that you'd be a fool to even use it. You can also just get on Youtube to find the solution to any given puzzle room, but it feels really unsatisfying to do things that way. There's a ghost of a hint system in place in the form of an extremely basic player message system a la Dark Souls, but it's not robust or effective enough to be of any assistance.
If you don't see any problems with that notion, and indeed if you relish the notion of bashing your head against puzzles aplenty, then this is the game for you. But if that doesn't describe you then I don't think you'll get your money's worth out of this game. I try to make a good-faith effort to complete the games I purchase, but after making it through about 70% of the game I eventually gave up on it. It's not that it didn't feel satisfying to make progress in the game after solving some thorny puzzles, and the game tries to encourage you by saying that it's testing you to make you better, but unless you're predisposed to like games of this type then I think the frustration will eventually catch up with you.
It's a bummer to think that a lot of the plot is locked behind a very high level of difficulty. While I'm sympathetic to the argument that games baby their players too much these days, I feel like the game would be better overall if the denouement was accessible at a lower level of completion, and structure the game such that the harder parts were optional yet encouraged instead of mandatory. I can tell that a lot of love was poured into this game, but when you're stuck, you're really stuck, and we're no longer in the days where the simple act of purchasing a game was enough to compel you to finish it. I feel bad that I have to confine my recommendation to a yes/no rating, but if someone's reading this to determine whether they'll spend money on this game or not, I want them to know that they should be careful about their decision.

Portal 1 is my favorite game of all time. As I may have been late to playing Portal 2 fully, I must say that it had some changes from Portal 1. While still a great game with even more great characters and puzzles, the way the game played is what really bugged me. While Portal 1 is much more about fast gameplay while still featuring some story at a small but still very suitable pace, Portal 2 focuses alot more on story. While some may say this is a good thing, I do not support big changes in most things, so that was a bad thing in my opinion. The only good thing I would say this change brought was how well played out the scene where you walk into GLaDoS' place and see her on the ground in different pieces while the lighting and music almost makes you feel bad for "killing" her in the last game.
That aside, the game did have some great features. Upgraded graphics, co-op levels and story, FREAKING GEL, and community made levels. The community made levels are a great option if you just want to take a break from all the story telling of the normal Portal 2 single player experience.
I would say overall this was a good game, even though I'm not too much of a fan of change. It is still another experience for die-hard fans of Portal, like me, and it sure is a mostly positive one.

A FPS designed without guardrails. If you want to know if you'll like this game ask yourself a question. "Can I enjoy playing a game against a hacker?"
There is no matchmaking, so you'll be facing some world-class players who can spin around and triple headshot you before you can pull the trigger. You'll be facing tanks with no counters spamming HE shells into an infantry fight then pulling behind a rock to repair. You'll be facing 3:1 odds on occasion across the entire huge, huge open battlefield because three times as many people decided to log onto Terran Republic characters that day.
From the end user perspective, there is no difference between playing someone with god-like skill or a hacker. If you can enjoy yourself while losing helplessly as you are outmatched/outgunned/outmanned then you'll like this game, because there's nothing else like it.

My last encounter with a Wolfenstein game was Wolfenstein 3D (if you can beleive that), so I was expecting to be a continuation of the concept: you have some guys and you have some guns, and you have to get from A to B killing of many of said guys with said guns as possible. So, when I first Started up Wolfenstein: The New Order, I was expecting a dumb shooter, but what I got was far more than that! What really struck me was the depth and quality of the story, which was probably the best for any First Person Shooter that I've played. The game was also boosted by a set functional and enjoyable game mechanics. It did have it's faults however: some levels were pluaged by AI issues, I practically stuck to one gun throughout the entire game because the rest were useless, and despite being a relatively new game (2014) running on Ultra graphics, some very low resolution bitmaps were a bit blatant and offputting.

Overall, I found the gameplay and story of Wolfenstein: The New Order to be highly enjoyable and I'm even considering going back through to play the other timeline - which I don't often do! The flaws, when they appear, are noticeable, but ultimately do little to detract from what is otherwise a great game!

I've been waiting, itching to try this game for ages, so I did.... This review will turn out to be a rant, but in short:
It's a game only for those who have the time and patience to get used to it.
-I tried it - I loved it.
-I played it and realized I it wasn't as good as my initial impression was.
-I got to witness the halloween events and finally realized this game is not worth much.
So why the change in heart? I'll try to summarize why I liked it and what changed.
I've been running around, trying all classes, running with other players - just participating in fights. So far so good.
I noticed some of starter weapons (like sniper rifle) needs a change bandly, so I looked at weapons and upgrades, in hopes adapting my weapons to my play-style, and realized that those are going to be a b**** to get. Most weapons cost 1000 certs and you get 1 cert / 250 experience you earn. To put this into perspective, that is roughly what I get by killing 1 normal enemy with 70% exp bonus. What's worse, a lot of the stats you see on the screen are REALLY deceptive, so you might buy a weapon that looks good for long ranged combat based on stats, but in reality is complete rubbish due to recoil (that is not mentioned).
This was the first real hit on my experience.
Then, halloween came! I was really excited to see what the game had to offer on events. I felt like I was playing one of those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ phone games when I saw what the devs offered on halloween.The only REAL change in the game is that you can run around like a goofball, looking for pumpkins (by the way you have to go out of your way to find a decent amount). That might sound like fun until you notice they are relatively rare and they don't REALLY give anything worthwhile until you find about 200 of them.
Then you have "achievements" with rewards, which are devided into 4 tiers. Only last 2 tiers give actual items as rewards and to complete those you need to do 4 and 5 of following objectives (see if you can spot a problem):
-Kill x people with mask on. (not a problem really).
-Destroy x pumpkins. (a lot harder than it sounds, because everyone competes for kills)
-Destroy a RARE pumpkin (close to impossible to find)
-Obtain x masks (can only be bought with pumpkin seeds you get from pumpkins. Mind you I'm on tier 3 now - I still don't have enough to buy 1 mask and I need to buy 2).
-Kill x people witha pistol that costs real money.
-Kill x people with a knife that costs real money.
This was the point when I realized this won't ever be a game I take seriously:
-2 of those require money, which means f2p players will never get the last tier (and that knife),
-1 of those is so rare it's close to impossible to find.... Killing one should immediatelly drop some kind of item - that's how rare it is.
-Buying masks is also a bit of a hard one (that's putting it lightly) because with ~100 pumpkins destroyed (and i've actually spent time looking for them) I have got 402 seeds and the cheapest mask is 750. You need 3/4 masks at higher tiers.
To put it simply, to get everything this event offers you need to spend money AND either be insanely lucky or spend the 2 weeks looking for pumpkins.
As a side note, I checked around the forums and they've had this exact event since 2012. People complained about it being impossible to complete since then. I can only assume they don't take this kind of feedback into consideration.
So yeah...
The good:
-Combat and conquest thing is pretty fun.
-It's fun to alter between classes.
The bad:
-Steep learning curve. You really need to sit through hours/days of fails to improve.
-It takes a lot of time and patience to get the weaponry and skills to suit your playstyle.
-Some weapons that might be completely useless for what the stats imply they are for.
-Huge accent on team play (Impossible to play alone for the most part).
-Horrible holiday event design: Insane amount of boring grind AND REAL MONEY PAYWALLS.
-Devs don't care about feedback on events.
-(not mentioned above) Quite a lot of trolls and such who will kill you (not neceserely by shooting you).

One of the most beautiful and most thought-provoking games I have ever played.  Most of the puzzles are managable, some are pretty hard to do and a few are really, really tough, however the game has a pretty balanced gameplay design, so that you will seldom feel overchallenged. The philosophical ideas that are intertwined with the gameplay are really clever and sometimes even mind-blowing. Nevertheless, you could as well just ignore them if you only like solving puzzles, but in my opinion the philosophy behind the game is what really makes it stand out.
This game offers different endings according to how you complete it and how many extra challenges you solve, which I think is a great thing! The save game system is a bit confusing though - only 10 previous autosaves will be saved and you cannot choose when to save. So you need to look out not to pass too many checkpoints if you plan to replay a certain part of the game without having to play everything all over again.
Apart from this minor flaw, this game is just perfect. I recommend everyone with enough patience and a liking for philosophy to try it.

So, in my first experience with this game I played the game for almost 10 hours straight on permadeath mode.
Decided to take the Randy Random storyteller as an option.
Here's my story. ..
3 crash landed survivors. 2 brothers, in a spaceship, and then a meteor hit...err...Yeah so they landed on the planet in the far northern reaches, and built a sweet settlement. Had some visitor’s quarters that could house like 10+ people (ty mods). As our three adventurers went along, they recruited another 7 wanderers to join their settlement. In the first year’s winter, the old lady of the group lost her mind and decided to walk nude into the wilderness...everyone was sad when she died and a few settlers visited her grave for months after. Many raiders attempted to steal what the settlers built and grew, but through blood and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ kiting tactics, they survived. After the first full year, there were now 11 people in the settlement. Traders were a common sight, and the raiding had cooled off through the second winter. There were squabbles here and there, and the occasional rampant animal or man hunting pack of wild beasts. Overall it was quite peaceful; the settlers were able to create a life on this wild planet. They had gardens, electrical systems, defense grids, and even a hydroponics farm being built...and then it happened...
They came from the sky, 3 of them. These monstrosities in metal armor crashing through the roof of the home. They started with the scientist, gutted her right in front of the youngest one. She lost it and ran into the woods. Then the settlers banded together. They waited outside of the laboratory doors. Those steel encased doors that can hold back even the wildest of beast or raider. 9 people fully loaded with every ounce of firepower they had to offer. Even some EMP grenades they had scored off a few raiders who were unlucky enough to catch a few settlers hunting. They didn't stand a chance. The doors came down like butter. The trade caravan that had been there, fled as soon as the fire started. There was nowhere to run. The metal beasts shrugged off every round fired, even the heavy machine gun couldn't penetrate their armor. They barely scathed these monsters. 7 people went down in the melee. Only two escaped to run to a safer place, maybe the doors of the freezer would hold them out, and they would leave with some goods and let them live? That's when the beeping started, ......... has burned to death, .......... has burned to death. It kept saying it, over and over until they were gone. All but two, but the monsters weren't done. They broke the freezer doors down, knocked the final two unconscious and lit the rest of the encampment on fire. They all died, slowly. First from stab wounds and power fist wounds and then they were burned to death...that was it...game over...maybe someone else will find use of the ruins of this place...?
Seriously though, I was stuck for 10 hours almost playing this. I couldn't step away from this crazy story that was unfolding. If you are even considering it, buy it. You can return it if you play it for less than 2 hours. BUT, I doubt you will be able to put it down.

Yet Another Zombie Defense is a fairly simple top down twin stick shooter with some tower defense elements thrown in. Basically, you are thown in with nothing but a pistol and fight off a wave of zombies. These are the nights. Then, once they're all dead, it goes into a section where you can use the cash you earned from killing zombies to purchase and build. These are the days. You can buy guns, ammo, turrets to place guns on that will shoot automatically, and walls that can be placed to help stop the incoming waves. During the night stages you can pick up drops from the zombies like ammo crates, money stacks, and full health. Health will come back between rounds, but if run out of it during the night, it's game over. The walls and guns become very necessary for later rounds as the zombies continue to increase not only in numbers, but in speed and health as well. You're going to die. It's just about how long you can survive. Eventually ammo will run out, walls will get destroyed, and you'll be overwhelmed. And that's basically the whole game. Simple, but with possibilities and strategies to try. Oh, and there's an endless mode with is similar except that... there's no day stages.
There's also mutliplayer, which is where this game really shines for me. You can play with up to three other people (meaning four players total including yourself). That means four times the firepower, and a game is only over if every member dies so... better odds. Just make sure not to get in each other's way and do your best to cooperate. Playing online is a great way to make this game more enjoyable and interesting, as you can see other people's skills and strategies. I've played much more online multiplayer with this game than single player, and it's one of the few games I actually play online anymore.
I also want to mention how cool some of the other things are in this game. It has some neat music, which is nice. The way you can build walls and turrets to create a defensive outpost between rounds is a lot like a tower defense game, and it's a cool way to implement that genre into this top down twin stick shooter type of game. It's basically what I think a new arcade game would be like. I like it.
But every game has some downsides. The online can be awfully laggy at times. That can be due to distance, but... it's still a major drag since there's no local co op for this game, another downside. Also, while graphically it looks alright, artistically it is a bit drab. It's a zombie apocalypse, I get it, but that doesn't mean I have to like the dark, dirty look. Just a personal preference thing I suppose. Also, there's this weird system that allows everyone to use the money to buy things in private games with friends, but in random online matches there's no way to do so. Only the host can buy things. It works out alright, but the fact that it's inconsistent is strange to me, and not really explained anywhere either. The heads up would help. Speaking of that, it'd also be nice to get a little warning on the turrets. See, you buy the turrets from the shop and then you can place them. Pretty easy to figure out. What's confusing is that you're supposed to mount a gun on them. This could've been conveyed a little better. Many times newcomers will buy a turret and place it then be confused as to why it won't shoot. Well you have to have another gun to mount on it. And that gun also uses ammo. You start with many extra pistols to mount to them, which is nice enough, but being given a small heads up on a few of these features might have been nice little things to add. Also, there are supposedly more updates coming... but they're taking long than expected as well as longer than announced. So don't base your purchase on new features coming as it's still a bit up in the air. However, let it be noted that, at the very least, more stages to pick from would be very appreciated.
It's still a pretty fun little game. Nice for a time killer. Simple. Easy to learn. And for two bucks, it's worth it. Wait for a sale even. I got it cheaper and even I think it's worth the full price. Yet Another Zombie Defense gets a 6/10 for being a fun, simple, arcadey experience in a more modern time.

In general, I have to say this game cover all my need for an FPS multiplayer game.

There are some things that I believe can be improved in terms of gameplay, but nothing big deal.
Call of Duty meets Counter Strike is Dirty Bomb in a nutshell.
You can play instense match with complex objectives. Or you can just play the old CS style which is planting and defusing bomb. Either way, it is a fun experience playing this one.

In it's current state (alpha 5.1), it's already an excellent game. It's not a military simulation like ArmA3, but it's also far more accessible than ArmA3, most people will be immediately comfortable with the controls if they have played other FPS games. The closest comparison might be Red Orchestra.
To win, it very much requires not only teamplay within the squad, but also coordination between squads. Amazingly, this mostly works. The game's VOIP works well, with different channels for talking locally, squad radio and (for squad leaders only) a command channel. Joining a public server, pretty much everyone has a microphone and tries to communicate meaningfully.
I would really recommend this game when it is on sale for 2$ over the summer it is a very good game and 2$ is a great price for it.

"The Talos Principle" is an excellent game.  It's epic in scope, yet modularized so well that it can be treated as a casual game.  It's got beautiful graphics, wonderful sound (except for the darn beeping of the terminals), excellent voice acting, interesting puzzles, and a wonderful story.  It's a darn fun game to play.  I got 42.5 hours of great gameplay out of my first run (I missed only one of the base game Achievements (darn)), so even at the current list price of about $40, it's worth the price.
I do have some issues with the game, though:
- a few of the "star" puzzles (three, I believe) are so obscure that they cannot be done without a walkthrough.
- there are a few instances where the developers break the wall between the player and the character.  You, the player, must do certain things in the real world to finish things in the game world.
- several sets of Achievements are mutualy exclusive.  To get them all requires either multiple playthroughs or restoring to a previous save point.
- the Restore function could be better designed.  The Checkpoint process in the game is fine.  But, the saving of backups to be restored (a separate function) doesn't have any visibility into when it happens and the number of available slots is very low (10?).  The reason I missed one Achievement is because the Restore points I needed rolled right off the list before I thought to do it.  It's really nice to have that capability, but we need to know when backups happen and there really should be far more slots.
- the list of Achievements includes the DLC Achievements even if you don't own the DLC.  I don't own "Road to Gehenna," so it's impossible for me to get 100% Achievements in the base game.  Not cool.  Achievements should be based on what we OWN, not on what the company PRODUCES.
Other than that, the game is excellent.  Highly recommended.

Castle Crashers is a brilliantly drawn, faced-paced and now 60fps delight. Knights, magic, humour and poo, all roll-up nicely into this side-scrolling quest to resuce the princeses and defeat the evil wizzard. Characters are surprisingly well developed and unlockable characters are achived through gameplay rather than DLC (although there are a couple of characters available via DLC too). Each has their own style, weapon and their own magic abilities that become availble through leveling up.
Controls are easy to grasp, and mastering the combos is a case of learning on the job. The humor is at a level that children and adults will find amusing, which is why I recommend playing this with your kids. My daughter loves Castle Crashers, and will forever ask me to play so she can level up her favorite characters.
I hope a Castle Crashers 2 will be on the books at somepoint in the future. For now at least there is very little like this, and as such Castle Crashers will be a timeless classic. Highly recommended

Great PvP, I appreciated this style and think more games should use it, the style inspires a LOT more tactical planning and coordination than most FPS shooters these days. And an amazing feature is a playtime currency, which you keep until you log out, or spend it, making an obstacal for the annoying players that waste the vehicles in other games by doing stupid things like, wasting a vehicle on just themselves or just completely obliterating an air vehicle for just one kill. The temporary currency is also great, because it restricts the number of Maxes (The Exo-Suit Class, standard with a minigun and Heavy Grenade Launcher) that can be deployed. Although, the curreny is difficult as fudge to achieve if you want a new weapon or an expensive upgrade, it is a SERIOUS pain to grind the currency if your saving up for base unlocks too, costing 1000 for each base item unlock. Also, the character customization is severly limited, only allowing you to set your Faction and Face in the beginning, and only your Helmet, Body Armor, Decal, and Camo, which you need the buyable currency to unlock almost all of the customization gear, limiting players who can't afford currency to the devastatingly few helmets that are unlocked through ranking up. But it is still an amazingly massive scale game with different biomes and opponents that always keep you on your toes. So, in short, this game has its downs, but it is ASTOUNDING none the less.

This game is not only a finely-crafted puzzle game but a work of art that drives the player to think deeply not just when solving spacial puzzles and patterns, but when contemplating the very facets of their existence, consciousness, moral code, and sense of self. The game boils down complex philosophical texts and concepts in a way very digestible by non-philosophers.
This game moved me, and I found myself spending late nights pondering the meaning of what I had read. It's been a very long time since I bought a game and became so hooked that I played it through to the finish in just a week or two without really playing anything else. The puzzles fall under muscle memory in time, and they become busywork for your hands as your thoughts linger on the curiosity and emotion spawned from ingame computer messages and voice logs. The game affects you as much as you allow it to. The more you think on the concepts presented, the more you find parallels in real life. I can name at least three things this game has changed my view on in real life, and many more things that I felt have been reinforced. Not since college classes have I been driven to have such internal conversations on existential topics.
The puzzles are also the single weak point of the game, as the tetromino puzzles grow frustratingly boring. They appear whenever unlocking particular secret zones and some of the late-game content for some of the possible endings. They get so long-winded and frustrating that they outright interrupt the otherwise beautifully-crafted trains of thought and emotion the game guides you along. But that's a part of it--the frustration. I understand the reason behind the mechanic, but I still feel like it's a bit TOO real--a bit too harsh a method of teaching patience and perseverance.
Anyone looking for an intelligent and wholly inspiring game should buy this. It's not flashy, it's not exciting (until the end!), and it's definitely more niche as it requires patience and attentiveness in a way very few games do...but beating this game was the most educational video game experience I've had, and easily one of the most fulfilling. The graphics and environments are beautiful, the voice acting is remarkable, and the pacing of the game is spot-on. You can tell the developers playtested the game rigorously, and they know very well the many ways players will approach The Talos Principle's challenges...and boy does that really drive the narrative.
As for me, I'm off to buy the DLC and blow my mind a second time.
Thank you, Croteam.

I have been playing this game for well over a year now. I was very impressed with its quality, even with it being in alpha.
For those who don't know, the game puts you in control of 3 random characters stranded on a hostile planet. You need to direct your characters to build shelter, secure food, energy, weapons, etc.  The goal is to build a spaceship to evacuate your team from the planet, but you can also just mess around in your planetary sandbox if you prefer. Your characters will encounter other 'tribes' on the planet who may trade with you or fight you. Raiders will attack. Animals will attack. Even the weather can cause you problems. Along the way, you will probably have more characters join your tribe, or you can capture prisoners and convince them to join you. There are lots of ways to play!
The best part of this game is the modding support. There are some amazing mods out there! There is also a 'dev' mode that lets you spawn things or otherwise change parameters on the fly.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys sandbox games, sci-fi games, or survival games. I would gladly buy it again for the full price.

Portal 2 is one of my favorite games of all time. Great characters, funny dialogue, fantastic gameplay mechanics, and a surprisingly deep story. While Portal kind of felt like a glorified tech demo, Portal 2 really feels like a full game.
The only real complaint is that aside from achievements there's really not much replay value unless you want to experience the story again. However, the Perpetual Testing Initiative DLC will provide hours upon hours of additional gameplay ranging from simple additional chambers to entirely new stories. I would also suggest checking out some of the stand alone mods such as Portal Stories: Mel and Thinking with Time Machine.
Great game all around, honestly good job devs.

TL;DR Fun game now, should be a fantastic game later. If you have AMD products wait for them to fix it.
Let's start off addressing the elephant in the room, AMD performance.
My specs are as follows:
NVidia GTX 970 4GB
16 GB of Corsair Vengence ram.
AMD FX-6300 6-Core CPU
Now with that setup I can run just about any modern game at Ultra 1920x1080 60+fps.
So I thought Squad would be no different. Squad seemed to agree with me, when it ran it's diagnostics
it set the settings on ultra.
So, I booted up the firing range; 120 FPS.
"Wonderful", I thought.
So, I joined a server and saw why everyone was complaining; 28fps with lag dips constantly taking me down to 5-10 fps for short moments.
A little sleuthing told me that it may be a problem with the audio engine. So, I edited an INI and changed a setting or two.
I scored 2 extra frames per second.
At this point you may be wondering why I would reccommend this game. "Why Zach", you might tell me, "If what you say is true, it's garbage; unplayable!" To which I would respond with this retort, "but it fun tho".
The game is incredibly fun, even with the lag spikes and poor frame rates.
For early access and only being in alpha, the game is coming along very well.
Graphics are mostly pleasing right now, although improvements should be made.
Audio is fantastic, everything really sucks you in.
Gunplay is great, bullets have a realistic damage model and bullet drop. Yet it isn't like Arma where I felt I couldn't hit anything.
What really makes this game for me though is the community. Most everyone is friendly, and I have yet to hear someone claiming to have "done the copulation" with my mom.
The complaints I have right now include:
AMD performance
Can be really difficult to see enemies.
Textures and general muddiness in the graphical area.
Overall this game is amazing. All it needs to make it a must have for anyone interested in more realistic style shooters is better performance.
It's worth getting right now if you are running an NVidia-Intel setup but if you have anything AMD, wait for them to fix it.

My favourite moment so far happened in my second game. My squad pushed up through a town, but quickly got pushed back by the enemy. I found myself alone in a compound in enemy territory. I was too scared to move, and expected to meet the enemy any moment. Nothing happened. Just the distant crackling of gunfire and explosions. I decided to make a run for it back to my own lines. Leaving the compound, I spotted two men on a rooftop. They were facing away from me, so I knew they were bad guys. I layed down in the grass and fired a few rounds at them. This seems to have angered them, as they quickly spotted me and the ground around me came alive with landing bullets. I moved behind a wall and waited for them to hunt me down. A soldier ran through some bushes towards me, and I fired. Sadly, the rounds hit the wall in front of me as I didn't realise my rifle wasn't quite peeking over the top. I stood up as the enemy began spraying machine gun fire at me. I ran sideways firing back hoping to shoot him in the face. We were about six metres apart and we hit everything apart from each other. Deciding I was outgunned, I ran back into the compound and hid, where eventually my squad advanced back to.
10/10 I'd run and hide again.

Castle Crashers is a brilliantly drawn, faced-paced and now 60fps delight. Knights, magic, humour and poo, all roll-up nicely into this side-scrolling quest to resuce the princeses and defeat the evil wizzard. The art sytle is brilliant, all drawn in Flash too, so it is crisp and clear. The soundtrack is also really good, and twins well with the quirkiness of the game. Characters are surprisingly well developed and unlockable characters are achived through gameplay rather than DLC (although there are a couple of characters available via DLC too). Each has their own style, weapon and their own magic abilities that become availble through leveling up.
Controls are easy to grasp, and mastering the combos is a case of learning on the job. The humor is at a level that children and adults will find amusing, which is why I recommend playing this with your kids. My daughter loves Castle Crashers, and will forever ask me to play so she can level up her favorite characters.
I hope a Castle Crashers 2 will be on the books at somepoint in the future. For now at least there is very little like this, and as such Castle Crashers will be a timeless classic. Highly recommended

Great PvP, I appreciated this style and think more games should use it, the style inspires a LOT more tactical planning and coordination than most FPS shooters these days. And an amazing feature is a playtime currency, which you keep until you log out, or spend it, making an obstacal for the annoying players that waste the vehicles in other games by doing stupid things like, wasting a vehicle on just themselves or just completely obliterating an air vehicle for just one kill. The temporary currency is also great, because it restricts the number of Maxes (The Exo-Suit Class, standard with a minigun and Heavy Grenade Launcher) that can be deployed. Although, the curreny is difficult as fudge to achieve if you want a new weapon or an expensive upgrade, it is a SERIOUS pain to grind the currency if your saving up for base unlocks too, costing 1000 for each base item unlock. Also, the character customization is severly limited, only allowing you to set your Faction and Face in the beginning, and only your Helmet, Body Armor, Decal, and Camo, which you need the buyable currency to unlock almost all of the customization gear, limiting players who can't afford currency to the devastatingly few helmets that are unlocked through ranking up. But it is still an amazingly massive scale game with different biomes and opponents that always keep you on your toes. So, in short, this game has its downs, but it is ASTOUNDING none the less.

Dirty Bomb. Dirty Bomb is a free to play first person shooter. I know many games with that tag have a bad rep, micro-transactions making them pay to win and them being low quality games. Dirty Bomb, on the other hand is different.
If I had money to spend in this game, can I spend it to improve my game? Yes, but the increase would be so minor it is non-existent. The game isn't a pay to win game. It is reliant on skill, similar to CS:GO. If I had an encounter with somebody and they won, that means they were better than me in that point in time, maybe a better aim, better positioning, better tactics. Even if I dished out hundredds of dollars into the game, getting every character a cobalt loadout, that doesnt make me a better player. To become a better player you need practice. Even then getting a cobalt is special, but nothing better, due to the fact that the strongest loadouts are bronze, anything above a bronze is just asthetics. A cobalt card wpuld have the same stuff as a bronze loadout, just with a blue gun and other things. Personally, I don't have a cobalt, but I have a gold, the step below. The difference between them is the colour of their equipment. If I compared a bronze and a cobalt, they would be the same. The exact same, other than maybe different guns BUT, they have the same amount of perks which is what defines a default, lead iron, bronze and higher. a default ahs 0 perks. A bronze has 3.
It is nearly a purely skill based game, witha  bit of luck, and a bronze default difference. This game is probably one of the best, if not THE best free to play first person shooter out there. Now for the Pros and Cons.

RimWorld is gold. If you like simulations and emergent gameplay, similar but not identical to Dwarf Fortress, this game is an absolute gem. I really hope the developer keeps adding additional gameplay mechanics, but even if they don't this is an outstanding simulation/survival/sandbox game as it exists today.
I originally played the default game mode where you have 3 colonists from the start, just to learn the game a little. I came back and started over with the solo colonist because I figured it would be an easier way to start with just one person and it was. So far it has been awesome. I spent a while using my single colonist working on a simple home and camp. Then I was notified someone was fleeing pirates and I could either help them or ignore them, I chose to help. I killed the pirates chasing her and then found out she was a cannibal. Unexpected to say the least. Later someone decied to join my colony, she was also a cannibal, we're talking 2/3 are cannibals and I never had any say in this, it was emergent. Suddenly I'm dealing with a colony that is mostly cannibals. So now when pirates raid me or folks fall from the sky in cargo pods that I can't get to right away, well.... lets just say they don't go to waste, in a disturbing kind of way ;)
This game is awesome, it's worth the money if you like this sort of thing, if you like Dwarf Fortress and just wished it had reasonable graphics and a far better interface (like use of mouse), this is your game, hands down. It's not as detailed as Dwarf Fortress, but it's also not shallow either.
I won't go into all the details but suffice to say:
- Detailed control over everything you build, down to the walls and doors
- Detailed control over your colonists, when they should sleep, what activities they are responsible for, etc.
- Use based skill system, the more a colonist uses a skill the better they are at it
- Detailed control over combat, control where your colonist goes and whom they target
- Emergent game play; colonists traits and weaknesses when observed will encourage you to do things you probably wouldn't normally do; some colonists would rather wield a ranged weapon, others would rather be awake at night rather than day
The ONLY thing I can complain about, is the lack of height, Dwarf Fortress supports multiple levels of elevation, but this game only supports one, it's a missed opportunity, but I understand the complexities of supporting it, it's a bit of a bummer but at the same time, it's a hell of a lot more manageable this way as well.

Ok, so everybody seem to love this game, so even though I think it is good and do recommend it, I will talk about what I don't like about the game and what actually bothered me with it.
Again, great game is worth your time. Perhaps you'll find the views below interesting:
This game is inspired by Portal in terms of mechanics. Sure, the mechanics are different, but you still feel at home if you have played portal. It is clear what the inspiration comes from. The game even makes nice references to that series in a couple of easter eggs. I mention this because even though this game is "seemingly" a bit more deep and clever in its story, I still find portal massively a better game in terms of length, atmosphere, story and mechanics. Sure it is developed by a studio with a different budget but I think what I don't like about this game has little to do with budget.
Mechanics and time:
This game massively overstays its welcome. Sure, the puzzle are fun, but after a while you start thinking, "there is more still?" And even if you complete the main storyline, there is still tons of extras if you feel like searching every nook and cranny for extra stars which will lead to other levels which will lead to more stuff. I tell you, finding all stars is only for people with lots of time and patience, and perhaps not too many other games in their library. You might say, there is lots of value in this game, you get a lot to do. Yes, but its gets boring and tedious. Harder puzzles are not so much more clever as actually just more work. Not fun, work. All the mechanics have already been played out two thirds into the game and then it just becomes repetitive.
Story:
I applaud the story and the route it takes. Clearly inspired by theology around the world, especially a more eastern philosophy, mainly mahaya Buddhism mixed with with european modernism. It is interesting and it keeps you playing even though you are tired of the puzzles. You fly through the puzzles as fast as you can just to find out what is going on next. But the timing is again slow, and you have to play this game in several installments to get through.
The games asks interesting questions that makes you reflect and this is good, especially for a conventional or pre-modern, prerational mind who is ready to grow. But if you are interested in philosophy beyond modernism and post-modernism the game becomes quite frustrating storywise, because this game is not for you. None of the questions or answers given are within that field of view beyond modern/post-modern values, so you just start to click some answers that you don't agree with just to get the story to move on. There are no answers that you would like to give. And then you get insulted for picking any answers (that the game has provided for you.)
Even though I get the idea of the questions, it feels a little cheeky to create questions and answers that are all wrong just to "teach" you something new, and then hoping you have gained some kind of enlightenment at them end. nope...
Yes, the has some interesting points, and it uses nice artefacts/myths to play with your mind, but it is a little forced down your throat for my taste, and also not too great if you think there is more to the world than the reniassance. Something far much more intersting would be to incorporate lower memes and values in a bigger view rather than just deconstructing everything in the past and throw it away. One's current view is still based on the a previous one and so just erasing the older point of view and your ground is crumbling. A metaphore that is actually really beautifully done in the game, and one of its highlights, but still not very enlightening (to me.) Oh well, this discussion is perhaps for another time. I just thought this game wants to go deep so...
I find that the swapper did a much better job in going deeper and being actually interesting. Much more room for interpretation there.

My review for Max Payne 2 can be seen here:
In short great gameplay confounded and♥♥♥♥♥♥on by multiple core flaws to keep you from said gameplay.
The actual fall of Max Payne. This is Max Payne 1 (In terms of mechanics and him suddenly not being over the death of his wife or any of the lessons learned in Max Payne 2.) with some interesting modernizations to the formula and fancy graphics. That said it's bogged down with more slow (mostly unskippable) badly written cutscenes than slomo. First the good. Unlike many of Rockstars ports prior to 2012 it's well optimized has a plethora of settings and looks excellent other than a couple of REALLY low res textures in the favela that you can actually notice large pixels on (that probably exist thanks to this games long turbulant development and it's console counterparts).
While the amount of weapons you can carry has been capped to three it's done in an interesting "realistic" way and the actual gunplay and act of shooting and being shot at by pretty intelligent AI is better (for the most part) than ever before! Which is why it's a shame that it's so broken up by cutscenes that are mostly unskippable to hide the loading it does in the background. Here's an example: Max talks to himself; some of the words he enuciates appears as text on the screen and then bad guys wander in while Max talks about it. They see Max and open fire and then you start playing. Not so bad so far right? You kill everyone an- oh another cutscene!? Again guys enter the room Max talks about how dumb he is for letting this happen rinse and repeat with no skipping even after you've beaten the game.
This destroys the pacing most if not all of the time and any other smartly designed game would have you enter the room yourself and see the bad guys (Possibly even overhear them talking) and let you shoot them but in Max Payne 3 even 5 guys entering a room or opening a door is a momentous occasion worthy of a cutscene as opposed to just letting a player see or do these things for themselves to begin with.
This is the biggest issue stopping you from enjoying it because more often then not you'll be watching than playing which in it of it's self wouldn't be an issue if you could skip them but even if you have already have seen the cutscenes or are replaying the game you still can't skip them. Even Kojima wouldn't pull such a stunt! The closest you'll get is New York Minute but even then cutscenes will play and still be unskippable for the most part. Worse yet, the story is actually pretty bad if you are even paying attention. Hell even if you aren't because of them being 90% unskippable you can't even force yourself not to. I'd get into more detail about the story but I guess you'll just have to take my word on it or see it for yourself (I don't wan't a headache).
If you wan't great shooting, an interesting story that can be skipped at leisure and don't mind dated graphics play Max Payne 1.
If you wan't great shooting, great graphics and don't mind a badly written poorly told story via unskippable cutscenes play Max Payne 3.

Great game when it runs. Continuing from the great story telling of the past games MP3 pics up at a time that appears to be several years after the events of the last game. You start out down in Brazil protecting a young wife and her older rich husband at a party. The story jumps around a little by including flashbacks and skipping forward a few days after some incounters. Max's look also changes from his self-admitted crappy suit back to his leather jacket from the earlier games to later his bald head and flowery shirt.
The story telling has always been fantastic in this series and it is well done here as well. This time largely with voice overs from Max himself while you play, vs. the comicbook style images in the past. But it is as good as previous games and some notable names/characters pop up from past games.
The game/gun-play are really solid here, since the game is in 3rd person and you see Max on screen it's great how they handled his weapons. You're always wearing a dual pistol holster on your chest and it's seen at times but they stick to that by keeping you limited to a max of 2 pistols which can include Mac-10s or other automatic pistols. You can also pick up 1 long barrel gun, be that a shotgun, AK-47, submachine gun, grenade launcher, sniper rifle, etc. If you are carrying that gun and want to use a pistol you then hold it in the other hand, if you want to dual-wield then you drop the long gun. It's a nice touch and better than seeing a gun on his back or disappearing/reappearing out of his back or thin air.
Graphics are good, nothing amazing but certainly not lacking. The screen 'tears' at times in both cutscenes and gameplay, but that is the look they're going for so it's not an issue, but did bother me a few times. I get that b/c Max is a drunk and you're not looking through his eyes (FPS) then I think they use that for effect and realism.
As mentioned I've had issues getting the game to run. I run Windows 8.1 and at first it ran fine, I had to stop AMD's Raptr game tracking tool to get the game to work, but once I figured that out it would run fine. Then it started crashing. At first it was randomly during cut scenes, then I reached the only QTE in the game and it would crash each time I failed (wasn't expecting the QTE and I use a Nostromo so I wasn't sure of the mapped buttons). Then it started to fail to load, crashing after the title screen. So I've been in touch with Rockstar's support and they've helped but as of this writing I've been able to play it once in the last week and am on the final chapter of the game. Hopefully it'll get resolved for me so I can at least finish the story and game that I've otherwise enjoyed so far.

TL;DR Fun game now, should be a fantastic game later. If you have AMD products wait for them to fix it.
Let's start off addressing the elephant in the room, AMD performance.
My specs are as follows:
NVidia GTX 970 4GB
16 GB of Corsair Vengence ram.
AMD FX-6300 6-Core CPU
Now with that setup I can run just about any modern game at Ultra 1920x1080 60+fps.
So I thought Squad would be no different. Squad seemed to agree with me, when it ran it's diagnostics
it set the settings on ultra.
So, I booted up the firing range; 120 FPS.
"Wonderful", I thought.
So, I joined a server and saw why everyone was complaining; 28fps with lag dips constantly taking me down to 5-10 fps for short moments.
A little sleuthing told me that it may be a problem with the audio engine. So, I edited an INI and changed a setting or two.
I scored 2 extra frames per second.
At this point you may be wondering why I would reccommend this game. "Why Zach", you might tell me, "If what you say is true, it's garbage; unplayable!" To which I would respond with this retort, "but it fun tho".
The game is incredibly fun, even with the lag spikes and poor frame rates.
For early access and only being in alpha, the game is coming along very well.
Graphics are mostly pleasing right now, although improvements should be made.
Audio is fantastic, everything really sucks you in.
Gunplay is great, bullets have a realistic damage model and bullet drop. Yet it isn't like Arma where I felt I couldn't hit anything.
What really makes this game for me though is the community. Most everyone is friendly, and I have yet to hear someone claiming to have "done the copulation" with my mom.
The complaints I have right now include:
AMD performance
Can be really difficult to see enemies.
Textures and general muddiness in the graphical area.
Overall this game is amazing. All it needs to make it a must have for anyone interested in more realistic style shooters is better performance.
It's worth getting right now if you are running an NVidia-Intel setup but if you have anything AMD, wait for them to fix it.

Give me hate and all, but this game is pretty good. and i'll give you a few reasons why and why not you should play it:
Good:
1: fun.
having fun is the goal of the game, and it's quite enjoyable, from older players to ones who just started.
2: creativity
yes. there are crap bots out there, sometimes shaped like crap itself, but as long as you enjoy making your bot, it'll be fine.
3: games
There are a few gamemodes as of new years eve 2016. i will be counting all other modes where you don't quite fight:
EDIT: where you build your bot and color it if need be
TEST: where you test your bot. press numpad + and - to see the overclocker levels and how it affects your guns.
TUTORIAL: Learn the basics of how to play. once done, you get a crate.
AI bots: basically singleplayer deathmatch.
Deathmatch: you and 4 other players fight aginst a team of 5. first to 25 points, or the most points before time runs out wins.
Battle arena: basically capture the flag. you each have a tower, and there are 3 other towers in the map. you win by destroying the other team's tower.
League: same thing as battle arena, but the game ranks you on how well you do in general.
Brawl: a gamemode where the rules change from time to time.
4: Early access
the game is still evolving and growing, despite the community not enjoying it.
Bad:
1: Crates.
there are crates that can contain parts. fron rusty to protonium, you can get parts for free.
you need premium to get the full power of the crate though (the top row)
2: Rarity
each weapon now has their own rarity, based off of how common you get them from the crates.
there are 5 types:
common (white), uncommon (green), rare (blue), epic (purple), and legendary (yellow)
3: the community
i've seen terrible reviews of understandably bad games, but for this game, it's a mixed bag, leaning towards the negitive now. most of the players are decent, but some *ahem* suck.
4: premium.
if you want all 16 colors, if you want 3X recycle rates, if you want the top row of crates, then you gotta get PREMIUM.
the game can be played F2P, but you sometimes gotta cave in. you may spend mabey a few bucks for a few days, but it'll run out.
go for the most expensive, but worth it option: premium for LIFE. now, you'll never have to worry about having to renew your monthly premium with your well earned money.
Overall, very great game, awesome weapons, and ENDLESS creativity.

My favourite moment so far happened in my second game. My squad pushed up through a town, but quickly got pushed back by the enemy. I found myself alone in a compound in enemy territory. I was too scared to move, and expected to meet the enemy any moment. Nothing happened. Just the distant crackling of gunfire and explosions. I decided to make a run for it back to my own lines. Leaving the compound, I spotted two men on a rooftop. They were facing away from me, so I knew they were bad guys. I layed down in the grass and fired a few rounds at them. This seems to have angered them, as they quickly spotted me and the ground around me came alive with landing bullets. I moved behind a wall and waited for them to hunt me down. A soldier ran through some bushes towards me, and I fired. Sadly, the rounds hit the wall in front of me as I didn't realise my rifle wasn't quite peeking over the top. I stood up as the enemy began spraying machine gun fire at me. I ran sideways firing back hoping to shoot him in the face. We were about six metres apart and we hit everything apart from each other. Deciding I was outgunned, I ran back into the compound and hid, where eventually my squad advanced back to.
10/10 I'd run and hide again.

Played for several years now (going on about 5 now actually, including the Beta/Alpha timeframe. Even bought premium time which i regret ever since it ran the hell out. Keep getting beggar-like messages from them insisting i need to get it back every time i log in, like Warthunder does.) racking up a little over 6,000 hours or so total over the span of 4 accounts. (recent mods changing the rules and banning people when they get killed has always been an issue in this game, talking to the support desk gets nowhere.)
So I'm going to be extremely blunt about this game when i review it. I'll break it down into 3 parts. Pros/Cons, personal view, and overall experience. Here we go:
Pros:
* strong emphasis on team-work when you want to get something done
* each faction has varied weapons available only to them.
* Air and ground vehicles for rapid deployment available
* Full control over how your character is outfitted with weapons, vehicles and attachments (player freedom)
* MASSIVE continental warfare all of which you can walk to (if you have the time to do so.)
* Large community
* Continental victories give bonuses to the winning side, which makes later combat more challenging (a good thing)
* Earn income slowly through killing and helping your team (engineer/medic) which urges players to play their classes like they should be played. (Still doesn't happen though)
Cons:
* Toxic chat
* horrid optimization for a game that has been out so long
*Steep learning Curve when it comes to flight. You will crash
* Help desk needs some work when it comes to working swiftly on issues. Retrieving an account from a false-pretense ban can take months and tends to be useless if you didn't pay money in the account.
* Mods/Admins who play the game regularly, especially on Vanu and occasionally on TR and NC, tend to ban players if they are killed repeatedly by the same individual under the pretense of "hacking"
* Excessive vehicle spam (would be okay it Vanu weren't so damn ridiculous with their 2 shot plasma tanks and Scythe with fast firing plasma pods.)
* mega-servers (meaning Asia players mixed with Russia/U.S players) cause severe lag when in a fight if you engage in a Zerg-battle (96+ allied/enemy battle Happens often in Bio-domes). Makes fighting a living hell when you shoot someone only to find out they never hit, but they killed you.
* Severe faction Bias. Vanu have plasma related weaponry, making Terran Republic and  Conglomerate excessively out classed. Not only this but they have the only aircraft capable of hovering practically nose-down on a target, with a splash/high damage plasma pod launcher dual-wing setup that leaves little to no ability of avoidance. This leads to very.... well, one-sided dog-fights *and* ground assaults. (will be hitting this hardest in my personal experience, having played all 3 factions.)
* Unreliable team communication, due to it being basically a giant free-for all Hardcore Deathmatch from Call of Duty. (Friendly fire DOES HAPPEN. It happens a LOT on the New Conglomerate.) This isn't a game problem, more of a player coordination problem.
* Extensively updated, little to no true value per update. Latest "big" update was the ability to make your own outposts, which is nice, the rest has just been behind-the-scenes work that you don't really notice nor think is needed unless it works to bring the Vanu a more balanced gameplay feel to them compared to the other two factions.
* Income is earned so slowly that 3 hours of gameplay, if your NC or Terran, will only net you around 2k credits. Whereas an *hour* flying a scythe will net you an equal profit.
Personally i "enjoy" the game, i rage hard as hell on it though from the lack of communication between players.
Now before i go too far into detail let me just make something clear. There are faction-specific weapons. The most common ones you'll encounter from each faction is the Warden and SAW for NC, the Trac-5, T9 - Carv and T7 Chain Mini Chaingun for the Terrans, and pretty much everything on the Vanu is exclusive to the Vanu, not including the weapons with NS in front of the name, meaning they could be used by all factions. Now let's get down to the nit-and-grit shall we?
I spend most of my time playing the New Conglomerate, which is where most of my rage ends up being dispersed, due to the fact that this faction seems to be where the newbies culminate before being brainwashed into the Vanu super-soldiers or Terran Juggernaut.
After 2 years of fighting for the NC, having racked up plenty of kills to consider it a decent faction with some fairly good weapons, (primarily i find the Warden my favorite; being both long range and short range capable but with a controlled fire rate and low recoil.) I grew sick of the raging at the constant blueberry zerg where you'd see 6-10 people die in seconds from a single grenade, medics not doing their job, and engineers running away from a fight the moment they saw a Vanu Max suit. NC Max's also seemed to be run by cowards, refusing to push forward, forcing heavies with their overshield to move forward into the slug-fest only to be knocked back into the pile of blue shielded mechs, now blocking the way to retreat.
So i switched, tried out the Terran. And my god was it like Oil and Water. Terrans have high damage, high RoF, and a semblence of coordination. Their weapons are more accurate to what the NC should be capable of using as well but seem to just flat out lack in all retrospecs. The T9 - Carve having the most freedom of availability and control in the list of weaponry i have played in the Terran, and the most i've killed with. Racking up the same kill-count as my NC in only a *month* of gameplay... It hurt, seeing how easy it was compared to the NC, especially when i could complately destroy an equally skilled Max from the NC, when i'm using a single MRC3 minigun and M1 Cycler switching between them only when reloading the other. But NOTHING compared to the difference i saw in my next test.
After shaming my NC with a TR gun in a single month, my max in the NC in even less time... i switched over to the Vanu. I've dealt with tons of the Vanu bias, even seen the differences in their weaponry. Finding *no* faction wanted to fight them, but the TR seem to actually *help* them in combat, making it extensively one-sided to the NC. And since only the NC seem to actually fight both factions simultaneously on a regular basis, it's rare to see a continent not controlled by Vanu Republic.
Played the Vanu for 3 weeks. using the Polaris (starter gun) and Equinox. out did my NC in 2 weeks, out did the TR in a week after that. I felt filthy. the ease of use for the Scythe compared to the mosquito, the shear obliteration capable from the Magrider and their Max mechs' with dual Nebula loadouts were absolutely insane! I can’t help but question what the hell the developers are thinking when they say that "each faction has their perks" when it's obvious only the Vanu have *any* perks actually worth bragging about. And brag they do, my god the chat was *FULL* of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥talking about how skilled they are as Vanu. The stench of high-classed entitled C-word was almost palpable. I couldn't stand being part of that crowd anymore, and deleted my Vanu character. I switched back to NC, where even though you were severely out classed
.
The developers need to work on actually making the factions special, rather than just clumping 2 sub-pars with an overpowered one and then dumping leftovers onto the middle-man while handing down bread crumbs to the 3rd. (Example: high powered plasma LMG for Vanu, AP capable miniguns to the Terran, and a dinky auto-grenade launcher that has no splash to the NC)
Overall Score: 3/5
Devs: 2/5

So, I've been playing this game since Alpha 8(it's currently 14c). I've certainly put in more than 100 hours, and have tried lots of different kinds of mods, but I mostly prefer a mostly vanilla+vanilla-like mods.
Rimworld has come a long, long way, and it has been consistently fun. The interface has improved quite a bit, and the features added have only made the game grow in depth. I'd still like to see the game move into the Z-axis(elevation) and thus give us the ability to build upwards, or dig underground, but for now being on a single Z-level is fine.
The mental and emotional sophistication of the colonists has improved by leaps and bounds, and where they used to be replacable fodder that you thoughtlessly sent into battle, they are now much closer to organic characters. They have need and relationships with each other. They fall in love and get married(no babies though?). They get into fistfights when they disagree, and care deeply for their pets. They hide in their rooms when someone they care about dies, or if they've seen too much battle. Some of them can be emotionless sociopaths, while others can be nervous wrecks. It makes you feel a lot more interested in replacing lost body parts, and doing your best to help them recover; not so they can be ready for the next fight, but so they can get back to living their lives.
If I have a complaint, it's pet animal AI. When you muster your colony to battle, the animals attend their masters and often hang around in line of fire, regardless of whether you've released them to attack or not. The only alternative at the moment is to attach all the animals to one non-combatant trainer(assuming their animal handling skill is high enough to handle the highest-skill-req animal) and keep that trainer well away from the battle, reducing your manpower. All I need is the ability to quarantine non-battle animals, or to get them to get behind the gunners until battle has closed to melee.
All in all, I think that Rimworld has a ton of love and care put into it already, and the potential for more only continues to unfold. Built in mod support allows for tons of expandability, and years of continuous development seems to only be ramping up rather than slowing down. This is a game that seemingly started out as a Dwarf Fortress-like in space with a better interface, and is quickly turning into its own legend as a uniquely PC-gaming experience. You could wait for the game's official release, but I will say now: the game is wonderful in its current state, and looks like it will only get better.

I was apprehensive when I bought Wolfenstein: TNO, as the "World War II FPS" angle has been played out time and time again since the original Wolfenstein 3D was released.  However, I was more than pleasantly surprised at the experience I've had.  Rarely do I ever spend $60 on a game and think it was worth it, but this was one of those occasions.  Fast-paced gameplay (whether you stealth in with a knife, or sprint down the halls blowing Nazi limbs off with twin shotguns), a catchy soundtrack, and great voice acting breathe life into what is arguably the gold standard for First-Person Shooters in this generation of console technology.
My one gripe is that the game is just that- a console port.  If you're picky, you may want to use a gamepad.  That being said, this game was a thrill ride and worth every penny.  If you can catch it on sale, good for you, but if you're on the fence and have $60 to burn I think you'll be satisfied with the purchase.

Each time you play a new session you get very random events and starting conditions, although you can tweak the settings before you start. Yesterday I had 3 colonists start completely nude in a subtropical area and had to build shelters in the ruins of some small town I found. After a while they had built up a nice little village (we had 4 settlers by then, we found a person wandering and they joined us). We even traded with passing traders and captured a raider who was attacking our village (he decided not to join us so we let him go, but we stole all his stuff). Hunted some beaver-things that were suddenly eating all the trees, made clothing out of their pelts, discovered some secret weapons someone had left behind in the old village, tamed some pets, had 3 different crops growing, life looked good.
But then disaster! First we had these giant lightning strikes that set ground fires which burned a lot of trees, animals and plants nearby, including ones with food. One of the colonists was a secret pyromaniac and decided to "help" after the stress of firefighting but we got her under control. Then we had a flash freeze so our crops that were outside all died, then (because they were starving) I had my colonists try to hunt a giant beast, which proceeded to kill two of the colonists. One surviving colonist went mad from the shock and tried to attack the other (and the pets) and was disabled by a pet warthog she attackd. So then finally the one guy left tried to do all the chores but went a little nuts with all the death and started wandering until a Worg (yes a giant wolf thing) ate his face. Poor guy had already lost an eye and a pinky toe (literally) due to an earlier fight with beasts so that was just the last straw. Hah, I had no more colonists then.
So that's an example of a 2 day game session I had. Every game is different. You can have different numbers of starting survivors with different conditions and skills and choose which AI will manage the events, also where you get to land on the planet. Different starting locations can have different climates, resources, plants/animals, and people (or even just the ruins of them).
Random events can range from weather issues, raiders (think of Borderlands), traders, crazed animals, rampaging robots, secret caches from ruins, diseases, madness, just all sorts of stuff. Also randomly you get drops of stuff that land from your old destroyed ship in orbit. Each colonist has different skills which determines what jobs they can do. Some colonists don't like to pick up things, some can heal people, some like to do research or train animals or plant things, etc. Also, each person has their breaking point or mental issues. Some like animals, or hate people or like to start fires, or get PTSD of different sorts. For example traumatic events or just nasty surroundings (like dead corpses lying around or dirty/bloddy buildings) can cause people to freeze up, wander randomly, attack others, or do bad things (like the Pyro). I once even had a weird alien probe send out a signal that made only females suddenly get more aggravated. Weird things like that.
It may not be the typical sort of game you guys play but it's very much like a rogue-like RPG but with multiple characters. You get a little bit of strategy and city building and plenty of combat, plus you have to research the higher level technologies. You can even research to build a new ship and have your people escape but it takes a bit of work and a lot of luck to survive.
