Wow. Max Payne 3 has as much action and explostions as a movie directed by Hollywood's Michael Bay. The game is a 3rd person action game that follows in the vein of the previous two Max Payne games.
Story: The story continues on from Max Payne 2. Now, Payne is no longer living in New York City and decides to move to Sao Paulo, Brazil for a fresh start. But, little does he know that the family he is working for is not exactly what it seems and the dark plot unravels itself as you progress through the game. The tale is intriguing and you will find yourself wanting to move from one chapter to the next. Each chapter is paced well so they do not feel too short or too long and the action is plentiful. As you reach the end of the game, the story takes a really dark turn and this is reminiscent of the older Max Payne games which I think is good that the developers retain the essence of what makes this franchise great.
Graphics: The visuals are great for a game released in 2012. Each character model is highly detailed with realistic cloth, hair and skin textures and the environments are great too. They really capture the atmosphere of Brazil and are beautifully rendered in high definition and vibrant colours that pop off the screen. Even in 2015, the graphics are still impressive and hold up well to today's standards.
Gameplay: This is the meat and potatoes of any Max Payne game. The action is frantic, cool to watch and most importantly fun. It is super satisfying to use shootdodge and see time slow around you (especially in specific action set pieces) while you take out heaps of enemies at once. Shootdodge is a great feature and is particularly useful when you have multiple enemies that are flanking you, or simply have no cover. On that note, Max Payne 3 implements a new cover system that lets you hide behind environment and shoot blindly at your enemies. I believe this works really well to add to the realism of the game, and ultimately make it more enjoyable (i.e so that you don't run head first into a firefight, but inspect your surroundings first).
Overall, Max Payne 3 is an amazing action game that ranks highly with other similar games such as Uncharted 2. It provides a fitting send off to one of gaming's most troubled heroes.

Max Payne 3 is the sequel to Max Payne 2, but was the wait worth it ? We play as Max Payne. Max is a man with nothing to lose, after losing his wife, daughter and his lover Mona Max quits his job and turns to a life of drinking and abusing painkillers but then one day a man named Passos offers Max a job in Brazil to protect a wealthy family and Max accepts, but the job turns from a simple protection job into a battle with the local law enforcement, private military and local gangs. So how is Max Payne 3 ? This is a fantastic sequel and probably one of the best third person shooters ever made. The game looks outstanding the environments feel alive with people in the city. When the gun battles begin all civilians run to hide, close the windows. The gameplay is very similar to previous Max Payne titles. In Max Payne there is no health regen. You have a health bar in the shape of Max in the side of the screen and during battle it fills up. You can use painkillers to heal yourself. There's also the last stand kill. When Max sustains too much damage he goes into slow motion and you can kill your shooter by shooting him. It will revive you and give a portion of your health back. The game has a cover system which will help you a lot cause the game is pretty difficult even on the lower difficulties. The game has a few bugs that are incredibly minor. The multiplayer is dead. I had to wait ten minutes to get inside a team death match and the game is filled with hackers. Overall Max Payne 3 is a very good game. Amazing story, great gun play and amazing graphics make this one of the best rockstar games ever. Well worth the money. I give Max Payne 3 a 9/10

Squad even in its early stages, has been able to find the perfect medium in the market between fast paced shooters and the more complex simulations like Arma 3.  I was really glad to see the implementation of ballistic physics such as bullet drop and also bullet travel time.  Yes, bullets don't automatically teleport to your target like in 90% of todays shooters today.  I've heard people refer to Squad as a "running/walking simulator", and if you come into this game with a counterstrike mentality, I assure you, it will be. The devs have managed to create a very realistic feeling tactical shooter, but stopped short of the clunkiness and overcomplicated controls that often come with that.  Graphically, the game needs some improvement.  in area's around buildings and when looking at close terrain, it already has an acceptable amount of detail, but when viewing off to the distance, it does look a little barren (Yes much of the game is focused around empty wilderness but I'm referring to textures).  That said, the devs are clearly focused on getting the bare skeleton of the game right before looking into cosmetics, and in my opinion, they have got it right.  Game performance for me has been excellent, but I do have  high end machine.  I have heard complaints that people have performance issues on AMD machines. Though this may have been addressed by now, it's worth doing a little research before clicking on the buy button.  Playerbase so far has been welcoming and mature, but fun to play with.
This game has real scale, so be prepared to travel with your squad. If seeing an enemy to shoot at around every corner is what you're looking for, then Squad is definitely not for you.  It's an expensive game for one so early in development.  Is the price justified at this stage? I think it may be a little high for some if you're looking for instant "pick up and play".  I wasn't under any illusions about what to expect though.  I bought this game because I know that buying it was inevitable at some stage.  It has a great dev team who are focused on the long haul, and have experience at exactly what they are doing.

Wow. Max Payne 3 has as much action and explostions as a movie directed by Hollywood's Michael Bay. The game is a 3rd person action game that follows in the vein of the previous two Max Payne games.
Story: The story continues on from Max Payne 2. Now, Payne is no longer living in New York City and decides to move to Sao Paulo, Brazil for a fresh start. But, little does he know that the family he is working for is not exactly what it seems and the dark plot unravels itself as you progress through the game. The tale is intriguing and you will find yourself wanting to move from one chapter to the next. Each chapter is paced well so they do not feel too short or too long and the action is plentiful. As you reach the end of the game, the story takes a really dark turn and this is reminiscent of the older Max Payne games which I think is good that the developers retain the essence of what makes this franchise great.
Graphics: The visuals are great for a game released in 2012. Each character model is highly detailed with realistic cloth, hair and skin textures and the environments are great too. They really capture the atmosphere of Brazil and are beautifully rendered in high definition and vibrant colours that pop off the screen. Even in 2015, the graphics are still impressive and hold up well to today's standards.
Gameplay: This is the meat and potatoes of any Max Payne game. The action is frantic, cool to watch and most importantly fun. It is super satisfying to use shootdodge and see time slow around you (especially in specific action set pieces) while you take out heaps of enemies at once. Shootdodge is a great feature and is particularly useful when you have multiple enemies that are flanking you, or simply have no cover. On that note, Max Payne 3 implements a new cover system that lets you hide behind environment and shoot blindly at your enemies. I believe this works really well to add to the realism of the game, and ultimately make it more enjoyable (i.e so that you don't run head first into a firefight, but inspect your surroundings first).
Overall, Max Payne 3 is an amazing action game that ranks highly with other similar games such as Uncharted 2. It provides a fitting send off to one of gaming's most troubled heroes.
I'd give the game a 9/10.

Max Payne 3 is the sequel to Max Payne 2, but was the wait worth it ? We play as Max Payne. Max is a man with nothing to lose, after losing his wife, daughter and his lover Mona Max quits his job and turns to a life of drinking and abusing painkillers but then one day a man named Passos offers Max a job in Brazil to protect a wealthy family and Max accepts, but the job turns from a simple protection job into a battle with the local law enforcement, private military and local gangs. So how is Max Payne 3 ? This is a fantastic sequel and probably one of the best third person shooters ever made. The game looks outstanding the environments feel alive with people in the city. When the gun battles begin all civilians run to hide, close the windows. The gameplay is very similar to previous Max Payne titles. In Max Payne there is no health regen. You have a health bar in the shape of Max in the side of the screen and during battle it fills up. You can use painkillers to heal yourself. There's also the last stand kill. When Max sustains too much damage he goes into slow motion and you can kill your shooter by shooting him. It will revive you and give a portion of your health back. The game has a cover system which will help you a lot cause the game is pretty difficult even on the lower difficulties. The game has a few bugs that are incredibly minor. The multiplayer is dead. I had to wait ten minutes to get inside a team death match and the game is filled with hackers. Overall Max Payne 3 is a very good game. Amazing story, great gun play and amazing graphics make this one of the best rockstar games ever. Well worth the money. I give Max Payne 3 a 9/10

Squad even in its early stages, has been able to find the perfect medium in the market between fast paced shooters and the more complex simulations like Arma 3.  I was really glad to see the implementation of ballistic physics such as bullet drop and also bullet travel time.  Yes, bullets don't automatically teleport to your target like in 90% of todays shooters today.  I've heard people refer to Squad as a "running/walking simulator", and if you come into this game with a counterstrike mentality, I assure you, it will be. The devs have managed to create a very realistic feeling tactical shooter, but stopped short of the clunkiness and overcomplicated controls that often come with that.  Graphically, the game needs some improvement.  in area's around buildings and when looking at close terrain, it already has an acceptable amount of detail, but when viewing off to the distance, it does look a little barren (Yes much of the game is focused around empty wilderness but I'm referring to textures).  That said, the devs are clearly focused on getting the bare skeleton of the game right before looking into cosmetics, and in my opinion, they have got it right.  Game performance for me has been excellent, but I do have  high end machine.  I have heard complaints that people have performance issues on AMD machines. Though this may have been addressed by now, it's worth doing a little research before clicking on the buy button.  Playerbase so far has been welcoming and mature, but fun to play with.
This game has real scale, so be prepared to travel with your squad. If seeing an enemy to shoot at around every corner is what you're looking for, then Squad is definitely not for you.  It's an expensive game for one so early in development.  Is the price justified at this stage? I think it may be a little high for some if you're looking for instant "pick up and play".  I wasn't under any illusions about what to expect though.  I bought this game because I know that buying it was inevitable at some stage.  It has a great dev team who are focused on the long haul, and have experience at exactly what they are doing.

I purchased RimWorld roughly a year ago during the somewhat early stages of its development. And since then I have sunk hundreds (if not thousands) of hours into it before it was finally brought onto Steam. I did not come from a background of Dwarf Fortress of Prison Architect, nor did I believe that I would be a fan of the methodical and careful harvesting, construction and management that RimWorld's gameplay prominently features. I bought into RimWorld because I saw my favorite streamer play it, and it seemed different than the masses of shooters and fighting games that I had invested so much time into.
When I first booted up RimWorld, I sat down with a glass of ice water and familiarized myself with its core gameplay mechanics. Each of your villagers is unique, with varying degrees of aptitude in everything from mining to creating artistic masterpieces. Your job as the player is to assign tasks that these villagers will complete based on their intelligent AI system; it is critical that you carefully manage what tasks are prioritized by which villager in order to ensure that your villagers are constantly working to build and improve your colony. However this is balanced by a Mood system that requires that you also manage your villager's health and recreational levels. That's the basic rundown of the system but I could go on for hours and hours and hours about the intricacies of the game. What's important is that you won't find yourself confused by how the game works at all.
By the time I was wrapping up my first session of RimWorld, I reached over to take a drink from my glass of cold water and realized that all the ice had melted and it was lukewarm. Somehow, nine hours had passed. I was hooked. When a mad boar gored a good man to death, I wept. While my men and women fought with raider scum, I shouted with rage and frustration. And when even in the midst of surviving in a harsh and unforgiving new world, my survivors still found time to find love, I celebrated. There is something beautiful about RimWorld's complex (yet simple) gameplay. It manages to reach out and grab you, to really make you feel invested in the tiny pixels that mill about on your computer screen. It's very appropriate that the game's AI systems are labeled as storytellers, because RimWorld tells a story - your story. How it develops and ends is entirely up to you, and that's what makes RimWorld so goddamned fun. All you need is a playlist of your favorite music and a nice glass of your favorite refreshment and you're ready to create a beautiful new world.
Buy this game. If you have even the slightest interest in base building or city building simulations, or have any sort of history in games of those genres you will enjoy RimWorld thoroughly. It's also incredible how amazing RimWorld's developers are at building and expanding upon the game. These are people who refused to release the game because they felt like the game "needed more features and depth," though I can say with certainty that at the time it had plenty of both. These devs are committed to making this game an amazing one, and I'd recommend you get behind it.

I love the game so far, here are some pros and cons.
+Pros+
+Large game map with a decent design for cover and flanking.
+Guns feel good and are LOUD, seriously it is so tense when you're in a firefight in this game.
+Character models are easy to distinguish from each team. I have had no friendly fire or even close to it in the three long matches I have played in as of the writing of this review.

+Realistic damage as far as I have seen.
-Cons-
-Performance issues, it seems to be poorly optimized and can dip to 25 fps (and I have heard this from many so it is not just me) in intense firefights.
-Map controls are slightly difficult in certain situations.
-It's not the prettiest game out there, some people may think that is a big deal so here it is in the list.
-If you have a bad team it could potentially ruin your enjoyment of the match. Now I haven't run into this problem yet but if you get a team full of people who won't cooperate and work together (trying to play this like COD or something) I'm sure you're not going to enjoy the match.
Overall I love this game to death and will be playing a lot more of it. Hope the devs work out the optimization issues in a short amount of time but other than that it's a great game for anyone who likes realistic tactical shooters in a large open space.

TL:DR Robocraft is a great game go get it.
Robocraft is an extremely diverse game with an everchanging meta and 4 main game modes The Pit, (FFA with respawns) Elimination, (Kill the enemy team no respawns) Battle arena, (Has respawns capture towers and kill the enemy team's Protonium Reactor) and my personal favorite, Team Deathmatch (reach 20 kills before the enemy team does, has respawns).
When you finish a battle you get a crate (Rusted Bronze, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Diamond, Protonium). better crates give you better chances for better items, but your items are still heavily based on RNG. Different game modes give you different amounts of item slots in a crate. Battle Arena gives you 4 slots, Team DeathMatch gives you 3, Pit gives you 3, and Elimination gives you 2. New items help you build a better bot. PLEASE don't use the same cheap rail tank sniper that requires no skill and kills the innovative bots.
Some great Robocraft youtubers are the Memers aka Gromek999, BobDaBiscuit, and jac733. SpaceKryptonite, Robot⇌Engine, and Vesperine32 are fun to watch. Awesomesoul will keep you up to date with Robocraft news.
All the  weapon types in robocraft are Chain Shredders, Proto Seekers, SMGs (The lasers that have like a million tiers, Plasma, Teslas, Ion Distorter/Destabiliser, Railguns, Flak cannons, and Nanos (Healers)

Easy to be part of something big, or a small group, or to go solo and do your own thing. Interesting selection of support roles, as well as support or aggressive vehicles and aircraft. Good looking landscape, love the blasts of differnet weapons flying across my screen!
It's a mix of easy-ish and hard. Hard to get into and really excel at. Takes a bit of getting used to so that you aren't crushed within seconds of stepping onto the battlefield.
There is a tutorial at the start which gives you the very basics. Then all characters, vehicles, and aircraft are unlocked each with their own weapons, tools, and add-ons (armor, grenade/explosive types, med kits, implants) which you can sort of swap around among the different classes (for the most part .... medics can't use sniper rifles, though, for example). With "creds" (points from experience, kills, completing achievements) you can buy new weapons, gear, upgrades.... these aren't necessarily "better" but they offer a different playstyle, for example Infiltrator (assassin) for one faction VR starts off with a semi auto style sniper rifle but you can buy single fire "bolt action" rifles. They're not better, but they're different and take a different play style. In this way you can be super effective as a newbie or as a seasoned player with tons of creds/upgrades.
The only drawback I'd say is that sometimes it can feel like you can't kill anyone, or the other team is just crushing you. This is a mix of learning how to control your fire/shoot within the hitbox, and playing with a good team. Sometimes, though, the other team just has better air support, sniper positions, and more spawn points, and you will be overrun. Just warp to another part of the map and start again.

I'm late to the party by about three years or so on this. I still remember when this came out and I'd always wanted to play it. Well, I finally got it after a few years. Good old summer sales, amirite?
Anyway, this game is immersive, to say the least. The camera angles and views that R* use are quite unordinary, but lovely in their own little way. The time sequencing between changing from normal time to slowed down is quite amazing too. It's not like a typical transition, as it seeps you into it in a way. Attention to detail, on even the small things, are what have established R* as one of my favourite game producers. The way they envision their games, from plot to small details, to even the final design itself, never ceases to amaze me.
To elaborate further on the immsersion, the game is also a bit trippy. Not like a Beetles' music video, but more so like when you sniff a little too much glue while listening to DnB then walk outside. It's a somewhat pleasant immersion. The camera angles offer literal different perspectives, but also show you a different part of the story. In the cutscenes when the protagonist (Max Payne himself) is drunk (he is an alcoholic, if you didn't know), the camera angle switching and the effects they use really are what make them game complete. I mean, it's a typical third-person shooter, with some more-than-usual fluid animations and time sequencing. But, a game is not only about the gameplay, but the story as well (in my opinion). The visual R* use to describe Max's life truly help one relate to him more. Not in an empathetic sense, but more of a sorrow sense. Player-character relation always is important, whether in games or in film.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes any of R*'s previous or newer games. If you enjoyed GTA V's gameplay, but wanted more story, play this. If you enjoyed RDR's smooth gameplay, but wanted something you can relate to more, play this. Actually, whether you've played any of those games doesn't matter. If you're bored and want to play something out of the ordinary, this is something I advise you to consider.

I purchased RimWorld roughly a year ago during the somewhat early stages of its development. And since then I have sunk hundreds (if not thousands) of hours into it before it was finally brought onto Steam. I did not come from a background of Dwarf Fortress of Prison Architect, nor did I believe that I would be a fan of the methodical and careful harvesting, construction and management that RimWorld's gameplay prominently features. I bought into RimWorld because I saw my favorite streamer play it, and it seemed different than the masses of shooters and fighting games that I had invested so much time into.
When I first booted up RimWorld, I sat down with a glass of ice water and familiarized myself with its core gameplay mechanics. Each of your villagers is unique, with varying degrees of aptitude in everything from mining to creating artistic masterpieces. Your job as the player is to assign tasks that these villagers will complete based on their intelligent AI system; it is critical that you carefully manage what tasks are prioritized by which villager in order to ensure that your villagers are constantly working to build and improve your colony. However this is balanced by a Mood system that requires that you also manage your villager's health and recreational levels. That's the basic rundown of the system but I could go on for hours and hours and hours about the intricacies of the game. What's important is that you won't find yourself confused by how the game works at all.
By the time I was wrapping up my first session of RimWorld, I reached over to take a drink from my glass of cold water and realized that all the ice had melted and it was lukewarm. Somehow, nine hours had passed. I was hooked. When a mad boar gored a good man to death, I wept. While my men and women fought with raider scum, I shouted with rage and frustration. And when even in the midst of surviving in a harsh and unforgiving new world, my survivors still found time to find love, I celebrated. There is something beautiful about RimWorld's complex (yet simple) gameplay. It manages to reach out and grab you, to really make you feel invested in the tiny pixels that mill about on your computer screen. It's very appropriate that the game's AI systems are labeled as storytellers, because RimWorld tells a story - your story. How it develops and ends is entirely up to you, and that's what makes RimWorld so goddamned fun. All you need is a playlist of your favorite music and a nice glass of your favorite refreshment and you're ready to create a beautiful new world.
Buy this game. If you have even the slightest interest in base building or city building simulations, or have any sort of history in games of those genres you will enjoy RimWorld thoroughly. It's also incredible how amazing RimWorld's developers are at building and expanding upon the game. These are people who refused to release the game because they felt like the game "needed more features and depth," though I can say with certainty that at the time it had plenty of both. These devs are committed to making this game an amazing one, and I'd recommend you get behind it.

I'm late to the party by about three years or so on this. I still remember when this came out and I'd always wanted to play it. Well, I finally got it after a few years. Good old summer sales, amirite?
Anyway, this game is immersive, to say the least. The camera angles and views that R* use are quite unordinary, but lovely in their own little way. The time sequencing between changing from normal time to slowed down is quite amazing too. It's not like a typical transition, as it seeps you into it in a way. Attention to detail, on even the small things, are what have established R* as one of my favourite game producers. The way they envision their games, from plot to small details, to even the final design itself, never ceases to amaze me.
To elaborate further on the immsersion, the game is also a bit trippy. Not like a Beetles' music video, but more so like when you sniff a little too much glue while listening to DnB then walk outside. It's a somewhat pleasant immersion. The camera angles offer literal different perspectives, but also show you a different part of the story. In the cutscenes when the protagonist (Max Payne himself) is drunk (he is an alcoholic, if you didn't know), the camera angle switching and the effects they use really are what make them game complete. I mean, it's a typical third-person shooter, with some more-than-usual fluid animations and time sequencing. But, a game is not only about the gameplay, but the story as well (in my opinion). The visual R* use to describe Max's life truly help one relate to him more. Not in an empathetic sense, but more of a sorrow sense. Player-character relation always is important, whether in games or in film.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes any of R*'s previous or newer games. If you enjoyed GTA V's gameplay, but wanted more story, play this. If you enjoyed RDR's smooth gameplay, but wanted something you can relate to more, play this. Actually, whether you've played any of those games doesn't matter. If you're bored and want to play something out of the ordinary, this is something I advise you to consider.

If you liked the original AoE II and basically want to replace that game with a slightly better copy (because your CD is gone or wont work), then this is for you.
If you want something different from AoE II, then don't get this because its basically the same.
I used my AOE II CD to play this game on and off on various computers for the last 15 years or so, starting as a kid. When I tried to use it on Windows 8.2, it was no longer compatible so I bought this. I'm happy with it because I would have been happy just to play from the old CD I got in the '90s, but my only curiousity is that this "AoE II HD" appears to be exactly the same as the origial AOE II. Unless my memory is failing me, everything looks exactly the same. They did add some options and clarify some writing in the random map set up, and now I can easily play multiplayer. And I can add free new graphics through community-made add ons. They said they improved the AI. But yeah, other than those things, not much changed, which is fine with me but some people might be expecting something new.
As far as the game itself goes, I've enjoyed this game for a long time. Theres a lot of creative strategies you can make with it (although the army and war based strategies are more robust and varied than more peaceful ones) and a long list of maps types and civilizations that add a lot of spice to your tactics. These sort of 2D graphics arent terrible but theyre not going to really impress compared to the modern 3D endless camera angles style of many games, but this game isnt really about graphics (although some of the community-made stuff is pretty beautiful). It's about strategy, building economy, reliving historial battles, and maybe going head to head with your friends in online multiplayer (or working together as allies to bring down random strangers from across the world lol). Its fun, and replayable. There's a reason I keep coming back to this game for the last decade and a half. :)

I have played the Age of Empires series since I was six. I've played Age of Empires One, Age of Empires Two, Age of Empires Three and then finally age of Empires Two HD Edition. I've also played Age of Mythology, and probably sunk a good few thousand hours in across the whole series.
Age of Empires 2 HD Edition is not exactly a HD edition. The game would probably be better named if they just called it "Steam Edition" in my honest opinion. Rather than just sticking the game on steam and leaving it at that, they also added two new expansions - the African expansion and the Forgotten expansion.
It looks the same as it did before, with new textures for expansion units and buildings. The game sounds pretty much the same too. The gameplay is unaltered as well, so for all intents and purposes this is a repurchase of the old game with steam functionality including achievments, mod support and the expansions - which are the selling points you should focus on, if you're comparing this game to the old one.
The expansions are definately worth it. While i've run into some inexplicable performance issues as of the African expansion, the units, buildings, and civs are definately worth the purchase. The campaigns are... hit and miss, but they're generally pretty alright.
The mods for this game are amazing. Ozhara is definately one to check out if you're interested in exploring and looking at excellent texture and sound upgrades to the game.
As for the achievments... well, i'd honestly say some of the achievments are a little silly, such as losing 50,000 buildings, and winning 100 games with each faction. Now, it did use to be a LOT worse - you used to be able to need to win 1000 games with each civ to get all the cheevs, which thankfully was removed.
All-In-All this game is definately worth the money to purchase it now. The steam implimentation and support for mods, achievments and expansions makes this a solid purchase and a solid, fun experience. Would highly reccomend.

First person puzzlers have been pretty popular since the first Portal, but this one is one of the most polished and beautiful ones I have played. The difficulty curve is not too steep and for experienced players the first few worlds might be a bit too easy. There are bonus stars to collect that require at lot more "out-of-the-box"-thinking though. The "Road to Gehenna"-DLC starts off at at higher difficulty, but is still never frustrating.
From a gameplay standpoint, there are multiple mechanics that are unlocked by progression
You are dropped into multiple hub-worlds containing a few puzzles each. The puzzles are self-contained for their primary objective but might need to be connected to get some easter-eggs and the always-elusive bonus-stars. Each hub has a different architectural design beautifully displayed by the engine that brought you Serious Sam.
From a story perspective, it is absolutely NOT comedy-based like the Portal trilogy but it tries to engage the player in interesting philosophical thoughts while also introducing them to excerpts from classic philosophers. It is not preachy though, but included into the game-world with (skippable) Terminals to interact with.

I've only played this game for a little while but I love it thus far.  The idea of an intelligent and independent robot has fascinated me probably since I was a little boy watching Star Wars for the first time (that is Star Wars IV A New Hope for you whelps...yeah I'm old)...R2D2 is my favorite Star Wars character.   I'm also fascinated by the achievements and lives of ancient Greek scientists and philosophers.  I also enjoy puzzle games so yeah observational bias...I know.   Still...this game has moved me in so many ways - the music is hauntingly beautiful, the setting is perfect, and the story (found at the network terminals or time capsules) is thought provoking.  But most important, for me anyway, while playing this superb game, I've found myself questioning what matters most to me in my own life.  What things do I find meaningful?  What direction is my life headed? Is my course that I chose headed towards ends that that I would consider desirable?  Why don't I trust myself? What motivates me?  I could go on...I will spare you.
In brief this game does what any great artwork should do - make us aware...of what, is up to the individual expereincing it.

I HIGHLY recommend you play on permadeath, as it will make the stories all the more meaningful when every action matters and can't just be rewinded or a previous save loaded.
To summarize what it is like playing:
Game deals you a handful of cards.
"What the hell? These cards are♥♥♥♥♥♥ they literally hate each other and one of them can't even lift anything."
The game stares you dead in the eyes, and says "Deal with it."
And so you do, you overcome challenges and face problems that if given the choice you never would have ended up in the first place having known the game systems and how it works.
In a non-permadeath video game, when I miss-click and accidentally have my doctor amputate the wrong arm on someone, I would reload the save. Here I don't have the option, I instead get to experience the story of what happens when things go wrong, and get to feel the joy of having won despite mistakes or suffer the real crushing feeling of failure when every action matters and there is no rewind. It's a classic sense of 'you made this bed, now you have to sleep in it.'.
Mind you sometimes the game deals you great cards, and when it does, it feels EVEN better because that hand could have been bad, but it wasn't, and every hand counts.

Really surprisingly well done shooter, especially given the relatively poor treatement the franchise had received in the last few years.  The weapons and perk progression are very well balanced out and satisfying, the missions tend to be varied and interesting, and the character progression caught me by surprise in a very good way.
On the techincal side this is running ID's engine so while not completely jaw-dropping, everything is extremely smooth/fast, the mouse control is perfect, and you never slow down/chug in the middle of the action.  The only down side is that for those with higher end displays, the output is locked to 60hz&60fps, and there are no truly effective ways to go beyond to 120/144 etc.  While patches and mods exist, they all have extremely negative side-effects such as doubling all animation speeds in the game etc.
Also one of the only FPS games where getting the collectables is often actually interesting/enjoyable and I wasn't comfortable calling the game 'done' till I hit my 100%.

This is a masterpiece.
It really is. It might not be perfect but it is one of these games that do so many things right. One of these that you complete and you sit back and think "i just witnessed/played something great, something rare".
In the core it has amazing addictive puzzles that will make you scratch your head but not frustrate you (too much, its kinda hard at the end). But what really makes this game shine, the cherry at the top, is the story.
No cutscenes, you are a silent protagonist so you dont speak, just texts to read, a voice that guides you and some interaction with some computer. Thats was enough for me be to be captured in one of the most interesting stories in videogames. This game will make you think. You will read, and then you will explore the world, you will listen and then you will think, even after you stop playing.
It will serve you a really interesting story, a mystery to solve, and will make you really think about what you really are. It will make you question your own humanity.
If you like puzzle games this is a must play. If you do not like puzzle games maybe its time to start liking them.

I have been playing this game since alpha 3.   I estimate, at the time of this posting, that I have put over 500 hours into this game if you include all the different alpha versions.  This game has come a long way and I expect there will be even more to come.   As the game is now, alpha 14 as I write this, it could be considered a complete game when you consider the amount of content.   It will keep you busy for hours.   At $30, it's well worth it.
Basically you start with a few resources and a handful of colonists and eventually grow your colony into something much more.   The end game idea is to build a ship and escape the planet you are on.   But the enjoyment is actually building up your colony and defending it against exterior threats.  There are many threats including raiders, weather events, and starvation/exposure (in the more diffcult biomes like desert and tundra).  Each threat is unique and has systems in the game to deal with them.  You can play any game type you like.   Meaning, you can deactivate threats you find annoying or unbalanced.  You can choose your biome as well.   Perhaps you want to play an easy biome with more raiders?   Or you want to play on the Ice sheet with minimal raiders?  It's up to you.
At the end of the day Rimworld would be labeled a Basebuilder when it comes to genre.   But in reality, there is so much to it than that.  And even if you want to use a mypopic definition like "Basebuilder" when classifying Rimworld that's fine.   Because even within that narrow definition, Rimworld would be the best "Basebuilder" I have ever played.

So, after playing the game for a while now, I really want to write a review, which is rare for me, but sometimes keeps happening ^^
I started to play when a few friends mentioned it to me and urged me to team up with them. Since it is f2p they didn't need to do much convincing, it was definetly worth a try.
I have to admit, that I would have some trouble in the beginning to really get into the game, since there are a lot of parts and the tutorial just covers the basics, but my friends told me what to focus on first and then everything else somehow explained itself. We quickly jumped right into the battle with some simple bots we created. That was the first thing that got me hooked. Even if there aren't that many parts to build your bot at the beginning, you still can manage to build something that fits your style. This works even better if you play as a team, as you can adapt your bot to the needs of the group. Nice!
Some matches later I checked out the payment system out of curiosity and was positivly surprised. In my opinion, it's one of the fairest payment systems that I've ever seen in a f2p game. One the one hand, you really don't miss much, if you don't pay. With premium, you just level up a little faster, get a little more loot and have access to some minor cosmetics. But the gameplay isn't influenced at all. On the other hand, the premium time is very fairly priced (like 3 bucks for 3 days, so you can for example just play premium on weekends, when you actually have enough time to play). If you start playing as much, as I do, I think it's really worth it to support the developers a little and get the before mentioned extras in return. It's also awesome, that I can buy premium for life, if I want to, also for the very reasonable price of a "regular priced game" (50$). You can get that even cheaper if you wait for a sale. I'm only saying that much on this topic, because nowadays fair pricing has really become an issue in the games industry, at least to me.
Back to the game. When I started playing, there were some matchmaking issues leading to unfair balance soemtimes, but with the latest updates it got much better. Now it really feels like I can build nearly anything and still have a chance. I don't  need legendary weapons to rain havoc on my enemies, I can do that from the start. It actually is more about player skill and smart tactics. That's how competetive multiplayer games should be!
I could go on, but it's easier to just try it out yourselves. It's free, it's fun, you can play in short doses or you can spent hours optimizing your bot. With a new bot it's also always a new experience and it's still early access, so it probably will continue to get better. I love what the developers have done so far and I'm looking forward to all future updates.

I've read the reviews made about the game and I also wanted to share my +600 hours experience with you, who are just starting the game, because oh boy this game was hard to learn.
Tutorial is mostly pointless, you'll learn the game by playing it. Don't quit easy!
You won't understand the cert mechanism and you'll look at all the 1000 cert weapons and say 'How in the hell am I supposed to make that many certs?'. Believe me, you can, but it takes practise and time.
You'll suck at air fights. I still suck at air fights, it's just so hard to practise with all the people who MAX upgraded their ESFs and learned all the flank moves, but you can give it a shot.
You'll probably won't be able to kill anyone effectively at the start, eventhough you have other FPS experiences. The fights are nothing like you've seen before.
Tanks and ESFs will be your main enemy in ground fights. You'll be bombed out of nowhere. My main advice is to buy those 2 packs of C4, eventhough it will cost you a fortune at the start. They pay you back, trust me.
Starting weapons are fine. Don't go ahead and buy a 1000 cert weapon. Upgrade your suit and utility slots. The only upgrade i'd suggest you is the bolt action sniper rifles for TR and VS. NC starts with a bolt action anyways.
Playing medic is a great way to make certs, but don't forget to upgrade your healing tool.
If you're looking for a good secondary, any NS pistol should do fine. Commisioner, Underboss or Blackhand. Emissary is an interesting choice as well. TR doesn't really need another pistol because the Repeater is too good already.
Do not initiate any target you see. This is the common sense for most FPS games because your target dies within less than a second, but not in this game. If you're a LA with a carbine and you see a HA 100 meters away from you and you try to gun him down, what will happen is that he'll turn on his NMG, aim between your eyes with his long range effective LMG and kill you before you know it.
Use your utilities. C4s and Concussion Grenades are lifesavers. They can also win a fight right away. If you manage to sneak onto that Prowler(Tank) who just had his 50th killstreak and blow him up with your 2 bricks of C4, you are the hero.
There are tons of things i'm forgetting here buy you'll figure them out by yourself. This is a splendid game and probably the best FPS game that I've ever played. Go for it, try it, you won't regret.

When The New Order was originally announced I was pretty convinced it would be a generic "kill all nazis" shooter that would lack any real depth. I was pleasently surprised when I started playing, however, and found that the game was more story driven and thoughtful than I had given it credit for.
BJ Blazkowics is a soldiers soldier with a jaw made of cinder blocks who's forced pretty suddenly to explore a world where the Nazis won World War 2. The characters are interesting, and BJ becomes a fairly compelling character that doesn't succumb to the Duke Nukem syndrom (the strong hard♥♥♥♥♥that is completely unphased by anything that goes on in the world.) The gunplay is fun, the mechanics of the game are sound, and there are some pretty intense sequences spaced throughout. In the prologue there's a choice that the player is forced to make that, admittedly, caused me to lean back in my chair and really think. This choice affects minor points in the game and does have a presence later on.
The game is not perfect though. As likeable as BJ is throughout the game, he survives events that would kill anyone else and this can sometimes break the immersion. In The New Order, veteran Wolfenstein fans might be disappointed to find that the Supernatural and occult aspects of some of the Wolfenstein games is almost non-existent aside from some allusions to it early in the game. The Nazis won World War 2 through technological superiority instead, though this does (as mentioned above) provide for some intense sequences and fights.
All in all, the game is deeper than it appears to be and there is a healthy amount of humor to be enjoyed. The set pieces are fantastic and the gameplay is solid with a competent story to back it up. Wolfenstein: The New Order is not perfect, but it's worth a play through.

K- I finished "The Talos Principle," and, well: I don't get it.
I am sure that those who believe that the emperor is wearing clothes will say "Oh- you didn't read all the stuff, and are too poorly educated to get the cultural/religious/sociological subtext."
No- I did read everything, and while most of it bored me to tears, I understood all of it. I mean- is the "big surprise" supposed to be that the protagonist is a robot fulfilling a task set for it by human progenitors, thousands of years ago, before humanity was wiped out?
I'm sorry, but that is pretty much made clear, in the first ten minutes of the game- hardly a revelation.
Is the "big surprise" that the game is a meditation on our collective relationship with the divine and the unknowable? Well- I guess such would be a "surprise" to someone of limited philosophical tendencies.
Like I said: within the first ten minutes of the game, you grasp that you are an AI running through a gauntlet set for you, by beings long past. I kept playing, because I hoped- I really hoped- that I'd be able to know what happened to humanity, and the "big payoff" at the end was you bringing humanity back to life.
But no, no, no. The "Big Surprise" of the ending is that humanity is dead (duh,) and you are awake in a dead world (again, we learned this in the first ten minutes of the game.) Not a single word nor snippet of information is imparted about what happened to humanity.
Glad I bought it on a 75% off sale, and didn't pay full price.
One last thing:
If I were setting up an AI to revive at a random point in the future to safeguard all that was human, I wouldn't force the AI to spend day after day collecting "tetris" pieces, in order to learn his purpose.
Throughout the game, you collect recordings of the lead scientist's voice, expressing her doubts and concerns about the Talos project, and humanity's demise. You hear the concern in her voice, as she wonders if what she is working so hard on is for naught.
Perhaps the "big reveal" at the end of "Talos" is that she was right.
It was all for naught- and you're the sucker who wasted his time on earth figuring that out.

First person action shooter. I feel this is some sort of a modern remake of older Wolfenstein titles, with it's own story.
You play as William "B.J." Blazkowicz, a one man killing machine. It's World War ll, and B.J. is a US Army soldier going to war with Germany. As all educated people, we know that Germany was defeated in WW2, but this game follows a different kind of view on history, where Germany actually won the war. To not give anything away, story is straight forward, good guys trying to kill bad guys with some friendly help on the way.
Game has decent variety of weapons: knives, pistols, shotguns, assault rifles, SMGs, sniper rifles, grenades, energy based weapons, turrets that you can carry with you, etc.. You can carry a lot of firepower, as well as use almost any kind of weapon in both hands, for those who like that weapons blazing approach. It's possible to kill enemies silently, via melee/knife takedowns, throwing knives or silenced pistols.
Game has decent amount of secrets, collectibles, side missions. You unlock different kinds of "perks" by completing combat objectives, that grant you some boost to equipment, ammo count, etc.. Game is about 20 hours long if you play casually, with exploring/looting.
Graphically game is decent, with some low resolution textures here and there. People with budget PC's will notice texture streaming (textures loading in while you turn camera), it's the way the engine works and does the textures. Animation quality is good, didn't notice any glitches apart from couple times stuck in vents. Voice acting is good, there's decent amount of character interactions, humor, emotional moments via cutscenes.
To be honest, from all the Wolfenstein games, this one I liked more than others. To close this off, I must warn that game has a lot of torture elements, as well as heavy gore, limb amputation and decapitation, so I don't recommend playing this under game's age limit.

I HIGHLY recommend you play on permadeath, as it will make the stories all the more meaningful when every action matters and can't just be rewinded or a previous save loaded.
To summarize what it is like playing:
Game deals you a handful of cards.
"What the hell? These cards are♥♥♥♥♥♥ they literally hate each other and one of them can't even lift anything."
The game stares you dead in the eyes, and says "Deal with it."
And so you do, you overcome challenges and face problems that if given the choice you never would have ended up in the first place having known the game systems and how it works.
In a non-permadeath video game, when I miss-click and accidentally have my doctor amputate the wrong arm on someone, I would reload the save. Here I don't have the option, I instead get to experience the story of what happens when things go wrong, and get to feel the joy of having won despite mistakes or suffer the real crushing feeling of failure when every action matters and there is no rewind. It's a classic sense of 'you made this bed, now you have to sleep in it.'.
Mind you sometimes the game deals you great cards, and when it does, it feels EVEN better because that hand could have been bad, but it wasn't, and every hand counts.

I may not have played the game too much, so don't take this review as if it's from some hardcore 1000-hour veteran.
I have recently begun playing Robocraft, & I would generally say that it is a fun experience. I find the idea of creating your own vehicle/mech/walker/etc. to use in battle attracting to me, even if it is possible to go into a match with a singular block.
However, if you are hoping to get the most out of this game for free, you may find it difficult, considering the following:
1: Premium is quite expensive if you are willing to have it for an extended period of time.
2: Making any decent amount of "money" ("Robits" are the in-game currency) is close to impossible without premium, as premium allows a 3x multiplier for earnings in recycling, & there is no other way to make money except the factory (which is already close to impossible with a free-to-play made machine)
3: The game is constantly teasing you about what you get with premium (Salvage-crates show you extra items you may receive with premium, most colours only being available with premium, etc.)
I also find it annoying that any first-time player can get his first deathmatch against a premium 5000-hour extreme player (This may change, as the game is still in development).
My last complaint is about map variety, as there are few maps at the time of this review being written.
Do note that all of the criticism in this review is subject to change as the game is in development. For example, multiple maps have been added to the basic gamemode. Still hoping for a matchmaking fix though.
Also, homing missile spammers need to be publicly executed. ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)

Rimworld is a sandbox sci-fi colony sim with elements of tactical combat, resource management, colonist and animal management, research, and disaster mitigation. The game lacks a few key features at this time like animal riding, vehicles, alien biomes, research tree, ect, that would greatly improve that game. However as Rimworld is still under development, being on alpha 14 at the time of this review, its list of features may grow.
While the base game has a slightly limited number of features, it was set up by the developer to be heavily modable. The mods for Rimworld are varied and numerous and can substantially change not only a few details but key mechanics of the game. As development of the game continues I can only assume that the effects of the mods will also grow, allowing for a greater level of replayablity.

Talos is a puzzle game. A puzzle game wrapped with a layer of philosophy and heady thinking. It is also beautiful and melancholy...and from the start, as an obvious robot/android in an otherwise empty world, it is clear something not-good has happened.
Where is everyone? Well, that's something you can slowly discover over time, provided you're curious to read the often-semi-corrupted files on the terminals, read the QC codes on the walls, and listen to Alexandra's time capsule audio recordings.
It was worth it to me, because put together, it all created a world in which solving arbitrary puzzles, one after another, with increasing difficulty, actually made sense.
For me, Talos was one of those Steam impulse buys that turned into total gratitude I'd taken the chance to pick up an enjoyable and diverting game, and what's more, a game that made me think. Imagine, if you will, feeding answers back into an in-game computer terminal where you're purportedly conversing with some kind of 'plain language' interface programs...when the program asks you why you care so much to prove you're a person.
"But I'm not a person," I thought at the time. "I'm a person, pretending to be a robot, playing a game..." The rabbit hole just gets ever deeper.
Anyway, Talos is a beautiful game and well-executed. I do not recall a single crash or glitch (aside from the deliberate graphic glitches intended to be part of the game itself). The puzzles, if taken in the obvious order, are very good at teaching the mechanics of the game itself. Even though "just a puzzle game", I found myself experiencing genuine emotions as the fate of the human race slowly became clear...  But the ending more than made up for the melancholy.
I highly recommend Talos, especially if one can get it on a Steam sale, as I did.
Gehenna DLC: First, I'll echo what others have said: The Gehenna DLC is for those who played the Talos base game and want more. I would also say it's probably for those who were completionist about the base game and want even tougher challenges.
Most of the puzzles in the Gehenna DLC are what I would consider "Red-Plus" at minimum. The ones in the level reached by acquiring enough stars are really tough. I would also hazard to say that the World 4 puzzles are also harder than anything in the base game. The Gehenna stars? OMG, they were brutal.
But it's really enjoyable, and I didn't mind taking the time to really figure out how to solve them. What I especially appreciated was the presence of other characters in the Gehenna world. In the base game, you're alone. You FEEL alone. Somehow even the QC codes make it feel like you're running around in an utterly empty world, with nothing but Elohim to nag you from time to time and the ever-melancholy time capsules.
Now, through the terminals in Gehenna, there is a realm of AIs who have decided both to try to make sense of their existences and to entertain themselves.
Although the developers said this is roughly four hours of game play, because I didn't cheat and use online guide help, I'd say I easily put 3-4 times that much time into it. Maybe more, I wasn't keeping track. The hub location and the individual worlds are just as gorgeous and evocative as the base game, albeit the DLC overall is smaller. Some of the puzzles seemed to be somewhat deriviative of the original (and required similar solutions, such as one with a hallway of energy gates), whereas others such as Open Field are completely different.
The only thing I didn't like about the DLC was the lack of a closing cinematic. Just credits and it's over. Still, one of the endings does give a hint as to the ultimate destiny of these uploading AIs... And it is good.
Top recommendation is to NOT (do not) play Gehenna until you've finished and mastered the base game. If you can't solve the base game's World C 'red tetromino' puzzles without help, Gehenna will be frustrating. Plus, the story narrative in Gehenna refers a number of times to the base game's ending -- so play that first, then go for Gehenna.
Major plus: I got to save D0G, along with several others whose names I recognized from the base game's QC codes.  :-)  Happy-happy.

Let me now tell you the tale of the town of Hurra...
Hurra started as a small crashsite wherin the only survivors were a planetary settler, someone's livein roommate, and the psychotic butcher. The butcher brought in loads of animals, each struck down with a single blow and chopped them into bits, the roommate cooked the bits and kept the settlement clean, and the settler did everything else.
The colony grew steadily, marked only with one person of particular interest, a scoundrel by the name of Mickey 'Ye' Huang. Having been a minstrel most of his life, Mickey was drunk, lazy, and incapable of any meaningful labor. But, Mickey was good for a laugh and liked to carve statues from wood that rich people from other worlds liked to buy so Mickey pulled his considerable weight. One day Mickey carved a legendary statue of incredible realism that depicted the death of his fellow colonists and a great fire. Despite how beautiful the statue was, (or Mickey clamed it was anyway) the rest of the colony hated it and marked it for export as it seemed to be an expression of madness. An expression of madness... or prophetic vision?
Hurra was a peaceful place, the peace only interrupted by the occasional wistless bandit taken captive and 'convinced' to join or be harvested for organs, and the infrequent mass boomalope chain explosion. Until one day 'it' arrived. It poisoned the land, killing crops and trees, and before the colonists could mobilize to deal with the metal monstrosity, another appeared, this time affecting their very minds. In assaulting the twin metal aberrations, many died, and those who were not killed were badly wounded. Immediately after the great calamity, the bandits whom had made Hurra rich and populous arrived in force, slaying with abandon, and burning that which could not be stolen. The sole survivor of this madness was a terribly old man afflicted with dementia, cataracts, and a bad back who had been welcomed by the colonists only a week prior as a means of trying to alleviate the guilt they had felt in inflicting attrocities upon even those who had meant them harm. For a day or two, the old man, kept it together and dug graves for the original settlers, unil overcome by grief, he beat his dog to death. Now with bleeding and infected wounds from his expired companion, he lay in the viscera covered hospital, slowly waiting to die. But before he could finish Mickey's prophecy, a wanderer came upon the colony and for reasons unknown even to him, he decided to join the colony. That man was former pirate captain, Tater Strahmn.
Tater heard the stories of Hurra, buried the old man, and rebuilt. In the years that followed, he lost all of his natural limbs and eyes defending his belief for a brighter future. Now today Hurra is a safe place where most are welcome, where slavery and organ trafficing are illegal. Tater stands above it all as a watchful cybernetic god clad in power armor, armed to the teeth, and followed by a horde of huskies. The only remnants of the old Hurra in the Pax Tatus are the graveyard where many colonists now come for silent contemplation after work, history having been rewritten to make the fallen into heroes, and a slightly burnt but beautiful statue in the primary cafeteria made by a forgotten artist prophesying the end of the world.

In short: Good game overall, but needs some serious attention to the matchmaking and game modes to make it more of a draw if it wants to remain relevant long enough to reach a full release stage and have anyone actually care.
I haven't played this game enough to be 'skilled' at it, but I've put in enough time and effort, interacted with enough people, and played enough games to feel like I can offer my review. And my review at this time is the game has a long way to go... and might not get there.
My points *for* the game:
- It's fun and exciting. When you get a well balanced match, where both sides are fairly well matched up, the games are fun, entertaining and enjoyable.
- the mercs are interesting. I like the personality of some of them, and the mechanics of some of them.
- The maps are... ok. Not great, but decent enough to give a lot of different players different options on how to play. Since it's still in beta, this is something they're already working on.
My points *against* the game are:
- not enough players, and far too many high level players being mixed in with new ones. Missions will often land you in a match against people who seem to have nothing else to do but play Dirty Bomb. This means, for example, that my lvl 8 character who is still learning the finer points of the maps and gameplay WILL get (and has gotten) matched up against a lvl 183 player who knows every nuance inside and out. This is a problem from both sides of the feild, as newer players get completely overwhelmed by higher level players and end up upset and irritated (NOT the point of a game), while higher level players have no time to deal with people who don't know how to play, kicking them out of spite or boredom, or just straight up abusing them during missions then mocking their lack of skill, resulting in bad times being had all around.
- an increasingly toxic playerbase. New players don't care. More experienced players don't care. Almost no one cares about what's going on in a mission, only about getting kills and making the other players look bad. The new players will kill themselves constantly trying to make something happen, then ragequit; the older players will camp the perfect spots, parkour to places no one knows how to reach unless equally experienced then snipe from an almost unassailable location, then troll the new players. People leave in droves and the new players who don't care just keep dying and rushing, while the older players just see it all as free EXP and keep steamrolling anyone less skilled than them with no mercy. And don't say anything about it; you'll get slowly pushed aside and ignored, or trolled until you lose interest.
- slightly steep learning curve. Not really because the game itself is hard. More because of the afformentioned situation. You WILL find yourself going through the meatgrinder to get better, and at the point of this review, there's no way to avoid being tossed in, or option to avoid people far above your skill level.
- the maps are a tad confusing. In a game like this, dead ends don't really make any sense, and there are a disturbing number of paths you can run down that lead exactly nowhere. The minimap doesn't really help, since if you shift your focus from the main screen too long, you're already dead.
- a little too fast paced (personal thing). The game is fine if you like dying a lot. But I can't help feeling that if you could live a bit longer, and there was a bit more strategy as compared to death almost as soon as you're found and 'twitch or die' mechanics, the game would be more fun. I say this is a personal thing because as of this review being posted my best and favorite mercs are on the lower end for HP, so of course they die faster.
- airstrikes and artillery and orbital lasers. I can see how these can be useful and seen as fine and cool to have within the game setup with one or two mercs to a side having it. But there's literally nothing preventing an entire team being the same people, so sometimes the entire mission is people airstriking each other. I'm not sure how constantly exploding is fun for some people, but... some people seem to enjoy it. And everyone else has to deal with it. For me, it was just annoying having people exploding everything in sequence for 15 or more minutes per mission. Might as well have a merc with a tactical nuke added in for laughs.
Overall, the game is fun; despite my misgivings on it, I kept wanting to come back and try again, which is a good thing. The fact that I get almost instantly repulsed, either by the horrible match-ups or the trollish players I run into (new and 12 year old mentality or older and fully entrenched 'you're nothing but a headshot to me' mentality) is something they will hopefully take measures against in the future.
A lot of people are saying the game is still in Beta, and it is. But if the game continues to collect people who don't give a crap about new players, and new players who don't give a crap about anything after being mauled repeatedly, and most importantly LOSING people who would like to play but can't fit themselves in between the two because all the fun is being leeched out, then when (and if) the game finally reaches completion, everyone is just gonna avoid it and play the dozen or so similar games out there instead.

Let me now tell you the tale of the town of Hurra...
Hurra started as a small crashsite wherin the only survivors were a planetary settler, someone's livein roommate, and the psychotic butcher. The butcher brought in loads of animals, each struck down with a single blow and chopped them into bits, the roommate cooked the bits and kept the settlement clean, and the settler did everything else.
The colony grew steadily, marked only with one person of particular interest, a scoundrel by the name of Mickey 'Ye' Huang. Having been a minstrel most of his life, Mickey was drunk, lazy, and incapable of any meaningful labor. But, Mickey was good for a laugh and liked to carve statues from wood that rich people from other worlds liked to buy so Mickey pulled his considerable weight. One day Mickey carved a legendary statue of incredible realism that depicted the death of his fellow colonists and a great fire. Despite how beautiful the statue was, (or Mickey clamed it was anyway) the rest of the colony hated it and marked it for export as it seemed to be an expression of madness. An expression of madness... or prophetic vision?
Hurra was a peaceful place, the peace only interrupted by the occasional wistless bandit taken captive and 'convinced' to join or be harvested for organs, and the infrequent mass boomalope chain explosion. Until one day 'it' arrived. It poisoned the land, killing crops and trees, and before the colonists could mobilize to deal with the metal monstrosity, another appeared, this time affecting their very minds. In assaulting the twin metal aberrations, many died, and those who were not killed were badly wounded. Immediately after the great calamity, the bandits whom had made Hurra rich and populous arrived in force, slaying with abandon, and burning that which could not be stolen. The sole survivor of this madness was a terribly old man afflicted with dementia, cataracts, and a bad back who had been welcomed by the colonists only a week prior as a means of trying to alleviate the guilt they had felt in inflicting attrocities upon even those who had meant them harm. For a day or two, the old man, kept it together and dug graves for the original settlers, unil overcome by grief, he beat his dog to death. Now with bleeding and infected wounds from his expired companion, he lay in the viscera covered hospital, slowly waiting to die. But before he could finish Mickey's prophecy, a wanderer came upon the colony and for reasons unknown even to him, he decided to join the colony. That man was former pirate captain, Tater Strahmn.
Tater heard the stories of Hurra, buried the old man, and rebuilt. In the years that followed, he lost all of his natural limbs and eyes defending his belief for a brighter future. Now today Hurra is a safe place where most are welcome, where slavery and organ trafficing are illegal. Tater stands above it all as a watchful cybernetic god clad in power armor, armed to the teeth, and followed by a horde of huskies. The only remnants of the old Hurra in the Pax Tatus are the graveyard where many colonists now come for silent contemplation after work, history having been rewritten to make the fallen into heroes, and a slightly burnt but beautiful statue in the primary cafeteria made by a forgotten artist prophesying the end of the world.

Buy this game if you are an AoE fan.  Buy this game if you are a RTS fan.  Buy this game because it is awesome.

I have been playing this game since alpha 3.   I estimate, at the time of this posting, that I have put over 500 hours into this game if you include all the different alpha versions.  This game has come a long way and I expect there will be even more to come.   As the game is now, alpha 14 as I write this, it could be considered a complete game when you consider the amount of content.   It will keep you busy for hours.   At $30, it's well worth it.
Basically you start with a few resources and a handful of colonists and eventually grow your colony into something much more.   The end game idea is to build a ship and escape the planet you are on.   But the enjoyment is actually building up your colony and defending it against exterior threats.  There are many threats including raiders, weather events, and starvation/exposure (in the more diffcult biomes like desert and tundra).  Each threat is unique and has systems in the game to deal with them.  You can play any game type you like.   Meaning, you can deactivate threats you find annoying or unbalanced.  You can choose your biome as well.   Perhaps you want to play an easy biome with more raiders?   Or you want to play on the Ice sheet with minimal raiders?  It's up to you.
At the end of the day Rimworld would be labeled a Basebuilder when it comes to genre.   But in reality, there is so much to it than that.  And even if you want to use a mypopic definition like "Basebuilder" when classifying Rimworld that's fine.   Because even within that narrow definition, Rimworld would be the best "Basebuilder" I have ever played.

This game is awful. Max Payne is a generic antihero who drinks because he's really dark. He has to protect these rich Brazilian dudes. And it's always nighttime and raining and Max dwells on the past and drinks a bunch.
Game is designed badly. It forces you to use bullet time by throwing a large number of enemies at you at once in certain areas, it's like... "Hey look now we have a bunch of enemies shooting at you from multiple directions! It's bullet time! Welcome to the Max Payne francise!" It's not organically integrated into the game. FEAR does a much better job of integrating bullet time into combat IMO. The game design is lazy.
Game is a brainless on-rails shooter. It's not even a question of it looking like there might be other paths or areas. The objective is really just always in front of you. You get to a door, a cutscene plays, then you fight a bunch of enemies until you reach the next door.
The game autosaves in awful places. I once got autosaved when I was out of ammo and 15+ enemies spawned. If you die enough at a certain place it starts giving you meds and ammo but that takes forever and you have to just keep dying. There's not really a way out of that other than restarting the level. I remember playing this boat level for like half an hour, trying to inch up the stairs to get angle shots on the 10 enemies in cover above me.
Movement is clunky and slow, probably because the camera is bad. The cover system is clunky. Things that look like they should be cover aren't cover, and things that don't look like cover are cover. Aiming is really bad. When you take cover, aiming is basically irrelevant because the camera shifts (exceedingly slowly) and makes pop-up shots impossible unless you use your bullet time. Damage modeling is really bad, but that's probably an homage to the previous Max Payne games.
The game crashes when I try to change the resolution so I have to play with a 4:3 resolution. Many random crashes to desktop, especially on load. Rockstar social whatever is mercifully ignorable.

Where do i start with this mixed bag?
Well lets start with developer support, i have had two major binges on this game, when it was initially released and i believe a month or so back, the first thing that struck me was how remarkably little had changed and how much empty space there was between announcement, updates and then eventually actual implementation of patches, as far as i could tell no new maps were added but reading through the reviews there was atleast one that did, they've added a few characters but the problem is that they don't really have anything else to conpensate for the space between new characters being added, be it new maps, or debuggings,  hotfixes, skins, anything.
The card system
Now i was already againts the card system because it is completly down to RNG if you get a good card or not, this is somewhat conpensated by the skillbased aiming but the problem is the game is objective based, the game is always in overwhelming favor to whoever has the "right" perk, or whoever happens to have picked the "right" character, since you don't get to pick your weapons or perks and since the game is based on a rotating roster you get pidgeon holed into using the same 4-5 characters wich again there is no guarentee they will be the "right" character and you are again at the mercy of RNG, you can get all the kills you want but if your team fails to produce a tank or the a quick defuse perk then you are ♥♥♥♥ed and no one can be blamed for it because it was no ones choice. But atleast they used to have a trade up system so you could take 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cards and trade up for an arguably better one...not anymore , now you scrap it to get a dozen or so scrap. Basically grind central , your best bet is purchasing cases ( thanks CSGO) and then you're at the mercy of the RNG gods once again, because if you use scrap you can atleast choose wich characters card you purchase, with cases you can just as easily get a card for a character you don't even have. Basically all around the card system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. They didn't even bother to remove the achievement for ♥♥♥♥ing system they removed, ♥♥♥♥ing hello?!
Asymetric Maps and Snowballing:
Now nothing inherently wrong with asymetric maps but the problem is mixed with the spawn points it all becomes extremly bias to one side, typically the defenders, no you would think if anyone would need a leg up its attacked but nope in almost all of the maps i've played the defenders are in overwhelming favor BECAUSE of spawn points and the map being set up in a certain way where everyone is conveniantly funneled. If you somehow manage to plant a bomb or repair a generater and no one manages to defuse it in 30 seconds then yes you can close or open other paths but the availability of these paths is always depended on everyone perks wich they don't choose, and if there happen to be two tanks on the defending team well good ♥♥♥♥ing luck.
Now what inevitably happens is the game starts to snowball, and its always snowballs, i have been in very few matches where there has been an actual tug of war or the results have been close, and the worst part is there is no inherent mechanism to stop the snowballing like say in CSGO where every round starts over, the fact that there is no start and stop system, that the maps are so heavily biased along with spawn, the fact that for the most part you are relying on peoples perks and characters to either hold a point or control it simply amplifies the snow balling.
I mean we all know the good stuff, the fast paced nature, the parkour elements but its all for nothing due to the drawbacks, i guess its fun if you play it in short burst and just basically ♥♥♥♥ around, but otherwise its a solid no from me.

This is an excellent first-person puzzler game; probably on par with portal in terms of ingeniousness of the puzzles. It has an incredibly deep philosophical bent to it as well which really stopped to make me think on more than one occasion when being pressed on various beliefs. The storyline of the game is very well presented, and you'll find yourself wanting to seek out all the hidden locations where more information can be revealed about who you are and why you're doing what you're doing.
While playing, I felt a slight discomfort; an existential dread that stuck itself at the back of my mind throughout the game. Reading the various stories about the people in the game certainly contributed, as well as the environments of the puzzles themselves. They struck me as intentionally designed to look like they were intentionally designed, but not by any typical civilization. They feel strangely alien and navigating them made me feel uneasy, though I was driven to continue. The puzzles also lend themselves to this strange feeling, since many of them have you doing unconventional things to unlock all the secrets, which require you to constantly step out of your comfort zone and question your assumptions as to what you are able, allowed, and required to do to solve them all.
I primarily speak about how it made me feel since it was so unexpected for me going into this game. In the end I have to say I loved it for the challenge it presented and for how much it drew me in emotionally. Definitely pick it up if you're a fan of these kind of puzzle games, and if you're intrigued at the prospect of a complex philosophical journey.

Taking place in an alternate timeline where the Nazis have won the war using forbidden technology, the player once again steps into the shoes of B.J.Blazkowitz in order to mow down swathes of enemy soldiers. Interestingly, what sold me on the game is that apart from being a solid shooter experience, it actually tells a pretty good story and has some really good world building. If you take the time to explore you will find letters and news paper clippings and other bits and pieces, all non essential, but all helping to lend depth and texture to this "what if?" world. Just being quiet and overhearing guards and other NPC's conversations also helps flesh out the world and make it feel like a living place, not to mention some of the conversations are pretty damn amusing . Between murdering the hun you even have some more peaceful moments back at your base where you can get to know your fellow underground fighters and even indulge in some easter egg throwbacks to earlier games.  It was the world building going the extra mile that really helped raise this game from shooter fodder for me and I really recommend it. The stand alone expac The Old Blood is spiff too so if you like this, check it out
