TLDR, buy Squad if you
- Like slow paced gameplay compared to something like Battlefield, but fast paced gameplay compared to Arma
- Enjoy really working in a team. Like, REALLY. You MUST work well with your team if you want to win
- Enjoy playing a variety of distinct roles
- Like longer shooter match lengths
- Enjoy a combination of strategy and action
- If you're a social gamer (not as necessary, you can get by without being massively talkative, but a mic is still an absolute must)
Avoid it if you
- Don't have a mic (seriously, just get one, they're cheap as chips)
- Want a large variety of game modes
- Want shoot-em-up action all the time
- Have little patience
- Don't like taking directions/advice from other players
- Want to lone-wolf/do your own thing
- Have an AMD CPU. There are some serious Unreal Engine issues plaguing AMD users right now. Probably avoid Squad until they iron them out.
Before I dive into my actual review, I want to mention that I've played over 500 hours of Arma 3, and that that's where the majority of my shooter experience comes from. I've also played a decent chunk of Project Reality, the BF2 mod that Squad is based on. In my opinion, Squad is a far superior game to Arma 3, and even though they both scratch different itches and are very different games, Squad is probably going to be my go to tactical/'realistic' shooter for at least the next 2 years.
Squad isn't the first game to do what it's doing. If you've played Project Reality (and if you haven't, I really recommend it before buying Squad, it's free) you've basically played Squad with vehicles and dated graphics. However, it does do what it sets out to do extremely well.
A lot of reviewers have described Squad as being 'slow-paced' and while there's some truth to that, I would put it a different way. Squad has a fair bit of down time where you're just walking between objectives, chatting and dropping banter with your squadmates. When you're actually engaged in a firefight, there's nothing slow paced about Squad at all. You're constantly forced to make micro decisions that could lead to your entire squad being wiped out if you screw up, especially if you're playing a vital role such as medic or squad leader.
Ultimately what Squad comes down to is the effectiveness of squad leaders and how well they can utilise their squad members' abilities. A single fantastic squad can turn the tide of a seemingly hopeless round, and this happens quite often. This means that even the currently winning team's squad leaders have to be really switched on and constantly on the lookout for game making plays from other squads. Understanding how the maps flow is pretty key to this. I won't talk about how to squad lead specifically, but a great squad leader can literally win the game for you. It doesn't matter if you've got 50 amazing marksmen on your team if there's no one to coordinate them into killing as many of the baddies as possible.
The gunplay is extremely satisfying and has a lot of really impressive visual and audio feedback. Full auto, or even burst fire is only really viable on the AK model weapons. The M16 and M4 simply recoil too much to be effective on full auto at anything over about 20 metres. The US weapons do come with pretty great optics though, which means that the US team will usually try to engage at longer ranges, while Insurgents will attempt to sneak up closer. This lends a pretty interesting assymetric balance to firefights.
The audio in this game is almost on par with something like DICE's Battefield 4 or Battlefront. It's seriously impressive and actually pretty important to your survivability. Tracing where gunshots came from, or listening to an enemy fireteam run through the field you're lying in informs all those micro decisions you're constantly making. The visuals are pretty much what you'd expect too, with some nice lighting effects and some really atmospheric and immersive vistas on some of the maps. Could probably use a bit more polish, but nothing to complain about really.
I could talk loads more about this game, but if any of what I said sounds interesting to you, go try out Project Reality. If you like that, get Squad. They're different, especially since Squad doesn't have vehicles yet, but they scratch the same itch. Some of the most tense and satisfying gaming moments I've had have been in Squad.

Where do i start with this mixed bag?
Well lets start with developer support, i have had two major binges on this game, when it was initially released and i believe a month or so back, the first thing that struck me was how remarkably little had changed and how much empty space there was between announcement, updates and then eventually actual implementation of patches, as far as i could tell no new maps were added but reading through the reviews there was atleast one that did, they've added a few characters but the problem is that they don't really have anything else to conpensate for the space between new characters being added, be it new maps, or debuggings,  hotfixes, skins, anything.
The card system
Now i was already againts the card system because it is completly down to RNG if you get a good card or not, this is somewhat conpensated by the skillbased aiming but the problem is the game is objective based, the game is always in overwhelming favor to whoever has the "right" perk, or whoever happens to have picked the "right" character, since you don't get to pick your weapons or perks and since the game is based on a rotating roster you get pidgeon holed into using the same 4-5 characters wich again there is no guarentee they will be the "right" character and you are again at the mercy of RNG, you can get all the kills you want but if your team fails to produce a tank or the a quick defuse perk then you are ♥♥♥♥ed and no one can be blamed for it because it was no ones choice. But atleast they used to have a trade up system so you could take 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cards and trade up for an arguably better one...not anymore , now you scrap it to get a dozen or so scrap. Basically grind central , your best bet is purchasing cases ( thanks CSGO) and then you're at the mercy of the RNG gods once again, because if you use scrap you can atleast choose wich characters card you purchase, with cases you can just as easily get a card for a character you don't even have. Basically all around the card system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. They didn't even bother to remove the achievement for ♥♥♥♥ing system they removed, ♥♥♥♥ing hello?!
Asymetric Maps and Snowballing:
Now nothing inherently wrong with asymetric maps but the problem is mixed with the spawn points it all becomes extremly bias to one side, typically the defenders, no you would think if anyone would need a leg up its attacked but nope in almost all of the maps i've played the defenders are in overwhelming favor BECAUSE of spawn points and the map being set up in a certain way where everyone is conveniantly funneled. If you somehow manage to plant a bomb or repair a generater and no one manages to defuse it in 30 seconds then yes you can close or open other paths but the availability of these paths is always depended on everyone perks wich they don't choose, and if there happen to be two tanks on the defending team well good ♥♥♥♥ing luck.
Now what inevitably happens is the game starts to snowball, and its always snowballs, i have been in very few matches where there has been an actual tug of war or the results have been close, and the worst part is there is no inherent mechanism to stop the snowballing like say in CSGO where every round starts over, the fact that there is no start and stop system, that the maps are so heavily biased along with spawn, the fact that for the most part you are relying on peoples perks and characters to either hold a point or control it simply amplifies the snow balling.
I mean we all know the good stuff, the fast paced nature, the parkour elements but its all for nothing due to the drawbacks, i guess its fun if you play it in short burst and just basically ♥♥♥♥ around, but otherwise its a solid no from me.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a fun, over the top shooter that shot towards the moon and missed, but is still a fun ride throughout.
Somewhat fundamentally, to enjoy this game the most, you need to be able to enjoy a game that has very over-the-top violence. The Nazis are made out to be carved out of evil with evil blood and evil hats. So no worries about killing them in any way you can think. Personally, I just have to laugh at the over-the-top evilness/violence balance (this isn't to say I think  any real world parallels are humorous, just the very one sided presentation to ensure you can have fun killing your enemies without feeling bad). But you also can't escape the violence, so it is something you have to be ok with. Also as a warning, there are cyborg dogs you have to kill. Not a ton, but it does come up.
With that out of the way, why is this game fun? Because it is a mix of Call of Duty style first person cover based shooting with Serious Sam's over the top explodey-shooty violence. You _can_ sit in cover and shoot at your enemies if you'd like, but the game doesn't seem to think you will, so ammo and health are spread around to allow you to march head first into battle with guns in both hands.
There are some stealth sections (I think only 1 is reaquired stealth which there is enough health to remedy if you mess it up) where you can sneak up and kill your enemies, but they are no where near as deep as the sneaking you'll find elsewhere. What is awesome at least is that failing your stealth isn't game over or some terrible outcome; you merely pull out the big guns and go to town.
The downside is if you like the stealth gameplay, it really is only some sections. Most of the encounters in the game are just outright shooting with the enemy already knowing where you are and no way to sneak up or even flank them.
By the end of the games, the encounters become quite intense and require a lot of diving in and out of cover, changing weapons as you don't have enough ammo to kill everything, and managing (to some extent) your explosives and big guns for the insanely armored enemies. Unfortunately, like stealth falling by the wayside, aiming generally does too. Armored enemies don't care about your petty headshots and precise aim. Instead, just throw a couple explosives at them or find a turret (or get ready to empty multiple clips directly into them).
But in the end, it's all a bit crazy, over the top violence.
Also, the story is, while also over the top, better than I feel it really needed to be. The ending I find to be a bit disappointing, but overall, it was a much better story than I think anyone needed in their shooter. But I for one am happy to have experienced it.
Is it all roses? No. There are some strange decisions/bugs you run into such as checkpoints remembering your health but not the available health kits. This means that if you happen to die but picked up health and armor between the checkpoint and your death, that health won't be there, but you will respawn with the same (likely low) health. That feels like punishing someone who might be having trouble or someone who got stuck jumping up a wall which also happens.
The stealth is underused and never becomes particularly deep even when it is there. The last few stealth-able sections really seem to want you to just get on with the shooting and involve a lot of moving through open areas.
The armored enemies are really annoying. They don't feel like a question of skill, just attrition. Your lazer guns do well enough against them, but if there's more than one, you feel like you constantly have to stand next to something to recharge them.
But in the end, these all feel like small nit picks to an enjoyable game. Definitely worth a play if you're looking for some fun but over the top first person shooting.

I have been playing this game since alpha 3.   I estimate, at the time of this posting, that I have put over 500 hours into this game if you include all the different alpha versions.  This game has come a long way and I expect there will be even more to come.   As the game is now, alpha 14 as I write this, it could be considered a complete game when you consider the amount of content.   It will keep you busy for hours.   At $30, it's well worth it.
Basically you start with a few resources and a handful of colonists and eventually grow your colony into something much more.   The end game idea is to build a ship and escape the planet you are on.   But the enjoyment is actually building up your colony and defending it against exterior threats.  There are many threats including raiders, weather events, and starvation/exposure (in the more diffcult biomes like desert and tundra).  Each threat is unique and has systems in the game to deal with them.  You can play any game type you like.   Meaning, you can deactivate threats you find annoying or unbalanced.  You can choose your biome as well.   Perhaps you want to play an easy biome with more raiders?   Or you want to play on the Ice sheet with minimal raiders?  It's up to you.
At the end of the day Rimworld would be labeled a Basebuilder when it comes to genre.   But in reality, there is so much to it than that.  And even if you want to use a mypopic definition like "Basebuilder" when classifying Rimworld that's fine.   Because even within that narrow definition, Rimworld would be the best "Basebuilder" I have ever played.

TLDR, buy Squad if you
- Like slow paced gameplay compared to something like Battlefield, but fast paced gameplay compared to Arma
- Enjoy really working in a team. Like, REALLY. You MUST work well with your team if you want to win
- Enjoy playing a variety of distinct roles
- Like longer shooter match lengths
- Enjoy a combination of strategy and action
- If you're a social gamer (not as necessary, you can get by without being massively talkative, but a mic is still an absolute must)
Avoid it if you
- Don't have a mic (seriously, just get one, they're cheap as chips)
- Want a large variety of game modes
- Want shoot-em-up action all the time
- Have little patience
- Don't like taking directions/advice from other players
- Want to lone-wolf/do your own thing
- Have an AMD CPU. There are some serious Unreal Engine issues plaguing AMD users right now. Probably avoid Squad until they iron them out.
Before I dive into my actual review, I want to mention that I've played over 500 hours of Arma 3, and that that's where the majority of my shooter experience comes from. I've also played a decent chunk of Project Reality, the BF2 mod that Squad is based on. In my opinion, Squad is a far superior game to Arma 3, and even though they both scratch different itches and are very different games, Squad is probably going to be my go to tactical/'realistic' shooter for at least the next 2 years.
Squad isn't the first game to do what it's doing. If you've played Project Reality (and if you haven't, I really recommend it before buying Squad, it's free) you've basically played Squad with vehicles and dated graphics. However, it does do what it sets out to do extremely well.
A lot of reviewers have described Squad as being 'slow-paced' and while there's some truth to that, I would put it a different way. Squad has a fair bit of down time where you're just walking between objectives, chatting and dropping banter with your squadmates. When you're actually engaged in a firefight, there's nothing slow paced about Squad at all. You're constantly forced to make micro decisions that could lead to your entire squad being wiped out if you screw up, especially if you're playing a vital role such as medic or squad leader.
Ultimately what Squad comes down to is the effectiveness of squad leaders and how well they can utilise their squad members' abilities. A single fantastic squad can turn the tide of a seemingly hopeless round, and this happens quite often. This means that even the currently winning team's squad leaders have to be really switched on and constantly on the lookout for game making plays from other squads. Understanding how the maps flow is pretty key to this. I won't talk about how to squad lead specifically, but a great squad leader can literally win the game for you. It doesn't matter if you've got 50 amazing marksmen on your team if there's no one to coordinate them into killing as many of the baddies as possible.
The gunplay is extremely satisfying and has a lot of really impressive visual and audio feedback. Full auto, or even burst fire is only really viable on the AK model weapons. The M16 and M4 simply recoil too much to be effective on full auto at anything over about 20 metres. The US weapons do come with pretty great optics though, which means that the US team will usually try to engage at longer ranges, while Insurgents will attempt to sneak up closer. This lends a pretty interesting assymetric balance to firefights.
The audio in this game is almost on par with something like DICE's Battefield 4 or Battlefront. It's seriously impressive and actually pretty important to your survivability. Tracing where gunshots came from, or listening to an enemy fireteam run through the field you're lying in informs all those micro decisions you're constantly making. The visuals are pretty much what you'd expect too, with some nice lighting effects and some really atmospheric and immersive vistas on some of the maps. Could probably use a bit more polish, but nothing to complain about really.
I could talk loads more about this game, but if any of what I said sounds interesting to you, go try out Project Reality. If you like that, get Squad. They're different, especially since Squad doesn't have vehicles yet, but they scratch the same itch. Some of the most tense and satisfying gaming moments I've had have been in Squad.

Robocraft has taken a very intersting route since I've first began. Many things have changed over the past 2 years. I still enjoy it, although it won't be the same when I first started.
The game's title speaks for itself: you craft robots. From a beginners perspective, its a somewhat straightforward process: you place blocks, add some guns and some movement part, and go into battle. For the most part, that's what everyone does. Dive deeper into the game, and you can see that there's more than meets the eye.

There's so much potential this game has, and it has taken some of it. The freedom to build basically whatever you want.
It isn't all glamorious. There's "meta" robots that are easy to dominate with, and certain weapons help with that. While Freejam has attempted to address these issues, they're not putting out the right corrections to fix them. Not to mention, the game is still lacking, such as a proper tutorial. I know that Freejam is still an indie game company, but they had several chances where they could fix a lot of issues and never took them to the fullest. I was hoping they would reach beta by the end of 2016, but no.
Overall, I give this game a 7/10. It's not what it used to be, and it's changed a lot from what I started with. I still like playing this game, but it needs the proper fixes. I hope Freejam surprises us in a good way in 2017.

I beat the whole game in about 9 hours on the normal difficulty (I switched it to the easiest difficulty towards the very end just so I could be done with it).
Great looking visuals, immersive sound, halfway decent voice acting for an FPS game, but the gameplay is just too flawed to make this an actually fun game.
Shooting in this game is the best part! Then you have many long segments where you aren't shooting or you aren't supposed to shoot - hunting around for stuff like this is Ether One or Dear Esther (for example, there's a section where you're looking for mold - I'm not kidding), or sneaking around with limited weapons. First of all, this is a problem because I got this game thinking it would be an intense, fast paced FPS. When you throw in these inane "look around for something" quests and these slow-paced stealth sections, you're keeping me from doing what I want to do with my limited free time. Second of all, the stealth gameplay is just not fun. It's not even a problem with the mechanics of stealth in this game, it's just that sneaking around, waiting, and sneaking some more isn't really fun when you're looking for an intense, fast-paced experience.
But, even if they got rid of all that other stuff, they managed to mess up the shooting gameplay as well. At first, when they only have the weak enemy types that go down in a few hits, the game is quite fun. Even with that, though, the guns  they give you aren't really precise, so even if you're aiming down the sights, it's not easy to pull off those headshots, giving you less of that feeling of mastery and control that you can get from other FPS games. That's fine if running and gunning is a viable tactic, but if you do that, it seems you'll take lots of damage and you have to find medkits to heal yourself. I know people claim to hate regenerating health, but I honestly would've had more fun if, during combat, I could just run and gun, hide for a bit to heal up, then do it some more. There's a lot of other ways to fix that annoyance than regenerating health, though.
More about the combat - as I said, when there's weak enemies that go down in a few hits, it's fun. However, they quickly start introducing heavily armored enemies. They kinda have weak points, but it's still going to be a frustrating experience  taking them down. It's just not fun when you have to empty entire clips into enemies, even if you're hitting their weak points, until they fall down. It ruins the fun pace of the game because you have to pop out, shoot, then duck back behind cover, and repeat until they're dead. You can't just run and strafe and shoot because you'll just take too much damage. It's possible I was not clear on what parts of these enemies were "weak points" or what the  best strategies were for taking down these enemies - I would blame that on the game's lack of clear feedback and guidance. These enemies occur way too frequently, and they continuously introduce stronger and stronger enemies that take more and more time to take down. It's just not fun. Compare this to games like Bulletstorm, Call of Juarez, or Shadow Warrior. They manage to keep the challenge up while still making the combat satisfying.
Also, the weapon switching is atrocious. I think you should've been able to switch weapons while the game is paused. They give you so many different weapons, which is great, but because of how weapon switching works, you'll find yourself not feeling like you should ever switch it up unless you run out of ammo. Why give players lots of weapons if you don't give them an easy way to decide between them and switch?
Also, I know people complain about modern games "hand holding" players, but if it improves the fun-per-minute, I'm all for it. In the case of this game, there were many times where I wasn't sure where I was supposed to go so I had to spend time wandering around. That's just not fun. When you have a limited time to play games, you want to spend it having as much fun as possible - so if they did a better job of indicating where to go, the game would've been at least less annoying.
So, overall, the FPS combat is the best part and it's rife with gameplay issues that make it frustrating and unsatisfying. The parts that aren't FPS are even worse - they are boring, slow, and totally not what you would want if you're looking for a fast, exciting FPS. However, I did at least enjoy the story, writing, voice acting, and animation during the cutscenes - the characters were memorable and their faces when talking didn't look too "off". Also, the visuals and sound in this game are quite polished and really help with the immersion. However, there just isn't the same intelligence, ingenuity, and creativity in the actual gameplay design.
I primarily recommend a game based on the amount of fun I have for the time I am playing the game. Wolfenstein: The New Order, only manages to be fun about 20% of the time through the game, so look elsewhere for a fun, fast-paced, thoughtfully-designed shooter.

I was expecting a mystery with a buttload of puzzles, but I wasn't prepared for the evocative soundtrack, the darker narrative undertones and discussing the nature of existence with a computer. The narrative has an excellent idea that although sometimes stumbles into Pretentious Village with segments from the bible and other historic texts and stories, is consistently thought-provoking and intriguing to the point where I personally started questioning my own philosophy, and which builds to a stunning conclusion, all without having to pull the massive twist card.

And just when you think you have things figured out, you realize that the puzzles also interact with each other. Each puzzle "room" is connected to another so you can find ways to cheat and make the rooms work with each other to reveal hidden goals.
Besides the great mind bending gameplay, there's an interesting story behind it. It's mysterious enough to be a puzzle all in it's own.

Ever since the Xbox 360 shipped with a headset packaged as standard, online games have yearned to create the kind of cooperative multiplayer seen only in advertisements and well-rehearsed E3 demos.
Outside of these scripted environments very few games have put emphasis on voice chat. Sure, we’ve had games like those in the SOCOM series and MAG which have tried to varying degrees of success but the simple truth is that outside a certain genre of game, voice chat just isn’t used. Hell, even in the most competitive games out there today it’s rare to find people using voice chat.
Squad, on the other hand, is one of the few games which seems to be doing voice chat right. Boot up Squad today and within a few minutes you’ll have a voice telling you where to go and what to do. If taking orders isn’t your thing you can be that voice telling others where to go and what to do. It’s actually very close to what MAG was trying to do, except it’s on a platform where people actually have microphones. You also probably won’t have to worry about servers shutting off making the game unplayable. Even though it’s still in an alpha state, Squad has a thriving active community of players. If anything about MAG sounded appealing to you, Squad is the game that actually delivers on those ideas.
The developers behind Squad started out making a relatively popular mod for Battlefield 2 called Project Reality. Project reality built upon Battlefield 2 adding new levels of realism and a vastly increased scope. It looked better, it played better, its custom-made maps spanned dozens of kilometers. It’s one of the best fan mods out there today. It seems that all of this experience has translated perfectly into Squad with its vast maps and team-focused gameplay.
Squad is unique in that in can take minutes to get to anything resembling action but good leadership will ensure you’re never out of the fray for too long. It’s as if someone took an objective-based first person shooter like Battlefield and added the massive scale and openness of DayZ. As a result Squad it definitely a game you’ll enjoy more if you’re playing with a group of people you know. That’s not to say you can’t have fun alone but just like in other games where communication plays a key role – like Trouble in Terrorist Town – you’re going to have more fun after you and the people you’re playing with have built up a rapport.
It’s hard to be too critical of Squad because it’s still in active development but what I can say is that the gameplay feels extremely solid. Most of the things that need to be improved before the commercial release are related to the UI and tutorials because as a new player it can be very difficult to know what you should do which becomes a very intimidating problem, especially when other people are relying on you to perform your role.
Unlike most early access games, Squad actually offers a fun playable experience. If you’re on the fence about spending the money, maybe wait until the official release but if you’re excited to play right now, it’s well worth the price.

There's a lot to say about this game, so stay for the ride. Ostensibly this is a fairly fast-paced first person shooter in which the ability to aim will put you at an advantage over other players and I believe this is paramount for a shooting game, unlike other shooting games on the market which focus more on pressing a button at the right time. However it still succumbs to the same issues as other games, including gimmicks and horrible developer support.
The Splash Damage website itself claims that they have 200 employees, but you would never guess that number given how glacially slow their work rate is. As of May 2017, a new map was released called Dockyard. This map was in development since 2015 and the last playable untextured version was the summer of 2016. It's taken a professional company nearly a year just to texture one map. If this were a small team of part-time hobbyists, I'd understand completely, but this is supposed to be a "AAA video game developer" (quoted from their own website). The community has been asking for more maps all along as the game originally only shipped with five levels.
Another big problem that Splash Damage is guilty of, as are most other video game companies these days is that they released a game before completing it, then whenever they are criticised for this, they pull out the tired cliché of "Oh it's in beta". The game exists in perpetual beta and will likely never officially go gold. One of the downsides of releasing and marketing an unfinished game is that people get bored of it and leave. The playerbase is stone dead. According to
, the average player count is somewhere between 1,500 and 2,100 players, which by the way is less than half of Farming Simulator 2017. This game doesn't even make Steam's top 100 online games. The game ultimately fails at retaining its playerbase and I can see why. It's stagnant with no development. Join a server and you'll see that more than 90% of players have under twenty or thirty hours in the game. They should have made the game first and then released it properly. The game is created on Unreal Engine 3, which since its release in 2007 I seem to remember being horribly unoptimised and the forums are filled with threads that support that hypothesis. Perhaps that also turns people away.
Dirty Bomb is a class-based shooter and Splash Damage has shown little to no originality when it comes to gameplay. In 2005 I played their previous game Enemy Territory, which had five classes and was on the whole not bad. It was a free to play game, had barely any maps and within maybe two or three years it died. Only the hardcore competitive players remained. Sound familiar? Most of the abilities from that game were directly ported into this game, such as a smoke grenade to call in airstrikes, artillery, medics that revive downed players and land mines, but split up to accommodate nineteen characters instead of five. I will admit that the character design is pretty good, but that's only aesthetics and not gameplay.
This time they expanded the roster from five characters to nineteen and as is the case with pretty much every class-based game, they're unbalanced. Medics had far too much of an impact in Enemy Territory and the same occurs with this game. A team with a medic or two will always win against a team without medics and I believe that forcing roles on the player isn't fun. Unfortunately, after playing the game for long enough, the attentive player will realise that there's a small group of characters that are much more effective than the rest. The most obvious of these is probably Fragger - a character with high health, damage, accuracy and his special ability is an instant kill hand grenade on a sixteen second cooldown. If you spot a player with a decent number of hours in the game, they will invariably have Fragger as their choice of character because he gets the job done better than anyone else.
The game has a dead playerbase, the developers have done almost nothing on this game in over two years. The most recent events have been "trinkets" which are akin to keyrings that hang off the side of the player's weapon. These keyrings could be made by one person in a day at the office and the events that accompanied them were simply a grinding exercise for points. The Christmas event involved Internet memes which strongly indicates that the developers are marketing towards twelve-year-old boys. The Community Manager Chris Mullins often creates videos on the Dirty Bomb Youtube page, but these are fairly lacklustre with vague promises of what's coming in the future or showing a community video that he enjoys.
The saddest part is that this game had a lot of potential and it was squandered by the developers releasing the game before it was finished. I still play this game with friends because it's easy to jump in for a few rounds and compared to all of the other horrible detritus on the shooter market, it's less repulsive than the rest.
Pick it up? Sure, but don't expect much from it or expect to stay. The game is dead, the developers either don't care, aren't up to the job or both. It's too late to salvage and Splash Damage's lineage of dead games ought to be a lesson in how not to produce a game by now. Oh, finally the community is repugnant. If you dare to be good at aiming, you'll receive abuse and player reports. I've yet to be banned thankfully, but that could always change.
Thank you for reading.

In my first game of Rimworld, a wanderer named Vladimir Black stumbled upon my colony from the desert and joined us. He proved useful as he had experience in performing medical procedures and one of my initial survivors had her legs broken in an attack from a man-hunting squirrel.
Unfortunately, as Vladimir got to work on his operation to fix her legs, he botched the surgery. She was most displeased, and he perplexingly got frustrated at her for the operation's failure. He returned to work on her legs and botched the surgery again, leaving her a cripple. He immediately fell into depression and was in a fragile mental state, and ultimately lost his mind as he was scouring the plains searching for food.
He took off his clothes, and began beating up the other survivors with his bare fists.
They retaliated in turn, but he proved too powerful for the colonists. One, a 94 year old man named Spiffy, had to be carried back to his bed in a critical condition. He beat on Patricia, the woman he had botched surgery on twice. He beat her to death.
Spiffy's wounds became infected and disease spread quickly throughout the colony. One of the colonists shot and critically wounded Vladimir, but out of some misguided notion of honour nursed him back to health. Vladimir once again turned on the colonists, who were already at breaking point.
Raiders came and saw the colony in disrepair and kidnapped the only able-bodied, sane members remaining. Vladimir, Spiffy and Hutch succumbed to madness and beat each other senseless.
10/10 would recommend.

Rimworld is astonishingly fun and addictive for an Early Access game.  Don't let the relatively simple graphics fool you (though they're certainly less abstract than, say, Dwarf Fortress which Rimworld is frequently likened to) ... the game feels quite immersive.  It becomes very easy to empathize with your colonists as individuals, to feel pride in their skill level, to want to please them by providing for their comfort in their bedrooms and ensuring proper entertainment.  Starting from scratch, you have to act quickly to build shelter and beds, get crops going and build production stations for cooking food, producing clothing and weapons, crafting art and building a variety of goods for trade when the traders come.
There are threats galore, of course -- pirate raiders, hostile primitive tribes, manhunter-maddened animals and disasters both manmade (toxic fallout) and natural (volcanic eruptions).
The gameplay and the characters are complex, and its easy to lose all track of real-life time.
This game has been absolutely dominating my gameplay time for over a year already (I bought the game back in Alpha 7 days; this review is a few days following Alpha 14 and the initial Steam launch).  I definitely recommend it!

This is a hard game to explain. I had read glowing reviews about this game and how deep and philosophical it was, and now that I've finished it I agree. I know it sounds strange (it certainly did to me before I played it) but playing through this game has _really_ made me think a lot about what it means to be human. It was a really rewarding (and heavy) experience.
The odd thing, though, is that I had to invest a significant amount of time in order to "get it", and most of that time is spent solving puzzles. In fact, when I first started I was actually somewhat underwhelmed by the narrative and philosophy, and I thought that the reviews were overrating how "profound" it was.
Gameplay-wise this is a first person puzzle game (like Portal). If that appeals to you you will probably like this game. There are a lot of puzzles, many of which are quite challenging in the best kind of way.
If you are interested in a deep philosophical experience I really _want_ to recommend this game because I think you would love it if you finished it, but unless you also really like puzzles I don't think you'll enjoy it enough to stick with it in order to get to the heavy stuff that everyone (including me) is raving about.
For what it's worth, though, I'm really glad I played this interesting and thought-provoking game.

As far as I know, there are little to no steam conflicting key bindings by default, and it does sync with your steam friends well. It integrates with steam nicely.
T - Trainability/Gameplay - 6/10
After abandoning this game for a while, I jumped in and was able to remember most of the controls and how the game worked. Personally, I remember hating how they replaced the rotate command from "r," a perfectly reasonable keybind, to the mousewheel with no indication of the change and 30 minutes later I finially figured it out. As a new player, I think I could learn the controls soon enough, but they could be better. The UI is in my opinion terrible, with editing being hidden under "Play," and other things. The gameplay was ok, and I didn't really like the newer gamemodes. Overall meh.
E - Execution - 8/10... but now it's 5/10
I really liked this game early on, minimal pieces to build with but enough to basically get anything done, decent matchmaking, and a clear goal (get to T10). Now it just seems like a cash grab (many colors to decorate locked behind a subscription fee or the lifetime price of about a AAA game, etc).
A - Ambition - 7/10
Eh. Voxel based builder shooter thingy, seen it before. This game was a bit different though, so a little bit of credit.
M - Moddability - 3/10
Online based games can't really be modded, but at least community servers? You can have an in-game replacement sorta thing for steam workshop for ships, but those are also paid with no way to try out the ships. A great example of mods in an online game is Team Fortress 2, where you can have custom maps, and client side things that only you can see and don't affect progression.
O - Optimization - 10/10
It's well optimized. Not much else to say.
S - Soundtrack - 5/10
Some ambient soundtrack, nothing great, and the sound effects are okay.
Final Verdict - 5.8/10
This is normally where I would leave it, and this is the unbiased score (as much as possible). My totally biased score as a player from about 2-3 years ago would be 4/10, just due to the downhill turn this game has taken.

Ever since the Xbox 360 shipped with a headset packaged as standard, online games have yearned to create the kind of cooperative multiplayer seen only in advertisements and well-rehearsed E3 demos.
Outside of these scripted environments very few games have put emphasis on voice chat. Sure, we’ve had games like those in the SOCOM series and MAG which have tried to varying degrees of success but the simple truth is that outside a certain genre of game, voice chat just isn’t used. Hell, even in the most competitive games out there today it’s rare to find people using voice chat.
Squad, on the other hand, is one of the few games which seems to be doing voice chat right. Boot up Squad today and within a few minutes you’ll have a voice telling you where to go and what to do. If taking orders isn’t your thing you can be that voice telling others where to go and what to do. It’s actually very close to what MAG was trying to do, except it’s on a platform where people actually have microphones. You also probably won’t have to worry about servers shutting off making the game unplayable. Even though it’s still in an alpha state, Squad has a thriving active community of players. If anything about MAG sounded appealing to you, Squad is the game that actually delivers on those ideas.
The developers behind Squad started out making a relatively popular mod for Battlefield 2 called Project Reality. Project reality built upon Battlefield 2 adding new levels of realism and a vastly increased scope. It looked better, it played better, its custom-made maps spanned dozens of kilometers. It’s one of the best fan mods out there today. It seems that all of this experience has translated perfectly into Squad with its vast maps and team-focused gameplay.
Squad is unique in that in can take minutes to get to anything resembling action but good leadership will ensure you’re never out of the fray for too long. It’s as if someone took an objective-based first person shooter like Battlefield and added the massive scale and openness of DayZ. As a result Squad it definitely a game you’ll enjoy more if you’re playing with a group of people you know. That’s not to say you can’t have fun alone but just like in other games where communication plays a key role – like Trouble in Terrorist Town – you’re going to have more fun after you and the people you’re playing with have built up a rapport.
It’s hard to be too critical of Squad because it’s still in active development but what I can say is that the gameplay feels extremely solid. Most of the things that need to be improved before the commercial release are related to the UI and tutorials because as a new player it can be very difficult to know what you should do which becomes a very intimidating problem, especially when other people are relying on you to perform your role.
Unlike most early access games, Squad actually offers a fun playable experience. If you’re on the fence about spending the money, maybe wait until the official release but if you’re excited to play right now, it’s well worth the price.

There's a lot to say about this game, so stay for the ride. Ostensibly this is a fairly fast-paced first person shooter in which the ability to aim will put you at an advantage over other players and I believe this is paramount for a shooting game, unlike other shooting games on the market which focus more on pressing a button at the right time. However it still succumbs to the same issues as other games, including gimmicks and horrible developer support.
The Splash Damage website itself claims that they have 200 employees, but you would never guess that number given how glacially slow their work rate is. As of May 2017, a new map was released called Dockyard. This map was in development since 2015 and the last playable untextured version was the summer of 2016. It's taken a professional company nearly a year just to texture one map. If this were a small team of part-time hobbyists, I'd understand completely, but this is supposed to be a "AAA video game developer" (quoted from their own website). The community has been asking for more maps all along as the game originally only shipped with five levels.
Another big problem that Splash Damage is guilty of, as are most other video game companies these days is that they released a game before completing it, then whenever they are criticised for this, they pull out the tired cliché of "Oh it's in beta". The game exists in perpetual beta and will likely never officially go gold. One of the downsides of releasing and marketing an unfinished game is that people get bored of it and leave. The playerbase is stone dead. According to
, the average player count is somewhere between 1,500 and 2,100 players, which by the way is less than half of Farming Simulator 2017. This game doesn't even make Steam's top 100 online games. The game ultimately fails at retaining its playerbase and I can see why. It's stagnant with no development. Join a server and you'll see that more than 90% of players have under twenty or thirty hours in the game. They should have made the game first and then released it properly. The game is created on Unreal Engine 3, which since its release in 2007 I seem to remember being horribly unoptimised and the forums are filled with threads that support that hypothesis. Perhaps that also turns people away.
Dirty Bomb is a class-based shooter and Splash Damage has shown little to no originality when it comes to gameplay. In 2005 I played their previous game Enemy Territory, which had five classes and was on the whole not bad. It was a free to play game, had barely any maps and within maybe two or three years it died. Only the hardcore competitive players remained. Sound familiar? Most of the abilities from that game were directly ported into this game, such as a smoke grenade to call in airstrikes, artillery, medics that revive downed players and land mines, but split up to accommodate nineteen characters instead of five. I will admit that the character design is pretty good, but that's only aesthetics and not gameplay.
This time they expanded the roster from five characters to nineteen and as is the case with pretty much every class-based game, they're unbalanced. Medics had far too much of an impact in Enemy Territory and the same occurs with this game. A team with a medic or two will always win against a team without medics and I believe that forcing roles on the player isn't fun. Unfortunately, after playing the game for long enough, the attentive player will realise that there's a small group of characters that are much more effective than the rest. The most obvious of these is probably Fragger - a character with high health, damage, accuracy and his special ability is an instant kill hand grenade on a sixteen second cooldown. If you spot a player with a decent number of hours in the game, they will invariably have Fragger as their choice of character because he gets the job done better than anyone else.
The game has a dead playerbase, the developers have done almost nothing on this game in over two years. The most recent events have been "trinkets" which are akin to keyrings that hang off the side of the player's weapon. These keyrings could be made by one person in a day at the office and the events that accompanied them were simply a grinding exercise for points. The Christmas event involved Internet memes which strongly indicates that the developers are marketing towards twelve-year-old boys. The Community Manager Chris Mullins often creates videos on the Dirty Bomb Youtube page, but these are fairly lacklustre with vague promises of what's coming in the future or showing a community video that he enjoys.
The saddest part is that this game had a lot of potential and it was squandered by the developers releasing the game before it was finished. I still play this game with friends because it's easy to jump in for a few rounds and compared to all of the other horrible detritus on the shooter market, it's less repulsive than the rest.
Pick it up? Sure, but don't expect much from it or expect to stay. The game is dead, the developers either don't care, aren't up to the job or both. It's too late to salvage and Splash Damage's lineage of dead games ought to be a lesson in how not to produce a game by now. Oh, finally the community is repugnant. If you dare to be good at aiming, you'll receive abuse and player reports. I've yet to be banned thankfully, but that could always change.
Thank you for reading.

Normally, I'm wary of modern "AAA" games. They always tend to be 'streamlined', which is simply their hidden term of saying they dumbed the game down for consoles. And that means lackluster textures, poor animations, poor ports and controls, et cetera, et cetera.
However, I have to say Wolfenstein: TNW pleasantly surprised me. In a nutshell, it's a very fun shooter.
Graphically, the game looks good, although I would advise against moving too close to various surfaces in the game as the textures there tend to still be rather blocky. However, the overall feel and design is very pleasing to the eye.
This big plus is supported by some excellent animations; the latter are always an important part in such games for me. When characters move in a clunky way, it simply takes away something fun, the feeling that you're fighting against living, breathing (or, in this case, mechanical) opponents. Not so in TNW. The animations are rather silky smooth and lovely to look at, especially the robots (although I would not advise looking at them for too long for obvious, lethal reasons).
Underlining everything is also an excellent sound design. Most of the effects and weapons have various clicks, pops, scratches, explosions, booms and other sounds you would expect to hear but in high quality and there's plenty of them. In fact, some of the weapons are so much fun to reload simply because of the extremely satisfying ratchet you'll hear when doing it. Admittedly, there are a few instances in the game where sound effects seem to be almost missing, although those are few and mostly contained in semi-cutscenes. But a few additonal effects would hurt there. Anyway, I digress.
The shooting mechanics are rather excellent. The weapons feel like they have a powerful impact and are fun to use, although, unfortunately, the game doesn't seem to care where you shoot a soldier. I believe headshots do count, but I have only been doing those with a silenced pistol, which brings down unarmoured enemies in one shot.
The AI is... okay. It never truly bothered me while in combat. In fact, I sometimes found myself flanked, although I believe that was mostly due to there being several paths the soldiers could take to get to me, so some simply did so. Where the AI does seem to be completely absent is in stealth. Kill an enemy silently and then receded to the shadows, then proceed to watch the other soldiers nonchallantly walk by their dead comrades as if it is the most normal thing in the world. Strange, but it never really detracted me from enjoying the game.
The level design is varied and fun. The game is almost completely linear, although (SLIGHT SPOILER IN THIS PARAGRAPH) you will get the option of two different timelines while playing, according to what choice you make. The ability to cut vents freeform is nice; a lot nicer than pressing a button and waiting for a repeating animation of your character cutting a piece of metal over and over. You can't do a whole lot with it - you either cut a hole or you don't. But it's still a nice touch.
The difficulty is a bit on the low side. Even when playing the game for the first time, I would suggest selecting the second-hardest difficulty or even THE hardest, "Über" difficulty. Only then will the game give you at least a bit of a challenge. Otherwise the enemies are a little too easy to kill.
Story-wise, there's not much I can say without spoiling it, but it does have a little twist in it (however predictable it is). The cutscenes, while unfortunately taking the player away from the first-person view of their character and thus disembodying you, are, for the most part, nice and very well done. This is accompanied by some above-average voice acting, helped along by, on occasion, funny script writing. The cutscenes sometimes DO tend to fast forward things a little bit. It almost feels like the developers ran out of time and couldn't afford to show, for example, an animation of (making this scene up now) your character making his way through a series of pipes to reach the restricted area. Instead, you might only see the character get into the piping system, then you will be promptly placed at the start of the next level. Feels strange in an otherwise rather polished title.
That's about it. The game is somewhere around 12 hours long, shorter if you don't want to enjoy the sights and merely rush through. There is another timeline available, but the differences will be most likely minor. However, I will be happy to replay the game on the hardest difficulty and enjoy it again.
Is it worth the full price? I think that's something for you to decide. I would probably wait for a sale and get it then. But, if you enjoy shooters, especially with a WW2 vibe infused with sci-fi, you will enjoy this game.

Also, the autralian server is literally dead, with a peak of 500 players accross two continents, which is low, very low, while Connery, an US server, is probably going to get merged soon enough due to lower and lower pop counts aswell.

If you're completely new to FPS genre, you're going to be eaten alive. - to get anything done in this game, you need a team. And it's either going to be completely moronic, or you're simply going to be outnumbered 4 to 1 on a base worth defending, while your faction has the biggest pop on the continent, fighting another base with 100+ players against 12 or something.
- 4 years, and the lore is still lackluster & almost absent from the game itself, even better, a lot of weapons are not from the factions, and the factions literally have 2 freaking vehicles for them : a heavy tank and an aircraft; while you have 8 other vehicles who look almost exactly the same, have exactly the same weapons accross all the 3 factions.
- No viable anticheat, there're cheaters who're going through the walls, the ground, who're spinbotting with LMGs in the sky yet still playing, I'm talking about more than 100 hours in game without getting banned, this is just sad.
- 4 years latter, lags and optimization are still garbage on battles with more than 100 people in.
So, let me ask you one question, is it worth for a new player to play planetside ?
I'd have answered yes in 2013, but in 2016 ? Unless you REALLY want to get into the bits of big fights left (which are going to disappear soon enough), be prepared to face huge frustration moments. Despite devs' recent progress for new players, it's already too late, since the new players don't stick around either way, nor even try the game. For a free MMO FPS game this is definitely worth a try. I have enjoyed almost every minute I have played. I have a few hundred more hours than shown.
[Pros]
-Massive battles with hundreds of players on at any given time.
-Massive maps
-Simple yet solid gun play mechanics.
-Good overall design and concept.
-Good variety of weapons, vehicles, and customization for both.
-Mostly cosmetic micro transactions.*
-Multiple character slots.
-Multiple factions.
-A lot of teamwork and communication in the community.
[Cons]
-Grinding Certs can take forever
-Extremely limited character/vehicle customization for free
-Can be confusing for new players to get into
-Requires a pretty solid rig due to the intensity of so many players on very large maps
*I say mostly because you can buy unlocks for real money to accelerate the process instead of grinding certs to unlock them which may give an unfair advantage so it can be taken as a con or pro. There are also a few gun finishes/paints such as black and gold that can only be unlocked via daybreak cash(paid currency) but offer no advantage statistically.
Overall I would definitely give this game a try if you are into larger scale FPS games with a mix of vehicle combat such as Battlefield. It takes some time to get into but once you get the right weapons and equipment it becomes much more enjoyable.
A tip to newcomers since I sometimes see blueberries running around squad less.. I highly recommend that you start off joining a squad that is active and listen up to the platoon or squad leader and follow directions to learn the game faster and have a good time. Remember that this game is not like call of duty and is not a one man army game. Teamwork is essential.

I just completed the game with 11 hours spent on gameplay. I loved the story and the story did a great job of getting me to care about the main character, Max Payne.  I never played Max Payne 1 & 2 and didn't feel like I was missing something since the Max Payne 3 story stood on its own merits. Still, with frustrating QTE portions aside, the game was great with weapons and the 3rd Person Point of View was good enough though I'd wish for 1st Person Point of View aiming.  Trying to find Golden Parts was at times in the way of the flow of the situations in the game; for example, after a firefight I have to keep moving to the next situation--sometimes due to time limits-- so I don't have time to treasure hunt.  Even so, aside from QTE, some frustration with 3rd Person shooting, and plot flow breaking treasure hunts, this is a great game because of a great story that makes you care about characters.

Dirty Bomb is simultaneously a new and old FPS. It really is a hard game to describe, something like overwatch, TF2, with a bit of a faster feel to it. Be warned, there is a learning curve, but the new tutorial does help with that. The game says beta but sometimes it feels more like a fully released game. I can say with confidence that it is the best F2P shooter on the market, and I would contend one of the top 5 you can play right now. There are claims that the game is pay 2 win, mostly from those people that watched the angry joe review of the game. That could not be further from the truth. While there is a portion of time where some people will have better loadout cards than you, you can buy ANY of them from the store at bronze level. The difference between the bronze and cobalt/gold/silver cards is merely cosmetic, you have access to the same perks, skils, and weapons. WARNING:
Rimworld is not for the casual players, this is a game you need to commit to. Be prepared to fail and start over, and over, and over again untill you have understood the game. Rimworld is a game that is so in depth, every choice you make matters and has consequences. I would recommend watching some Youtubers first and to start easy and work your way up.
Having said that, rarely have I seen a developer that is so active within the community. Tynan is active on the ludeon forums and actively responds to suggestions and he has taken inspiration from the community, and even integrated some of the popular community mods into the vanilla game. The game is very solid and after about 100 hours hasnt crashed or glitched out on me once. One of the only two annoyances I have with game is that the starting character system is weird, as it partially allows me to get the colonists I want, but at an extremely inefficient way. The other thing I find annoying is something I love and hate, the randomness of it. Having random events makes the game unpredictable and fun but also unfair at some points, which sucks if you spend 20 hours making a colony to then see them die by the plague and flu hitting simultaneously.
Is this game expensive? Define expensive. To me this game is so in depth and with modding this game is worth the price it has, although it is indeed one of the more expensive games in its category. On the flip side, I feel like the price benefits the game. This game is not about selling the most amount of copies, this game is about delivering an amazing experience to player looking for a challenge, and the price means you are commited to the game.
If you are looking for a management game with a challenge and you are willing to learn by failing then this is the game for you.

-Summary-
Great game for those looking for more than a match-based FPS. This game is a persistant, large-scale war fought over an entire planet... not over a single city or spick of forest. Well Recommended to try it out (it is free, after all) if you are looking for a futuristic FPS of this scale!
-Review Details-
Pros:
* Good Graphics (runs pretty well on low-end PCs) for an arcade-like game.
* Great variety in classes, weapons, and factions/playstyles.
* Large-scale warfare.
* In-game music is EPIC (music fits each faction's style, and is unique to each faction).
* Teamwork is well rewarded.
* Not a match-based game. Is Massive-World Engine.
* FREE-2-PLAY
* Support roles are actually rewarding!
* Easy and comprehensive Squad system. Play with friends, or with random players!
* Combined Arms with vehicles, aircraft, and infantry all fighting together.
* If you find a favorite in-game faction, it is hard not to become a loyal soldier for the said faction... inter-faction rivalry at its highest!
* Base-building for RTS players, and resource-gathering for non combat-oriented players.
* Clans and Zergs.
Cons:
* There is a PAY-2-WIN Grindy feel (everything bought with premium CAN be earned in-game however, but it takes a lot of earning).
* Some difficulty dealing with hackers/cheaters.
* Still bugged here-and-there (but usually pretty stable for a game running 500 players a map).
* Not a match-based game (a con for some).
* Relatively high learning curve for infantry/vehicle crews (EXTREMELY high learning curve for aircraft pilots).
* NS weapons (usable by all factions) ruin the feel of being part of a unique faction, are often overpowering, and are usually bought for (not grinded)... money grabbing?
* Clans and Zergs.
Zerg
A massive blob of around 50-100 or more players attacking and swarming the map. Extremely difficult to stop. In Planetside 2, Zergs usually take over most of a continent ("map") while active. (Good news: non-zerging factions get a bonus to XP for resisting the Zerg!)
Match-based game
Common mode of game where a set number of players play for a set time. Winner(s) get the majority of the match's rewards, while the loser(s) get very little or nothing at all.
Massive-World
An Open-World type game mode where any number of players can compete over any amount of time in a massive open world. Players are rewarded for actions done during play, and less so for the end result of a conflict. However, the winning side usually still recieves a hefty reward for all of the work done to win (especially when a single "battle" can last for several hours, and a war for a day!).

There's no doubt this game deserves a positive review.
Why?
Well, I'll just put all of my reasons down into this one review.
--------------------------------------------------------------
Number 1) Creative idea.
There's no doubt that when you look at Castle Crashers, you see no resemblence of any game out there. That, my friend, is the beauty of Behemoth. Their games are all origanal ideas, and Castle Crashers is no exception. This is only one reason I recommend Castle Crashers, you never know what might happen next.
Number 2) There's always something to play for
What do I mean by this? What I mean is that whenever you play Castle Crashers, you always have SOMETHING to do on it.
For example, you might be trying to unlock a new character out of about 31 of them. You may be trying to own everybody in an arena match, or playing the mini games included in Castle Crashers. You may be grinding for a larger level and more gold, or trying to beat Insane Mode for the beautiful golden skull.
Number 3) Stratagy
Now, first off it's important to note that Castle Crashers is a button mashing game. It seems like there's no stratagy involved, when truely, there is. There's times when you have to cast a magical spell, or times when you need to sling an arrow. Times when you have to bash rival's skulls with weapons, times when you need to dodge all of their attacks.
This is a small reason I recommend this game, but I think it's sort of worth mentioning in this review.
Number 4) Simple controlls
Now, when I say this, I also want to note that Castle Crashers is SO much easier with a plug-in controller. That being said, this number is all about the simple controlls with a CONTROLLER.
Here are the only controlls you need to memorize: Light attack button, hard attack button, use item button, scroll item buttons, and toggle magic button. Oh yeah, and jump.
It seems like alot, but it is SO easy to memorize.
Number 5) Large amount of playable characters
When I say this, I mean LARGE. Well, about 31, including 2 cheap DLCS and an unlockable character you can only get if you get Battle Block Theater.
The others are unlocked by certain paths, beating arenas or levels, and beating bosses in Insane Mode. There's all different character paths you can do, such as the Red Knight being Red knight > Skeleton > Bear, each one unlocked by beating the game with another. Each character has their own looks, names, and unique magic abilities that makes the player really want to unlock each one.
Number 6) (Final) Very creative rivals, bosses, and playable characters.
When I say this, I mean very creative. Some of them may have some inspiriation, but for the most part they are all orgianal ideas. They all have their different attacks, and the bosses are each hard and annoying in their own ways. These make each different boss and characters unique as can be, a small reason I recommend this game, but still a reason.
I hope you enjoyed this long review, and I hope that I made up your mind whether or not to buy this game if you haven't already.

This game is a puzzle game on all kinds of levels. You got the obvious puzzles you got to solve where you are free to chose which one you do first and which later. Then you got the storyline which you are solving by yourself by constantly thinking about the scripts you read in each part of the world. The only difference is, that you're not allowed to type in your own answers but instead to chose between different answers. Though these answers are pretty much almost all you'd like to put in anyway so it's not a negative point in any way.
You get in this game:
- to chose which puzzles to solve first
- the opportunity to do puzzles only if you like
- different endings (don't expect too much difference^^)

Dirty Bomb is simultaneously a new and old FPS. It really is a hard game to describe, something like overwatch, TF2, with a bit of a faster feel to it. Be warned, there is a learning curve, but the new tutorial does help with that. The game says beta but sometimes it feels more like a fully released game. I can say with confidence that it is the best F2P shooter on the market, and I would contend one of the top 5 you can play right now. There are claims that the game is pay 2 win, mostly from those people that watched the angry joe review of the game. That could not be further from the truth. While there is a portion of time where some people will have better loadout cards than you, you can buy ANY of them from the store at bronze level. The difference between the bronze and cobalt/gold/silver cards is merely cosmetic, you have access to the same perks, skils, and weapons. The game is not overly grindy, and you can bang out loadout cards in an afternoon if you just complete your missions. Personally this is my favorite FPS on the market right now, the only downsides I can see to the game are that content updates are a bit scarce, but with the developers seperating from nexon, I am hoping that they will be able to produce content more quickly. Just recently a new map, dockyard, was released, with a teaser to another new map being in production. Overall dirty bomb is a well rounded, if slightly rough game. The gameplay is solid, and progression is fun and not too hard. I give this game an 8/10, with the 2 points being deducted for a little lack of content, and for general bugs and glitches.

This review has troubled me more than most as I’m still trying to decide exactly how I feel about WOLFENSTEIN: THE NEW ORDER. There’s much to like here. Visually, the game is impressive, the combat is fun and quite challenging on the higher difficulties, and the story, although a little cheesy, and not a match for such franchises as BioShock or Half-Life, is pretty good. And the voice acting is solid throughout. There are also some impressive cut-scenes and very enjoyable set-pieces. Despite all this, however, the overall lasting impression of the game is that it somehow falls a little flat. Perhaps it’s the fact that there are so many cutscenes where control is suddenly wrenched away from the player (I like a good cutscene as much as the next gamer and they are necessary to flesh-out a full story, but here there are so many of them it sometimes disturbs the rhythm of the game). Or maybe it’s the rail-like, linear nature of the game and the lack of variety in the environments. Or it might be the fact that, although the game tries to offer a mix of stealth and run-and-gun it really only gets the latter right. Or maybe it’s just me. It’s true to say the same can be said about many good games and it would be unfair to criticise WTNO too much for having these traits. But at the end of the day, although I enjoyed WTNO, and will stick with the franchise, I’m left with mixed feelings about the overall experience. Oh, and it’s yet another game with no quick save, which is annoying.

-Summary-
Great game for those looking for more than a match-based FPS. This game is a persistant, large-scale war fought over an entire planet... not over a single city or spick of forest. Well Recommended to try it out (it is free, after all) if you are looking for a futuristic FPS of this scale!
-Review Details-
Pros:
* Good Graphics (runs pretty well on low-end PCs) for an arcade-like game.
* Great variety in classes, weapons, and factions/playstyles.
* Large-scale warfare.
* In-game music is EPIC (music fits each faction's style, and is unique to each faction).
* Teamwork is well rewarded.
* Not a match-based game. Is Massive-World Engine.
* FREE-2-PLAY
* Support roles are actually rewarding!
* Easy and comprehensive Squad system. Play with friends, or with random players!
* Combined Arms with vehicles, aircraft, and infantry all fighting together.
* If you find a favorite in-game faction, it is hard not to become a loyal soldier for the said faction... inter-faction rivalry at its highest!
* Base-building for RTS players, and resource-gathering for non combat-oriented players.
* Clans and Zergs.
Cons:
* There is a PAY-2-WIN Grindy feel (everything bought with premium CAN be earned in-game however, but it takes a lot of earning).
* Some difficulty dealing with hackers/cheaters.
* Still bugged here-and-there (but usually pretty stable for a game running 500 players a map).
* Not a match-based game (a con for some).
* Relatively high learning curve for infantry/vehicle crews (EXTREMELY high learning curve for aircraft pilots).
* NS weapons (usable by all factions) ruin the feel of being part of a unique faction, are often overpowering, and are usually bought for (not grinded)... money grabbing?
* Clans and Zergs.
Zerg
A massive blob of around 50-100 or more players attacking and swarming the map. Extremely difficult to stop. In Planetside 2, Zergs usually take over most of a continent ("map") while active. (Good news: non-zerging factions get a bonus to XP for resisting the Zerg!)
Match-based game
Common mode of game where a set number of players play for a set time. Winner(s) get the majority of the match's rewards, while the loser(s) get very little or nothing at all.
Massive-World
An Open-World type game mode where any number of players can compete over any amount of time in a massive open world. Players are rewarded for actions done during play, and less so for the end result of a conflict. However, the winning side usually still recieves a hefty reward for all of the work done to win (especially when a single "battle" can last for several hours, and a war for a day!).

Max Payne 3 is not a fun game. It is a game you should only play if you like a 'challenge'. What it has going for it are interesting levels and a half-cooked story that at the very least, serves as excuse to have those levels. What it has going against it are
- a protagonist who progressively gets more and more repetitive about the things he says, like a broken record,
- a last stand mode that doesn't work half as well as it should because of serious camera issues and the inability to reload if you just happened to have no bullets left,
- certain areas of the game that simply pit you against people with no options for tactical play, turning something that could be about tactics and skill into something that is a matter of luck,
- "interesting" mechanics such as enemies who, when shot through the head, keep their weapon aimed perfectly at you and keep their finger squeezing down on the trigger tightly;
- when you finally masterfully headshot an enemy, it turns out you've only shot off his helmet and he is in fact perfectly willing and able to return the favour on your sadly unhelmeted head,
- enemies remaining fully on their feet for seconds after you've already killed them, making you doubt you've actually killed them while getting shot from all other directions,
- enemies swaying and skittering around like cirque du soleil acts as you're forced to try and aim for their head because their bodies can take about 1,231 rounds before they die of lead poisoning,
- keeping your crosshair aimed at an enemy who is behind cover, waiting far too long until he remembers his job is to kill you and he finally pokes his head out,
- finding yourself with your handgun equipped after EVERY cutscene, regardless of whether it's empty and whether you actually need bullets in your gun for the enemies rushing at you directly after said cutscene,
- and one particular recurring miniboss whose one weakness is that when he runs out of bullets after half an hour, you have two seconds to shoot him in the head - neither challenging nor fun, nor necessary.
Finally, this game seems confused about its pace. It clearly wants its action to be engaging and heart-racing; it has characters specifically and very annoyingly screaming at you to keep moving, yet at the same time it expects you to stop and comb every level carefully because there might be painkillers, clues or golden gun pieces in any inconspicuous part of any level. Add to that that it is often unclear which way will progress the story and that you cannot return once the game has checkpointed unless you redo the whole level, and finding these things becomes tedious as well. All of these design choices are conflicting and become yet another mind-numblingly tedious aspect of the game. All things considered, this game lacks fun, lacks an interesting main character, and even generally lacks a sense of satisfaction at overcoming the challenges-turned-tedium. Not really worth the money, definitely not worth the memory it eats up on your hard drive.

So if you've been wanting to get your fix of mute-protagonist-alone-in-dystopian-puzzle-prison-world-versus-disembodied-omnipotent-antagonist-jailkeeper-voice genre games, Croteam would appear to be the only studio currently delivering. The game is gorgeous, the puzzles are challenging but extremely logical and progress at just the right pace, and the story as delivered largely through Elohim's voice and text logs is both compelling and thoughtful. The game is full of "aha" moments, both in terms of the puzzles as well as the story, and it all wraps up in a satisfying conclusion with a great final set of puzzles that manages to turn many of the mechanics on their head again.
There are really only a couple of faults I can think of, and none of these were bad enough to at all spoil my enjoyment of the game.
Firstly, as with any puzzle game of this nature, replay value will always be limited - a lot of the fun is in figuring out the solutions and uncovering the backstory, and you won't ever be able to repeat that experience, short of someone inventing some kind of mind-wipe technology. That still hasn't stopped me enjoying replaying Portal multiple times, but it's never the same as your first time. Sadly the Steam Workshop has very little in the way of new levels even 8 months after release. At some point I would like to go back through and unlock the bonus levels, however.
Secondly, the hint system seems ... a little pointless. You have to complete a solid chunk of the game even to unlock it, and it is rather hard to find - I actually had to look up a spoiler to find out how to access the messenger worlds, and hints are extremely redundant once you're looking up spoilers. Even then you have to complete even more non-trivial puzzles to earn even a single hint! It's a nice bit of extra content but the complexity of it makes it seem more like a joke than a serious attempt to deliver hints.
I suppose the only other thing here is that in terms of mechanics, this game doesn't really bring anything actually new to the table. All the puzzle mechanics have been done before - but the way they are executed against such a rich background, and the way they play off each other to create ever more intricate Rube Goldberg-type puzzles, is truly fantastic, and it certainly never feels like it's lacking.
So, a resounding thumbs up - this is one of my top games of all time. Just buy it.
