This game is the definition of deceptive.
Shotguns double as sniper rifles with how high their damage and how low their bullet spread and falloff damage is. Actual sniper mercs with sniper rifles have their hands held by the game in a lot of matches with most maps having too much wide open space and too little cover where the attacking team moves in from, and "grenades" that give them temporary wallhacks for those rare moments when targets actually do find cover. Most explosives often don't have enough of a giveaway for it to even be possible to avoid them, or they're simply too powerful. Common audio glitches can eliminate the sound of air strike markers entirely and give players no cue whatsoever. Proxy, a typically defense-oriented merc who uses landmines, can actually kamikaze into enemy teams and get a triple-kill or better just by abusing the way explosives work. SMGs can't deal damage worth a damn without consistently headshotting. The starting medic, who also gets an all-purpose overpowered shotgun, drops a healing station which is far too strong, and effectively turns anyone standing near it into an unkillable tank, simultaneously putting most other medics' healing abilities to shame. EMP and flashbang explosives specifically have absolutely no concern for balance put into them, being able to blind/heavily disorient anyone hit for several seconds, essentially a death sentence in a fast-paced FPS like this. And the grind, for ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥'s sake, the grind.
Everyone praises this game for "the number of different ways there are to earn credits" which you need an absurd amount of just to unlock a single merc, but these people, who must be mathematically inept, at least need to learn that zero times any number is still zero. Devs always want you to pay, but the ones behind this game make it shamefully obvious, even giving new players 30,000 free credits (which might sound completely contradictory, but bear with me on this) so they can get their first merc that much sooner, which will, of course, make future merc grinding feel like absolute hell by comparison. It's basic psychological manipulation and preys heavily upon people easily addicted or vulnerable to instant gratification. The first 6 levels fly by with very few rewards to receive for them, and at that point, the game tells you that you "get a free LOOOOOOTBOX every levelup from now on," but there's a MASSIVE spike in the amount of exp needed to level up after getting to level 7. There's a chokehold on players to spend money rather than grind through what should be, and even sometimes is fun objective-based combat and gunplay, and anyone who doesn't play ALL day and do ALL their missions and gets turned off by the obvious lack of balance with some guns will asphxiate before they reach their goals.

Thought-provoking story, as long as you inspect the in-game terminals that provide exposition etc. Requires a great deal of reading if you want to achieve the maximum effect. Puts into perspective both the purpose of human life, as well as what defines humanity in an AI. If you found interesting the moral dilemmas of acknowleging the legitimacy of synthetic life as presented in the Mass Effect franchise or the Ex Machina movie, you will enjoy it.
The actual puzzles kind of feel like what Portal 2 would be without the portals. Laser puzzles are done in a better way, albeit a tad over-used over the course of the game. The testing elements in The Talos Principle kind of snap with each other in a more predictable way, which allows - in contrast with the Source engine - repeatability in specific "solving techniques", while at the same time almost zeroing the margin for alternate solutions. It's just a change of pace compared to more realistic first person puzzles, nor better or worse. A lot of easter eggs and bonus puzzles.
The DLC is decent too, with a lot more organic activity in the terminals, and nice puzzles.

Kind of hard to sum this one up without giving too much away, at least with regards to the plot (which is heavily philosophical and unlike anything I've dealt with in a game so far), but you have choices to make that will influence how the game unfolds and ends for you.
Gameplaywise, this is a puzzle game, and you will be solving a variety of puzzles with a growing number of tools to collect tetriminos, which allow you to unlock more puzzles. The puzzle design is seriously top notch. I have never felt more proud of myself in a puzzle game than I was after solving some of these puzzles. Just when you start to get comfortable with certain techniques, the puzzles use that casual reliance against you and require you to think differently. There are over 100 puzzles in the game, with optional stars to collect for an exceptional challenge (it hurt my brain too much to collect them). Without completionist tendencies, the game should provide you with roughly 15 hours of puzzling ecstacy.
All in all, this game is a super unique experience that has continued to preoccupy my thoughts since I completed it.

Alright, here is the story of my first game:
I start up Squad, giddy als all hell to get going. I was really interested in getting this game for a while already, the moment was finally there!
I join a server, as well as a decent looking squad with 2 clan members. I was nervous as a bag of d1cks because all kinds of things were still very unknown to me; how are the people in the community in a random round in a random squad, can I pull my own weight, do I know enough already about the game to really benefit my squad and the team?
Turns out I really did not have to worry. I silently linked up with the squad leader after spawning in and basically just followed him and the rest of the squad around, moving from position to position, giving covering fire, keeping an eye out for contacts and so on. All the while getting more and more in communication with the various helpful, kind and cool deviants from the squad.
My confidence about my capability's was starting to grow and mayng, was I going to need it.
Our squad was the one who had to capture and defend the ruins that is Castle. We spread out accordingly and even set up a support detachment on the ridge next to castle so we'd have a lot more sightlines on the place and some great covering fire. Slowly but surely enemies started to appear and trickle in. I was perched in one of the higher structures in Castle so I had good vision over the place as well as some good cover from the direction we knew the enemies were coming from. And massively attack they finally did, with multiple squads.
It was complete carnage in the castle. Thrilling, adrenaline pumping, PTSD inducing close quarters combat. For at least 10 minutes, it was insane. Bullets flying around all over the place, grenades going off everywhere. Slowly but surely our numbers were dwindling giving out loud screams wherever they fell. Nonetheless, we were making it incredibly hard for the enemy to push up and set up an effective position. Our medics risked everything to just, try and keep as many as they could alive.
The supporting fire from the ridge made it so the enemy couldn't really push on my position and I in turn was able to make it very hard for them to find good cover to do anything with. They were pinned in castle. This did not stop them from flanking attacks, using smoke to move in cover, using the little bits of cover they had left as best they could to fire back at us. They were giving it everything to get Castle.
After spending almost all of the ammunition in my weapons, sweating like a pig and shaking from the adrenaline, we had won! The enemy team ran out of tickets because of the ferocity of the fighting in that round, as well as our succesfull attempt to defend Castle.
I sat back in my chair in awe, feeling spent because of this first round. I was actually the top player on the server on points by far since I was defending from inside the capzone, and our squad was the top squad. My kd was only 5-2, definitly not the most kills in my squad, but my role in being there on that little perch in that godforsaken castle was (at least it really felt and looked like it) crucial. And that was fckn amazing.
So, I can truly recommend this game already in it's alpha state. I played a couple of other rounds after that on different servers and had similar experiences each time.
The immersion is great, the people are pretty dang cool, strategy and communication completely win games and that is so incredibly satisfying to experience and play with. The graphics are pretty good as well I must say, the sounds are awesome.
I'm really looking forward to all the updates and how this game is going to develop. There's still a lot of things that aren't fully fleshed out or functioning, but from what I've seen the developers are doing an awesome job updating it. The game itself is really stable for me but if you're an AMD user, wait till they've fixed the problems with it.
It's like a huge complicated chessgame, you can chose the role you play and how you go about defeating the enemy with your squad and team. It's completely up to you. If you even remotely love anything that comes closes to that, Squad will probably be a great thing to add to your life.

This game is the definition of deceptive.
Shotguns double as sniper rifles with how high their damage and how low their bullet spread and falloff damage is. Actual sniper mercs with sniper rifles have their hands held by the game in a lot of matches with most maps having too much wide open space and too little cover where the attacking team moves in from, and "grenades" that give them temporary wallhacks for those rare moments when targets actually do find cover. Most explosives often don't have enough of a giveaway for it to even be possible to avoid them, or they're simply too powerful. Common audio glitches can eliminate the sound of air strike markers entirely and give players no cue whatsoever. Proxy, a typically defense-oriented merc who uses landmines, can actually kamikaze into enemy teams and get a triple-kill or better just by abusing the way explosives work. SMGs can't deal damage worth a damn without consistently headshotting. The starting medic, who also gets an all-purpose overpowered shotgun, drops a healing station which is far too strong, and effectively turns anyone standing near it into an unkillable tank, simultaneously putting most other medics' healing abilities to shame. EMP and flashbang explosives specifically have absolutely no concern for balance put into them, being able to blind/heavily disorient anyone hit for several seconds, essentially a death sentence in a fast-paced FPS like this. And the grind, for ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥'s sake, the grind.
Everyone praises this game for "the number of different ways there are to earn credits" which you need an absurd amount of just to unlock a single merc, but these people, who must be mathematically inept, at least need to learn that zero times any number is still zero. Devs always want you to pay, but the ones behind this game make it shamefully obvious, even giving new players 30,000 free credits (which might sound completely contradictory, but bear with me on this) so they can get their first merc that much sooner, which will, of course, make future merc grinding feel like absolute hell by comparison. It's basic psychological manipulation and preys heavily upon people easily addicted or vulnerable to instant gratification. The first 6 levels fly by with very few rewards to receive for them, and at that point, the game tells you that you "get a free LOOOOOOTBOX every levelup from now on," but there's a MASSIVE spike in the amount of exp needed to level up after getting to level 7. There's a chokehold on players to spend money rather than grind through what should be, and even sometimes is fun objective-based combat and gunplay, and anyone who doesn't play ALL day and do ALL their missions and gets turned off by the obvious lack of balance with some guns will asphxiate before they reach their goals.

"Croteam, the guys who made the ultraviolent Serious Sam games, have released a non-violent puzzle game? Say, what!?"
Well hot damn was I surprised at first! And hot damn am I surprised now, that I've beaten the thing and realized that it's the bees knees.
The Talos Principle is a contemplative, philosophical puzzle game, in which you explore a virtual reality world in order to find out what it means to be human and to determine if you are, indeed, a human.
The game takes the simple first-person-shooter mechanics, but removes the guns and adds in a much-needed precision jump to keep the player from sliding around too much. This results in a most pleasant gameplay experience, allowing you to focus on solving the actual puzzles. There are a lot of puzzles in this game, starting from♥♥♥♥♥♥easy and ramping up to hair-pullingly frustrating. And if you are a genious and can easily solve all the puzzles, there are hidden stars that require even more devilish puzzle-solving! Yaaay!
To top off the gameplay, The Talos Principle sports great storytelling via audio logs, e-mails, chatlogs and text files, as well as the best interactive dialogue I've ever had in a game. The game is pretty as heck (top tier skyboxes) and sounds very lovely.
I heartily recommend this game!

A first person puzzler very much in the style of portal. the level of polish and care given to this game is clear. There's a rich lore, interesting story, compelling imagery and narrative, and a world changing mystery to solve.
pity it's not fun.
the puzzles, while mechanically interesting, quickly become a slog as you trudge from one beautiful, classically inspired vista to another, to do yet another puzzle lazer bounce puzzle and collect yet another not-at-all-Tetris-trust-us sigil, in an attempt to unlock another not-at-all-tetris lock on a door that is hiding the interesting bits of the story.
this feeling of drudgery isn't helped by the isolated nature of the puzzles making them all feel like little roadblock work-units disconnected from and cordoning off the rest of the game. the checklist presentation of the finished and pending puzzles is also clearly distracting, daring you to leave one unfinished, gleaming colorfully and defiantly uncrossed on every nearby signpost, breaking you out of the immersion and reminding you there's work that needs doing, once your done all this interesting introspection on the nature of AI vs consciousness.
Some of the puzzles, especially the later green and yellow unlock puzzles, and almost all of the red progression puzzles, seem to be designed as gotcha traps. many introduce new mechanics without any warning, leaving you banging your head using the well tested strategies from other rooms, unaware the deadly froblinators have another function unlocked by approaching them while standing on one foot. some puzzles are specifically designed to mislead the player, i.e. including an important looking door that looks very much like it's required, but can't actually be used to solve the puzzle, and is only designed to use up resources that are needed elsewhere.
I'm especially bitter about the messenger system; it's originally presented in a way that strongly implies a progression barrier on the (red) story puzzles, suggesting they can't be solved without first the unlocking messenger system. once i finished doing all the work to unlock the messengers, i was disappointed to find it was just an in-game hint system, render obsolete by 20 years of the internet, locked behind the exact same puzzles they're meant to help solve, insult to injury. more grating, each messenger requires 15 or 20 minutes or work, and you can only ever have 3 for the entirety of the game, making the in-game hints too rare to be used and too costly to be horded. and then i still had to back-track through all of the levels to do the same red gotcha puzzles that lead me to believe the red puzzles were progression locked in the first place.
i really wanted to like this game. interesting trans-humanist introspection, slightly askance view on the sacred nature of thought, and a truly interesting mystery; it was straight up my alley. after 8 hours with it, my exhaustion with the gameplay overwhelmed the compelling and interesting story.

Age of Empires II: Headache Remastered edition.
Don't take that the wrong way, I love this game. I'm just not good at it. In strategy games, there's usually a counter for every unit on the field, we call this The Law of Rock Paper Shotgun. Age Of Empires II takes that and adds to it where not only do units counter one and other, but civilizations do as well. With 20+ civs to choose from, what works good with one sucks with the other, there is no bread and butter.
Oh and if you're not good at multi tasking? Sorry. You'll get steam rolled. You have to manage your own resources by choosing what to build and when, military to train yes/no and how much and when, civilian population levels, and all factor in what your enemy is doing so you can get a few steps ahead of them and crush em. Long story short you need to be a phsychiatrist to win at this game.
Campaign stories are good and there's a fair amount of history that's real to peak your interest. Got a history passion about Ghengas Khan? Play his campaign levels. Just don't try it online, some Spaniard is gonna just wipe you all up and down the street.
Good game that I'm just not good at. Rates well regardless.

WARNING:
Rimworld is not for the casual players, this is a game you need to commit to. Be prepared to fail and start over, and over, and over again untill you have understood the game. Rimworld is a game that is so in depth, every choice you make matters and has consequences. I would recommend watching some Youtubers first and to start easy and work your way up.
Having said that, rarely have I seen a developer that is so active within the community. Tynan is active on the ludeon forums and actively responds to suggestions and he has taken inspiration from the community, and even integrated some of the popular community mods into the vanilla game. The game is very solid and after about 100 hours hasnt crashed or glitched out on me once. One of the only two annoyances I have with game is that the starting character system is weird, as it partially allows me to get the colonists I want, but at an extremely inefficient way. The other thing I find annoying is something I love and hate, the randomness of it. Having random events makes the game unpredictable and fun but also unfair at some points, which sucks if you spend 20 hours making a colony to then see them die by the plague and flu hitting simultaneously.
Is this game expensive? Define expensive. To me this game is so in depth and with modding this game is worth the price it has, although it is indeed one of the more expensive games in its category. On the flip side, I feel like the price benefits the game. This game is not about selling the most amount of copies, this game is about delivering an amazing experience to player looking for a challenge, and the price means you are commited to the game.
If you are looking for a management game with a challenge and you are willing to learn by failing then this is the game for you.

Visuals: (on ultra atm) Certainly good enough, occasionally feel like a bit of a work-in-progress (because they are). There are odd player model issues - like when someone is applying a field dressing. Not quite as polished as some other games but still immersive - and there are updates forthcoming with visual improvements in the pipeline. Most of the weapon, and visual, effects are already great.
Sound: Excellent - the sound of your own guns firing have satisfying 'weight', and the crack-and-thump of incoming rounds (along with the visual distortion) is very effective. The radio chatter (if your in a decent squad) is very immersive.
Gameplay: Excellent. I've already lost count of the immersive games on random public servers, in a random squad, where everyone  in the whole team is working together on synchronised objectives. No other FPS game has managed to acheive teamplay like this on random public servers imo. Microphone is essential - I never bother with a mic on any other game but this game is different.
There's been quite a lot of additional content announced, but the game is so good as an infantry focussed team game right now, I hope the addional content enhances rather than unbalances the gameplay.

9/10. As far as puzzle games go, The Talos Principle had me fully invested and I definitely had to rack my brain to work out the more difficult ones. It's a beautiful game and it has great gameplay mechanics. There's the philosophy component as well, which is an integral part of the game's story.
While I enjoyed solving puzzles and debating a computer about what it means to be a person, I didn't feel like the two meshed well together. When I purchased the game I was actually expecting to sit in a room with a robot and debate the meaning of life and personhood. Instead, it's basically Portal with an exploration of humanity woven throughout the story.
One of the star puzzles required outside research (The Eagle Has Landed), which I found unnecessary. A few of the others were so well hidden that I had to do a google search.
All in all, The Talos Principle is a great game and well worth the price. I sunk over 20 hours into it. My only criticism is that I didn't feel that running around searching for Tetris pieces is the best avenue for exploring what it means to be a person.

9/10. As far as puzzle games go, The Talos Principle had me fully invested and I definitely had to rack my brain to work out the more difficult ones. It's a beautiful game and it has great gameplay mechanics. There's the philosophy component as well, which is an integral part of the game's story.
While I enjoyed solving puzzles and debating a computer about what it means to be a person, I didn't feel like the two meshed well together. When I purchased the game I was actually expecting to sit in a room with a robot and debate the meaning of life and personhood. Instead, it's basically Portal with an exploration of humanity woven throughout the story.
One of the star puzzles required outside research (The Eagle Has Landed), which I found unnecessary. A few of the others were so well hidden that I had to do a google search.
All in all, The Talos Principle is a great game and well worth the price. I sunk over 20 hours into it. My only criticism is that I didn't feel that running around searching for Tetris pieces is the best avenue for exploring what it means to be a person.

After learning the game, I did my first play through as a single colonist trying to get by.  I had to build, hunt, cook, clean, mine, and do everything by my lonesome with my pet dog.  After some time went by, my sister shows up to the colony to help me in my endeavors.  We keep building, eventually we get defenses set up and we even buy some slaves and bring them into the community.  My sister falls in love with one of the slave girls, and they set up to get married.
My life would change that day.  We have fought many men and women to keep our home, our supplies, and our food.  My dog went from a loyal companion to a trusted fighter.  I set our turrets a little further down the mountain at a choke point, but I then got an alert that men were trying to tunnel past the defenses straight at our base.  I set my troops up to prepare for a big skirmish.  This would be a bloody wedding.
The mountain side burst open, and the first lady that came out started throwing grenades.  She killed off one of my men, but then went down in the process.  The next person to come through had a bow, and hit my dog, but was taken out in a melee.  The last person out was my father.  I couldn't believe it.  The closest target to him and his shotgun was my sisters wife to be, and before I could stop him, he unloaded the shotgun right into her side, nearly killing her.  In a fury, I shoot my father before he can get another shot off.  We take my sisters bride-to-be into the hospital, which wasn't as advanced as I would have liked it.  My sister, also our doctor, stayed with her lover every day, trying frantically to heal her.  After a few days go by, she passed away.
This game allows you to create a story, and is really worth the investment.  Some stories will suck, but every once in a while you will get one that makes you really, really enjoy the game.

After playing a game like Alan Wake, its rather refreshing to find a game that appreciates the platform it was brought into, being the PC, which is notorious for subpar console ports. Forcing anti aliasing and having a very limited graphics options menu does not equate to a great port. Reason being why I should gush over how buttery smooth Max Payne 3 ran on my rig, with its rather extensive graphics menu and fantastic optimization. You never really appreciate a good port until you run across a♥♥♥♥♥♥one.
Anyway, lets get down to business…
Theres a lot of good in Max Payne, and quite a bit of bad to compensate. One is something the franchise has never really been able to accomplish, being, having an engaging narrative. Max, finding himself in the crosshairs of a New Jersey mob boss, travels to Brazil with a man named Passos, promising tons of cash and escape from his current predicament. What ensues is, from what I’m able to muster from my playthrough, was just a ♥♥♥♥ ton of noise and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It’s standard action movie fair, with little creative flare. You’ll end up forgetting this the entire thing, along with its unique setting.
Forgetting my two sentence limerick, I like Passos. He’s a funny guy and always has your back in the middle of a fire fight. But everyone else are simply cardboard cutouts, completely two dimensionally with zero personality. Whenever someone is killed off, you don’t really give a flying ♥♥♥♥. You just want you mate to stop crying so you can move onto the next shootout.
That’s another issue, as Max Payne 3 seems to fall into this cycle of moving from shooting gallery to shooting gallery. While, yes, that pretty much describes every single FPS in existence, they at least offer engaging combat mechanics to compensate and enemy variety. While bullet time remedies the issue slightly, a dude with a gun is virtually the only dude you're going to kill. Still, it retains tension and is engaging with the bullet time (effectively slowmo) mechanic, which is a godsend in hotter fire fights. Longer play sessions will tend to get grindy and feel as if Paul W. S. Anderson was behind development.
Going with the theme of combat, the gunplay is fan-♥♥♥♥ING-tastic. Whether it be magnum, pistol, shotgun or assault rifle, every round expended has kick and power. When you clear a room of enemies, you can’t help but feel like god. Contributing to this is the expertly balanced difficulty here. Powering through on Hard Mode, I couldn't help but feel a sort of Dark Soul’s type of challenge in which it is completely fair and challenging. If you die, you died because of you, only amplifying the euphoria of victory.
Now, what I learned from Alan Wake was animating a models lower jaw and hiring the most inept voice actors does not lead to a satisfactory audial or visual experience. So, I feel I should note Max Payne 3 has some pretty good talent with is animators and voice actors, feeling very close to real thing. And NOT the atrocities that walk Bright Falls, with cold, unfeeling eyes. Expressionless faces and barely moving mouths, you can understand why Alan Wake was a horror (as well as learning experience) for developers.
Moving away from the mechanical aspects, the game looks fantastic. Its has a widely variant color palette, with bright colors and high contrast for sunny Brazil. To the drab brown and greys of a snow blanketed Hoboken, Max Payne 3 is quite the visual treat. You’ll often be left in awe at the detail that was carved into the world. Bullet impacts, soaked fabric, creasing cloth, and trash on city streets all contribute to immersive side of the overall experience.
Despite its forgettable story, characters shooting gallery mentality, Max Payne 3 is still an enjoyable experience. With tight gunplay, bullet time mechanic, and decent voice acting, I’d dare to say that Max Payne 3 is a pretty good game overall. Though, don’t expect much to think about when you set it down.

+ Great Gun play. I mean really great. Things are flying all over, shooting stuff, glass getting smashed and so on..
+ Great Setting. São Paolo and Brazil is a great setting for this, with all the grittiness, corruption and violence that is Max Payne
+ The new mechanics. I like how the developers implemented a cover mechanics and how you can keep shooting while lying down for instance.
+ The story is good and fits in the Max Payne universe, there might have been some clichés and some predictability but all in all good.
+ Sound and Soundtrack. Generally good overall, adding to the atmosphere of the game.

Come on. Do you really need to read the reviews for a free-to-play game? I'll give you all the information to know in less than 10 words: It's fun and not pay2win. Yes, you have to purchase Mercs for a pretty hefty amount of credits BUT luckily you don't need to purchase them with real money. You want to know WHY? Every Merc is balanced. If you die, it is purely because you were outplayed, not out-paid(does that make sense?). Each Merc has their own weaknesses and strengths. They are all incredibly fun. Yes, there are loadout cards with more powerful guns. BUT the good thing is that a  bronze card and a cobalt card have no tactical difference, despite the the extremely low drop rate of the latter.(Order of rarity is lead, iron, bronze, silver, gold, etc to cobalt. you only need at least a bronze card to have the maximum advatage of your merc.)There are many things I love about this game that sets it apart from other fpses:
-Every Merc can jump off walls, giving a lot of mobility options for everyone in the match
-Hip fire is recommended 90% of the time because most guns in this game have very little spread and are very accurate
-cases can contain new mercs(yay) and you get them about every 3 matches
-Completey team-based because of objectives and payloads(I love that you can't 1v6 the enemy team like in other games so you actually need half a brain to play)
-Loadout cards bronze rarity and higher do not give any tactical advantage, purely aesthetic
-When you get shot down to 0 health you get "knocked out", so any teammate can help you up after as long as the enemy doesn't finish you off first.)

As spiritual successor to Project Reality, its probably the most fun I've had playing an fps since the first time I played Battlefield 2. First and foremost this is not a game for lone wolfers. Grab a goddamn mic, join a squad, and partake in jolly cooperation. The visuals, environments, and gameplay are all top notch, and every match is dynamic and feels completely new. It may take a few matches to get familiar with everything but the community is very mature and welcoming (for the most part) and will gladly give you tips and advice as you play. Although my perferred loadout is either the marksman or the optics rifleman, each unique role within a squad is equally enjoyable and rewarding. Probably my favorite match happened when playing a combat medic. This game rewards teamplay more than K/D and actually hides such stats until the round is over, helping to prevent players from getting so hung up on it. Overall, 10/10 will get mowed down by an autorifleman again.
Sidenote: The only downside to this game at the moment is the issues with AMD proccessors.  I currently have an FX 8350 and do experience significant issues. However, turning all your settings down to low, while not visually appealing, allows you to properly enjoy the game for the most part. I'm sure this issue will be fixed come release of this game however, so worry not. Keep in mind that this game is early access.

WARNING:
Rimworld is not for the casual players, this is a game you need to commit to. Be prepared to fail and start over, and over, and over again untill you have understood the game. Rimworld is a game that is so in depth, every choice you make matters and has consequences. I would recommend watching some Youtubers first and to start easy and work your way up.
Having said that, rarely have I seen a developer that is so active within the community. Tynan is active on the ludeon forums and actively responds to suggestions and he has taken inspiration from the community, and even integrated some of the popular community mods into the vanilla game. The game is very solid and after about 100 hours hasnt crashed or glitched out on me once. One of the only two annoyances I have with game is that the starting character system is weird, as it partially allows me to get the colonists I want, but at an extremely inefficient way. The other thing I find annoying is something I love and hate, the randomness of it. Having random events makes the game unpredictable and fun but also unfair at some points, which sucks if you spend 20 hours making a colony to then see them die by the plague and flu hitting simultaneously.
Is this game expensive? Define expensive. To me this game is so in depth and with modding this game is worth the price it has, although it is indeed one of the more expensive games in its category. On the flip side, I feel like the price benefits the game. This game is not about selling the most amount of copies, this game is about delivering an amazing experience to player looking for a challenge, and the price means you are commited to the game.
If you are looking for a management game with a challenge and you are willing to learn by failing then this is the game for you.

I bought this game on a sale on a premise that it would be some sort of Portal like puzzle game to "pass my time". In the end, it is so much more. The game mixes a challenging puzzle gameplay with a developing plot (that requires the player to search for bits of information across the multiple maps and areas of the game), and surprisingly, philoshopy. The player is confronted throughout the game with multiple philosopical questions on humanity, morality, existence, free will and much more, and the player's own stance will influence the outcome of the plot. As if the great challenges of the game were not enough, the search for scraps of a well thought plot line alongside famous mythological, historical and philosopical texts make this game a new kind of experience in terms of gaming. Deffinetly recommend it for anyone looking for an intellectually stimulating game.

Age of Empires II is one of the most popular RTS games of all time. It established Ensemble Studios as a top tier company in the time and corroborated the success they got with Age of Empires and the expansion Rise of Rome. It fixed every single aspect that lacked in the first game, like refarming, being able to start a building over a unit, better AI players and a better unit behaviour. Also it introduced new feautures like the domestic animals, formations, unique techs, tech trees and bonuses, up to 200 population capacity and many more.
AOE II still has a lot of popularity outside of steam, where people gather on IRC channels to share IP and play; however, over the time the rate of new players to the game was decreasing in relation to leaving players. Many causes of leaving were related to the graphic bugs the game had with newer OS like Windows Vista, having magenta all over the grass, water, etc. With the appearance of AOE II HD the game got fixed and the base of players increased again.
Pros of AOE II HD version:
- New graphic features
- Added more population cap
- Re-balancement of units
- Graphic fix with support of widescreen
- Music now sounds in every PC
- Integrated multiplayer with other Steam players (No more TCP/IP to play)
- Compatibility with Steam Workshop. Mods and campaigns all over the place
- Developers always working on the game adding 2 DLCs with new content including civs,          campaigns and sounds.
- The posibility to play the game in multiplayer even if you don't have the DLCs. You can play      with other players that have them with the cost of having a reduced choose of civs, with  possibility of choosing an expansion one.
Cons of AOE II HD:
- SUPER IMPORTANT: Needs multiplayer tweaks - Crashes players and/or disconnects them
- High Latencies: Some players (like me) experience high pings whereas in services like voobly with classic AOC don't
- Reduced performance: Even with all the new graphic features disabled the game still has a considerable fps drop for players with old PCs (like me, again).
Overall the Steam version acomplishes the objective of revitalizing the game with new possibilities and ideas while adding new content to the game over the time. Old-School gamers, new gamers and nostalgia gamers, like me who played this on my childhood, are going to enjoy this version as the old MSN Zone times where the multiplayer was extremely fun. Needs some tweaks however but in a scale of x/10 it deserves definitively a 9.5/10.

This game is like any other class based shooter,but its more focused on gunplay than abilites.Assault characters with abilities geared towards killing are obviously better in combat but that doesnt mean you cant kill anybody with medics,engineers and such.What i mean is that you can have fun killing people while playing a support character,because every character has a good rifle/smg/sniper in their arsenal.You dont have quirky primary wepons that is based on charachter,you have abilities that you can switch to.Every character can defend themselves well ,while having an ability that differenciates them from others.
Every character has access to 9 loadout cards and 3 primaries.Gun balance is very good,every gun has its own pros and cons,makes them more situational than being better or worse.They are just more "useful" than eachother in different situations.There arent few OP guns that you have to grind for to actually have a chance against better,more experinced players.There are no gun progression,you just buy cards(meaning loadouts) with in game currency and you are done.Threre are paid games like Battlefield or Call of Duty that do this,and you get better progression in a f2p game like Dirty Bomb.The time you are "handicapped" against players with more hours is very short.This f2p game is less pay to win than any f2p game(except dota) and some paid games that i played.
The progression goes on like this: You start off with only 2 characters and every week theres a free rotation of 3 characters other than first given 2 so that you can test them.Every chacter like i said has 9 loadout cards and each card can have max 3 augments.Theres a rarity system,lead(1 augment),iron(2 augments),bronze,silver,gold,cobalt,special event(3 augments).Everything beyond bronze is purely cosmetic and you can buy any bronze card you want with in game credits as well as any character you want.You also dont have to buy cards to use characters as you already have blank cards.To sum it up you can buy anything that gives you an edge,permanantly no renting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t,with in game credits.Nothing is locked with a paywall except cosmetics.
You earn these credits realy fast too.There are 3 missions that refresh in 3 hours and give about 2250 credits in total,base playing time credits rate,daily bonuses and one leveling bonus.In a ~1.5 hour session where you complete 2 sets of missons daily you get about ~5500 credits with some case drops. Every merc is 30-40-50 k credits.So you can roughly unlock one in every week or so.You also get cases,meaning cards and sometimes +bronzes.They might have good augments,so you dont have to buy the best card from store.I reckon that i had most mercs with handful cards in first 150 hours,which is absolutely phenomenal in a f2p game.
Gunplay is amazing.You can just rely on your primary as a non-assault character and destroy everybody if you simply have better aim.You dont get killed just by a headshot.The game rewards precise aim tracking more than anything.If you are dying in a balanced match you are just bad and bad because enemies are aiming better than you and not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting their way with abilites,for the most part.
About the bad parts,first comes performance.The game runs on unreal engine 3 which can have bad fps even on high end pcs.The ui,coherent ui is simply bad.Game lags more on main menu than anything ffs.Splash Damage are saying that they are working on it and they better should.Additionally they recently introduced a skin system.akin to CS : GO and the community are backlashing because Splash Damage put every skin behind RNG.You cant buy a skin you want with irl money,you have to gamble.I also hope that Splash Damage makes a change.

Now before you believe I'm going to spout out that this game is terrible because it has changed too much, give this review a chance.
So I'm an early 2014 player of Robocraft. As you may already see, I don't recommend this game, but would I say it's a bad game? Of course not.
Once upon a time I'd come home excited to load up Robocraft and grind out as many games as possible, trying to reach a higher tier to get a nicer, cooler colour. I would even go on the hunt for some of freejam's hidden promo codes online! A lot has changed since then, and honestly, a lot of it I liked!
Coming from an age where people would once attach a helium block, a pilot and a sniper all in one and camp at the top of the map, I'm glad to see they managed to prevent that. I also love the new weaponry and attachables.
The idea of giving other players a 5% boost when a premium player was on your team was a great addition that not only rewarded you but also your team!
The gameplay is fun and the community is friendly enough, although the interaction really only goes as far as "good game". The only way to communicate through voice is through overwolf which nobody ever uses unless they wanted the free promotional codes. The player base seems mature enough, albeit at times a minecraft kiddie would appear.
So why don't I recommend this game?
The part you've all been anxiously waiting to see.
Put simply, its too difficult. Progression back in my day as a Robocraft veteran wasn't that difficult, at the time of typing this I have 40 hours of playtime (would be a lot more since I used the standalone previously). In my day, you could spend a whole day and reach tier 4 - 5, it was a game where you and your friends would rush to be the better robocrafter. But now its just competitive, and the rewards seem... bare.
Now I know someone - anyone - could say "but its an early access game!", they've been expecting to end their early access sometime around the end of 2016 and its about to hit 2017. If this is the game that I expect to see on a full release, then I'm not too impressed.
Side note:
Is it possible to make a crane bot with your mate acting as a hook to attach to you? Wouldn't work previously due to players practically being brick walls.

This game is one of Valve's most classic games, and it's a pretty good one too.
First things first, I wouldn't recommend playing this tired, since some of the puzzles in this game can be really annoying if you can't concentrate well.
Right, to the review.
This game offers a lot of challenge and a plot in the singleplayer mode, which is on some parts pretty hilarious too, I'd say. The puzzles are usually fairly easy or medium of difficulty, at least in my opinion. They, however, are the main thing about the game, and the challenge they give to your brain is good.
The basic idea is to complete levels with your trusty portal gun, This gun creates a blue and an orange portal, and you can go through them once both portals are at place, or make lasers or other stuff got through them that have something to do with the level itself.
I'm not going to go in-depth into the plot since I don't want to spoil it.
The multiplayer mode is pretty fun too, it's a bit like the singleplayer mode, but there isn't such a clear plot. It's more of just a brain twister with friends. You try to get through levels that have been made in such fashion, that you need to have multiple players in your team to get through them.
As a whole, I'd give this game a 7.5/10 since it's a pretty good game, but some parts might be a bit buggy etc. (or maybe it's just me).

I've played RimWorld since Alpha 7 (It's now currently on Alpha 14). I've seen this game take shape through the hard work of the devs and the beyond supportive community. It has everything you could possible want from a base building/micro-management/survival style of a game. Here's my take on the game if you're on the fence on buying it:
The end game consists of you trying to survive long enough to build a spaceship to get your colony off of the planet you crash landed on. Along the way you'll have obstacles like diseases, wild animal attacks, pirate raids, solar flares that hinder your power, storms that destroy your entire harvest, and tons more. There are endless possibilites on what can happen at any moment which creates this constant fearful mindset: "Will I be ready for it?" Well odds are you won't be. I've never had the same experience twice in this dynamic game (And future mods developed by the community will continue to keep RimWorld refreshing).
On top of all the crazy dynamic events, every single colonist has special traits and passions that make them effective towards certain tasks, such as hunting, cooking, growing crops, crafting, mining, etc.. As you grind these tasks the colonist grow in levels which then allows them to produce better quailty work. But just like life, everyone will have a weakness alongside their strengths. For example, there are negative traits that will effect a colonist such as cannibalism, being a nudist, the need for bioinic body parts, greed, being anti-social.. Both the stengths and weakness' will effect the way you play out the situations thrown at you.
If you love survival games with a challange, I'd recommend this game 100%.

I really love this game. It is engrossing, saddening with little bits of elation here and there, and just very special
Several times I have started a new colony when i get home from work at 5:30, and stay up until 3:30 at night trying to keep all my little guys and gals alive.
You get really attached to some of your colonists, others you kind of just tolerate because they are useful. But the game centers around these little people, and there is just something special about that.
A colonist from one of my most recent saves was named Starl. She was the first to join my colony, just waltzed right in one day. I didn't think that much of her at first, just a jack of all trades type character with little boosts in medicine and growing.
As my colony grew, the storyteller kept drawing attention to her, and I realized just how ♥♥♥♥ed up her life is.
First in comes her husband, he was part of a visiting tribe. The saddest part about this was that the whole time he was visiting, not once did he talk with her, acknowledge her, or interact with her in any way. It was a very cold relationship from what I gathered. But Starl never stopped being faithful to her crappy husband that lived far away. So many romantic attempts failed on her, but she never took on another lover.
Then her brother fell from the sky. He wasn't exactly a skilled guy, so I figured I would just rescue him and send him on his way. It was Starl that patched him up. I like to think that the Deep Conversation they had while she was tending to him was something akin to "Live Long and Prosper", but Chris didn't. He died of hypothermia trying to leave the map.
Last but not least, her father was a sniper for a siege party. The long range sniper battle between him and Starl was long, terrifying and awful, but it had to be done. I like to think that all of those misses were warning shots, but in the end Starl put one right between his eyes. The worst part is she didn't even know him, shortly after Starl's conception, her father was put to sleep in a cryo-chamber for unknown reasons, and came out 49 years later. He was biologically 17 years old, while Starl was almost 50.
When Starl was killed, one shot by a sniper with a shooting skill of 2 or some crap like that, I was caught by surprise. I remember shouting "NO!" to my screen, and staring at her little sprite in real despair and sadness.
This is why I recommend Rimworld, for the moments like this. You may not always care about your colonists in every playthrough, but then you get one like Starl, and you get attached, and care, and then despair.

is a unique 3d puzzle game. You play as a grey autonomous robot, exploring worlds crafted by the omniscient Elohim, seemingly as a rite of passage. You slowly unlock several different tools that are used to solve the puzzles. While The Talos Principle leaves a visually striking impression with its beautiful environments, the world seems to lack structure and personality. There are wide open areas that lead to nowhere, and many puzzles have lots of empty space. It's possible the world was intended to have this 'abandoned' look, but the puzzles could have been crafted differently to support the world they exist in.
That leads me to the puzzles themselves, at around world B, you haven't unlocked every possible tool that the puzzles eventually implement into the game, but you feel like you have seen everything the game has to offer. The difficulty curve on the puzzles ramps up instantly and then quickly stagnates, with some random puzzles being far too easy. The 'empty space' I discussed earlier is used mainly to arbitrarily make the puzzle take longer to solve, placing tools you need at the ends of long winding halways for no reason. While the game offers about 100 puzzles, it feels like there's only 3 or 4 puzzle archetypes. Once you've solved one "use two jammers on one door", "make the connector self-powered etc" puzzle, you've solved them all. Even the best puzzle games suffer from this flaw to some extent, so I can't really subtract too many points for it. You want the game to offer you more, but it continuously gives you the same options. This combined with the heavily restricted movement and placement of objects makes it feel at times like you're just following the guideline to solve a puzzle, and not finding a unique solution. The game really shines during some points however, when the puzzle design is at its best and there are different solutions to one puzzle.
I was considering making this review a not-recommended one, but The Talos Principle offers just enough to justify a purchase. I purchased it on sale for $14, and I think it's worth around $20, but I wouldn't say it's worth the $40 price tag it has attached.
If you like puzzles games, definitely check it out. It's a worthwhile game experience despite its flaws.

Early Access, my muscular buttocks. I've been playing Rimworld off and on throughout development, and even the very first alpha version I tried was remarkably solid and fun to play. Granted, there's a lot more content now--and I mean A LOT more--but at its core Rimworld has always provided a smooth and entertaining experience. Tynan Sylvester's work ethic and quality control are unmatched by literally any other developer or game I've followed, and Rimworld could easily have shed the EA moniker a long, long time ago.
In fact, Rimworld is one of the rare games--and I'm struggling to even think what might have been the last one--that I've been more than happy to pay full price for. In the era of bundles and Steam sales, that's saying quite a lot.
The AI Storytellers and customization options for a new game allow players to tailor the experience to their whims. If you're looking for a challenge, you can pit yourself against the ever-increasing threat of hostile raids. More interested in the opposite end of the spectrum? Virtually eliminate threats altogether and focus your efforts on building your fledgling outpost into an impenetrable fortress. Or a vacation resort, if that's more your thing.
But besides all the incredible gameplay mechanics at work--farming, animal taming, base-building, fortification, defense, combat--the most incredible aspect of Rimworld is the attachment you develop to your colonists and their stories. Even when the game lacked much of the depth and complexity that's been fleshed out over the past two years, you still got to know them as individual entities--traits, personalities (based on a few key variables), every injury they suffered, every mental break your other colonists had to wrangle them back from. When one dies, you may find yourself scrambling for a recent save file to bring them back. Not because you want to cheat the outcome, but because he or she was there from the beginning and it just doesn't feel right continuing without them.
I got into playing Rimworld because I was excited about the base-building aspect, but there's so much more to enjoy here. It's sort of a top-down, base-building, survival, people sim. If that doesn't entice you, I don't know what will. I guess that makes this paragraph the TL;DR.
It's absolutely worth full price. If you see it on sale, don't even hesitate.

Many ups and downs in this games history, like the removal of megabots.  With these negative looking updates a lot of players fail to see the things they gain from removing something.  For example after the removal of megabots your team's probability of winning didn't depend on if your megabot was a troll, or had a half full frame.  Now it depends on teamwork, with the added bonus of more CPU.  A lot of people complain about the "3x recycle rate with premium".  This is NOT pay to win, it is pay for a faster progression which does not mean premium players win more often.  Freejam wants you to buy premium, is it all that bad, what do you expect from a team of about 30 people?  Have you ever seen a free to play game with monthly updates that doesn't have some kind of "premium" or pay for something system?  There would probably be more negative feedback if they slapped a 10$ game price on it.  I would also say that most the updates are debatably positive or negative.  For example the removal of repair costs allowed more players to get into T10 because they didn't do good enough to make a profit before which is good for them, but some pre-update T10 players said it was a different feel when you had to work really hard to get in T10.  Robocraft is still very incomplete, if you are quitting come back in 6 months and see what they have accomplished.  Freejam cannot address every single community suggestion, and a lot of people seem to not realize that.  You can't complain that they don't listen to their community look at QoL poll results, on both of them they implemented the top wanted feature into robocraft, that is called listening to the community.  I think that freejam has made it pretty clear that they are not bringing back megabots and removing epic loot.  I truly believe that they can see a bit further than us into the future and that all of this is for the greater good of robocraft, after all it is their vision.

Switching back to you preferred weapon is a chore as the mouse wheel feels like a poorly ported analogue stick. As each cutscene precedes another fight this can cause some cheap deaths, and maybe its my setup but on quite a few reloads the game would crash. That doesn't mean that it's bad: quite the opposite, in fact. I really like playing this game with friends. But once you take off the nostalgia goggles, you realize that the game's shortcomings means there are substantially better and more modern RTS games out there.
The pathfinding is atrocious, the base management and economic development are unnecessarily cumbersome, the civilizations are not diverse enough, the single-player campaign is uninspired, and the dated combat system favours sending large swarms of junk units and early rushes over careful planning and execution.
In many, many ways,
, which was released in 2005, is more modern and fun than Age of Empires 2, and isn't in need of an "HD" remake. Hardcore RTS fans might've snubbed AoE 3 back in the days because they felt like the gameplay was "dumbed down" compared to that of AoE 2, but the fact is that sometimes, less is more. Especially when it's done right.
But since all your friends are nostalgic 90's kids, you might as well grab this one when it's on sale. Otherwise, I know this is an unpopular opinion, but you should really stick to Age of Empires 3.

Age of Empires 2; one of the most iconic games from the late 90's and a must play on every lan party is now (mostly) playable on newer OS's ? A thought I found highly enjoyable, since I've played thousands of hours on the original steamless version released about 17 years ago; right to the point when did no longer work properly through changing the system from XP to 7. Soundbugs and purple water were just a few of the problems making it unbearable to play. Hearing that it would actually get an hd adaptation fixing incompatibility bugs filled my heart with joy. I bought it right upon release and gave it a few hours of gameplay and I must say its kinda good but not the same.
First of all, they fixed most of the bugs, which is ofc a huge step and raised the AI's ability to actually play kinda well. In the original release, a 1 vs 7 match on the highest difficulty was just like shooting fish in a barrel and many players jused it as a warm up for multiplayer matches. Through the workshop you now can still patch the difficulty even higher, which brings some sort of challenge even to the most veteran players. Target finding is still like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ monkey on crack trying to run backwards trough a maze of broken glass bottles - the units still get stuck anywhere at anytime and won't hesitate to take the most stupid and unsafe route possible. Always watch where your folks are goint to.
Some gamechanges regarding the old one were made too. For example the maximum limit of units on all sides has been raised from up to 200 to up to 500, which is quite nice since you can comandeer way bigger and complexer formations of troops while sill maintaing your ressource gain trough your workers. No more sacrificing to make room. That change, I like.
Sadly, the game feels kind of heavy and bulky. Meaning with to much movement (which you'll get quite fast) on the map, it starts to lag. And not just a bit, it will get completely unplayable even in matches with only 3 to 4 people especially if your playing with AI's.  I play on a fx8350 8x4,4ghz, 32gb ram with a gtx970 gaming and I still had to guit dozens of matches against just 3 or less AI players because as soon as i'm acually moving my 400+ soldiers into battle and the enemy does the same, your frames per second will become frames per minute. Online, its even worse. The few rounds I tried to play with my girlfriend vs AI, we had to leave after around 10 minutes because the lag was unbearable. A problem which is still there, even nearly three years after the release of this version. The old version never had those kind of problems with lag and we've always played with 8 players (human and/or AI).
So if you can, play the old version. Try a virtual machine with XP or W98 or something like that. If you want big battles with many units then this version is not for you. I will do the same since after three years, a patch fixing those problems is rather unlikely.

This is a review strictly for the single player mode, as I've never touched multiplayer.
Max Payne 3, is a very solid 3rd person shooting game. I'll list out what I enjoyed and what I didn't enjoy below:
Good:
-Unlike Max Payne 1 & 2, you can aim any weapon with surgical precision.
-Shot locations play a pretty crucial role in the game. For example, shooting a guy in the leg will cause him to fall to the ground.
-Bullet time makes a return, and it is amazing.
-Many small challenges in the game, such as "get this many kills with pistols/smgs/shotguns."
-Collectibles in the form of golden gun pieces.
-Clues make a return in the game.
Bad:
-Long loading times. Cutscenes play during the loading screen, so at least you can watch the cutscene, rather than looking at a blank screen that reads "loading."
-You can only carry up to 3 guns(2 pistols and a long gun). If you dual wield, you automatically drop your long gun.

Well, where should I begin?  Squad is something special.  It sores very high while it’s flying, and perhaps falters ever so slightly when it’s not, mostly due to other people.  The development team has laid out a yellow brick road that seems to be on track.  Make no mistake, if you have hungered for something real, something tactical and representative of intense visceral infantry (and perhaps in the future, vehicular) combat, this is that game.
The genius of squad lays in what it creates.  Emergent, medium scale infantry combat based around team play.  Switching weapons takes a bit of time, as does preparing a grenade or smoke grenade to throw.  Moving is not very quick.  These are all good things, because it creates an environment where you need to think before you act.  It really isn't that hard to understand what this game is about.  Think of an instance that countless people have shared and that seems to be the staple of amazing moments in Squad.  You and your 8 person squad is moving to an objective on a map that represents a few square miles (they are big map).  You have a general idea of where you’ll meet the enemy, but there are no guarantees. It seems slow.  You all decide to stop and drop a rally point.  You here a hiss of bullet cross your plane past you nearby.  There's no 'snap' so you know it’s not exactly on you, but it’s nearby.  Maybe you hear a few more hissing bullets scream by, and then a snap.  You hit "B" to engage squad comm's and begin to tell your squad you think you’re being shot at.  An explosion of gun fire erupts, everyone’s on comms screaming, all hell breaks loose, your SAW gunner starts unloading in hopefully the right direction.  You and your squad are frantically trying to communicate where the fire is coming from.  You notice your rocketeer launch an RPG, and for a moment are dazzled by the beautiful animation of the back blast before you get your head back in the game.  Smoke is being deployed ahead of you to cover your retreat.  The other side launches a rocket and decimates your squad.  It’s all over.  And it all took maybe 3-5 seconds.  That, at its core, is squad.
The audio is a dream.  The graphics are absolutely gorgeous (although this is the only department I can think of where EA is really apparent.  The anti-aliasing is not finished, so some maps in the desert with lots of shrubs look rather gross atm).  For the most part, if you land in a good squad, you'll have a great time.  If you land in a bad squad, you may need to switch squads or teams.  Sometimes you need to find a new server altogether.  You may waste 10 minutes doing so until you get in a good server with a communicative squad.  But once you do, you're in for an amazing ride.
Let’s address some of the cons, and if you follow the forums you may have been misled into believing there are a host of problems without realizing there mostly client side.
1. My game runs like crap/balls/low fps etc.:  This is primarily people running old computers.  I upgraded (spent $400) recently on an i3 6100, gtx 950 and 4 gigs of ddr4 ram, and this game runs like an absolute dream.  Go to twitch, watch people play.  It runs absolutely amazing.  Bugs are not very prevalent.  Your windows is not fully updated, and before running updater and installing all of the updates you decided to get on the forums and start b*******?  Well that’s your problem.  BUT, you’re REALLY lucky that the community is so amazing that people are going to help you.  No one is going to troll you, and rarely do people get on your case about not using the search function if you're sincere.
(One small side note, if you’re running an AMD cpu you may get mixed results.  I don't know much about it since I'm luckily running an intel cpu, but I've seen and heard people with AMD's are able to run this game).  The point of this paragraph is to set the record straight.  This game is VERY well optimized at this time if you have a decent rig.  If you're running a potato, then either upgrade or wait for more updates.
2. "Peoples suck and I can't play with a good team" bla bla bla.  Right, just leave your squad and find another one.  Switch teams and repeat.  Still no good, leave the server and do it again. Maybe you lose 10 minutes of your time.  If that’s unacceptable to you and you can't invest a small amount of time to have a great experience, then I think COD is going to be on sale this week, it’s that way _______>
Almost every issue is resolvable thanks to the amazing community that is Squad.  That community involves the developers who are extremely active on the
forums, redit, and twitter.  I avoid the steam forums bc it’s mostly COD people who try this game out for 20 minutes and begin complaining.
Is this game for me?
Great question, let’s see if we can get that sorted out for you.  Are you mature minded?  Are you patient?  Does the idea of brief moments of intense fighting interspersed with moments of boredom as you walk large distances and communicate with your squad excite you?  Are you okay using a mic and having real living people listen to your voice and talk back to you okay with you?  Maybe this games for you.
On the other hand.  Do you think COD is the best thing since sliced bread?  Do you frequently get into arguments with people on forums even though your right and he is wrong?  Is it other people’s fault that you died and your team sucks?  Move on, COD is your game.
This is an experience that will be remembered for a long time because it does what so many of us have yearned for for the first time.  Take a risk and you may find yourself having a lot of fun.  Or maybe you hate it.  It is well worth the risk to try it out.

Still the gold standard for real-time strategy games more than 15 years after its release, Age of Empires 2 didn't age
well. "HD" in this case quite literally means that the game supports higher resolutions and has crisper details: don't expect a complete overhaul. Sure, the AI was improved, and there are a few new civilizations to choose from (if you buy the DLC), but ultimately, the game plays and feels like it's 1999.
That doesn't mean that it's bad: quite the opposite, in fact. I really like playing this game with friends. But once you take off the nostalgia goggles, you realize that the game's shortcomings means there are substantially better and more modern RTS games out there.
The pathfinding is atrocious, the base management and economic development are unnecessarily cumbersome, the civilizations are not diverse enough, the single-player campaign is uninspired, and the dated combat system favours sending large swarms of junk units and early rushes over careful planning and execution.
In many, many ways,
, which was released in 2005, is more modern and fun than Age of Empires 2, and isn't in need of an "HD" remake. Hardcore RTS fans might've snubbed AoE 3 back in the days because they felt like the gameplay was "dumbed down" compared to that of AoE 2, but the fact is that sometimes, less is more. Especially when it's done right.
But since all your friends are nostalgic 90's kids, you might as well grab this one when it's on sale. Otherwise, I know this is an unpopular opinion, but you should really stick to Age of Empires 3.

Still playing, will write more and better soon, but so far I have to say this is a very frustrating game to play because of how it controls and plays with a mouse and keyboard. I'm really saddened and disappointed because I enjoyed Max Payne 1 and 2 so much back in the day.
But in this game Max animates clunkily and awkwardly, moves slow, sticking in and out of cover is messy, there's no rolling from cover to cover or anything, aiming down sights sometimes decides to switch which shoulder you're viewing from, messing up your shots. The guns hardly feel any different from each other, it's pretty much dumping bullets from whichever weapon you have. There are some "set piece" situations where you have to shoot something or some guys more specifically and sometimes it's not clear what that is, which lead me to fail over and over without a clue of what I was supposed to do. Usually my play sessions end with me rage quitting after hitting one of these sections... If you have at least one painkiller and are about to die you automatically enter into a kind of "bullet time" where you're falling to the ground and have to shoot the guy who's killing you, but only that guy; problem is, if you are travelling behind some cover and can't get a shot, or if you're out of bullets, you'll just have to wait 5+ seconds knowing you'll die, without being able to do a thing. Even if you succeed, you are lying on the ground and Max is very slow and clunky to get up and it's difficult to quickly move back into cover, sometimes making the whole point completely moot. Enemies sometimes die with a pistol shot to the head, but not with 5 AK-47 shots to the chest, even if they aren't wearing any protection, like no clothes at all from the waist up, damage is highly variable, so when using bullet time is impossible to predict how it is going to go. This isn't helped by the fact that some of their "death animations" take way too long, like 3-4 seconds to fall to ground, making it hard to tell if they are dead or not, especially since it's visually similar to them being just "stunned", which is surprising when they take clear shots to the chest from supposedly good weapons like AK-47's.
In sum, the shooting part doesn't feel anywhere remotely good, not even decent. God, do I miss Mass Effect 3on the PC! Even picking up weapons from killed guys or interacting with some elements with the "E" key (like inspecting stuff) is difficult because you're forced to swing the mouse and move around trying to aim the "right way" so that the keypress pop-up shows, even though you're standing right there, which is very frustrating especially during a firefight.
Other than that, during each sections of the game there are clues and golden gun elements hidden in the environment, that you are encouraged to find, but that is in conflict with the hectic pace of gameplay and pretty chaotic shootdown situations where you don't have time to explore around. This is especially evident when your companion keeps shouting to you so you hurry up and making bad jokes about it, and also is frustrating because the clues particularly give some more depth to the story that you'll miss otherwise. Am I supposed to rush my first playthrough of the game and focus on those "secrets" later? And finding them is not an easy task with how the keypress pop-ups are difficult to show up, like I mentioned before. And what's up with no 5.1 sound, only stereo? Not that it is that great of a deal, but, on this day and age on PC...
Man, this is a real shame, since the game runs very smoothly and looks absolutely beautiful, with loots of detail! I particularly like the special FX used to portray that Max is wasted from booze and painkillers all the time. Also, the story is enjoyable and gives a faithful nod to the atmosphere of the older games, helped by the fact you have the original voice from Max Payne, and though there's  no "comic book like" sections those were replaced with a more cinematic direction with nice slow-motion shots that are very nice and stylish.

I've been playing Rimworld for, well, years.  Time above only shows post-Steamkey conversion.  The game is terrific!  By far one of the best, most in-depth and rewards survival games out there.  It has a definite stuggle phases, an entertaining midgame and a clearly defined endgame with actual victory conditions; something that most survival games never get around to finishing.  Tynan has always been on the ball with rapid updates and plenty of communication & hands-on time with the community.
The game is also designed from the ground-up for being moddable, and the sheer amount of mods out there would give a Bethesda title a run for their money.  The amount of stuff you can add into the game is simply amazing, and expands the options for storytelling to an incredible degree.  You can start off as anything from a high tech colonist blazing bases across the landscap or primitive tribals who are still struggling to enter the Iron Age.
The graphics may not be the best but they're certainly good enough, and I find the abstraction actually helps emphasize the story telling aspect of the game.  Combat, on the other hand, is brutally realistic and it is entirely possible to lose you favorite colonist to one unlucky head shot from out of nowhere.  That's right, kids, if you set the difficulty of this game on high it will most certainly kick your sorry butt, so don't say you didn't ask for it.
The western theme music is a nice touch of fan-service to Firefly, although you'll find the "western frontier" theme is actually a mercifully thin veener that is easily researched past in short order.  Of course there is nothing stopping you from abandoning all research & living the luddite dream if you really wanted to.  The amount of choices the player has is excellent, as you're never forced down any particular playstyle by anything other than the climate (meaning surviving certain biomes will require you to prioritize and develop a few things in a certain order, such as air conditioning for deserts and hydroponics for tundra).

Anyway, great game and you should totally buy it.  I know $30 seems a bit much, and maybe you want to wait for a sale (I won't begrudge someone just being thrifty) or maybe you don't trust Early Access (in which case kudos for showing uncommon wisdom) you should at least add it to your "Want" or "Follow" list. I'm not the one for writing reviews, so the fact that I'm writing one for RimWorld is a feat in itself.
What is it? It's a beautiful mixture of Dwarf Fortress, Prison Architect and the hardiest survival simulators available. Hell, even The Sims might be compared to this. Tynan Sylvester's hard work, sweat and tears have poured into this beautiful piece of software, to create an incredible, awesome digital experience. The Talos Principle is both a puzzle game and a philosophical exercise. Gameplay-wise, it takes its cues from games like Portal, Q.U.B.E. and Antichamber, but the existential philosophy of the plot gives the game an interesting and deeper spin.
The mix of philosophy and puzzles works very well together… Getting stuck in a puzzle often means you wander off to explore another puzzle, giving your mind space to consider new answers, and at the same time the themes and heavy questions posed by the game’s plot brew in your mind. You are asked questions and explore these ideas at points between the puzzles, and I found going back and forth between logical puzzle-work and ethical considerations quite interesting.
Content-wise, the game is pretty big. There are three distinct worlds with over two dozen puzzles in each, then there are hidden stars to collect in the game offering additional puzzles, along with many other hidden secrets and easter eggs. Gathering all the stars feeds into a secret ending, which I found a fun task (although ultimately I needed a guide to gather some of the more elusive stars), and some of the secret areas offer a deeper look into the plot.
Whilst the plot is fairly predictable, I found it so well written and thoroughly explored that I was compelled to find everything I could about it in the game. Whilst the plot could be seen as almost optional, and many of the puzzles can be skipped if going for a quick completion, the themes explored had me hunting down every last puzzle and scrap of information.
The Talos Principle is a fantastic puzzle game with an interesting story that lingers with you long after switching it off.

The Talos Principle is a first person puzzle game at its core. The puzzles are interesting and gradually become more and more difficult as additional mechanics are added and more and more mechanics get combined within a single puzzle.
In terms of the story behind the puzzles, it reminds me of Dark Souls; there is some story there, but it requires you to seek it out and think through it. It's great because it's there if you want it, but you can completely ignore it if you're only interested in the puzzles.
There are also some additional secret stars which can try to explore and find; they often involve an additional step after you've already completed a puzzle in order to access it (which can be quite a step up in difficulty) or figuring out how to connect one part of a puzzle one one side of the map to another puzzle on the far other side.
I'd put it up there with the Portal series in terms of the structure of the puzzles, in that you have a few core mechanics that you'll continue to play around with while thinking through how they would help you reach the goal that the game is setting out for you. What I mean is; the game appears very basic, with only a few mechanics involved in solving the puzzles, but these mechanis are used in so many various ways that no two puzzles will feel the same.
As you go along, it is likely you will find a puzzle or two that you just can't quite figure out at the time. This is totally fine; as you complete puzzles, they open up new areas, meaning you can come back to these tougher puzzles at a later time in order to solve them.
If you're looking to invest a few hours into a well executed puzzle solving game with philosophical undertones and a subtle story that is there if you want to find it, The Talos Principle is it.
