Still playing, will write more and better soon, but so far I have to say this is a very frustrating game to play because of how it controls and plays with a mouse and keyboard. I'm really saddened and disappointed because I enjoyed Max Payne 1 and 2 so much back in the day.
But in this game Max animates clunkily and awkwardly, moves slow, sticking in and out of cover is messy, there's no rolling from cover to cover or anything, aiming down sights sometimes decides to switch which shoulder you're viewing from, messing up your shots. The guns hardly feel any different from each other, it's pretty much dumping bullets from whichever weapon you have. There are some "set piece" situations where you have to shoot something or some guys more specifically and sometimes it's not clear what that is, which lead me to fail over and over without a clue of what I was supposed to do. Usually my play sessions end with me rage quitting after hitting one of these sections... If you have at least one painkiller and are about to die you automatically enter into a kind of "bullet time" where you're falling to the ground and have to shoot the guy who's killing you, but only that guy; problem is, if you are travelling behind some cover and can't get a shot, or if you're out of bullets, you'll just have to wait 5+ seconds knowing you'll die, without being able to do a thing. Even if you succeed, you are lying on the ground and Max is very slow and clunky to get up and it's difficult to quickly move back into cover, sometimes making the whole point completely moot. Enemies sometimes die with a pistol shot to the head, but not with 5 AK-47 shots to the chest, even if they aren't wearing any protection, like no clothes at all from the waist up, damage is highly variable, so when using bullet time is impossible to predict how it is going to go. This isn't helped by the fact that some of their "death animations" take way too long, like 3-4 seconds to fall to ground, making it hard to tell if they are dead or not, especially since it's visually similar to them being just "stunned", which is surprising when they take clear shots to the chest from supposedly good weapons like AK-47's.
In sum, the shooting part doesn't feel anywhere remotely good, not even decent. God, do I miss Mass Effect 3on the PC! Even picking up weapons from killed guys or interacting with some elements with the "E" key (like inspecting stuff) is difficult because you're forced to swing the mouse and move around trying to aim the "right way" so that the keypress pop-up shows, even though you're standing right there, which is very frustrating especially during a firefight.
Other than that, during each sections of the game there are clues and golden gun elements hidden in the environment, that you are encouraged to find, but that is in conflict with the hectic pace of gameplay and pretty chaotic shootdown situations where you don't have time to explore around. This is especially evident when your companion keeps shouting to you so you hurry up and making bad jokes about it, and also is frustrating because the clues particularly give some more depth to the story that you'll miss otherwise. Am I supposed to rush my first playthrough of the game and focus on those "secrets" later? And finding them is not an easy task with how the keypress pop-ups are difficult to show up, like I mentioned before. And what's up with no 5.1 sound, only stereo? Not that it is that great of a deal, but, on this day and age on PC...
Man, this is a real shame, since the game runs very smoothly and looks absolutely beautiful, with loots of detail! I particularly like the special FX used to portray that Max is wasted from booze and painkillers all the time. Also, the story is enjoyable and gives a faithful nod to the atmosphere of the older games, helped by the fact you have the original voice from Max Payne, and though there's  no "comic book like" sections those were replaced with a more cinematic direction with nice slow-motion shots that are very nice and stylish.

From what i remember from the first 2 games, this one is different in it's presentation and style. The first game was a brilliant mind ♥♥♥♥ of a game that took Max to really dark places, and i really liked that aspect of it. The second was a really stylish noir style take at romance with bullets. This one is more of a typical washed out cop tries to redeem himself in a place where he's not familiar.
When you play this, you follow Max from his drunken beginnings as he's had a pretty tough life, but you do tend to think he's taken a turn for the worse with the amount of drinking he does, not sure i remember him drinking this much in the first 2 games.
Just when Max thinks things can't get any worse he's driven from his home town and pretty much forced to start over and leave everything behind, which includes his past, which is definitely a good thing..... or so he thought. The situation goes from pretty grim, to terrible.
The gameplay is still very familiar, nothing really to add; you've still got bullet time, bullet time dives, not much has been added in terms of mechanics. What they have added though is more style! so slowmo deaths, and slowmo riddling baddies with bullets and watching them fall in very cool fashion! I think it's also more detailed when an exit wound appears on someone you've dispatched.
A different but good continuation of the series, and i don't think the day will ever get better for Max lol, but hopefully he'll be less washed out in the next one!

Just finished it.  Good game..but not perfect.  Pretty, surreal and monumental backdrops play host to the many, many well designed and clever puzzles.  I've always liked this sort of thing, and must thumbs up, because it's so rare now to see such a nice example.  However as good as it is, there are a few minor flaws:
* The puzzles gain in complexity over a very long, shallow and almost linear learning curve and at times it feels like a particularly long set of tutorial maps.
* You'll only play through this once, as there's only one correct way to solve each puzzle.
* The puzzles are well balanced and a few are challenging, however once you've got the hang of the basic puzzle elements, the problems generally become easy because you know that there are so few ways to actually go wrong.
* Part of me liked the philosophical texts in the game, it's an unusual twist, but they do get boring and increasingly irrelevant after a time and both hide and confuse the pretext story, particularly early on.

* Each level is broken down into a number of discrete and sealed off sub-sections cotaining one puzzle each.  While some of the puzzles might allow you to make use of the elements from a neighbouring sub-section,  to gain a bonus point, there's not enough of this going on.  Missed opportunities to make it really interesting every-where.
* There are a number of messages left on the walls around the game, to add some depth to the core story.  The fictional authors vary so much and the texts are generally so pointless that it's hard to gain any sense of the characters involved until near the end of the game.
* There's a secondary tetris style jigsaw puzzle sub-game involved, used to unlock some of the doors.  Early on these really are not challenging in any way and so are pointless..later they become much more complex but also mind-numbingly boring, as there's no real logic to solving them generally, beyond rotating the puzzle pieces until one fits.
* Crashed a lot initially, due to some kind of persistent graphics issue.  Had to switch from DX11 to OpenGL in the end, to get it stable.  Not as pretty.
Despite all of the above, I still recomend the game.  The primary game puzzles aren't bad, and not even repetative particularly, they just lack variety and complexity a little in places.  One of the puzzle tools is particularly novel and interesting to use.
This is an enjoyable game, though the puzzles can get tedious at times.

Very elegant puzzle design that almost never relies on overlong tedious solutions or overly complex chains of actions. If The Talos Principle was just a serie of puzzles, it would be a very good game, but the narrative context in which these puzzles are placed elevates the game to one of the very best of the last few years.
Multiplicating the narrative supports and story lines, the game weaves a very engaging tale steeped in philosophy, but, more than that, it's one that is at its more powerful in video game form, and not only because there are different endings.
The only two slight reservations I have about The Talos Principle are that the nature of the puzzles does not have much to do with the story (having to solve puzzles is part of it, but why this type of maze navigating puzzles?) and that the most narratively satisfying ending, the one that sheds a new light on the whole game and that allows everything to fall into place, is very difficult to obtain (mostly because it involves finding objects hidden in many different ways in large areas). It makes perfect sense that it is, but it is also a shame to see that a number of people never reached it. I highly encourage people to go as far as they can and then check the many guides in written and/or video form to help them experience what must be one of the pinnacle of video game writing.
PS: The DLC expends on the game's world in a very clever and satisfying way. Of course, it also provides a healthy dose of slightly harder puzzles and, more surprisingly, a healthy dose of text based interactive fiction! Well worth your time even if the conclusion is not as brilliant as the one of the core game (but how could it have?).

You play with squad. You listen to orders.
This game is not Cod or Bf4. There is no crazy kill streaks here.

Still its not about kills . You wont even know until end of the game how many kills you got.
Its about playing objective and teamplay.  About tactical gameplay, cold head thinking and hard choices.

This game is amazing. I've played others like it - Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria, Towns, Timber & Stone, and others, and they all pale in comparison. (Ok, Dwarf Fortress has more complexity, but, honestly, who could every play it with the horrible interface?)
It's similar to other colony-management games, but much more interesting. The basic premise is that your people crashland on sparsely-habited planet on a rim world, and have to survive, and eventually build a spaceship to escape. (The new scenario editor opens up other options, but this is the premise of the basic game.) You will battle hunger, disease, injury, hostile enemies, random events, and even interpersonal relationships.
The game features three different 'storytellers' which control how often events occur and how dangerous they can be. You can play a relatively safe colony-building game, or a 'This planet hates me' game. It's your choice.
The interface works well, and while there is a bit of a learning curve, it's part of the fun, and the game never gets tedious or overly complex.

An *okay* game that was honestly a little more fun back in its earlier versions. As of right now, the dev seems to be falling for lots of typical mistakes you make when you're trapped in a 'dev bubble'. First hes added in a magnitude of negative disorders for your colonists (like pyromaniac where they randomly set♥♥♥♥♥♥on fire...) as a way of making the game interesting, only to end up discovering that a majority of the events weren't working which is why the game felt bland in the first place... and so now we have endless random disasters hitting us with the additional 'benefit' of having pyromaniacs and 'jealous' people having mental breaks before you 2nd month is up. On top of that, man eating animals can promptly destroy a new save file you've created by wiping your 3 colonists in a matter of seconds. I dunnoo..... I really feel like its just so typical of a dev that is consumed in writing coding or theorizing, instead of actually playing his game.
Taking 1 hour 30 minutes to make a 3 man team that only has 1 disorder each was an absurd waste of my time and they still struggle to keep up with the day-to-day needs let alone dealing with raids, sickness and events. The dev just really needs to hop on for several 10 hour or so sessions and actually write down some notes.
The only reason I do not recommend this game is because the general games purpose and end game is sloppy and under thought. You could put 300 hours into building an amazing colony only to end up being raided by an impossibly difficult force that wipes you in 10 minutes flat, meaning its all fun and games while your head is in the clouds but after reality hits you, its hard to find a point in playing this game.

Max Payne 3 confuses me. On the one hand it retains 'the shoot first ask questions later' feel of old school fps games, marries them with some ridiculous (but admittedly cool) set pieces and together manages to produce an extremely fun bullet riddled campaign of destructive justice. Pretty much what defines Max Payne to be honest. It true Rockstar fashion, the cinematic presentation is excellent, as is the score.
On the other hand, the game suffers from some terrible design ideas like last stand (basically leaves you a sitting duck on the floor being shot at from multiple directions), clunky controls, incredibly cramped environments, over reliance on closet mobs that literally spawn out of thin air, annoying monologue by Max about everything.. (and I mean EVERYTHING) and some of the worst follow NPC's in recent history. The story isn't particularly well written, characterization is average at best and the (thankfully) few 'boss' encounters are average at best; frustrating at worst.
So why would I recommend this game then? Because it is FUN. Also, explosions everywhere. Really, for $5, it's totally worth it.
P.S. You are going to have to deal with Rockstar Social Club so prepare yourself.

The most important information that I myself would have liked to have known before purchasing "Squad" at its current beta build would be...
1) Without needing said; this game is entirely squad dependant... to play this game affectively, you need to be a team player. Likely chances of you capturing a base by yourself is nill; work together and observe the battle acitvely to take points and aid eachother with cover fire or medical aid. Medics btw, require you to first "bandage" someone once they've been shot or taken down, at which you can then proceed to using a medical bag to restore the rest of the individuals health; it is a two step process. There is also the factor, that when someone is taken down (and is no longer a threat) they are still alive and can be revived by a medic, as long as the person was not shot in the head. A medical emblem will be easily seen above those on your team who can be revived.
2) Weapon Customization is limited at the current time and only few weapons are given to each squad position. There are only a few attachments for each weapon (but, they are still being added with each update). The last recent update included new acogs and other attachments for select weapons; due note, this game does not allow you to share attachments on other weapons... Weapons, as well as their attachment choices are squad position dependant.
3) Some squad positions (such as the sniper), do not become availible for a squad choice until a given amount of members have filled a squad; this leaves the sniper position locked and unavailible until at least the 4-6 person is added. This makes it nearly impossible to attain the sniper position on purpose; getting the sniper is only likely to be availible once you've joined an active squad which is nearly full, and you get lucky to see the position unused. I've always enjoyed rifles and long range sniper battles...But, be warned; this game intentionally attempts to limit sniper use due to maps being very open.. this could maybe change in the future, but at this time it seems to be a set feature. Snipers also use a smaller acog, instead of a medium or long range scope.
4) At this given time of writing this review, the beta still currently does not have vehicles. Maps are very large, and walking distances are beyond boring. To make it worse; your character has stamina, which you must pay extra careful attention to so you can have enough to accurately aim and fire your weapon with percision when needed. When running from behind one cover to the next, you will lose your stamina almost entirely. Stamina is also regained slower than most other FPS titles...; you will have to literally sit and guard your position until you can continue running. Is it realistic? Maybe... But in real life, there is also troop transports and humvees... Which for both, Squad devs have clearly shown pictures and videos displaying humvess and transports which are in the mix for future updates. Right now though, running sucks, so be warned.
5) To spawn at any other location which does not include a captured enemies FOB, the squad leader must (with the proximity of other squad mates) create a spawn FOB or rally point so you don't have to walk all the way from base to the next objective. To create a FOB or rally point, squad mates from your squad must collect on the squad leader to allow the placement of such equipment (essentially a rallypoint looks like 3 bags placed on the ground, and a FOB looks like a radio on a table); these are usually meant to be placed in a building or location that you can then build fortifications to protect the FOB spawn point. If an enemy squad/team over runs/takes/captures the FOB, they can then continue to use the FOB as an enemy spawn location. FOBs, can also be destroyed with explosives ect..
6) Building is reserved to only certain locations, which are usually small compounds centered near or around objectives. Once you walk into or around the vicinity of the compound, a given amount of "construction points" are displayed in the top left of the screen. The points are used by squad leaders to build sandbag walls, barbwire fences ect. Once a squad leader places a fortification, it must then be built by other squad members using the "shovel" tool. A whole compound can be fortified leaving all windows and entrances blocked by choice of the squad leaders; anywhere within or directly near the compound, fortifications can be built. Construction points are shared between all squad leaders, so it is important to be smart with placement of items... It should be obvious, but if you place a sandbag wall infront of a window, try not to leave any cracks between the sandbag wall and the window itself... enemies will use said cracks in the fortification to wreck everyone within the compound... It should be remembered, as its easy to know; if you can see out, then the enemy can see in.
7) As squad leader, you must be helpful to your squad by way of communication; since FOBs and rallypoints can only be placed by squad leaders, it is imperative that squad communication is present; less so by other squad members, but it is absolutely necessary for the captain of the squad as he conducts the progression of the game. Without rallypoints or FOBs placed, the game quickly turns into a walking simulator for all other players and it guarantees a loss when the other team is using such tools accurately. Again, this game is "squad/team" dependant; you must be team player. Which to mention, the community seems at this time, to be far from Toxic; players work together and with a proper team (even without vehicles) the game can be quite enjoyable.
8) The game runs at 50-60 Frames for myself, and most if not all settings are set to max. Frames in game, are entirely dependant on the quality of the server being played, as well as the current or allowed population. If I were to play a max 40 player match, I can maintain the 50-60 FPS no problem; but if I join a 65+ man server, I get about 30-40 frames tops.
Because I didn't read it anywhere, and didn't realize until after I purchased the game, it should also be known that the 100 player servers as advertised have yet to be added to the game; most likely due to the fact that smaller servers are already having difficulty with frames, ping ect... With the fact that most servers provide low FPS with higher player count; most servers to me at least, are simply unplayable due to high ping or FPS instablity; this has left my server choices rather limited if I choose to play with the best experience. Just to say, in case people are wondering; I have a 4GB GTX 970, i7-3820, 12GB ddr3 and I play at a resolution of 1080p.
9) The major hangups I have with the game at this current time, which I believe is hindering it from becoming perfect, is primarily the lack of vehicles... Running the long distances sucks terribly, and like me, you'll probably learn to hate your stamina; not only because you're always waiting for it to refill, but because it takes nothing to deplete it; which means about 75% of your game time, is spent hunkered down in the bushes waiting for your bar to fill. I'm sure this is a tactic by devs to force players to linger in the bush intentionally instead of simply rushing objectives nonstop, or is a way to force squad leaders to always be aware of placing FOBs or rallyponts; either way, I very much despise it. Personally, I believe at the games current beta build, stamina should be increased for the enjoyment of the game; that is until vehicles are added.
- Now, I completely accept that this game is very early beta, but considering the results of other Steam betas which eventually slowed and nearly stopped with worthwhile updates; I review my games as if they are not to recieve another update and are standalone... Yeah, I'm talking to you Ark Survival... You can keep adding different dinos, but you can't fix your 10 FPS code?.. Shysters.

While the original Portal was an awesome game, it's short lenght made it feel like a prototype. Portal 2 is the sequel that the original deserved, picking it's original ideias, adding some new ones, and it's one of the best videogames of all time. It's a first person puzzler where you use a gun to create 2 portals in different locations that are connected in space, meaning that if you enter the first you'll exit in the second. Add to that plenty of different environment mechanics and you have lots of different puzzles that are well designed and with the right amount of difficulty. The main story is well written, with good characters that are well voiced, and filled with humor. It's also around 3 times bigger than the original, lasting around 9-10 hours. That is enough to recommend this game on every Steam account, but the game also has an amazing co-op campaign for two players, with completely new puzzles that have the same quality of the main campaign. Having 2 characters and 4 portals makes this mode more complex, but not exactly harder, especially if you have a good partner. It'll last around 5-6 hours. And there's also lots of great community made levels for both single and co-op, which can make the game last for at least 20 hours of amazing quality content. On sale, it's a steal.

It's similar to other colony-management games, but much more interesting. The basic premise is that your people crashland on sparsely-habited planet on a rim world, and have to survive, and eventually build a spaceship to escape. (The new scenario editor opens up other options, but this is the premise of the basic game.) You will battle hunger, disease, injury, hostile enemies, random events, and even interpersonal relationships.
The game features three different 'storytellers' which control how often events occur and how dangerous they can be. You can play a relatively safe colony-building game, or a 'This planet hates me' game. It's your choice.
The interface works well, and while there is a bit of a learning curve, it's part of the fun, and the game never gets tedious or overly complex.

Oh man this game.... this gem, the Max Payne series were the first games that I've played on PC ever.
Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne is for me, the epitome of a great noir-crime game.
When I heard that there was a Max Payne 3, which was completely unbeknownst to me, I IMMEDIATELY bought it. And did it deliver...?
Yes, it did.
Max Payne 3 looks very different from its predecessors. The rundown, bleached buildings and shadowy sidewalks of New York have been replaced by the hedonistic nightclubs and baking heat of São Paulo, where Max has taken a job working private security for wealthy businessman Rodrigo Branco. Unsurprisingly, things don’t work out for Max: Rodrigo’s trophy wife, Fabiana, is kidnapped on Max’s watch, which sets in motion a chain of events that draws Max into a much larger, more sinister story that just left me in shambles.
Story: 10/10
It touches on the disparity between rich and poor, and how resentment and desperation can fester in the slums and the penthouses alike. This isn’t only tackled in the main story, but also in nice scraps of incidental narrative recovered in clues dotted about the meticulously-crafted environments.
The single-player story lasts around 10-12 hours.
Graphics 8.5/10: Not the best looking game around but environments are impressively detailed and performances sensitively captured.
Cinematics: 8/10
The action set-pieces seem a little muted, especially when compared to, say, the spectacular recent capers of Nathan Drake. But this isn’t necessarily a bad thing.
Sound: 9.5/10
Stirring and evocative soundtrack by the LA rock band ''Health''. Bound to get you pumped.
Final Verdict: 9.5/10
New gameplay elements like the cover-system are implemented very good, but the lack of innovation makes the action a bit tedious towards the end. Nonetheless Rockstar delivers a good game and even more important: it deserves the name Max Payne.
There are plenty of games which are critically acclaimed for their gameplay but lack anything in way of story or character. Max Payne 3 is a different type of proposition. The gameplay is simple yet.. satisfying, but it’s entirely in the service of a strongly-authored narrative. Players aren’t at the liberty to roam, to explore, or to shake things up. Some might find this too controlling, but in return for your freedom, you’re rewarded with a mature genre piece which is also a finely-realised character study.

I was reluctant to pay the steep price for this EA game. But I was lured in by the realism and hardcore nature of this shooter. I'm a Battlefield fan. I'm an Arma fan. What SQUAD brings is the best of both of these worlds.
Your enjoyment of this game is mostly dependent on how well you will work with others, and how well your squad leader is. Team work is vital. If you don't have a squad leader that can lead (ie. maintain order, keep your group together, coordinate with other squad leaders, make the right call at the right time, etc). then you won't really enjoy the game.
That is why it is imperative that you put your time in. Be a private. Learn the ropes here. Once you log 100+ hours in this game you'll understand enemy behaviour. You'll know the terrain. You'll be able to strategize. Once YOU become squad leader and once YOU can lead your team to victory...that's when this game REALLY has you for good.
This game is light in content at this point, but there's something very pleasurable about hardcore "infantry only" game play that I'll probably always want to revisit even after they add all the things the DEVS are promising. What are they promising?
-Fastropes from helicopters
-Various Land Vehicles

-Ladders added to Breacher and ladders revamped.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

This game is unreal. The stories and narratives that evolve as you play are endless. Let me tell you the story about Joe.
Joe crash landed in a pod with two other survivors. Joe was not too bright, he loved to fight, and make art. That was all. He refused to cook. He refused to clean. He refused to haul things. He couldn't heal people. Joe was in his 80s. He was the only hunter in the colony.
Time went on and the colony flourised. Stockpiles were high, foodstores were significant, many different varieties of meals and all were happy. Then the raiders hit. A significant force. Joe, being the only competent fighter, took to the fields. Frightened colonists in tow. The fight was fierce.
Scouring the area, he discovered a couple of colonists were injured, he took them to their beds to die. There was nothing he could do for them, but offer them comfort in their final days as their conditions slowly worsened. Soon. Only Joe remained.
Days and weeks passed. Winter, came and went. The stores of food were plentiful. To pass the time Joe created great works of art from the materials his dead too soon friends had gathered. Just an old man. Waiting to die. Making beautiful art.
He made art that told the stories of his friends. Murals of beavers representing honesty. Frescos of winged marmots representing strength. He created art in rememberance.
Suddenly. A call over the communications relay. Someone was in trouble. Looking for help. He offered assistance. Grabbed his weapons and charged outside. A young man, tribals on his heels. Joe charged. He slew bandits left and right. He cut them down like a man possessed. Til the arrow caught him. Then another. With one final swing of his mighty club. He took his attacker out. Fell to the ground. Dead.
Joe may have died, but the colony lived on. The youth he rescued rebuilt. With Joes art, the only evidence of those who left it behind.
This is just one of many different stories that happen in this game... This particular one took place over a year ago. There have been so many additions to it. So many great and wonderful things.

Ignore my playtime - I have 1000+ hours since around alpha 7, this game is superb and an absolutely fantastic investment for the amount of time you can get out of it.
To start, this game in its purest form is about controlling randomness. The planet is randomly generated. Your colonists are randomly generated. The events that transpire are random.
You start with nothing - a few colonists with randomly generated abilities, personality traits, and possibly injuries or other health conditions. You have a handful of building materials, enough food to last a week, and some simple weapons. From there, it's your job to help them survive.
However, you don't control your colonists directly. You give them orders, and they will try to carry them out. This isn't an RTS game - at its core it's a procedural story generator, and your role is basically to keep your colonists alive for as long as possible as their lives play out. You are like a mostly powerless god, able to guide your colonists but can never overcome their free will or innate personality traits for long. Things will never go exactly as planned, and that is part of the joy of the game. Traders will visit your colony, you will get raided by pirates and tribals and even mechanoids, colonists will get to know each other better and even fall in love, random disasters will happen, your colonists will get sick... their lives play out while randomness happens all around them.
Once you get accustomed to the basic mechanics, the purest and arguably most fun way to play this game is 'iron man' mode - don't just reload an autosave whenever anything bad happens to your colony. When someone dies, they die. In some circumstances, that will mean the end of your colony. But sometimes you will continue, hampered by the loss of a colonist but hopeful for the future, eventually thriving without them. This is RimWorld at its best - a rich simulation that allows for some incredible storytelling. There are few games where you will ever find yourself so attached to what are essentially randomly generated pawns.
A lot of people in the reviews are comparing RimWorld to Prison Architect, but it's only like PA in the sense that the art style is similar - the graphics are simplistic and representative. The game does not play the same way at all. It's much closer to Dwarf Fortress, but really it's a little unfair to compare RimWorld to another game because it doesn't really feel derivative of anything else. It's very much its own thing.
I think it's easier to say who I
recommend this game for:
- If you like to have tutorials and hand holding throughout, this game is not for you
- If you don't like challenging games, this game is not for you
- If you want action and constant battles and explosions, this game is not for you
- If you like predictability and hate randomness, this game is not for you
Overall, RimWorld might not be the prettiest game in the world, but what it lacks in looks it makes up for tenfold in replayability. Ludeon are constantly adding more content, they listen to community feedback, and even though it's Early Access this game has vastly more content and replayability than most completed indie games.
I've invested hundreds of hours into this game and will probably invest thousands more. Couldn't recommend enough.

I want to start off this review with a basic conclusion. Should you buy this game?
YES!
When I first heard this game was coming out, I was skeptical. The last Wolfenstein wasn't that good and Bethesda wasn't really doing well in choosing games to publish (but their developed games are top notch). Also it was the developer's first game. My friend was hyping all over it, so I kept an eye on it. When it came out, I looked at the reviews to see that it did really well. Like, REALLY WELL. This was back when I didn't have a great laptop. Now I do, so I can actually own it.
But I allowed my friend to come over and let me play it on his computer. And I absolutely loved it.
You could tell the developers were huge fans of the older Wolfenstein games and wanted to make sure that this did the series justice. And♥♥♥♥♥♥ did they do their work. Let's start with the story.
You play as the series protagonist since the beginning, William Joseph "B.J." Blazkowicz, an American soldier who is trying to take down an old enemy: Wilhelm Strasse, or Deathshead during 1946, which was when World War 2 was over in our actual history. You storm the castle, killing all Nazis that get in your way, only for it to end in failure. You get captured and are given a choice by Deathshead himself: which of the two soldier friends you have should he kill?
This decision is important for how the game will go, not in story but in gameplay. And this was the prologue.
You escape after one of your friends are killed, but you're hit in the side of the head by shrapnel and put into a coma. You wake up fourteen years later, in 1960. You find out that the Nazis won, America was bombed to hell, and that Germany is now the major superpower. So what do you do?
You try to bring them down of course. And the story is phenominal, very smart and it focuses a lot on the characters, especially B.J.
The gameplay is utterly amazing, really. The HUD is very similar to Wolfenstein 3D's, you got your health and armor right in the bottom center of your screen, with ammo to the right. A new thing to the game is the fact that you can dual-wield almost every weapon you get. Assault rifles, sniper rifles, pistols, shotguns, all of them. I will get to the weapons in more detail later.
There is stealth, which if done well can make a game excellent. This was done well. It's rather simple. Kill them with a not-loud weapon, stay out of sight. Take out the officers before they can call in reinforcements. Then you can go guns blazing. Or you can just say screw it to stealth and go guns blazing the whole time, except for certain parts.
Now to the weapons. I thought that it was just amazing that the developers put a lot of detail into every weapon. Even the ones you use for a single level, they make sure it looks good. The fact that the weaponry changes from 1946 to 1960 is great too. And there are upgrades you can find that can give you things like bouncing lasers or rocket launcher attachments for both assault rifles that you carry. Simply endless.
Finally the visuals and how the game plays. The characters look amazing, with the eyes looking very well done and the skin detailing every part of the person's history. The explosions, both fiery and gory, look great. Lighting, shadows, shiny guns, it all looked amazing. And it played very well, good optimization.
Now...any complaints about the game?
Uh...not really.
Machine Games hit every note, being able to provide a great story that also has great gameplay and great graphics to combine into a well-polished game. I hope they continue to make fantastic first person shooters in their future.

Age Of Empires 2 will always be my favourite strategy game.
The campaigns are in depth and detailed, knowledgable and intuitive, providing a closer look into each civ you may play as. There are multiple sandbox modes where you can face up against AI opponents, or you can create your own scenarios to beat.
The original game, by all means, is a masterpiece. The civs don't seem rushed, and the bonuses seem balanced and fair which complements itself for multiplayer. Tech trees reflect the steps in technology each civ made in history, and the unique units are fun to master and learn to use.
One downside of this game, for me, is the expansions they released. I think the campaigns felt a little rushed, with lack of a narrator which for me was the only reason I played the campaigns, often just using 'black death' so I could hear the story of El Cid or Saladin one more time. The civilisations which are bought in with the forgotten kingdoms seem to lack balance, and you can tell the devs are thinking more towards the incresingly popular multiplayer with civs like the Italians and Portugese. The extra settings for map size make for some longer games, and the population cap increase makes for some larger fights and more thorough strategy vs the ever updated AI, which in hardest mode can probably wipe you out before you even reach castle.
This game is however made more challenging by the expansions, and for players who may have only played Age Of Kings and The Conquerers, the new civs add new challenges and AI makes for some harder gameplay.
All in all, if you're a fan of strategy and RTS, you should buy this game, but only buy the expansions if you're up to the challenge.

Age Of Empires 2 will always be my favourite strategy game.
The campaigns are in depth and detailed, knowledgable and intuitive, providing a closer look into each civ you may play as. There are multiple sandbox modes where you can face up against AI opponents, or you can create your own scenarios to beat.
The original game, by all means, is a masterpiece. The civs don't seem rushed, and the bonuses seem balanced and fair which complements itself for multiplayer. Tech trees reflect the steps in technology each civ made in history, and the unique units are fun to master and learn to use.
One downside of this game, for me, is the expansions they released. I think the campaigns felt a little rushed, with lack of a narrator which for me was the only reason I played the campaigns, often just using 'black death' so I could hear the story of El Cid or Saladin one more time. The civilisations which are bought in with the forgotten kingdoms seem to lack balance, and you can tell the devs are thinking more towards the incresingly popular multiplayer with civs like the Italians and Portugese. The extra settings for map size make for some longer games, and the population cap increase makes for some larger fights and more thorough strategy vs the ever updated AI, which in hardest mode can probably wipe you out before you even reach castle.
This game is however made more challenging by the expansions, and for players who may have only played Age Of Kings and The Conquerers, the new civs add new challenges and AI makes for some harder gameplay.
All in all, if you're a fan of strategy and RTS, you should buy this game, but only buy the expansions if you're up to the challenge.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

I have a lot to say about this game (most of which are positive) so to not waste anyone's time, I'll summarize my points at the beginning before moving on to go into detail about them.
Pros
- Fun and fair gunplay
- Unique and fun progression that gives more insentive to keep playing the game
- Very responsive controls and movement
- Highly stressed on being objective based
- Not at all pay to win
- Very few cheaters (if any)
- Overall fun core gameplay
Cons
- Tons of grinding (though the game helps you out with it by throwing extra certs at you for playing the game)
- Not many maps nor variations of choke points within those maps
- If you dislike grinding or very objective based gameplay this game is probably not for you
- If you are a beginner or just not very good at shooters, you will (probably) get merked ;)
The gunplay feels extremly comfortable and fun. Whenever you die in the game, it's clearly because the opponent was better than you rather than any glitch or exploit. Especially not even the level or tier of weapon they have.
All the tiers of loadout cards past bronze being purely for asthetic not only makes the game more fair to those who don't want to spend money on a game but also supplies the player with some extra long term things to stride for. It's set up in such a way to let the player see it as something they will be rewarded with and get if they keep playing in the far future.
The not pay to win esk nature of the game also gives any player the chance to do really well against anyone, considering they do well in any particular match. I myself have been at the top of the leaderboards at level 6 and even without bronze cards or spending a cent (though I will later in my support of this game and its creators).
All the mercs and their guns (as far as I know) are responsive and viable. Every single one doesn't seem like a potentially great weapon if and only if applied to a good situation in the right hands.
I've also not met any hackers (so far).
The ability to recycle unused or unwanted loadout cards and craft specific tiers for specific mercs makes it and even more fun thing to unbox a random card from the crates. It gives you the suspense of knowing you have a chance to get something amazing but that even if you don't, you'll still not be missing out on much.
A big potential negetive of the game is that it involves a lot of grinding. Like TONS of grinding even just to unlock a single merc. Despite this however, the enjoyabily of the core gameplay lets you not get bored or feel like you got ripped off throughout your playtime. And this is helped greatly because the game basically throws extra certs at you for playing the game with different boosts and daily bonuses. Not to mention how it has merc cycles that let you try out different mercs so you can see which ones are to your liking.
I also especally like the highly stressed objective based gameplay throughout. The fact that you can't keep track of your overall kdr during a game is a nice touch to tell the player, "focus on the objective, not your pride."
Overall, I very much like this game and all the reasons above are why I feel so strongly about recommening this to anyone who enjoys shooters and has the capability to play this game. (P.S. Notice how half of the cons I could think up are conditional statements that don't apply to me? Ye, another two reasons why I like this game. P.P.S I will send this in as a steam review and as feedback for the game.)

The Talos Principle is remarkable. It takes somewhat simple puzzle mechanics and weaves in philosophy and mystery that makes the game feel… Grand. Very grand. This feels more like an epic than many games that shove that buzzword down your throat.
The people who made this game must’ve been ♥♥♥♥ing intelligent. The way they give you info, what info, and how it’s delivered keeps you in a state of reflection and speculation while you wrap your brain around the puzzles. It's a great balancing act.
I was really intimidated by this game at first, for as engaging as it was I feared for a brick wall that could impeded my progress, or the game becomes so obtuse that I leave it out of frustration. And while the game is open really open ended, going through it in order never felt like a gradual curve up to impossibility. They sprinkle the tricky puzzles, but never where it feels like the difficulty curve is too uneven.
It’s also long, Steam says I’ve put 26 hours into it. And for it’s length, I think like 2 or 3% of it’s content and story was repeating itself. Finishing it was immensely satisfying too, I haven’t been that satisfied from beating a game for a while.
So yeah, ♥♥♥♥ing buy this game and play it immediately. It was worth it at $35. Hell, it would be worth it at $60. 10/10 GOTY 2014, 15, & 16.

I really liked this game, I will play it aqain and I recommend it to anyone who plays anything.  It demonstrates good character and story, Level design and concepts,  there are some lack -luster bits in there, like the collecting of 'gold' weapons which  make your gun more powerful as well as how you have to connect online to play it, but they are worth overlooking for this frenzied frag fes This is Max Payne melded into the new ages of games like Gears of War etc( the dynamics of combat(I have not played Gears of war, but the hiding behind cover is central to this game an I beleive it was a good decision too, it works.. to some extent)
Game is VERY challegning  -a testaemnt to 'REAL' games, unlike games like Bioshock infinte amongst other newer games which are a walkthrough....   If you dont like challenging games, then I suggest you try at it - it is innately rewarding and I beleive some of the easier games are actually led by you own happiness at success rather than it being a good game, hence I reinforce my tatement that this can deal out punishment but still keep you interested... There is so much that is in this game that a gamer, let alone a story driven gamer or FPS freak cant ignore!
Adding to the story,  Max goes through a 'tranistion' where he changes and his environments change... I will say no more, this is hard to do in a game or story without each side of the game feeling 'detached' I think... These guys did a wonderful job, and whats more the level design is compliments it.
The game's story structure is not linear either, it shows parts of Max's life after Max Payne 2 (which is sub-standard to this) and it jumps about, but does not make it hard to follow... In a  way, you could easily forget about the story and just FRAG!
On story matters:  the commentary is in a more gloomey and Gritty,  but still just as 'Romantic' (I mean reflective and thoughtful and intersting , NOT 'in-love') in a Max Payne kind of way. It does kind of hold true to the original, but changes it slightly and as Max Payne is an old-boy now, that makes sense.  However, it can be a bit depressing as a result... But the end does kind of feel more 'uplifting' or balancing in contrast, so even better reason for you to complete it I think!
Level design is wonderful... It almsot feels like most parts of the level have been given a good amount of attention  to challenege the player (unlike Alan Wake whcih has poor and dull level design(in my oppinion)... There are some parts of the game, just like Max Payne 1, that are iconic and VERY memorable... Some are just SO epic, it is to be played to be seen... and perhaps this is one of the best thigns that goes for it...
The levels vary from big multi layered slums to large elaborate, open Buldings.. Each work really well and it is a pleasure to not only be challenged with finding different strategies to fight, but also to see how Rockstar's Developers and Level designers can make a level to make the expereince feel different.
As for the art side... Eveything looks ok... my machine is not great and I had it on low settings, so please dont think it looks awful... maybe the shine came off through that...   There are still a few extras likethe TV shows and various stuff to look at as with MaxPayne 1 and 2, so thats also a good plus, something that Alan Wake was also good for and perhaps did a better job of... But I consider this a better game in genreal (FPS).
The guns are good and it is an intersting kind of set up... For you Pyro players on TF, sorry, they're mostly ballistic  weapons, so you will have to aim hard and rush in fighting or snipe with concentration.. this adds to the difficulty I think(AND REWARD! Dont be a Plank and skip the challenge!)...  but lots of machine guns, pistols and sniper rifles... And a sign these guys are true to the FPS genre in general, at the end you are given a pretty nice Battle rifle (a sniper rifle without a scope which can be fired with accuracy)... I love these guns and feel the introduction only twice in the game , specifically at the end really was a nice addtion... As with the statisics on Rockstar - Socail club  (which is nothing I want anything to do with...), you will notice there are more kills with dual single wield weapons than with big 2 handed weapons, I did not use them much and found at times they were quite ammo hungry... But they are excellent Assault weapons, but given their strngth it is interesting to find once you do dual weild, you cnnot carry  a bigger weapon( so when your ammo rusn out , your left with nothing... a nice dynamic given they are so powerful... Plan your assault well!
I will add - I played this on Hard, did not play noraml, so maybe easy and normal are more reasonable... in saying that I am not the best gamer and the third person perspective (HUD) can be annoying at times and get you killed, so it may take some getting used to , but this is Max Payne and good on the Dev's and Rockstar for keeping this true.  Also this is differnt to most FPS, by feel and application! There needs to be some variation!  There are enpough standard FPS  games out there, so even better reason to play this...
The problem with Max Payne 3 is  - that it is gltichey - I get CTD or Crash to Desktop  all the time, - often it is not an issue whilst playing and can play for many hours without any issues, the problem is when you open the menu (eacape) and leave it or leave the game idle ... it will crash and it can be tricky getting the game to close.. (lots of alt-tabbing - annoying)
Also as I mentioned Rockstar 'Social club' (which is a proper-chavvy name if you ask me:P) is a requirement to play. I hate this method of authenticating and even then, Rockstart have made it a standard that you MUST be connected to them before playing ... THUMBS DOWN ROCKSTAR!(I dont care how intersting statistics are), its not right!
Additionally the Golden waeapon thing and some of the clues are quite hard to find and is borigng. Perhaps they could have made more obvious level design... or perhaps I should play it again and is a good reason therefore to incite extra play to fans...  In case you ask, I hate walkthroughs - they are for the braindead if you ask me... why ask when you can work it out yourself... gain-something from it...
Finally my last annoying point is cover shooting.... I played this on hard, so cover shooting for longer than 4 seconds will get you shot easily and more than likely make you use a pill to heal...  so I will have to say Rockstar DID NOT play test and calibrate this enough... Or maybe I am missing something, it feels like you cannot aim or prepare before hand, the function of cover shooting is 'different' and dis-orientating in relation to 'freeshooting' if I could have a starndard FPS PoV (Point of View) then I would... and it would make this game easier... In saying that , it is something you can get used to and the dyanamic makes the game more intersting.... Additionally to that, some of the reticles are Horrendous! This is a difficult game to recommend, but I feel I must.
It's ultimately, just a miserable game. I don't know quite how else to describe it. Obviously with the Nazi setting, it would have been inappropriate to make it a fun romp, but I came away from the game quite disheartened by it. Technically it's very good. Realistic graphics and great action set pieces, but the game world is just too grey. I suppose it makes a change from the "realistic is brown" trope, but no matter where you are, everything is grey. They even try to justify it in the storyline in a subplot about concrete that never really goes anywhere. The action is good, but tends to swing from either annoyingly easy to frustratingly difficult several times through each level. You either have an abundance of health, armour and ammo, or you have to scratch your way through. Very rarely is there any middle ground, so you'll either stick with one gun throughout the game, or just throw everything you have at the baddies. There doesn't really seem to be a lot of point in some of the weapons, especially the shotgun.
The biggest criticism I have about the game though is that it is just too miserable and frankly the ending sucks. When I finished the game, I felt no real sense of accomplishment. The final boss battle relies too much on good luck rather than skill to make you feel like you've really "won" and the payoff to the storyline is a despressing as anything else.
There is a plucky Scottish ally who adds some comic relief, but it's few and far between. Halfway through the game he has a breakdown, so you even lose that. There are two branches to the game which change the storyline slightly depending on which choice you make in an early level, but to be frank I don't really feel like I want to even bother with the second path. It just seems like a chore. And forget about trying on a harder difficulty, I can't imagine that'll be much fun at all; just frustrating. Ultimately a good game that needed some lighter moments, a better ending and a bit more colour.

While the original Portal was an awesome game, it's short lenght made it feel like a prototype. Portal 2 is the sequel that the original deserved, picking it's original ideias, adding some new ones, and it's one of the best videogames of all time. It's a first person puzzler where you use a gun to create 2 portals in different locations that are connected in space, meaning that if you enter the first you'll exit in the second. Add to that plenty of different environment mechanics and you have lots of different puzzles that are well designed and with the right amount of difficulty. The main story is well written, with good characters that are well voiced, and filled with humor. It's also around 3 times bigger than the original, lasting around 9-10 hours. That is enough to recommend this game on every Steam account, but the game also has an amazing co-op campaign for two players, with completely new puzzles that have the same quality of the main campaign. Having 2 characters and 4 portals makes this mode more complex, but not exactly harder, especially if you have a good partner. It'll last around 5-6 hours. And there's also lots of great community made levels for both single and co-op, which can make the game last for at least 20 hours of amazing quality content. On sale, it's a steal.

I came into this thinking it was going to be a dumb macho shoot em' up but what I got was a truly harrowing story about the human condition. Aside the main villian who could be easily named Dr.McNastyBadMan all the characters are well rounded and relatable but have flaws which themselves have consequences for themselves and others. You'll find yourself wanting to punch your fellow resistance members in the face for their hostilities towards you but at the same time completly understand where they are coming from. The story ends at kind of an odd place that leaves room for a sequel but it's hard to say. It's not sequel bait though so it gets a pass.
Gameplay is fun, and while there is a sense of realism in the story, combat is just as old school wolfenstein as it get's with plenty of overpowered badass weapons and unique kill options. The perk system is also lots of fun adding a nice set of bonuses for completing passive tasks with only very few being a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get.
We need more AAA games like this; good story with characters that do more than growl moody one liners but still has fun gameplay. 10/10

I have played a fair bit of Robocraft. I got in fairly early, and saw the game develop into what it is today. For the greatest part I was eager to see the development, and happily played along.
A year ago Freejam started to change the game. The way it used to work was with progressively stronger tiers, culminating in truly massive megabots. It wasn't a perfect system, but it was satisfying. So I grinded my way all up to the megabot, and mere weeks later Freejam removed them. And later, the tiering system entirely. The game that it is now is not a game I enjoy anymore.
Oh, also, the crate system with which you gain loot is incredibly annoying.
Edit:
So after almost a year of inactivity, I returned to the game after hearing about a new update that fixes aerofoils and brings back megabots. It's even worse than when I stopped playing. The flow of the gameplay has been completely ruined, and a match in the game resembles a hectic slapfight. Tactical gameplay is gone, and you just B-line for the nearest cap point and occasionally shoot at enemies. The game's art still shows fanciful bots, but all I ran into were ugly metabuilds. Boxes of blocks with legs and rotors, and there seems to be no point to playing anything else. There are some small improvements (like the aerofoils not being total crap anymore), but it doesn't balance out all the poor decisions that were made. Also, for some reason it now runs like crap on my brand new, top of the line PC.
I'm gone. Definitely, and forever. There is no hope for this game.

This is a difficult game to recommend, but I feel I must.
It's ultimately, just a miserable game. I don't know quite how else to describe it. Obviously with the Nazi setting, it would have been inappropriate to make it a fun romp, but I came away from the game quite disheartened by it. Technically it's very good. Realistic graphics and great action set pieces, but the game world is just too grey. I suppose it makes a change from the "realistic is brown" trope, but no matter where you are, everything is grey. They even try to justify it in the storyline in a subplot about concrete that never really goes anywhere. The action is good, but tends to swing from either annoyingly easy to frustratingly difficult several times through each level. You either have an abundance of health, armour and ammo, or you have to scratch your way through. Very rarely is there any middle ground, so you'll either stick with one gun throughout the game, or just throw everything you have at the baddies. There doesn't really seem to be a lot of point in some of the weapons, especially the shotgun.
The biggest criticism I have about the game though is that it is just too miserable and frankly the ending sucks. When I finished the game, I felt no real sense of accomplishment. The final boss battle relies too much on good luck rather than skill to make you feel like you've really "won" and the payoff to the storyline is a despressing as anything else.
There is a plucky Scottish ally who adds some comic relief, but it's few and far between. Halfway through the game he has a breakdown, so you even lose that. There are two branches to the game which change the storyline slightly depending on which choice you make in an early level, but to be frank I don't really feel like I want to even bother with the second path. It just seems like a chore. And forget about trying on a harder difficulty, I can't imagine that'll be much fun at all; just frustrating. Ultimately a good game that needed some lighter moments, a better ending and a bit more colour.

The good: The Talos Principle is a bit like a less humorous, more philosophical version of Portal. The mechanics are different than Portal's, but the idea of going through a series of self-contained logic puzzles is similar. The puzzles range in difficulty from fairly simple to challenging, and there are bonus type puzzles to complete in some levels. There are lots of little Easter eggs referencing other games and pop culture. You can actually leave QR codes that others on your friends list can find as they play the game, which is interesting. You have lots of mechanics to play with in each level (boxes, force fields, lasers, fans, etc.), which helps to make for a really varied puzzle experience. Unlike a lot of "player choice" games that have different endings which turn out to be different cut scenes, the Talos Principle has a couple of completely different endings with totally different ways to get to each. The level design is beautiful, and it makes the game very atmospheric and fun to look at.
The bad: This game seems to have a motion sickness problem. I don't normally have trouble with games and I got pretty sick after playing a couple hours. Apparently it's a common problem; I found lots of hits online from others experiencing the same issue. There's actually a motion sickness reduction menu setting, and that did help some, but I was still a little queasy. Something to beware of if you are inclined to have problems already.
General info: You play as an AI tasked with solving various logic puzzles. There's a lot of really interesting back story to discover if you take the time to read all the documents and listen to the voice and the various recordings. The philosophical nature of the game questions the nature of humanity - what are the defining traits of a human being, how does AI compare, etc. Whether you agree with the conclusions or not, there's some good fodder for thought/discussion. There is a little bit of back and forth in the game (when you have to fetch an axe, for example) that is tiresome, but overall, the level design flows pretty smoothly.
Overall: If you are into puzzles, good stories, or philosophical debates, I strongly recommend this one.
System Specs Used: Intel Core i7-3610QM, Nvidia GeForce GTX 670M / 3GB GDDR5, DDRIII 12GB RAM, Windows 7

A really fun, scripted FPS with a full cast of supporting characters and much more of a story than I would have expected from a game called Wolfenstein. The villains were off-the-charts loathable, and the friendlies were "I'm going to miss them" lovable.
I'm not particularly good at combat in FPS games, but the "BRING'EM ON!" ("Medium Difficulty Setting for the Average Gamer") was just right for me to have enough of a challenge without wanting to quit in frustration. Pacing was great, with good interspacing of homebase time or exploration between intense battles. Perks are awarded for certain actions (like stealth kills or crazy carnage) so the game can become a little easier for your preferred style.

Probably one of the best first person puzzlers ever created, it's got some really rad gameplay with some really rad story bits going on. The puzzles will have you questioning your intelligence, while the narrative simultaneously has you questioning your existence. Mechanically, everything seems to fit together perfectly - though personally I disliked the self co-op stuff (it's always the same thing, and it's always annoying!).
The story is loaded with that philosophy stuff that all those philosophers like to talk about, but they did a good job at not pushing anything on players. There's a lot of notes to read at a lot of terminals, so if you dislike reading you should probably keep that in mind. The various notes and messages and audiologs available throughout the campaign offer a lot of backstory into the 'world' and the people who built it. There are quite a few ways the game can end, which is impacted by decisions you make throughout the game that you may not even realise are decisions. I don't have a problem with this, but it'd have been nice to know going in.
If you're a completionist, I feel really bad for you. There's entire puzzles and endings locked behind collectibles, which a lot of the time require you to break the levels. I mean, the idea is nice - smuggling items from one puzzle into another to break the rules - but it really just feels like breaking the game.
I got the game on sale, but I would have easily paid full price for it. Definitely pick it up.
Drop the philosophy, pick up the sociology. Road to Gehenna is everything the main game did right, with a little bit less of the stuff it did wrong. There's a lot of really cool stuff they did with this, like terminal minigames and a "forum" where you could speak with other people/robots/whatever. Because it focuses on a society and the people in it, the way the story is told is pretty different and there's a lot more comedy. As with the main campaign, it does have a handful of endings - though the choices that impact the endings are a lot more obvious this time around.
The puzzles in the DLC are more of the same, don't expect any new mechanics. Instead, it forces you to use all the old mechanics in new ways. Jamming something then launching the jammer, using lasers to cut off other lasers. It's all stuff that was possible in the main game but never utilized. The puzzles aren't necessarily harder than the main stuff, but they're still pretty difficult - and they start off that way. So make sure you play through the normal campaign before diving into this.
This expansion is also worth the money, in my opinion, but don't be expecting anything new.

For those of you looking for memorable characters and a good story, stay away from this game. Stick with Portal 2.

One of the best first person shooters I've played in years.  The New Order manages to feel like a classic 90s FPS, but without all of the antiquated design elements that make those games annoying to play today.  It has surprisingly good story and characters, and excellent voice acting (if you can get past the "I'm a tough guy" main character's voice).  The atmosphere, though, is the best part of this game.  They did an absolutely flawless job in that department.  You really feel like this is a real world, and that is an extremely chilling and unnerving prospect.
The game runs well, and has good customizability -- it feels like a PC game, not a console port, which is hard to say for a lot of triple-A FPS on Steam these days.
The game did what it set out to do, and honestly, for $15 on a Steam sale, what more could I have asked for?

The evolution of a Splash Damage objective based game. If you liked RTCW, ET, ET:QW, then you will easily get a feel for this game. It is as much a game about moving (and firing on the move) as it is about aim. Deaths are seldom due to an infuriating single shot and a respawn is never more than 24 seconds away. As a result good team play, smart positioning amd timing are needed to win a map.
There are a range of mercenaries to choose from with 9 relatively easily obtainable loadouts each allowing you to customise the character to suit your style of play. You start with 2 free mercenaries, with another 3 on guest rotation and you should be able unlock 1 extra within the first hour of gameplay (even if unlocking others may take a little longer).
If you like the game and you want to support more development (or get impatient to unlock more mercenaries) the in game store sells extra merceneries individually and in discounted bundles. You don't get a sense of pay to win because of how well the game is balanced - you have enough tools at your disposal to be competitive from the start.
And hey, it's free to play so what have you got too lose?

Pacing was great, with good interspacing of homebase time or exploration between intense battles. Perks are awarded for certain actions (like stealth kills or crazy carnage) so the game can become a little easier for your preferred style.
The AI is nothing fancy, so it was often easy to hide in a crawl space and take out a dozen soldiers by shooting at their knees. But the boss fights were fun! The roles of each team mate and how well they are performed have a direct impact on the outcome of the game.
If your looking for a tactical fps that demands teamwork with large-scale teams then I would definitely give Squad a try. Wolfenstein: The New Order is a first person shooter videogame from MachineGames. The last entry in the popular Wolfenstein franchise, it follows the exploit of the allied soldier B.J. Blazkowicz as he wakes up fourteen years after the climax of World War II and discovers that the Nazis, thanks to a huge leap in technology engineered by general Wilhelm "Deathshead" Strasse, won the war and conquered all the known world. Blazkowicz decides to join a resistance cell and try to undermine the Nazis by killing general Deatshead himself.
Much like the previous games in the series, the New Order is your typical FPS fare: you are given grenades and a wide array of weapons (some of which can be even dual wielded) to destroy the various kinds of enemies thrown in your general direction. The game also features some stealth elements: some sequences involve enemy officers that can bring in reinforcements against you if they aren't killed silently, with the rest of the Nazi soldiers unaware. It's worth mentioning however that these sections can be also played in a more direct manner, as to say shoot everything in sight. Therefore, stealth becomes a useful tool only during small portions of the game (later in the game these sequences also feature armed soldiers and cyborgs, who are basically immune to knife attacks, making direct assaults a more viable option).
By following your own playing style, you can unlock various perks. Every perk is unlocked by completing a specific challenge of some sort and award you a permanent bonus. There are four classes of perks: stealth (self explanatory), tactical (for players who like to switch between weapons often), assault (self explanatory) and demolitionist (for players who like to deploy explosives often). In short, if you stick to your favorite play style you are bound to unlock perks that benefit it and make your life easier on the long run (for instance, by killing a lot of enemies without being detected you are awarded the ability to run more silently).
The New Order also feature rather unique boss battles: instead of being just more powerful targets, the game's bosses are more like puzzle bosses, which require you to take certain steps in order to damage them. While this makes some bosses a bit frustrating if you don't get what you have to do right off the bat, it also makes bringing them down all the more rewarding.
In each level of the game there are also several collectables you can find as a self-imposed challenge: precious treasures, parts of a secret code which unlocks new game modes, pieces of lore.
The story of Wolfenstein: The New Order has been especially praised, and truth be told the main plot is pretty solid and the game's action is often paused by NPCs interaction, but always keeps you interested, which is a very strong bonus for a FPS such as this. Moreover, in true Wolfenstein fashion, the antagonists of the game are also so over the top evil that going after them is a reward in itself (they are Nazis, so this was to be expected).
Wolfenstein: The New Order is truly a very special and enjoyable FPS and I would suggest it even to people who never played a Wolfenstein game before (this is my case, by the way)

In today’s world of microtransactions, games releasing before they’re finished, glitch-ridden open world engines, and games that overall fail to live up to their artistic vision, sometimes there will come a game that’s so perfect that it’s hard to believe it even got made.
The Talos Principle is a single-player puzzle game made with full triple-A production values, arguably leaving Portal 2 in the dust at what it does. I liken it to Dear Esther, but twenty times longer and filled with actual gameplay, while keeping the beauty of the world and the philosophical overtones intact.
The game consists of walking through majestic-looking outdoor areas to find closed-off puzzle areas, then solving puzzles using only a small handful of simple and easy-to-understand machines. The puzzles themselves are eloquent and very well-tested. There are over a hundred of them in all, but each puzzle introduces a new idea or uses old ideas in new ways, so they never feel repetitive or stale. The game’s environments are simply breathtaking with their huge draw distances and ridiculous detail, while the puzzle areas feel aptly like claustrophobic rat mazes while never losing the area’s sense of atmosphere. The puzzles get very challenging near the end, but expert level design makes them all very rewarding to solve. And if you’re particularly clever, the game’s third ending requires you to figure out how to break the level design and take items out of their designated areas to find secrets hidden in closed-away or out-of-bounds places. It’s rather mind-blowing and something that I’ve never seen incorporated into a game intentionally before.
The icing on the cake is the storytelling. The story is that you’re a robot who wakes up in a garden and follows the commands of a god-like figure constantly talking in your head. It quickly becomes apparent that the whole world may or may not be a virtual reality simulation, which may or may not have been programmed by humans for a specific yet unknown purpose, and you are given the choice of blindly following the god’s orders or trying to unravel the mystery of who exactly you are and what lies outside of the simulation. The game has three different endings, and you will find whatever answer you seek if you search hard enough.
The game poses a few difficult philosophical questions and studies them from countless different angles. I know that some people will find the philosophy pretentious and trite, and I know it’s completely up to personal preference, but for me it really, really worked. I was hooked on the story the whole way. I think that even if some of the game’s lines fail to impress you, there’s enough material here that you’ll find at least something that will strike a chord and challenge the way you think. Besides, if you don’t like the story, it’s easy enough to skip everything by ignoring the computers, but you might miss out on the brilliance of some of the game’s endings.
I give The Talos Principle a perfect score. It’s got sublime puzzle design, mind-blowing secret collectables, gorgeous environments that put Dear Esther to shame, above-average voice acting, a professionally-written and well-presented story, nearly zero glitches, and depths and depths of content. It’s truly one of the best games I’ve ever played. Go play it if you haven't already; you might come out feeling like a different person.

Talos Principle: a game about solving puzzles and suffering existential crises.
And that is what makes it great.
I've always been a fan of the scenic puzzle game, something with a glorious vista sa you try to fit pieces together or find the way over a seemingly-insurmountable obstacle, and Talos Principle definitely presents that sort of thing well. Can you find better graphics? Almost certainly, but there is a great deal of direction and setting of scene in Talos that is effective in evoking what the game wants you to feel... awe in the face of the divine, doubt as to what you believe and the meaning of your goals. In terms of the puzzles trhemselves, these are not challenges requiring the fastest of response times nor a deep grasp of the underlying physics engine, some are rather simple, some are very challenging, some are so simple the challenge is breaking all the mistaken assumptions you've been building up solving other puzzles. This sort of puzzle game is not much for replayability, but in the case of Talos, where the puzzles are constructed to care about getting the end result not the process, there were sometimes several different solutions to the same challenge, you may have solved it one way, but can go back and try another.
In terms of the game's story, another puzzle... piece together fragments of diaries, documents, observations. Another puzzle, of a different sort, but one the game knows you're trying to solve and has ways of interacting with your efforts, force-fields and tiling locks for one's thinking not one's physical being. If the story itself is not groundbreaking, this approach to it buoys it upwards, taking advantage of what games can do as a storytelling medium. It is quite well done.
If you hate solving puzzles, or if you need certainty in your stories, there probably isn't much for you in Talos Principle. But if you enjoy figuring out the world around you, how do you get to the next step, or if you sometimes muse on what it means to be human, I'm sure you'll enjoy it as immensely as I did.
