I played this game back when you would earn RP and there was a tech tree and it was very enjoyable. One part Portal style puzzle play, one part philosophy lesson and it succeeded as both. The gameplay isn't as polished as Portal but it's still quite fun, especially if there's someone watching and offering advice. A few of the puzzles are ingenious, and thankfully ony a few are frustrating. The objectives on the final level in particular aren't very clear and unlike the rest of the game the last round is on a timer. But even then it's not so punishing that you'll want to smash your  keyboard in two.
The philosophical side is what really surprised me, though, and I found myself wanting to complete the missions to chat more with Milton, an AI you meet early on in the game, and to read and listen to the logs left throughout the levels. Many games use auto/text logs to progress the story, but I've never played a game where they were as compelling to follow as in the Talos Principle. The story behind the project and the reasons for the individuals doing what they did were quite moving and seemed very real. The writers of the game deserve a lot of praise for creating a story that could have been overwrought and manipulative, but was instead grounded and credible, and was much more powerful as a result. It seems silly to say, but this video game made me think and not just in the sense of solving puzzles. I actually learned something from the Talos Principle, and I hope it sticks with me. As one of the ideas explored in the game, free will is a personal choice, so I guess that's up to me.
Highly recommended if you like puzzle games, philosophical debates and really excellent stories about the nature of artificial intelligence.

***WARNING*** There are some minor spoilers found in this review - I try to keep it vague so as not to ruin your experience, though.
The Talos Principle is, at its gaming core, a puzzler.  It's a damn good one, too.  The puzzles don't necessarily get harder after the first ones, but they seem to get more unique in their approach.  There is some amazing design in the puzzles which makes the game both enjoyable and frustrating.
The scenery of the game is a visual feast.  It's beautiful, serene surroundings drew me to explore and just take in the calming charm of it all.  The music matches the setting, hauntingly gorgeous.
There is an interesting, albeit somewhat hidden, story of why you're there, why are you doing these puzzles, and what purpose does it serve?  There's a hefty philosophical influence in dialogues made with the computer system found in game and towards the end of TTP, I found it to be the most enjoyable portion.  The longer I played, the less I worried about puzzles and the more eager I was to get to those philosophical conversations.  For now, I'll skip this (and come back to it later).
The major plot of the story takes a backseat to everything else in the game, but it feels as if that's part of what makes your playthrough so good.  As you learn how to work the puzzles, learn more about your environment and learn more about why you, the character, exists, you, the player ALSO learns more about what's going on, why you're there and why you're doing the puzzles.  Every bit of progression and every conversation with the system computer draws you ever closer to the ending.
Now, there are multiple endings to this, each one making sense for the game's various philosophical outcomes.  When my chosen ending was about obtaining a sense of humanity, I felt a very real sense of accomplishment.  It wasn't that I just completed a game, but I felt as if I made the right decisions to seem human.  It's been an interesting thought-provoking experience.
On that note, the philosophical base for all of this game SOMEWHAT boils down to "What makes a human being a human?"  It's incredibly amazing to go through the development process of that simple question as it turns into a complex discussion.   It could be argued that the game was purposefully built around that single question, with every puzzle and conversation somehow blossoming the question into dozens, into hundreds, etc.  All in all, pairing all those thoughts and philosophical queries with a beautifully crafted ending left me with a satisfied mind, still full of questions.
This game is a solid 9/10 for me.  The puzzles were challenging, the philosophical aspect was incredible and the plot, while vague, was well formed and wonderfully carried out.  It's not a 10/10 only because by the end of the game, I was starting to become weary of the mildly repetitive puzzles and just wanted the philosophical chat.

The Talos Principle is a very good puzzle game, framed by an interesting philosophical theme and wrapped up in very nice graphics and a beautiful soundtrack.
The story is told as you discover partially corrupted emails, blog posts, and time-capsule audio logs, slowly unravelling bits and pieces about who you are, what this place is and what happened to the world of man. This was very well done and I enjoyed every snippet, with the time capsules being my personal highlight of every level (Compliments on the voice acting).
I definitely liked the puzzles in general, while I have to say I vastly preferred the Sigils to the Stars (which are semi-optional). With the sigils, there's always a solution, all the pieces are there for you to put in order. For some, the solution may be instantly apparent, while the more challenging ones will probably baffle you for a moment, but guides should never be necessary here.
The same cannot be said for the stars. Some of these will require the consultation of a guide. That is unless you search every dark corner of the map for a hidden switch or passage and randomly aim at every cloud and tree, cause who knows where the connector you need may be hidden.
I guess I just prefer puzzles where I am given all the pieces, as opposed to the manufacturer having hidden one in a secret compartment in the box.
The philosophical aspect is a bit over-hyped, in my opinion, and if it weren't for this hype, I wouldn't feel the need to put things into perspective, but here we are. My goal is to keep you from going into the game with unreasonably high expectations, as mine were.
Yes, Croteam did a great job of creating an interesting framework out of it, but the subject matter (Is a true AI a person, and what does a person make?) is nothing new or groundbreaking. It may not have been examined in-depth before in any games I can think of, but certainly in film and literature (and around bar tables).
Yes, some of the questions the player is presented with are thought-provoking, but then the answer you would actually give is often not among the options. I know this is due to the limitations of the medium and I can't imagine anyone else could have done a much better job of it, but to be able to lead truly deep philosophical conversations with a computer terminal in a game, we'll have to wait for the development of an actual AI. And wouldn't that be lovely, to have a meaningful conversation about whether or not an AI can be considered a person... with an actual, true AI!... in a video game... for our entertainment.
Once again, I really enjoyed playing The Talos Principle. So should you, seriously.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a first person shooter videogame from MachineGames. The last entry in the popular Wolfenstein franchise, it follows the exploit of the allied soldier B.J. Blazkowicz as he wakes up fourteen years after the climax of World War II and discovers that the Nazis, thanks to a huge leap in technology engineered by general Wilhelm "Deathshead" Strasse, won the war and conquered all the known world. Blazkowicz decides to join a resistance cell and try to undermine the Nazis by killing general Deatshead himself.
Much like the previous games in the series, the New Order is your typical FPS fare: you are given grenades and a wide array of weapons (some of which can be even dual wielded) to destroy the various kinds of enemies thrown in your general direction. The game also features some stealth elements: some sequences involve enemy officers that can bring in reinforcements against you if they aren't killed silently, with the rest of the Nazi soldiers unaware. It's worth mentioning however that these sections can be also played in a more direct manner, as to say shoot everything in sight. Therefore, stealth becomes a useful tool only during small portions of the game (later in the game these sequences also feature armed soldiers and cyborgs, who are basically immune to knife attacks, making direct assaults a more viable option).
By following your own playing style, you can unlock various perks. Every perk is unlocked by completing a specific challenge of some sort and award you a permanent bonus. There are four classes of perks: stealth (self explanatory), tactical (for players who like to switch between weapons often), assault (self explanatory) and demolitionist (for players who like to deploy explosives often). In short, if you stick to your favorite play style you are bound to unlock perks that benefit it and make your life easier on the long run (for instance, by killing a lot of enemies without being detected you are awarded the ability to run more silently).
The New Order also feature rather unique boss battles: instead of being just more powerful targets, the game's bosses are more like puzzle bosses, which require you to take certain steps in order to damage them. While this makes some bosses a bit frustrating if you don't get what you have to do right off the bat, it also makes bringing them down all the more rewarding.
In each level of the game there are also several collectables you can find as a self-imposed challenge: precious treasures, parts of a secret code which unlocks new game modes, pieces of lore.
The story of Wolfenstein: The New Order has been especially praised, and truth be told the main plot is pretty solid and the game's action is often paused by NPCs interaction, but always keeps you interested, which is a very strong bonus for a FPS such as this. Moreover, in true Wolfenstein fashion, the antagonists of the game are also so over the top evil that going after them is a reward in itself (they are Nazis, so this was to be expected).
Wolfenstein: The New Order is truly a very special and enjoyable FPS and I would suggest it even to people who never played a Wolfenstein game before (this is my case, by the way)

is quite a simplistic but very fun game. The game offers two types of game modes.
The basis of the first game mode Defense is to 'build your base by day and defend it by night'. This game mode is basically wave defense, every wave the zombies get faster, more health and deal more damage. This means that the standard pistol that you start off with will no longer be doing any real damage to the zombie horde. Another possible inconvenience to factor in is the lamp-post, the lamp-post is your only source of light in this game which means you will most likely be building your base around this lamp. There are 12 means of defense, these include; the wooden and steel palisades, the autoturret, pistol, SMG, Shotgun, Flamethrower, Assault rifle, Sniper rifle, Rocket launcher, Tesla coil and the Laser. Each of these weapons and defense mechanisms costs cash from which you gain killing zombies and collecting random drops off their dead bodies. All of these means of defense go on sale randomly through the waves which is quite cool, as if you are $2,000 off buying the laser and it goes on sale the wave after, you can purchase instead of going through another round without it. The cost of ammo is variable through the weapons however they generally cost $40-80 although the flame thrower is more at $200. Once again, these can go on sale and you can also loot them randomly off zombie corpses.
The other mode Endless Nights is about 'fighting zombies in never ending darkness'. In this mode the base-building and shopping element to the game is dropped, for a more shoot-em-up style of gaming. But don't worry, just because you can no longer shop for your favourite weapons, it doesn't mean that they won't drop from the zombies as they crumple to the floor. I mean, who doesn't love having a rocket launcher after thirty seconds? During this game mode you will most likely find yourself frantically running around the map trying to avoid the zombies but also trying to gun them down one-by-one. As in both game modes, there are three characters available to choose from; the guy, the girl and the swat.
The game is quite entertaining although it is best played with friends to maximize the most fun you can have with it. I have played both game modes with and without friends and they are both enjoyable. The game is a port from the Xbox 360 version and plays quite well on my system and also offers full controller support. The system requirements are also generally quite low so that is always nice to see with games. Lastly, the multiplayer is very easy and quick to set up and have others join, which is a positive due to the fact that some games these days are very difficult to set up.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who likes relaxing, simple and enjoyable zombie games. Although I would not recommend the game at the current price as on sale, it becomes a lot more cheaper! Depending on your region, the price for a 2-pack would be £0.49 / $0.74 / €0.49 and at this price I would immediately recommend it.

General Gameplay
I love Aoe2 and played my original version since it came out at least every second year. It kept pulling me back in with it's compelling gameplay elements other RTS games of the time (and still today in many regards) can't offer. Although it has no hero units with special abilities to activate, the stances and formations combined with the great unit balance offer many possibilities of influence for the player controlling his armies. Micromanagement like changing the formation to split a group of archers to prevent them being hit by an onager shot followed by focus firing it is a rewarding experience and lets the skilled player win in fights which he would loose if fought in a more static way (just letting onager and archers fire at each other). At the same time the economic gameplay elements aren't too plain either (as I find them to be in a starcraft or warcraft) and exploration of the map for new resources as well as thoughtfull placement of buildings are always rewarded. All in all the Gameplay follows the "easy to learn, hard to master" principle, whats always a good thing, regardless of genre and age of a game.
Campaigns
I personally love the campaigns although it could be nostalgia clouding my judgement. There has to be a certain amount of roleplay, imagination and will to explore to be going on (as well as a certain interest in history) to get immerged into the campaigns since their presentation and guidance fall short compared with warcraft or most other bigger RTS titles. It's basically a short narrative intro with text on a campaign specific background and narrator (over emphasising the accent hes supposed to speak). Ingame you get goals and mapinformation as text. Except of some triggers with unit spawns, short messages or tracking shots over some town or battlefield there's not happening much. But the goals and difficulty as well as the map design are great.
First HD Edition
Oh boy..... Now comes the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ part. This "HD" re-release of Aoe 2 sucked in every aspect as it came out. A big shitpile of bugs and subtle but stupid graphical changes (E.g. wrong animations for some units, changing the cliff-graphics to some ugly lowres picture of a bad 3D cliff or the farms to childish paint art). Nobody really needed animated water and I still don't understand the benefits of having the terrain being 3D with textures instead of the sprite terrain... looks exactly the same.
At that time I prefered playing the original Game with userpatch and/or "The Forgotten" mod which ran perfectly fine on any machine I have owned and also offered higher resolution and the biggest graphical plus in my opinion: More frames for unit animations. Something the HD edition never implemented despite all the addons and maybe never will.
"Single player mode now operates at 60fps instead of 20fps in v1.0c."
HD today
After all the patching and addons, Aoe 2 HD offers vast singleplayer content with many new civs and great campaigns. But after playing through all the SP content I tried to play multiplayer online (what I never did regularly in all the years I owned the game). It's totally ♥♥♥♥ed up. I really can't feel the difference to the technical issues the first release version had. It's laggy, the lobby buggs, out of syncs, bad pings of few guys ruin the experience for everybody, out of syncs, bad ranking system dropping you in with a 1600 ranking so if you're a total noob you have to get yourself stomped down to 13XX before having any chance (and therefore fun), and did I mention out of syncs?
If there happen to be the rare scenario of everybody having a good ping and the game doesn't go out of sync, the matches still suffer from the bad ranking system and the vast amount of brain-afk newbs playing games today. Seriously, as much as I want to like younger gamers, they often play careless and stupid. More diplomatic people call it "casual". There's no fault in that and the issue comes with the time consumption and focus on teamplay Aoe 2 requries: Having total ♥♥♥♥tards in your team isn't always obvious in the first 10-20 minutes of the game. So you build, survive or raid in the early game, applying the the micro and multitasking intensive pro tactics just to reach castle age and finally notice how derpy and utterly useless your team members play. Often the enemy came to the same conclusion scouting their bases and there comes the combined derp army of all the enemies to steamroll me. Even if I fight like a lion and punish them hard while going down, the ranking system doesn't honor that. Compared to other games, e.g. team based Shooters like Insurgency which let you respawn fast and always offer a comeback for individual players, in Aoe I wasted a big chunk of time for no reward without anything I could do to at least prevent my own dignity to be destroyed. Moving your base behind the brain-afk idiots of your team to at least have some meat-shield? Not how the game works. No team means no map control means no resources, and with the start base burned to ashes the economy is weakened too hard to get going again against multiple opponents.
Alternatives
The great voobly community. Personally I don't have the time or interest to become a good enough player to join their ranks, but it's certainly the most competetive way to play Aoe 2. And if you can live without some of the content of the two HD addons, picking up the classic AOE 2 + The Conquerors still offer many options:
- The Forgotten Mod -> The Forgotten before they bought the modders to co-develop the HD addon
- Userpatch -> I think what the voobly version basically uses. Many great fixes and upgrades like the mentioned 60FPS animations
- Age of Chivalry - Hegemony -> A nice total convertion, set in the time period Aoe 2 The Conquerors ends. All civs renewed (more than HD with African Kingdoms) and basically all Buildings and units reskinned and many new added.
- Game Ranger -> Tool to set up matches over the internet (I guess technically comparable to Hamachi but more comfort and with a server browser)
- Vast amount of community scenarios and campaigns as well as special multiplayer maps (e.g. tower defense or smoosh blood) -> Most of the content reaching the workshop was originally created in this community.
Conclusion and recommendations:
For me Aoe 2 is the old wise Wololo-priest of my gaming childhood and will always be a shiny milestone new RTS titles have to be checked against.
For people who played it back in the days or new folks who want to dig into the game:
-> For maximal singleplayer campaign experience: Get HD with all addons
-> For a stable and competetive multiplayer: Get the classic version and play on Voobly
-> For a great mix of SP, Coop and fun with friends: Get the classic version and keep it fresh and free of bugs with userpatch and total conversions. Play over GameRanger or Hamachi.
For todays "casual" folks
-> For a fast multiplayer experience: HD edition (+ addons if you need the civs) despite the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ stability and bad start-ranking, this offers the most careless derpists to play with and therefore the most casual multiplayer experience.
-> For oldschool singleplayer experience: HD with all addons for maximal content. If you're not sure how long you want to play it, get the HD edition without addons first. The addons don't change the classic campaigns in any way.

The Talos Principle is a very good puzzle game, framed by an interesting philosophical theme and wrapped up in very nice graphics and a beautiful soundtrack.
The story is told as you discover partially corrupted emails, blog posts, and time-capsule audio logs, slowly unravelling bits and pieces about who you are, what this place is and what happened to the world of man. This was very well done and I enjoyed every snippet, with the time capsules being my personal highlight of every level (Compliments on the voice acting).
I definitely liked the puzzles in general, while I have to say I vastly preferred the Sigils to the Stars (which are semi-optional). With the sigils, there's always a solution, all the pieces are there for you to put in order. For some, the solution may be instantly apparent, while the more challenging ones will probably baffle you for a moment, but guides should never be necessary here.
The same cannot be said for the stars. Some of these will require the consultation of a guide. That is unless you search every dark corner of the map for a hidden switch or passage and randomly aim at every cloud and tree, cause who knows where the connector you need may be hidden.
I guess I just prefer puzzles where I am given all the pieces, as opposed to the manufacturer having hidden one in a secret compartment in the box.
The philosophical aspect is a bit over-hyped, in my opinion, and if it weren't for this hype, I wouldn't feel the need to put things into perspective, but here we are. My goal is to keep you from going into the game with unreasonably high expectations, as mine were.
Yes, Croteam did a great job of creating an interesting framework out of it, but the subject matter (Is a true AI a person, and what does a person make?) is nothing new or groundbreaking. It may not have been examined in-depth before in any games I can think of, but certainly in film and literature (and around bar tables).
Yes, some of the questions the player is presented with are thought-provoking, but then the answer you would actually give is often not among the options. I know this is due to the limitations of the medium and I can't imagine anyone else could have done a much better job of it, but to be able to lead truly deep philosophical conversations with a computer terminal in a game, we'll have to wait for the development of an actual AI. And wouldn't that be lovely, to have a meaningful conversation about whether or not an AI can be considered a person... with an actual, true AI!... in a video game... for our entertainment.
Once again, I really enjoyed playing The Talos Principle. So should you, seriously.

This game was an absolute gem to play and deserves a place on everyone's bucket list.  Combining Portal-esque puzzle mechanics with deep philosophical themes was a brilliant move on Croteam's part and it made for a video game experience unlike any other.  The puzzles are very fun to solve and never once did I feel overly frustrated by any unfair game design.  Even the hard-to-obtain bonus secrets are cleverly hidden as intriguing challenges, encouraging out of the box thinking in a variety of unexpected ways.
The story is mainly told through text and audio logs left behind throughout the world, letting you slowly uncover the truth of those before you.  As I progressed through the game, I was constantly pondering the nature of being human, and hearing godly voice of Elohim affirm or deny my beliefs was an wondrous experience.  Though the character I controlled was a robot, I found the story to be astonishingly human, making for one of the greatest video game narratives I have ever experienced.
Did I mention the graphics and art design are oh-so-goddamn gorgeous?  Also, I was able to run the game smoothly on my mediocre laptop and still maintain great visual quality.

In terms of structure it reminds me of Portal (you solve puzzles and they're each contained in their own room) but in atmosphere it reminds me much more of Myst. Alone and isolated, you have just the occasional mysterious voice or text program to communicate with. Everything else are scraps of the past you have to find and piece together which helps build into the atmosphere of exploring not just ruins but history. It's a game about making you think, not just about how to solve puzzles but about the very essence of existence.
Some of the puzzles are frustratingly difficult because of the lack of any explanation of the puzzle tools and finding most of the gold stars are just unfair, with a good number of them relying less on logic and more on hiding the puzzle pieces under the sofa where you'll never find them. That said, the gold stars are optional (except for us OCD 100%ers) and I rarely ran into a manadory puzzle I couldn't solve. I just needed to leave it for awhile and come back later with a fresh perspective. Part of it is probably because I read a few reviews of the games that mentioned a few of the quirkier mechanics that would be hard to figure out on your own.
Overall, I greatly enjoyed the story and the puzzles and would recommend it to anyone looking for a thoughtful, slow-paced, thinking game with a great atmosphere.

"Yet Another Zombie Defense" is a co-op game where you and your friends have to kill zombies on a small map, that is the only point ... but that is pretty fun ! Up to 4 players can fight together, using a man, a girl or a member of the SWAT (the only difference is the skin, nothing else).
There are two modes.
The first one is the defense mode. You have to survive waves of zombies over and over until the end of your lives. Each time you kill a zombie, you get some dollars plus from time to time money, medic kit (enables your team to recevor health) or ammo (you need to have at least one weapon to get ammo, that does not take into account the pistol that you have at the beginning because you have infinite ammo for this specific weapon). After each wave, you recover your health but the zombies get stronger : they will deal more damage to you if they bite you, they will be faster and you will need more and more hits to kill them.
In order to survive, you are able and you have to use your money between each wave. You can buy different weapons (rifles, shotgun, flame thrower, tesla, rocket launcher, laser, ...), but always remember to have enough ammo tu use them ! Tip : I think the best way to go is to buy only one weapon so that, when a zombie drops ammo, you only get the adequate type of ammo. If you have two or more weapons, you are going to drop at random two types of ammo, and if you are looking for one specific kind, you might be unlucky and get the other one.
You can also buy barricades (wooden and steel) and auto-turrets and place them on the map, almost wherever you want within a medium circle from the center of the map. You can build up to 5 turrets, and for each of them, you have to buy and mount a weapon on it to get it active. Them, each time the turret shoots a zombie, it will use your ammo, so be carfeul with your stock ! The idea is to protect your turrets with barricades because zombies can destroy them, and since they are pretty expensive, you have to keep them alive.
Remember that only the host of the game can buy stuff and place items. You can ask for specific weapons, but the host has the final decision. I think that you should spend the first four or five waves killing the zombies with your pistol (which is free thanks to inifinite ammo), then you are likely to buy the weapon you like the most. There are also "sales !" : at random, between each wave, some items are going to be cheaper (-25% I guess), so you might want to wait if you are looking for a specific item and maybe get lucky after the next wave, unless you die ...
In the end, you have to get the highest score you can to get your name on the leaderboard.
The second mode is the endless night. As indicated, there is only one wave of zombie, but there is no end to it ! No money on this map, no barricade or even turret to build, you have to kill zombies with weapons. There is a lot of zombies and they can drop weapons : as soon as you pick one of them, you have to use it, you cannot get your previous weapon back (unless you drop it again). The aim is to survive as long as possible, so try to gather medic kits when you need one of them, and never stop running !
To conclude, this game is pretty fun, maybe it is lacking a little bit of content, but with two modes, Steam trading cards and 18 achievements to unlock (5 hours should be enough to get them all), it is worth its price, which is quite low currently :)

CONS:

- Little replay value despite a decent length story mode.

Please note: I've only played the main game. I don't have the Road to Gehenna DLC yet.
Folks that know me know that I have a... thing... for puzzles. So when the demo first came out for this, I grabbed it out of curiosity. And I grabbed it recently, when the opportunity presented itself. I was glad that my graphics card could handle it, because the worlds in this game are beautiful. There are plenty of things to get you ooohing and ahhing to the point where you might miss out on things here and there, whether it be something key to a puzzle, or one of the boatloads of easter eggs the devs put in this game.
But let's get to the nitty-gritty here: the puzzles. Plenty of free roaming areas within the puzzle rooms, much like what was done with the Portal series, and some bonus items can only be gotten with some interaction with different puzzle rooms. Each of the puzzle rooms has a sigil as its goal, which can be used with others to unlock different areas and different objects to be used in later sections. Outside of the free roaming ability, the game also uses the idea of building on pravious puzzles, so that you don't feel too overwhelmed. Still, some of these puzzles can turn into That One Level pretty quick.
The storyline you get from accessing terminals, throughout the levels, as well as getting into a pilosophical/spiritual argument with another AI. This made for a nice little twist.
Replay value? Well, it's mainly going to be for getting the rest of the achievements, and maybe the variants of the multiple endings. Or just seeing how well you can speed-run through it. But on the whole, this game was a nicely delivered package and certainly fun to explore. It gets an A.

The Talos Principle is a first person puzzle game that does an excellent job combining an immersive story and puzzle solving. I can confidently say it would be an epic (if not legendary) item in a MMO.
Main puzzles are closed areas with everything required to solve it is inside. There are also stars. Getting stars requires combinations of advanced puzzle solving and exploration. Stars are wild cards in my opinion in this game. Some people will love them and others will hate them. I am in haters group because I don't mind trying to solve a puzzle for hours, but spending hours trying just to find where a star is not for me. Note that, as I said before this is not necessarily a bad thing.
The game tells its story via consoles placed puzzle areas. Some consoles are in main areas, others hidden and requires some exploration. You can totally ignore them but doing so is definitely not recommended. Without the story, it becomes a classic solve-this-to-advance type puzzle game. As a result, game is best suited for people who like to read everything and check every corner.
Difficulty of the puzzles is just enough. They are easy enough not to make you rage quit, but hard enough to feel satisfied. At this point I need to point something. Some of the puzzles have extra things. It may be a gadget, a door or a laser receiver. They might be there to provide multiple solutions or I might have solved them differently. But in case they are there just to mess with your mind, I am saying that, keep your mind clear and don't focus on the goal door.
The game also has lovely scenery in almost every main puzzle area. I personally took some screenshots. It is nice to stop once in a while and relax. It also feels nice after a challenging puzzle.
Environment has high texture quality, objects are detailed
Usable objects snaps without a problem, there are no small unnecessary things that would get in the way.
Most puzzles provide just enough challenge.
If you play as intended, you feel how people felt and can empathize.
There are about 130 puzzles and lots of reading.
Few puzzle games actually have a story that makes solving the puzzles mean something.
This is a puzzle game so it is normal. Only reasons to replay are having the "Serious DLC" or getting the achievements. (Some people can challenge themselves to find "off the book" solutions for the puzzles, but I don't consider it a factor)
Some puzzles are big, and makes you to run from one end to another end several times. You solve the puzzle in 30 seconds but spend 5 minutes to finish it.
The Talos Principle gets a definite recommendation. It is best suited for people who like to read everything and check every corner in addition to solving puzzles.

Game is dead in 2016. Unless you are playing peak hours, you are fighting the same 20 aimbotters.

This update was supposedly to help new players by increasing the time to kill in a vehicle vs vehicle battle and to reduce the farming of infantry players by vehicles. If those were the updates' goals then it has failed miserably. While the amount of players actually playing the game during peak hours has increased, the actual fights still devolve into vehicle columns farming infantry. Also changed were the various ranks of armor upgrades which now give 90% of effictive resistance at rank one versus previous rank 5 upgrades, making a brand new player 90% as effective as someone who has maxed out all of their suit upgrades. While this is also a step in the right direction, this does not solve the core issue of vehicle lines farming infantry fights. Overall the last update is the last gasp of a dying game whose updates have come too little too late.

Ahh.. The New Order.. After the success which was the Return To Castle Wolfenstein, fans were waiting 8 years for another Wolfenstein, which turned out to be good, which was it's biggest issue. It was just "good", a decent FPS shooter, but without the feeling and climat of the 2001's RTCW. 5 years after, in 2014 we got Wolfenstein: The New Order. Bethesda, Machine Games and id, promised, that the new Wolf, will stand up to the level of it's 13-year old brother. But is it actually worth to be called "RTCW's heir"?
HOLY F*CKING YES! Where should I start? The plot. The beginning takes place during WWII, which should not be a surprise to anyone. Like in previous games, you play as a B.J. Blazkowicz, once again with a goal to finally kill "Deathshead" Unfortunately the assault on his fortress ends up with a failure, you lose your squad and find out that 20 years passed by and nazis has taken the control over the world! It is your job to at least try, to do something about it, if it's still possible that is.
During the game, you'll visit various places, even the concentration camp in which you can experience the particle of suffering from people that are held there. You can hear them talking about their families, how they got seperated from each other, etc. In RTCW you had castles, secret laboratories, catacombs, etc. and if you actually thought you saw everything, and it can't go further than that, then bruh... you haven't seen anything yet.
The game looks and plays great, even on my crappy PC, with the lowest details it looked really good and still gave me a lot of fun.
When it comes to music, it's really good, but to me, there's only one track that truly stands out. Unfortunatelly it plays once and very late into the game, but when it plays, man.... Chills all the way down the spine. You did a great job with it, Mr. Gordon. Hats off.
Someties you get to choose the way of killing the nazis, that is when the "signal detected" message appers in the upper-right corner. It means that there are commanders around which can call for support if they find you, you can eliminate them one-by-one and be sneaky-peaky, or just say BRING IT ♥♥♥♥♥! Rush forward and vaporize everything that breathes. Personally, I recommend the first way in later stages, especially on higher difficulty settings. Overall when it comes to gameplay there's nothing wrong about it and your weapons can be upgraded too (f.e. your assault rifle can shoot rockets!).
But of course there always have to be some flaws, here's no exception. It took me 15 hours to beat the game on "Bring em' on" difficulty, which seems preety short to me, also some of the later stages follow the similar scheme. Kill nazis in a big hall or something like that, move through corridors and tunnels, kill nazis, move through tunnels and repeat till the end. The game also lacks bosses, there are 3, maybe 4 in total, which wouldn't be bad, RTCW had the similar amount of bosses, but here, they all appear near the end! I almost started thinking that there may be no bosses at all! Who doesn't like to take down the giant mecha and make some noise from time to time? The worst thing about this game is the ending, the motherf**king ending which just begs to be different, and i don't understand why it ends in such a way, it could easily be different, why they decided to put out something like this, I have no god damn idea...
*SPOILER WARNING* If you haven't beaten the 15th chapter - don't uncover the text below!
To sum up, I'd love to give this game 10/10, but I can't, instead I have to give it 9/10 because of the flaws I've mentioned above and the price this game's asking for. 50 Euro is too much in my opinion, so just wait for the discout and then pick it, you won't regret it. I f*cking recommend this game to everyone, despite some flaws it's still an amazing game that will blow your balls, or boobs. And I can see why TB picked it as "The game of 2014."

I recommend the game, but I recommend it with the note that it may not be for everone, especially if you don't like losing to a dice roll.
Pros:
The game is a fairly sophisticated and fun colony-survival game. You collonist each have different personalities and skills which makes planning your colony and its activities and interesting challenge. The game is in many ways similar to Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria and the like, and challenges you to efficient build colonies, complete with air-coonditioners and automatic defense turrets.
Cons:
While the game is challenging on its own, at least to a new player, it also employs a generous amount of 'fake difficulty'. By this I mean random events which can screw over any player no matter how prepared or smart they play the game. For example, a solar eclipse can shut off your defences right in the middle of an invasion by dozens of tribal warriors giving a colony little chance to repell the invaders.

‘Max Payne 3’ is a highly stylized, cinematic, third-person shooter that is in many ways a throwback to the visceral, brutally violent, crime genre popularized by the likes of Pacino’s ‘Scarface’, or the more recent ‘Tropa de Elite’. A brooding background score, well crafted cut-scenes interspersed with ‘slow-motion’ action sequences, and ultra-violence personified make this a title that will well please its target audience.
Released by Rockstar Games in 2012, ‘Max Payne 3’ is the final installment in a trilogy of games which began with the cult-classic ‘Max Payne’ in 2001, and ‘Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne’ in 2003. Now nearly a decade later, Max, an ex-NYPD police officer, finds himself washed up, out of work, addicted to meds, staring down the bottom of a bottle, and taking a job as head of security to a powerful real estate tycoon in Sao Paulo, Brazil. The campaign is a dark sordid journey of betrayal, revenge and murder winding through the twisted underbelly of inner-city Sao Paolo and its favelas. As with most Rockstar games, the background setting is the real star here - with considerable effort clearly expended in replicating the vibe and authenticity of wealth, corruption and gang-warfare in Brazil’s second city.
Well conceived cut-scenes deftly transition into a fairly standard third-person shooter with a multitude of weapons, melee attacks and explosive devices at your disposal. Gameplay is fast, smooth and fluid and the standout feature of all the ‘Max Payne’ games – “Bullet-Time” – is well represented here in all its slo-motion, headshot, blood-spraying glory. It is usable in both Regular (slowing down time) and ‘Shoot-Dodge’ forms wherein you can leap in slo-mo in any direction across furniture, down stairwells, across rooftops taking down adversaries in cinematic fashion. A departure from the run-n-gun gameplay of the earlier titles, a newly introduced and quite serviceable cover system also adds a tactical element to gameplay to counteract the scores of hostiles that converge on your position as you progress. Beyond the main campaign, the game also features a strong multiplayer component – with both competitive and cooperative gameplay options - and expandable with 4 DLC packages (each with 4 MP maps, weapons and upgrades). K&M and Controller are both well optimized, and graphics, lighting and sound are excellent overall as well.
In considering its shortcomings – perhaps the game’s biggest flaw is its inescapable linearity, and the lack of any real variation in gameplay as you move from one (albeit gorgeous) shooting gallery to the next. Lengthy and unskippable cutscenes (when you want or need to replay a section), an uneven difficulty curve, an oppressive 30+ Gig install requirement, limited replayability and the need for ‘always on’ Rockstar Social Club 3rd Party-DRM blemish an otherwise great title.
‘Max Payne 3’ is a gripping, action-packed, brutally violent shooter with phenomenal gun-play, slick visuals and a great storyline. By almost any measure, this is an impressive title and ultimately a great example of a ‘shooter’ done right – but! as a ‘Rockstar’ game (specifically, the folks responsible for genre- and industry- redefining works like ‘Grand Theft Auto’ and ‘Red Dead Redemption’) – you, as I, might be left feeling a tad bit wanting of more innovation or variation in gameplay, by the end. Generally, Very Well Recommended! Rated (8.6/10)

Grimly obsessed with its' own brand of sun-kissed hyperviolence, Max Payne 3 is about as vacuous and as shallow as some of the people the eponymous character is trying to protect.
★★☆☆☆
With both wife and daughter dead and buried, our titular lead finds himself in the employ of a rich Brazilian family with ties to the seedy underworld of Sao Paulo, heavily armed and even more heavily drunk. As an ex-cop-turned-private-security Max is charged with protecting the Branco family, although quite why anyone would want to protect such a flakey band of character stereotypes is largely unclear at first hand. There's nothing special about the individual portrayals of these characters - Rodrigo, the rich big brother with a trophy wife, Victor, the conniving politician, and the insufferably irritating and gaudy Marcelo, but the foundation of a unsettled and troubled family is set, and for the first two acts, feels fairly credible, even if their own arc ends up disappointing and underdeveloped.
Underdeveloped, too, is a word worthy of describing what exactly you *do* in Max Payne 3, as you'll start the opening sequences as you mean to go on for the next 9 hours: shooting a whole bunch of guys, watching one of the well-directed cutscenes before entering another room where you shoot.. a new bunch of guys. And so the cycle continues. Once you've headshotted your way through the first few waves, you've pretty much seen all the gameplay Max Payne 3 has to offer. There are brief moments of particular showmanship, though scripted, are enough of a change of pace so as to not keep you from getting all too bored from the tedium of wave after wave of identikit gang members and paramilitary squads. These scripted bullet time set pieces look great, too - as does the entire experience, more colourful and exaggerated than previous games.
The non-scripted usage of bullet time works less well, with an introduced cover mechanic taking my own personal favour after several failed attempts at diving my way through encounters. There are exceptions, of course. One location early in the game has you at the top of a soccer stadium seating area, and it's satisfying to dive down to the lower sections, cleanly and precisely knocking off targets as you go. However, I never really felt there were enough variations in encounter design for me to be able to really pull off some of the cool, slow-motion dives I really wanted to. On more than one occasion I found myself trying to leap through a glass door or similar, only for Max to hit it at an awkward angle, thus snapping me out of the experience and left me resorting to sitting behind cover all too often instead of trying exciting ways to use the bullet time I had left.
Story-wise, Max Payne 3 never really goes through the gears so much as it plunges from first into 5th, eschewing the idea of a progressive narrative and falling back on grudge - and grungy - tropes. At times, there are glimmers of hope: the forays into Max's introduction to Brazil are well realised and shed some light on his relationship with his work partner-turned-friend Passos, but are all too brief and ultimately stifled by the same simple gameplay you've been grinding through. Sao Paulo itself is a beautiful host to the graphic and overindulgent shoot-outs, and with a heady variety of locations, too, from the dirty streets of the favellas, to the anaemic, well-polished floors of the Branco estate.
In the end, Max Payne 3 just about covers its' cracks with enough flashy gunplay and a Brazilian sun tan that the larger events of the plot soon wash over, though ultimately, the experience falls short of anything memorable.

I would have expected a game that came almost out of nowhere to be one of the best of the year, but here you have it: The Talos Principle. This game fits neatly into the niche of esoteric adventure puzzler with its classical landscapes, mind contorting puzzles, and philosophical discourse. Unlike others of its kind, The Talos Principle doesn't just play at esotericism like a freshmen after their first philosophy 101 course. While you may not come away from The Talos Principle any wiser, the subjects being discussed are done so in a manner befitting a developer who is flexing their philosophy degree or who has at least done their homework. The result is a game that actually feels smart instead of just feeling like it wants to be smart.
The puzzles are handled excellently in a style similar to portal, with a gentle, but significant learning curve leading up to the late game brain benders. While the puzzle locales are generally horizontal mazes or collections of rooms, the variety of tools to be used in solving them and the fact that they are rolled out over time keeps things interesting till the end.
Beyond the philosophical discourse present on several fronts in the game, the writing itself is equally superb and offers a narrative adventure-style discovery experience, adding another dimension to the game.
If you're a fan of Portal 1/2, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Mind: The Path to Thalamus, or The Swapper, then you can probably find something to like here. So far it's one of the year's best.

I've been playing games for about 25 years, and this game remains the best architecting/engineering game I've played to date.  It uses elements from Dwarf Fortress, the Sims, Tower Defense, and SimCity (among others), and has fantastic depth without being overwhelming.  There is a learning curve (perhaps it's biggest downfall is a lack of decent tutorial), but once you see how all the pieces fit together, it leaves a lot to be explored and developed.  There is a metric heck-ton of customizability in how you play a particular runthrough (especially with the new scenario system), the AI is well-polished, and just enough RNG to keep things from becoming repetitive or formulaic.  I'm probably 40 hours of gameplay in and am still learning more about how the pieces of the game relate to one another.

An astoundingly complex and deep game that suffers from a bit of early game difficulties.
Please don't misunderstand me, this is one of my favourite games of the decade - before playing on Steam, I've played every Alpha adding up to hundreds of hours. If you're willing to put in some effort, the rewards of watching your little ♥♥♥♥ed up ant farm of colonists is exceptionally rewarding.
But I would be remiss if I didn't point out how excruciatingly difficult it is to learn the early game of RimWorld. You start with very little (in the base version) and have to learn by constant trial and error what's necessary to survive past the first winter. "Oh, I should probably dispense nutrient paste until I have a way to easily replenish stocks. And I'll need a lot of tuques and parkas if I want to get work done during the winter. And don't skimp on cleaning and hailing, or else you'll find a lot of carcasses go to waste and people go insane from their sorry surroundings (?!)."
But I suppose that's also part of its charm, if you're willing to learn the hard lessons the game teaches you.
Overall, this game is worth the praise by leaps and miles, but it still needs some fine tuning.
Even if it is in EA its still the best milsim shooters out there, it also has a great community with devs who are very involved with the players.

All in, I had a great time playing it and highly recommend other FPS fans get it.

You start with very little (in the base version) and have to learn by constant trial and error what's necessary to survive past the first winter. "Oh, I should probably dispense nutrient paste until I have a way to easily replenish stocks. And I'll need a lot of tuques and parkas if I want to get work done during the winter. Overall, this game is worth the praise by leaps and miles, but it still needs some fine tuning.

I bought this game because I had a 90% off voucher and I knew for a fact that I'd be able to sell the trading cards I got from the game for more than I'd paid for it. For the price I paid for it, I think this game was worth it, but for full price I'm not sure I would have bought it.
The game feels like a student project, albeit a good one. The whole thing feels about as barebones as you can get, three playable character models, a handful of zombies, and a single map which consists entirely of grey concrete wasteland and a lamppost which makes the whole ordeal feel like some bizarre dystopian Narnia fanfiction. Zombies just sort of pop into existence at the sides of the map and are almost completely harmless until about night six, by which point they've lost any feeling that they might pose a threat. In fact, there barely ever feels like there's any sort of tension, with weapons barely ever running out of ammo due to frequent drops (on many occasions I found myself gaining more ammo than I was using), health drops and free refills left little fear of death until around night nine where, unless I boxed myself into a 5X5 box with four turrets, I inevitably got outran by the sizeable crowd of Zombies and killed. In a harder or longer game this might feel rather punishing, but here I could breeze through the first six rounds on my first try without even buying anything, so it just felt boring. The infinite night mode was better for me due to its faster pace, but it was still pretty generic. Even the game characters seemed bored, with both zombies and players alike barely reacting to damage. This combined with the awful gun sound effects made the weapons feel like toys; I was genuinely amused to find that the shotgun sounded like a Nerf gun (though it actually shot bullets like a real shotgun, which is a rarity in games), and the flamethrower ended up feeling more like a hairdryer than anything else. Plus there was some bizarre zombie behaviour, with them stopping whenever they attacked even if the player was still moving away from them, with the attack visibly missing and yet still causing damage. Zombies also had bizarre AI at times, attacking barriers or turrets rather than the player, or ignoring gaps in they could easily flood through to trap the player.
However, I did feel that this game has a spark of potential: I'd love to see the devs really go forward with the self-awareness shown in the title and closing "we hate DLC as much as you do" message, even if in the game's current state those are the only signs that this is anything but yet another Zombie game; I loved the way that you actually mounted your weaponry on the turrets rather than the several types of turret that most games would offer, despite it being a bit irritating to set up due to the clunky choice to only let you buy weapons when you didn't own one; and I liked the sale mechanic, even if it was a pain to see what was on sale due to the badly designed shop UI. And, in spite of my issues with it, I still wanted to keep playing until I'd unlocked everything. With a few tweaks and improvements, this would be well worth the asking price but in its current state it's just mediocre. If you want to play this, wait for a sale. Kind of makes me wish Steam reviews had a less binary review system.

It pains me to say/write it, but I definitely cannot recommend this game. It is not good.
Avoid if you're feeling nostalgia and want some old-school action. The game does not offer it.
SHORT VERSION:
Recommendation: Avoid. Watch cutscenes on youtube, if you want to watch cinematics ingame, set it on easy and complete. Definitely avoid, if you want some old-school shooting action, there's none of it. Bad combat AI, bland levels, frustrating save system and ridiculous story, that only starts picking up 1 hour before the game ends. That is definitely not worth 11 hours before that.
LONG VERSION:
The most annoying thing here is that developers actually tried very hard to make a great title, yet failed. They spent a lot of effort making alternative reality world ("where nazi won the war"), and went even as far as re-imaginining some popular songs from 1960 - making versions of those songs for their world. Concept art also loooks fairly good.
So... why is that a negative review?
Although someone put a lot of love into project, that did not result in proper product.
Combat mechanics and actual gameplay do not live up to expectations. Save system is furstrating, level design is bland most of the time and story is ridiculous and hard to believe most of the game.
I played most of the ID software titles (Quake 1/2/3/4, Doom 1/2/3, Couple of WWII games, return of castle of wolfenstein, Rage) most of them are superior to this.
Combat:
Combat mechanics in this game are incredibly weak. For example, there is stealth mode, and patrolling guards occasionally ignore you in plain sight, walk over corpses of their  fallen comrades and thoughtfully stare into windows in rooms full of dead guard dogs and slaughtered germans. No reaction whatsoever. That is the worst stealth AI I can remember.
In active battle, enemies are bullet sponges. The walk toward your position, jump out of the doors into line of fire and just keep firing. They do attempt to dodge and take cover, but generally it is just getting enough bullets into them. This is worse than RAGE where combat was spectacular.  Surprisingly, when they DO spot you their they all turn into snipers and can shoot you in the head with full auto fire from very large distances.
That results in incredibly boring experience, most of the time you're just aiming at some faraway muzzleflash hopefully hitting that spot that is probably the head. That does not compare, say, to original Doom, where combat was close and personal and involved firing shotgun straight into someone's face. It is worse than RAGE, where enemies could try to parcour over, jump roll and had some kind of personality. Here, you just keep feeding nazi with bullets. Or maybe you're feeding the same nazi with bullets because they all look similar.
If you do increase difficulty, they don't get smarter, they just require more bullets and deal more damage.
Enemies also occasionally spawn right behind you from previously checked doors.
By the way, the game does not let you manually save. Saves are checkpoing based, so if you just killed 3 robots and 50 people then got killed by stray bullet because you made a mistake, you'll have to do it all over again.
Annoying attack dogs start unescapable quicktime event when they jump at you. If there is "ally" involved (which thankfully doesn't happen often), the ally often will push you into line of fire with glee.
There's "skill tree", and there are kinda sorta cover and stealth mechanics, but they are not really fun, are not really interesting and are not very useful. Not sure why they bothered even adding those.
There are absolutely NO fun weapons in the game. Yes, you can dual-wield two assault rifles, but you'll run out of ammo in 30 second. There is double-barreled shotgun, but compared to "death to everything in front of you" version of it in original Doom, it is unsatisfying. Every weapon feels more or less similar, does not affect your playstyle much.
VISUALS:
The game looks surprisingly bad and bland most of the time. It would've been much better if it was even remotely comparable to its concept art, but apparently something went wrong. While level geometry resembles concept art fairly well, the lighting is off, and in outdoor scenes it does not look like the game from 2014. I'm not a person to complain about graphics usually, but that was incredibly noticeable in this case. At the very first level I frankly was very surprised how bad it is. It did get better in the very last level, but before that...
Most of the levels are fairly uninspired and boring, and resemble dozens of other games. I've seen it all before elsewhere. I saw it in FEAR, in Blood Rayne, in No One Lives Forever 2, in Painkiller and in many many many other games. No level is original here, it was all done before.
STORY *minor spoilers*:
Oh, boy... devs tried to go cinematic route. Apparently they got kinda jealous of Witcher in the process and added two "special scenes" that frankly come out of the blue and don't add much to the narrative. There's area that greatly resembles "civilian hub" zone I saw in Metro2033, so it looks like they tried that too. The area somehow resembles borderlands at the same time, but its only purpose is to make you feel sorry for the horrible state of the world and find missing toys for people. Yep, you read that right. The whole story will leave you in permanent facepalm for the most of the time if you know anything about history. Apparently small number of guys can survive "fighting" nazis for 14 years right under their nose despite global surveillance and army of robots. Seriously?
Halfway of the game Blazcowic apparently gets bored and starts musing over childhood events and saying "thoughtful" stuff. It doesn't add much to the game, but it is surely annoying. Then they start reading you diaries over the radio. Sigh.
By the end of the game once you lived through ALL the absolutely ridiculous story events. It suddenly starts getting better but the game ends very soon after that. Occasionally they manage hit the spot with their short letters and that diary they insist on adding to your journal for the last X hours of game, but when that happens the game just becomes depressing in a bad sense.
SOUND:
I do not remember anything about sound for the most of the game, but at its very end they fired heavy artillery and used all the good tunes they have. Music at the end of game is good. Before that... I don't really remember any of it.
BOTTOM LINE:
If you're looking for story, it'll be probably faster to just watch it on youtube or just set game on easy and complete it.
If you're looking to shoot stuff, then pretty much every shooter will be better choice. I would recommend Return to the Castle of Wolfenstein, if you really want to shoot more nazis. It has been years since I played it, but in the years when there was endless stream of "another WWII shooter"s, that game was one of the best, despite being set in fictional world.  There's also Blood Rayne 1, Painkiller Black Edition, and Original Doom 1 and 2, and original Quake, if you can handle "old" graphics.
This game made me think that perhaps it is time to give up on gaming industry and stop hoping that they'll ever produce FPS that could be as much fun as original shooters when I played years ago. Perhaps people forgot that it is not about cinematics and cutscenes but about killing stuff and having fun first.

Yet ANOTHER zombie defense is a decent entry in the zombie/survival genre despite the over-saturation of zombie games in recent years.
Choosing one of three characters, you must survive for as long as possible by constructing and buying resources by day and defending by night either alone, or with friends and strangers up to four players.
The game presents you with an assortment of weapons and accessories to aid you in your zombie slaughter. Ideally in zombie shooters the most expensive weapon is the most effective. That concept is no different on Yet Another Zombie Defense: Expensive = Effective. You can either buy weapons during day break at full price, or wait for a discounted sale to hit in later days. You will burn through money fast; therefore sales provide you with an option to cash in on low-price gear. You can effectively create your own “safe zone” through the use of auto-turrets and two variants of palisade walls: Wood and steel - the latter being more durable to zombie attacks. You can have all sorts of combinations, though their effectiveness will be tested in combat.
The online portion works just as well as the single player with a drop in/drop out feature. I had some lag drops here and there, even during my own hosted lobbies though not too often that would ruin the overall experience. Players can communicate via the in-game chat box and host is able to kick players who are otherwise trolling or lack contribution. From the several games I played the community is rather active, friendly and helpful which is a major plus.
The current offering is satisfying, though for a limited time. The game lacks weapon/fortification upgrades and variation in terms of maps. Once you breach wave 20 you will stop and question whether it is possible to progress any further as zombies become ridiculously over-powered in terms of speed, durability and damage. Future updates are promised by the developer (most recent being 14 August 2014) possibly free of charge, therefore it would be nice to introduce additional features to build on the current game.
I only played this game with an Xbox controller, therefore cannot comment on the functionality of keyboard and mouse. Xbox controls handled well without any problems.
Aesthetically nothing impressive. The character and zombie models are almost identical to those in Garry’s Mod. Delivers an entertaining game of mindless zombie killing.
Between 4-5 different tracks; nothing major in terms of variety. Some sound effects were off-sync – i.e weapon shots and zombie growls.
A fun but limited zombie shooter with a not-so-ridiculous price tag. In dire need of additional content to bolster its current offerings.
+Two modes which can be played alone or co-op + supported by leaderboards.
+Nice assortment of weapons and tools to change gameplay.
+Ridiculously cheap.
+Developer is opposed to the idea of charging players for additional content (DLC).
-In dire need of additional content – especially map variations.
-Unexplainable lag in single player and online.
-Some sound effects off-sync.
This game will test your head and your mind and your brain too.

This isn't a game... it's a movie in which you get to do the shooty bits.
Seriously, it's about 60% cut-scenes to 40% gameplay. Whether that's a good thing or not depends on your patience, and if you really want to sit through the hours of storyline which this game boasts. I was surprised that it needed 35Gb to install, initially, but now I'm not; much of that is evidently the mass of pre-rendered scenes required for the "cinematic experience".
So, is the heavily detailed story any good? I think it has its strong points, though it does drag at times. The voice acting was very good, but this game is very different to the earlier
and
. No longer set in the dark underworld of New York, nor in grimy back streets and slums,
is notably brighter, even if Max's personal story aims to be dark and morbid. With the story moving from the present to past events, the game does use material from earlier in the series to keep us in touch with the character and his tragic past.
The graphics are sweet, the sound good. Gameplay is engaging, though not overly difficult; enemy AI can often be clever but regularly just stays behind cover allowing you to take aim and pop it as soon as it pokes its head up. There isn't much in the way of sneaking around so trying to be stealthy is a waste of time – just get in there and fight. Good range of hand guns, uzis and rifles, plus the odd grenade launcher available. Maps are decent, offering plenty of cover. As with earlier
games, this has very linear design, follows a pre-determined path, leads to the same goals and conclusions. Personally, I don't see much in terms of replayability.
It's worth playing, as are all the games in the series. Just don't expect to be "playing" so much as "watching".

Been supporting this for about 2 years, great to finally see it on steam! These devs are phenomenal the amount of changes I've watch RimWorld go through is mind boggling, it's so far from the game I first played in 2014, and every step of the way it's been non stop improvements. These guys don't mess around!
As for gameplay, this is a game for EVERYONE. Casual gamer? No problem, relax and build your base with an occasional interruption of a small invasion or alien attack. Looking for a challenge? Turn up the difficulty and prepare to spend every week in game fixing yourself up from the last attack, only to be hit again by the time you finish fixing up.
If you like roleplaying there's an endless world with amazing stories to be had, the characters are all unique and as are their interactions with one another, and how they handle the environments and events around them.
If you're more like me and just like to build a huge colony and not worry about the lives of the characters - go right ahead! They are yours and will do your bidding (within reason), just keep them relatively happy and you'll have yourself a massive compound with an unstoppable army in no time.
Well, that's about all I have for right now. This game is 100% worth the money, I'd highly recommend looking into it if you haven't already, I've had hundreds of hours of fun adventures on this game and it's never been the same twice. I look forward for many more adventures in the future!

I have just around 6 hours and I have decided to tab out of my game to write this review on why i believe you should buy this gmae. The following harrowing tale has just taken place in the space of about 15 minutes irl time and nothing i am about to recount has been made up. It has all just unfolded in front of my eyes and i just had to share the experience before i forget all the minor details.
It is the 6th of summer. After being banished from their previous tribe this band of plucky cavemen and women set out to start a new.
After a month of toil and food all but run out. Today is the day of the big harvest, at least, it was supposed to be.
It is a chilly morning. 3 degrees c but the sun has risen and its warming up niceley. Everyone is ready to take in the harvest when V3trox spies some raiders to the north. Fortunatley we have prepared for this. The tribe is all skilled in the use of bows and our recent addition "toad" has been working hard to equip everyone with a bow.
V3trox calls the whole tribe to arms but leaves toad behind as she is an outsider and has no place fighting for the tribe and is left to perform the cleaning duties.

So, played thru once and am running it again.  PC version.
The game is what it is - a first person shooter.  If you're looking for more than that, you're going to be disappointed.  The graphics are good, the story gives you an excuse to kill Nazis.
The controls are horrible.  Fortunately, there are very few places where you need to run-and-slide.  Even so - pushing three buttons with your left hand (W, left shift and left crtl)?  Who thought this was a good idea?  Most of the controls are your basic WASD and mouse combos.  For times when you need to contort your fingers to lean and sneak, etc, you almost always have time to look at the keyboard first and plan it out.
Maps are linear.  There are only one or two ways, at most, to get from point A to point B.  The fact that the maps are linear doesn't bother me, but it might some people.
You start each chapter with no weapons.  Not a big deal, since you typically get them all back rather quickly, but still.  Most FPS you get to keep what you find.  Here, you have to keep finding the same weapons over and over.
You don't get to make your own saves.  You reach checkpoints, and the game saves for you.
Graphics are *very* nice.  There is attention to detail that makes the graphics worth turning up.  Eyes look wet.  Dusty hallways have dust motes.  Lots of little things you can easily overlook, but make the overall experience realistic.
Exploring pays off.  Even with linear maps, there are lots of places to check out.  They typically don't move you forward toward your goal, but you can often find some of the harder to locate weapons tucked away in these places.
Very little jumping.  I *hate* jumping games.  I bought a FPS to shoot things, not jump around.  This game only has a couple of times you are required to jump.  TIP:  Don't dual wield while jumping.  Hold a single knife and you'll jump further.
Sneaking is pretty easy.  Apparently Nazis aren't that observant.  There are times when you can clear an entire room using just your knife and a bunch of take-downs.
I know checkpoints is listed as a con, but the developers put some thought into when they happen.  You typically get a chaeckpoint right before a hard room, or a boss.  The repetition is there, but not as bad as some other games.
If you're looking for a shooter, this fits the bill.  Lots of shooting, not a lot of story to get in the way.  Advanced moves (sprint/slide, lean around corners, etc.) is awkward, but fortunately not necessary most of the time.  Love the "Easter Egg" - you get to play the original Wolfenstein in a dream sequence.  Linear maps.
If all you wants to do is shoot stuff, this fits the bill.

This game gives you immersive graphics, sounds, and communication.  If you're coming from Call of Duty, Battlefield, or other "military shooters", you will be in for a learning curve.
Communication and teamwork is a must.  If you are part of a squad and stray from your squad with your own personal agenda then you hinder the ability of your squad.  If you see enemies and fail to report them to your squad then your squad could be quickly eliminated.  If you're a squad leader and fail to communicate and strategize with other squad leaders, then your whole team will suffer.  This is a tactical squad based game. Any lone wolf or heroic maneuvers are frowned upon.  If you want to be the squad to steal the glory and rush an objective, leaving a gap between your lines, then you and your other team squads will be flanked.  Stop. Plan. Communicate.

This game is bad, really really bad. Bad to the point where I'm having difficulty understanding the praise it received. Were these reviewers paid off? I don't know.
I've played the first two games and I understand that a bad poetry narration is part of the package, but those games were meant to be sort of noir comic books. This game on the other hand, I don't really know what it is going for aesthetically.
There is weird blurring vision and weird colorful effects that fade in and out of scenes. Occasionally, lines of dialogue will have selected words appear as text on the screen to provide emphasis. Why these words? I don't know, it almost feels like the words were selected at random because the emphasis adds nothing to the scene. I assume the blurry/colorful effects have to do with our protagonist being a drunk that abuses pain killers but it isn't aesthetically challenging in a way that is fun or interesting, just nauseating, which may be contextually appropriate but doesn't provide an experience I see much of a point of putting myself through.
The rhythm of the game this
1. cutscene with blurry/colorful effects and bad narration.
2. shooting gallery style gameplay.
3. repeat
The shooting isn't particularly fun and it is so often broken up by long cinematic sequences that I never found myself getting invested in the experience I was having. It's like reading a bad book and having to turn the pages very slowly, but I'm not sure which part is the reading and which part is the turning. I guess it doesn't matter since neither experience is really worthwhile.

I should probably preface this buy saying that is this my first 8th gen game so I won't be talking graphics. So, what can you expect from this game?
Awesome mechanics
Fantastic artistic direction
Great characters
Loads of polish and small details adding to this well realised world (alternate 1960s Beatles are amazing, and the enigma code breaking was wonderful tangential learning)
Is there anything for me to criticize: Yes:
I was shocked that a game with the scale and budget of a hollywood blockbuster would have such a poorly handled story. Locations in which you play take place all across the globe, and most of them are in sections of areas, meaning there isn't much world building/exploration which results in the main problem: cohesion. The plot explains where you're going and drops you off so quickly you don't get the feeling of traversing the face of the earth, leaving a schizophrenic feeling in the level design and colour pallet. A conversation will start in the rebel base and end in:
- London at night
- A Nazi concentration camp in the Fall
- A REKT bridge in the middle of the sea
- The moon… THE MOON! WHAT?
The constant jump cut story telling almost killed any investment in the plot and completely ruined the ending for me, leaving a very bitter taste in my mouth: after the climax, you have a cinematic that probably lasts a minute before the credits roll. THAT IS NOT HOW YOU CONCLUDE A 14 HOUR STORY, AND THE PRECEEDING CLIMAX WAS AMAZING BY COMPARISON!
I only point out this problem because everything else by comparison was beyond fantastic. What they fail at with the over arching plot, they make up for with the small details. Asside from a few level locations, I refuse to spoil anything else, but be aware, this game's storytelling really don't flow well at all. I guess the acid test is: “Would I ever replay this game from beginning to end?” and my answer is: probably not. I may comeback for some of the moments that made my jaw drop, but I'd be using the chapter select feature.
