Wolfenstein The New Order certainly is an enjoyable game. But it's got it's flaws and hiccups. I'll try and review it.
The game takes place in an alternative universe, where Nazi-Germany managed to obtain scientific secrets, won the 2nd world war, and eventually conquered the world. With their half-robot army and cruel regime, nobody dares to rise up against them anymore. You play Blaskovic, a soldier that somehow survived WW2 and is out to kill the man behind the Nazi war machine. The setting certainly is one of the better parts of this game in my opinion. Not only do I think it's fun to play around with alternative history, it's also done very well in this game. From the big lines to the small details, everything in the world makes it look like it's truly a worldwide nazi dominance. On top of that, some of the missions are incredibly fun. I don't think I'll forget the mission with the bridge of Gibraltar anytime soon!
The game plays as your average shooter. You've got different guns, cover systems and health packs. The gunplay is decent, with some guns feeling far better to play with than others. My personal favorite was the Assault rifle. That said, there wasn't an overly big amount of different weapons. You had your pistols, assault rifle, shotgun, heavy rifle and the occasional two hander. You can also chose to 'akimbo' (dual wield) your weapons, but that results in not being able to use cover. Sadly, there wasn't a lot of variation per weapon category. Throughout the entire game, I only came across two different assault rifles. That said, the energy powered weapons look nice and are great to fire. Their recharge mechanic is also a nice feature, so no real complaints there.
The complaints I do have, however, is the extremely clunky way you switch weapons. Either you remember every gun per head and you will find yourself smashing keyboard numbers in the middle of combat, or you have to scroll through a weapon wheel which was obviously designed for consoles, which barely works as well. If it would've frozen time ingame when you switched weapons, it would've been far better.
The story progresses through missions. Inbetween missions you often find yourself at your team's secret base. This is one of the biggest annoyances I had with the game. The base 'missions' where you literally fetch tools and other crap, ruins the pacing of the game. Instead of gunning down nazis mission after mission, what you'd expect from a game like this, you're swimming after a ♥♥♥♥ing welder tool, grabbing toys for some mental lightweight or other nonsense. Totally unnecesary.
The characters are also not really all that great. I found myself having great trouble to like any of them. The main character keeps making pseudo-intelligent comments to himself and seems like a wannabe poet at times. Then there's some army dude who hates you for no rational reason, and your love interest you are supposed to care for as a player is just plain annoying. This part, however, is all subjectional, and can be disregarded.
Lets start with the visuals. The game looks pretty nice. There's sweet light/dark effects, gunfire looks amazing and the textures are overall good. The performance is alright. I experienced occasional framedrops (780TI) which weren't caused by my card, but by the game's performance. They, however, only seemed to happen around areas with lots of NPCs, so I'm not sure what that was all about. No biggy though. Texture pop in, however, IS a biggy. A big annoyance. The game does this at literally every turn. As soon as something comes in your line of sight, the textures quickly pop in and I didn't like that one bit. Other than that, no real complaints here.
Wolfenstein: The New Order is an enjoyable shooter with a great setting, some nice visuals and decent optimization. Small issues with performance, pacing and certain missions make this a flawed game, but still enjoyable nontheless.
7/10

The end goal is too build a spaceship and presumably escape with whoever is still alive plus whatever random people you have managed to brainwa- I mean recruit into your colony. But the real joy is watching your rag-tag team of misfits attempt to survive against disease, fallout, winter, and other people on the planet.

Age of Empires II is by far one of my favorite real-time strategy games, I have spent quite some time playing the game and found that the game is consistently fun. However I'm going to be honest when it comes to the game of being HD I can't really see much evidence of that. I was playing AOE 2 on CD before I found out steam had released the game in HD.
I played a match on CD and then immediately started playing the steam version to see if I could tell the difference and I'm sorry to say, I can't quite tell the difference. The only thing that is remotely different between the CD version of the game and the steam version is simply the texture of the water looks slightly nicer. Beyond that, all of the textures for the vanilla game are identical to what the game looked like on the CD version. The only difference I can see is that the steam version has built-in widescreen support whereas the CD version does not.
Now don't get me wrong the game is fun and I wholeheartedly recommend the game to anybody who likes the real-time strategy genre, however in my opinion when I saw the game I honestly thought more effort would be put in to making the textures look better, maybe something along the lines of what AOE 3 looks like.
The forgotten empires expansion from what I have heard is mostly a fan made expansion pack for the game that was initially available for people who owned the CD version of the game free to download, so I was somewhat disheartened to see that this was available in the steam version of the game but with a price tag. Personally the civilizations are fun to play, however the campaigns that go along with them could be better. When I say that though, I mean I wish that they had voice acting to go along with them. Other than that though, the forgotten empires campaigns are just as good as the campaigns that come with the vanilla game.
The African kingdoms expansion is an expansion made by the developers who are now working on Age of Empires 2, and in my opinion is a lot better than the forgotten empires expansion. The campaigns are very interesting, the stories are compelling and more importantly the civilizations are all fun to play.
So overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys real-time strategy games such as command and conquer, it has proved to be a very entertaining game for me.

It would literally be more fun to attempt to remake the old Brink game than play this. Balancing and generally interesting setting and characters are out the window with cliché, oversaturated character ideas such as 'the guy who goes invisible' or 'the guy that lights things on fire'.
Dirty Bomb is a game I was relatively hyped for as I was in the small minority of people who actually enjoyed Brink and its heavy objective based gameplay, and to hear there was a possible successor in the world I was quite interested. Back then there wasn't many Mercs in the mix so things such as balancing wasn't much of a problem. Some of the characters were interesting such as Arty with his artillery abilities. Fast forward to today, and we have a crisis in original ideas in characters. We have the stereotypical 'man with sword' that goes invisible, which has been done several times before in many games, the 3 (I think? I didn't count since they all look the same) snipers that are more or less glorified spotters. However, in Dirty Bomb, the key to success is supports and oh boy, are there so many supports. They all do the same thing, but slight differences set them narrowly apart. Some revive from afar and some might as well perform surgery there and then cause it would be quicker than charging up the flipping defibs!
So because of the overabundance of unoriginal character ideas, balancing would obviously be a problem. You'd expect an LMG to do more damage than an invisible man with a katana right? Bullets generally kill quicker and cleaner than a big sword but nope! If 'man with sword' gets anywhere near you you're dead. Even supports are unbalanced. Every support apart from Sparks (the one that revives from afar) is at a disadvantage due to her ability to revive a long way away. Why play someone who takes 4-7 seconds to charge some defibs when you can just shoot a gun to rev? Such a waste of time and effort designing playstyles when you just have these obvious characters that are objectively better than the rest. Why not put that time to actually making essential updates towards balancing and making worthwhile characters and abilities?
The maps aren't all that interesting either and is basically a checklist that goes as follows:
1. The same colour palette consisting of several browns, some mixed with green, and grey (all of these are cool colours, but a constant shade of it plastered on every wall is very boring.
2. Some fancy pants future triangles with an ugly shade of either lime green or banana yellow that are taped on to the side of everything.
3. Clear one-sidedness in most maps. Not single match goes by without the defending team getting steamrolled.
Its shoddy work, to say the least. I will applaud them on flank routes and layout, its fun to cap side objectives to open up a new route for your team.
I dislike this game but I still encourage and lost Brink fans to at least try it, maybe you'll like it or maybe you're like me and you'll dislike it.

TL:TR This game made me jump more than anything I've ever played or watched in my life! Very good game and lots of fun. 8/10 in my books!
So, I started playing the game and it doesn't really explain♥♥♥♥♥♥ but that's okay because it didn't take long to for people to guide me on how to play.
So after about 20 minutes of walking around aimlessly I started using the map more and figuring out which squad was doing what, and read the map legend which basically made the game 10x easier.
Anyhow, as the US, we're fighting in I think Afghanistan? We're trying to take over this little town with sand walls all over and lots of vantage points for the enemy.
We get extremely close and hear nothing but silence. So I pop up out of a crouch to peek in the window and at the same time a terrorist does the same! His face took up my whole 28" monitor and my heart dropped into my pants. I've seriously never been so startled in my life! We both ducked back down and then the grenades started going off all over.
It was super intense and made my adrenaline rush more times in a few games than any other game. There's no mini maps and the main map doesn't really show enemy positions at all other than what they are in control of or taking over. So you never know what to expect!
You can only hear your squad mates unless your close by to the other team members on other squads. And then squad leaders can talk to each other as well. Makes for a much more intense experience!
8/10 Still in early access but really does not feel like it! Maps are HUGE, graphics are very good, and the teamwork is unmatched. The fact the game does not explain anything at all might make this hard for people new to the genre or only casual to it. US is extremely over powered because they are the only faction to have scopes on guns besides the snipers. You can counter the scopes with sneaky movement and using cover to get close but it requires TONS of teamwork. Game is definitely not for casual game players but to players who like a hardcore realistic game, this is definitely for you!

This game is a great arcade-esque style shoot em' up and I adore it. I played for a few hours with a friend and it was a lot of fun but I have a few suggestions to improve gameplay:
1. SKILLS
-You can put a point after every round into a skill
-Skills could be like: accuracy, damage, run speed. and scavenger (get more from cash/supply drops)
2. GUN UPGRADES
-Pay to get various upgrades/attatchments to your guns
-Such as: incendiary (does dmg over time) explosive (hurts more than one target) or like an increase in damage, accuracy or firing speed
3.CHARACTERS
-We need just a little bit of character development, who is "The Girl"? Or "The SWAT"?
-I suggest adding MORE characters and giving them each starting attributes depending on who they are like: The SWAT gets a defense bonus due to his bulletproof vest.
4.TRAPS
-You should add more traps and trap like elements to the game
-Such as a bear trap that costs, say, $50 and you could put them in a 1/4 space of a normal tile
-Fire traps would be cool
5.PALISADES
-Palisades should decay with damage and you should have to pay to repair them
-The advantage of this would be you could add in palisade damage. As in they do damage to zombies based on how new and freshly repaired they are.
These are just a few suggestions that I thought could make this game better, even though it already is pretty addicting.
-Zac
P.S. Add some detail to the map, just a few cracks in the concrete or litter. Something to make it more immersive.
EDIT: Nearly a year later, I played this game again and saw that the devs practically took all my ideas and implemented them and I couldn't be happier! Skills and traps have been added and so have harmful palisades! They also added a couple of aesthetic details to the map! Awesome work guys and thanks for using my ideas :D

Hi Everybody !
I've been playing since the first alpha release, like 2-3 years ago, and let me tell you that this game is a pure bomb ! As someone who was fond of Dwarves Fortress, but wasn't skilled enough to read into the Matrix, Rimworld was a Messiah for me.
The game bsaics are easy to understand and very intuitive. The first and only true goal you have is surviving. For everything else, it's up to you to decide : Merchant city, wild scavenger, Altruistic township, or even warmongger that feed of the prisoner they capture. The games is not fully completed yet, as I think there is a lot more cool stuff that could possibly be added (Underground Mine, advanced diplomatic with other tribes, and why not, a Multiplayer version of the game without any mean of pausing the game), but you have still a decent amount of items and customization possibility.
The Graphics are nice. It's obviously not GTA5, but it's good at what it aims. You can grasp what is going on in a single look, it's clean enough so you can attach yourself with the character, and it isn't too ressource costly, so your computer isn't gonna Rip into peperonni when lots of stuff are gonna happen (and they will, trust me).
The sounds effects are kinda the same. Good and Distinguishable, and the gunshot, coupled with the fact your characters can die pretty fast, are clean enough to give you some thrill.
The OST is very nice and adapted to the context. it's not something i'm gonna listen to everyday, like the Halo/Civilization OST, but it's pleasant while ingame.
Oh, another point : The game is fairly cheap for what it gives, and i never experienced a bug of anykind. Okay, my computer got good stuffs, but i could run the biggest map, with tons of objects, without having the game crashing or lagging out, and that's something i respect from Ludeon Studio for a game in Alpha with those possibilities.
So, if you are fond of Management games/Sandboxing/ Roleplaying, Rimworld is definitely a game you should give a look at !
have fun, Fellow Colonists !

So after getting the trilogy on sale I played through the first two again to refresh myself into the series and in this one so far I'm in chapter 10 or 11.  This is my first playthrough of this game and most likely my last for many different reasons.  The linearity and graphics of the game didn't bother me at all (since the other two are linear as well and had ok gfx for their times as well) and I'm playing through this on the hardest difficulty before whatever unlocks.  But that being said
Pros:
- The golden gun pickups are interesting and pretty easily findable without any help
- The new weapon "ring" for consoles isn't bad since you can't really carry much more than 2 one-handed and 1 two-handed guns anyways
- You can blind fire from cover and still get hit (making it more "realistic")
- Max feels a little more "alive" with how he can hit things jump dodging and flip around and how he will duck down or move back slightly when being shot at in cover
- Cutscenes are now skippable (which from looking at other reviews was a problem before) so kudos to R* for fixing that (although I didn't skip them as I want to get "the experience" from my first playthrough of how the game is supposed to be)
- The "last man standing" idea where if you get hit while you have a painkiller you are knocked down. (I'll explain a little more in a bit)
- There are some funny things Max says from time to time and for each different area he had something to say when you pick up painkillers.

It would literally be more fun to attempt to remake the old Brink game than play this. Balancing and generally interesting setting and characters are out the window with cliché, oversaturated character ideas such as 'the guy who goes invisible' or 'the guy that lights things on fire'.
Dirty Bomb is a game I was relatively hyped for as I was in the small minority of people who actually enjoyed Brink and its heavy objective based gameplay, and to hear there was a possible successor in the world I was quite interested. Back then there wasn't many Mercs in the mix so things such as balancing wasn't much of a problem. Some of the characters were interesting such as Arty with his artillery abilities. Fast forward to today, and we have a crisis in original ideas in characters. We have the stereotypical 'man with sword' that goes invisible, which has been done several times before in many games, the 3 (I think? I didn't count since they all look the same) snipers that are more or less glorified spotters. However, in Dirty Bomb, the key to success is supports and oh boy, are there so many supports. They all do the same thing, but slight differences set them narrowly apart. Some revive from afar and some might as well perform surgery there and then cause it would be quicker than charging up the flipping defibs!
So because of the overabundance of unoriginal character ideas, balancing would obviously be a problem. You'd expect an LMG to do more damage than an invisible man with a katana right? Bullets generally kill quicker and cleaner than a big sword but nope! If 'man with sword' gets anywhere near you you're dead. Even supports are unbalanced. Every support apart from Sparks (the one that revives from afar) is at a disadvantage due to her ability to revive a long way away. Why play someone who takes 4-7 seconds to charge some defibs when you can just shoot a gun to rev? Such a waste of time and effort designing playstyles when you just have these obvious characters that are objectively better than the rest. Why not put that time to actually making essential updates towards balancing and making worthwhile characters and abilities?
The maps aren't all that interesting either and is basically a checklist that goes as follows:
1. The same colour palette consisting of several browns, some mixed with green, and grey (all of these are cool colours, but a constant shade of it plastered on every wall is very boring.
2. Some fancy pants future triangles with an ugly shade of either lime green or banana yellow that are taped on to the side of everything.
3. Clear one-sidedness in most maps. Not single match goes by without the defending team getting steamrolled.
Its shoddy work, to say the least. I will applaud them on flank routes and layout, its fun to cap side objectives to open up a new route for your team.
I dislike this game but I still encourage and lost Brink fans to at least try it, maybe you'll like it or maybe you're like me and you'll dislike it.

Easy to learn but difficult to master, Rimworld offers a surprisingly complex and addicting village-building/survival simulator set on an alien planet. I'm reminded of the Majesty games when playing this in that the player does not directly control the colonists- instead they place commands all over the map while each colonist gradually adds tasks to their daily routine. The ability to turn down or increase the challenge to a significant degree means that the core gameplay experience can change dramatically- from a grueling, rogue-ish race for survival against constant attackers, to a more relaxed, Sim-City like experience.
Personally I prefer the more slow paced approach, and I had a lot of fun organizing a complex town with animal pens, a variety of crops, a complex power grid and a variety of facilities for my villagers. Wild animals and pirates are always a threat regardless of settings, but a few security turrets in the main base should take care of any intruders. There's lots of little interactions between villagers and pets that keeps the world feeling vibrant, and once the town starts becoming truly self sufficient it's hard not to feel significantly invested in continuing to grow.
My main complaint with the game is that the UI feels clunky and unintuitive. I would have preferred easily identifiable icons stuffed in a corner to represent "ANIMALS" "WORK" etc, not the oversized text boxes we get currently. Also, the list of items showing the player's current resources lacks organization and can extend past the boundaries of the screen. Some tweaking in this area would make the game significantly more enjoyable, though the core gameplay is so solid already that it's easy to overlook the game's faults.

Friends said I'd love this game.  I watched many YouTube playthroughs but they seemed long and boring.  I was not impressed.
Eventually, peer pressure got the best of me so I bought it.  Though I don't have many steam hours, I probably have 300 hours having bought from Ludeon.   It is an excellent game rich with content.
While I enjoy building a strong base with traps and mazes for raiders, What I want to concentrate on in this review is the content.
What the videos don't convey well to someone who has never played RimWorld before is the attachment you have for certain characters in the game.  You will rely on your favorites to keep your colony alive.  When the inevitable happens and one of them loses a leg or worse dies, it changes your whole strategy.  You may decide to scrap the game and start over.  You may try to bribe a prisoner to join your colony.  One colonist can mean the difference between success and failure.
As I said, there is content on top of content.  See a statue in a room?  Take a look at it, each one tells a different story.   And that's just a simple example.  Each character feels a certain way about all other characters and vice versa.  Think that doesn't matter?  It does.  What other video game have you ever played where you cared whether two characters hated each other or not?  In this game you will.  You'll celebrate the former enemies who mend fences.  You'll curse when a colonist loses his spouse.
That not enough?  Every action has a reaction.  Is one colonist highly skilled at medicine, but making many mistakes?  Have you checked to see if he's drinking on the job?  Many weapons have their own stories too.  And so do the tombstones.  Many are hilarious.
To conclude, if you are sitting on the fence about whether to buy or not.  I'd recommend it to people who like building games.  I don't know what games to compare it to.  It has alot of the traits of Craft the World, resource management like Sim City, Banished (though it's far more entertaining IMO) and maybe some Age of Empires.  I don't think the let's play videos can do it justice until you actually learn the game.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is basically "Nazi Punks ♥♥♥♥ Off" the video game (with a healthy dose of cyberpunk mixed in).
Game developers have took notice of the demand for games resembling the fps games of generations past and have tried to blend more modern elements of current first person shooters into the mix. It's a difficult compromise when games have gotten slower, prettier, and more forgiving in diffculty. Games have come a long way from the stretched out .jpg Mars space stations of DOOM or the endless bright blue hallways of the original Wolfenstein. We've seen honorable attempts to recapture the fun and speed of those classics (i.e. RAGE, DOOM 3, Serious Sam, Duke Nukem: Forever) but few have been remotely successful.
I think W:TNO has been the best effort in a long time. id managed to find a near perfect sweet spot between these two eras of first person shooters. The graphics settings should be reasonable for most modern machines and my time with the game maintained a silky, buttery smooth framerate.
Shooting feels very satisfying, game mechanics are generally pretty refreshing, and your arsenal of weapons provides lots of fun variety.
On top of it all the plot managed to hold my attention the whole way through and manages to keep a steady pace through the ten hour campaign. If you've at all felt burnt by previous reimaginings and sequels of classic fps games you could do a lot worse than to try The New Order.

This game is a fun and sometimes crazy ride of colony management and survival, in a world that is as easy or as difficult to handle as you like. For extra fun, use the random storyteller - you never know what you're gonna get, but you know it is going to be epic.
The game is at its best when it does stuff you didn't expect. Or when something happens that you thought you were prepared for, but it turns out you had no idea what was coming.
If you like games about building homes, farming, taming animals, trying to save your cats from all sorts of predators, battling raiders from hostile factions then capturing them and trying to turn them to your cause if they have useful skills and/or personality, as well as facing the challenges of heatwaves or extreme cold, this is the game for you.
It's still in development, but has kept getting great updates the whole way and is getting very close to the full release - and the whole time it's been very much playable and enjoyable.
Where on the planet you place your colony/tribe will decide a lot of the challenges you face, especially when it comes to weather and growth season. The storyteller you pick has a significant effect on what events occur, and of course you can also set their difficulty level to whatever you wish.
If it's your first time in, here's a few tips:
Look over your people's skills before you start. It's a good idea to cover all bases, and check their traits to see if anything could cause trouble.
In the Architect menu, click on what you want to build. You'll get a list of materials you can build from. Choose wood, unless you have a ton of stone around you. Wood is renewable, stone is not. Use stone later, when you're established.
Items with a red X on them can't be picked up by your colonists/tribesfolk. Click on the item(s) and free them up for use. Make sure you equip your people with the basic weapons you start with, according to their skill. Check that no hunters are unarmed.

Most of my complaints are not about the game itself, but some of the misleading reviews. They're quick to compare RimWorld to Dwarf Fortress, but it honestly seems like most of them have just heard of it in passing and don't want to be teased for not knowing what a dwarven atom smasher is. RimWorld is somewhere between Prison Architect and Dwarf Fortress in complexity, and would best be explained as diet, caffeine-free, dolphin-safe Dwarf Fortress in a nice-looking can just as willing to run your colony into the ground with misfortune you can't help but laugh at.
The tutorials aren't the best, but if you're relying on those to teach you how to play, you're going to have a bad time. Take some time to explore the menus available to you and the map around you. There are no Z-levels, so you're stuck playing on and gathering resources from only one plane. Steel is not produced as an alloy, but gathered from salvage and compacted steel, the latter of which is dug out from any terrain you might happen to have on the surface.
And the game really doesn't need multiplayer, not that there is any at the time of this review. Honestly, that's just a recipe for disaster in a colony management game like this. If you want multiplayer, roll the same seed as your friend and pick the same starting zone, then compare how you both do.
So I guess I recommend it if you really like colony management games, because this one is already more finished than most of the ones on Steam. Not entirely certain about dropping 30$ on it, but I figured I've been spoiled by enough sales that I don't mind playing full price to give a game like this a go.

The ridiculously slow bullets make sniping (and aiming in general) completely pointless. It's like trying to throw stones at somebody far, far away - if they simply move around a bit they can easily dodge the projectiles forever, even if they are not trying. Your skill in aiming is made absolutely irrelevant.
In fact, unless the enemy is standing within knife-distance, your best bet is to aim wherever he is currently NOT. Practically always the player WILL have already moved away from the spot he was at when you fired, but if you are lucky he ran in the direction you guessed. Do expect target hit-rate at about 5-10% of your normal FPS, like CS or COD or whatever. This completely ruins the game for me.
The broken bullet physics is a real tragedy, in particular because the game has everything else required for a true epic FPS. Huge landscapes, tons of players, guns, vehicles and all kinds of things. But when the enemy can literally run away from your dead-on-center headshot bullets, none of that really matters.

Rimworld is about creating a story with the lot you are given by the game. Imagine Dwarf fortress and Prision Architect had a baby. The baby was then adopted by Stardew Valley and taught to fight crime. Along the way it became the sidekick of Firefly but swore revenge when Firefly was killed in front of them. But I digress.
You start out with one of three scenarios (currently) built into the game. The original, (and my favorite) is of three crash landed survivors of some ship in orbit. They are not colonists, they are lawyers, mobsters, artists, programmers, slaves, bar keepers. Hell, I once had a guy who became a butcher because he thought animals were speaking to him.
The end goal is too build a spaceship and presumably escape with whoever is still alive plus whatever random people you have managed to brainwa- I mean recruit into your colony. But the real joy is watching your rag-tag team of misfits attempt to survive against disease, fallout, winter, and other people on the planet.
Overall I rate 8.9/10

When Wolfenstein (2009) flopped, things looked grim for the oldest FPS franchise. Then around 2013, I saw the first impressions of the newest Wolfenstein and I just thought this was going to be another cash-grab off an old license. Oh boy, was I wrong. The New Order is a great game. Let's get this out of the way: The New Order runs of the id tech 5 engine, which has bad pop-in problems (which means graphics popping in when you look at them). Make sure you have a powerful enough PC to run this game (you will still have pop-in, but it will be severely reduced). Okay so the TNO is set in the alternate reality where the Nazis won World War II. That is all you need to know because the story is just amazing and trust me, you will love it. The gameplay is described as "old-school" and it is, but at the same time, it is very refreshing compared the crap FPS that come out nowadays. Picking up health and armor (in my opinion) is better and more realistic than the covering behind something mechanic to get your health back. It just fits this game very well. You can also duel-wield weapons which is very fun. If you want a new, amazing FPS experience with a story up there with Half-Life and Bioshock, then get Wolfenstein: The New Order.

The puzzles are interesting enough on their own, but the main draw to the game is the story. It waxes philisophical about what it means to be human, the nature of consciousness, and the implications of civilization. I know it sounds like it's going to be some freshmen-level analysis of the human condition, but it isn't. It doesn't preach, it doesn't try to smugly bludgeon you with terms and names of philosophers or fallacies - it assumes you've heard all of that and makes little observations here or there. Enough to ask a question, or make you wonder about something, but it doesn't pretend to know the answers.
While you aren't immediately explicitly told exactly what is going on, you can infer it pretty easily from terminals, voice recordings, and notes left around. By the end of the game you're expected to have figured it out, but it's not trying to be a mystery. No spoilers, but the story itself was strangely
for me. I'm not the sort of person who seeks out feel-good stories, and I didn't expect this one. But for a story that involves total destruction, its ending is a surprisingly hopeful and positive one. It ties together human desire for revelation and our drive to invent into one strangely satisfying conclusion. It's the sort of ending that I think might be ok with if human history actually followed in its footsteps
The story is really what cements the game as excellent, to me, but let's talk gameplay. Each puzzle is bite-sized, I don't think i spent more than ten minutes on more than one or two. And every puzzle gives you a set of items and obstacles, and says "here is everything you need to solve the puzzle - just put the pieces together correctly". The solutions get more complex at time goes on, but the game introduces you to machines and concepts slowly, and I never felt unprepared for any puzzle.
The difficulty curve is exceptionally well-done, I never felt like it threw any impossible challenges my way, and I didn't need to Google anything to beat the whole game. A lot of puzzle games tend to go from zero-to-impossible a little too fast, or never seem to pick up steam, but this one nails the curve. Even if you can't beat the later levels (and believe me, it took time), you'll still have a good handful of hours into a remarkable game.

Ridiculously well done game. I give this a full recommendation in its current alpha state (7/16/2016). It is well worth the $30 I paid back in April (pre-steam). I get so attached to my colonists that their inevitable deaths will bring me to near tears and rage quitting. It is so sad to spend hours watching their skills improve, seeing them recover from illness, fall in love, and get married...then have that bond ripped away as they get mauled by a bear or sniped by raiders or shredded by an exploding turret or accidentally shot in the back by another colonist or two. No other game has given me that experience.
You build, you farm, you hunt, you mine, you develop your colonists, you fight off countless raids, and you get to experience a great story about the development of your colony in Rimworld.

As of Jan 31 2016, the game has a lot of potential, if you got a rig that can max out setting, then the game runs prety smooth. Ive only experienced issues on the 100 player servers. This game focused on coordination of small units (Squad)  in order to complete the objective. You need a mic to be a valuable player.

When Wolfenstein (2009) flopped, things looked grim for the oldest FPS franchise. Then around 2013, I saw the first impressions of the newest Wolfenstein and I just thought this was going to be another cash-grab off an old license. Oh boy, was I wrong. The New Order is a great game. Let's get this out of the way: The New Order runs of the id tech 5 engine, which has bad pop-in problems (which means graphics popping in when you look at them). Make sure you have a powerful enough PC to run this game (you will still have pop-in, but it will be severely reduced). Okay so the TNO is set in the alternate reality where the Nazis won World War II. That is all you need to know because the story is just amazing and trust me, you will love it. The gameplay is described as "old-school" and it is, but at the same time, it is very refreshing compared the crap FPS that come out nowadays. Picking up health and armor (in my opinion) is better and more realistic than the covering behind something mechanic to get your health back. It just fits this game very well. You can also duel-wield weapons which is very fun. If you want a new, amazing FPS experience with a story up there with Half-Life and Bioshock, then get Wolfenstein: The New Order.

Rimworld is about creating a story with the lot you are given by the game. Imagine Dwarf fortress and Prision Architect had a baby. The baby was then adopted by Stardew Valley and taught to fight crime. Along the way it became the sidekick of Firefly but swore revenge when Firefly was killed in front of them. But I digress.
You start out with one of three scenarios (currently) built into the game. The original, (and my favorite) is of three crash landed survivors of some ship in orbit. They are not colonists, they are lawyers, mobsters, artists, programmers, slaves, bar keepers. Hell, I once had a guy who became a butcher because he thought animals were speaking to him.
The end goal is too build a spaceship and presumably escape with whoever is still alive plus whatever random people you have managed to brainwa- I mean recruit into your colony. But the real joy is watching your rag-tag team of misfits attempt to survive against disease, fallout, winter, and other people on the planet.
Overall I rate 8.9/10

Pretty alright shoot-shoot game. I can appreciate a series as stilted and nonsensical as Wolfenstien now trying to have some semblance of a narrative, but it's more or less filling or setpieces to explain why you're Shooting All These Nazis. The few sex scenes were really dumb/hilariously out of the blue, and there are a few torture porn-ish scenes that really left a sour taste in my mouth, so be aware.
The gameplay is pretty fun; it's more or less your standard run-and-gun cawadooty shooter with a few holdover elements brought over from shooters of yore (health & armor systems & dual wielding, for example). The game also has a very basic stealth element that can be very easily broken or bypassed.
You're encouraged to explore the level in order to pick up upgrades or collectables, and of course health & armor. A lot of the exploration, however, is usually done after you've cleared the entire hallway of enemies so sometimes it's a bit of a moot point to do so, other than seeing some neato concept art or fringe dialogue.
All in all, a pretty decent way to blow off a couple of afternoons.

Great game, F2P at its best.

Massive battles that can turn on a dime, from assaulting a fortress with a swarm of allies to being driven off as your Anti-air is knocked out and the skies fill with mosquitos/scythe fighters and gunships while a column of magriders/prowlers move in.
Pro:
Free to play. Literally. You dont need to buy a god damn thing.
HUGE fights, you're never alone if you dont want to be. Just hit ''i'' ingame and it will jump you into a firefight somewhere.
Multiple classes with their own playstyle.
Classes are:
-Combat Medic: Heal your allies and revive the dead. play as rear support or be in the thick of it.
-Combat Engineer: Repair MAX suits, vehicles and aircraft as well as deploy turrets. Assault rifles and shotguns for the NC
-Infiltrator: Take on the role of cloaked sniper OR close range SMG assassin
-Heavy Infantry: Heavy machineguns with massive ammo counts, RPGs and an energy shield
-Light Assault: Jetpacks and assault rifles. Get in, get out, kill everything
-MAX: Powered armor with multiple options. TR get friggin MINIGUNS, NC get shotguns, VS get lasers
Multiple vehicles for you to play with, adapt and tinker:
-Quadbike with weapon mount

Very few games these days serve to challenge the mind in a way that The Talos Principle does.
Gameplay wise, it's very similar in structure to the Portal games in that puzzles are laid out for you to solve, but with one key difference: you're given a lot more freedom to do the puzzles in any order that you want. That is to say, you're not allowed to skip to the much more challenging puzzles right away, but if you're stuck on a puzzle and just want to move on, there usually are a myriad of puzzles that you can choose to do instead of doing everything in numerical order, which makes the game a lot less stressful. Sometimes just doing another puzzle can inspire you to solve the one you're stuck on. Increase in puzzle challenge usually involves introducing gimmicks, and then combining those gimmicks to test your mettle. Honestly, the comparisons to Portal are unavoidable, but in my opinion, this game lives up to that standard.
On a different note, this game exceeds in what I think is the most important aspect of a puzzle game, and that is its story. No one wants to solve puzzles if there's no motivation to solve them, but this game makes sure that you are dedicated to traversing its interesting and immersive world. It is, at heart, a Science vs. Philosophy story, and your mind will not only be focusing on the game's many puzzles, but also the interesting philisophical ride that it will take you on. Adding on to that, this is a game that leaves you shrouded in mystery.... You're thrown into this world knowing just about nothing about yourself, and its up to you to figure out what you are and your true purpose. It's endearing, inspiring, and its a smart look into prospect of Artificial Intelligence. You will not be dissapointed.
All-in-all, if you've been looking for a puzzle game that will inspire you, challenge you, and leave a strong impression on you, get this game. It's up there with some of the greatest puzzle games of all time, in my humble opinion. It's simply a masterpiece of charm and intelligence, and it deserves more respect. GIVE THIS GAME A LOOK!!

A good FPS and an excellent reboot to the series without dropping the essentials of Wolfenstein.
Wolfenstein has always been about mowing through hordes of Nazis in the most rediculous manner possible and this game delivers that and then some while adding legitimate storylines to the gameplay that connect the player to the game world more than the quintessential hero B.J. has ever done. Those same stories never over stay their welcome and have some very satisfying conclusions (depending on your personality type).
Gameplay is built around the stealth vs Run-n-Gun, but for the most part eventually devolves into a series of set piece gun fights where stealth is only useful for initation (or not at all).  In fact, the final chapters end up being a series of running gun battles with on-the-rail world space to connect to the next "battle arena". Not something that should be too much of an issue for an FPS, but the game does such a good job of introducing and implementing the stealth mechanics early that its slow removal is noticable and disappointing.
In any case, one item of note is the dichotomy of difficulty vs battle length makes the firefights in general (and the ending in particular) fairly unsatisfying. Basically, the entire game is fairly easy, even on its hardest setting (at least if you are a veteran to the FPS genre), but the firefights typically take several iterations to figure out the cadence. This means for the ending (and at various points in the game) you are stuck between playing on easier levels that you will (probably) finish on a single play through, but not really feel any satisfaction from doing so, or play on harder settings and be forced to suffer load times and restarts as you slowly figure out game idiosyncracies (I respawned after a first death and didn't realize none of the health/armor/weapons/ammo I was supposed to have access to were spawning...that took be 20 minutes before realizing it and restart the level).
Speaking of the games limitation...while the gunplay is fun its rather limited to pistol, machine gun, shotgun, sniper rifle, and laser gun. Variety is added by allowing most weapons to be dual wielded and adding secondary fire options / ammo types.  Additionally, enemy types are fairly standard throughout the game and the game takes the "bullet sponge" mentality of increasing game difficulty by adding new versions of Nazi soldiers that simply take more and more punishment to kill.  IMO, in a game where dual wielding rocket launching machine guns is considered "normal" I think it would have been much more fun take the "zerg" approach and just have "endless waves" of enemies to wade through.  In any case, enemy variety is a problem.
Anyway, don't let this games limitations turn you off from buying it. Killing Nazis has never been so much fun and its easily worth full price...let alone whatever Steam sale has it for now.

It pains me to do this, but I can't recommend Wolfenstein: The New Order.
Why?
Well to put it bluntly, I've seen this all before. You may as well be playing FEAR, or Half Life 2. Sure this is prettier, but mechanically there is nothing new on offer. There is an entirely ignorable "perk" system that feels tacked on, an array of basic FPS weapons that all have alternate fire modes and the possibility of dual wielding, and lots and lots of Nazis to shoot.
For style points, it gets 10/10. The alternate history they imagined wherein the Allies lose World War 2 is an interesting conceit. The graphics, sounds, music, voice actors, and presentation are top notch. The characters the plot introduces are believable and well written. This is pretty much the limit of nice things I can say about the game, however.
The well written characters, while welcome in their own right, also serve to highlight how poorly the protagonist fits in among them. While BJ (William) manages to have SOME emotion and even fall in love with his nurse, he seems to switch that off and become a robotic murder machine akin to the Nazi ones you're constantly fighting once the player assumes control of him. Granted this was not really something video game writing is typically prepared to deal with; the best game to tackle the issue of player character as a mass murderer to date was Spec Ops: The Line. Spec Ops, this is not.
I already mentioned this earlier, but the gameplay just falls flat for me. There is a very loosely structured cover system that is entirely unnecessary and feels as tacked on as the perk system. You could honestly ignore it entirely and beat the game just fine (just like the perk system). The basic weapon types are all here, knife, grenades, pistol, assault rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle, and gravity gun (I mean Lazerkraftwerk). That you can dual wield 2 of the same weapon type doesn't really matter, just like the cover system. More interesting is the alternate fire modes with each weapon, but even this is not anything amazing, so much as a way to increase weapon variety somewhat (the assault rifle is also the rocket launcher when alt mode is engaged, the sniper rifle is also a laser gun with a battery in alt mode).
Gameplay that isn't innovative is fine as long as it does it better than other games somehow, and this really doesn't do anything better than any other shooter I've played in recent memory. My recommendation, go play Ziggurat if you like fast paced arena shooters. Go play Dishonored if you want a game about sneaky stealthy first person gameplay. Wolfenstein allows for both of these styles of gameplay, but brings nothing new or interesting to either of them.
If you've played every other FPS on Steam and are looking for a way to kill 8-12 hours, then by all means, pick up W:NO, but there are more fulfilling experiences out there that serve specific tastes better. That is unless killing Nazis is a fetish for you, then this is probably your game.

One of my early SQUAD experiences was a cache destruction mission. These can often feel like a really complex game of whack-a-mole. We had a rough idea that one of the caches was located in this small village in a valley to the south of our squad's position. We set out with support from the rest of the company in the valley, while our squad hugged the lower part of a ridgeline. At about 600m we started taking LMG fire, so myself and the other SAW gunner started putting down suppressing fire and letting our team follow our tracers.
At the bottom of the valley there was a small river running perpendicular to our avenue of approach that was proving serious trouble to cross. RPK rounds and RPGs detonating everywhere. The other elements were getting nowhere. Our squad circled around to the right side of the valley to take up firing positions that looked over the village. Myself and one of our medics were prone on this hill with good visibility of the rooftops and quickly spotted several hostiles. At first we just put down suppressing fire but the medic started calling out targets over local comms to me. "Near building, crouching next to the tires." Three round burst. "Next one, building to the west, moving to the stairs." Another burst. Return fire started to get heavy so we were forced to re-position and find a new spot. By this time though the enemy team had sent a small unit up the hill to engage us and it devolved into a messy firefight until the match ended.
We lost but I didn't particularly care. I had just spent an hour and a half of maneuvering, suppressing, and directly engaging equally organized enemies with a bunch of people I had never met before.
10/10 would suppress again.

Its hard to recommend this game. As much as I like Max Payne, I'm willing to admit that the only reason why I enjoyed the game is because of the gameplay, and whatever connection I had to the protagnist was because of what I knew of him from previous games.
+Gameplay. Bullet time seems to run out quicker forcing you to use the cover system in many instances. Some may think its not as run-and-gun but I found it made you think more tactically, choosing when to use what kind tactic. Using cover and picking enemies off, jumping out guns blazing or dodging and shooting if you can take out the last few. The damage on enemies makes them respond realistically, and I also like the melee attacks and how Max holds his secondary weapon in his left hand, also I appreciate separating the shoot dodge and roll (eventhough its awkward trying to go into cover after rolling). You fight enemies with armored vests early on so your in for a challenge.
+The Showdown mechanic, where a shot that would have killed you instead drains out all your bullet time to go slow motion giving you a chance to kill the enemy before you die. If you kill him your saved. It feels odd to rely on this to avoid death. However it ends up turning into a clumsy attempt at trying to cover the issue of headshots killing you, so you end up relying on the Showdown mechanic to much.
+- A change that some may appreciate and many probably won't, is the limit to 2 dual wielding weapons and 1 secondary (two-handed gun). I never like limiting weapon use but given that the game is taking a more realistic route I don't mind so much mainly because dual wielding is what its all about.
+Visuals, the city is beautiful, physics and destruction to the things you shoot at. Its not noir anymore, and the comic book style cutscenes have been replaced with these discoloured or zoomed in shots in regular cutscenes, with occasional popouts of words said kinda of like everything has happened already and Max is only seeing fragments of memories. I liked it but I think it was overused a bit. As was the amount of cutscenes.
Aspects of the gameplay that came close to ruining the game:
-Headshots kill you (relying on the showdown mechanic to save you)
-Very few guns
-Shoot Dodge uses to much bullet time, making its use limited to when your out of bullet time or if its the last few enemies
-Max's Character, hes all brooding, nihilistic old ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. He spends almost all of his dialogue complaining, self hatred & seems to have a death wish. While it does seem like Max as a character with no one he cares about left alive, seems like a natural evolution, what made the series work before was not just his cynicism and metaphors, it was the fact he was a good guy underneath all that.. having something to fight for.
Nihilists on the other hand are self absorbed (which I'm alright with) but they also complain alot. We hate having to listen them go on, unless its something they keep inside of themselves.
Not just that, but alot of people can't relate to the whole drinking problem thing. What exacerbates the problem is we never get to see him try and see the lighter side of things. It make sense to me that after losing everyone he cares about and killing so many, he would no longer be able to live like a normal person but theres not even a single moment where he enjoys himself. We need a silver lining at the end of it all to make it worth caring about all the strife he goes through.
A change of scenery, a new pair of bad guys, but it just seems like hes doomed to repeat history. Never being able to be normal again, and no one left alive that can slap some sense into him to set his priorities straight. The exception of Bravura, but him and Max weren't exactly in the best of terms.
- The only reason why I enjoyed the game is because of the gameplay, and whatever connection I had to the protagonist was because of what I knew of him from previous games & the voice actors attempt to add personality to a otherwise bland story & characters, alot of dailogue to explain rather dreary moments, uninteresting "clues", characters we know not little about.
-Max's looks. If they thought Max is your every man that the look could appeal to, they chose the wrong game and he doesn't really look like Bruce Willis yet they gave him that look half way into the game.
Max speaks in metaphors and is way to cynical to be your average man.
If you go into the game not expecting a Max Payne sequel, I see it as a continuation of Max's life, different developer starting a new story (and not a very good one), then you might enjoy it if you don't mind the negatives & love the gameplay alone.

Great story-driven game - one of the better stories I've experienced in a while. I'll try to review this without spoiling anything.
This is a pure singleplayer game, which in itself is all it needs. Story takes you on a long ride and to me, it's crafted out so well, it felt like I was watching a movie at times (even though the cutscenes aren't even that long) because of the depth of the character development. It brings you to another level of gameplay experience, as you can sympathize for the characters and actually feel the way they feel. The immersive storyline kept me away from other games and I plowed through this game in about 3 days (3-4 hours each time). Bringing in a love story, it adds another element to it. Voice acting was nearly flawless. Authentic accents (actually used people from Germany, Russia, and Scotland to name some) provided an amazing feel to the game.
There are times when the game puts you through a very depressing scene, making you ponder how much life is actually worth. Then there are times where they put you through a vigorous environment, only for you to slaughter as many people as you can.
It's hard to stop playing because it's so well written and the gameplay itself is so much fun. You have a variety of weapons to choose from and has something I haven't seen since Halo 2 - dual wielding guns. However, I feel like the weapons are fairly limited. Other than the first part of the game with some gun changes, you only have a choice of like 5 different weapons, only modifications to those weapons afterwards. The game itself ran smoothly on my 660Ti on high, with minimal FPS drops. The gameplay mechanics were smooth and the motions felt good.
The only thing that would stop me from getting the game is the price. I feel like CDN $66.49 is a bit overpriced for this game, since it only has a singleplayer element. I picked it up on sale for something like CDN $16.49 from the summer sale and I can say it was worth every penny. I'd probably pay a max of CDN $40 for it. Singleplayer games that are fairly linear (like this one) just aren't worth it at full price.
Story: 9.5/10 (fantastic)
Gameplay: 8.5/10 (very good with some flaws)
Graphics: 8.5/10 (very good with some flaws)
Voice acting: 10/10 (best I've experienced in a while - authentic voices)
Price: 6/10 (CDN $66.49 isn't worth it - pick it up on sale)

Friends said I'd love this game.  I watched many YouTube playthroughs but they seemed long and boring.  I was not impressed.
Eventually, peer pressure got the best of me so I bought it.  Though I don't have many steam hours, I probably have 300 hours having bought from Ludeon.   It is an excellent game rich with content.
While I enjoy building a strong base with traps and mazes for raiders, What I want to concentrate on in this review is the content.
What the videos don't convey well to someone who has never played RimWorld before is the attachment you have for certain characters in the game.  You will rely on your favorites to keep your colony alive.  When the inevitable happens and one of them loses a leg or worse dies, it changes your whole strategy.  You may decide to scrap the game and start over.  You may try to bribe a prisoner to join your colony.  One colonist can mean the difference between success and failure.
As I said, there is content on top of content.  See a statue in a room?  Take a look at it, each one tells a different story.   And that's just a simple example.  Each character feels a certain way about all other characters and vice versa.  Think that doesn't matter?  It does.  What other video game have you ever played where you cared whether two characters hated each other or not?  In this game you will.  You'll celebrate the former enemies who mend fences.  You'll curse when a colonist loses his spouse.
That not enough?  Every action has a reaction.  Is one colonist highly skilled at medicine, but making many mistakes?  Have you checked to see if he's drinking on the job?  Many weapons have their own stories too.  And so do the tombstones.  Many are hilarious.
To conclude, if you are sitting on the fence about whether to buy or not.  I'd recommend it to people who like building games.  I don't know what games to compare it to.  It has alot of the traits of Craft the World, resource management like Sim City, Banished (though it's far more entertaining IMO) and maybe some Age of Empires.  I don't think the let's play videos can do it justice until you actually learn the game.

This game was surprisingly disappointing. The first two Max Payne games are classics, but this is terrible. It is so not like them, it's unrecognizable as a Max Payne game. I don't play the Grand Theft Auto series, but can only presume this was a GTA game that had the Max Payne logo attached to it for branding purposes. I do not play GTA  because GTA does not interest me. I want to play Max Payne. And this is not a Max Payne game. In fact, it seems the developers go out of their way to make this game as un-Max Payne as they could.
The story is different. Instead of a film noir setting about a widowed cop trying to salvage his life while investigating mob conspiracies, we have a Brazilian setting about street gangs kidnapping the daughter of some wealthy guy for no reason but they want money. I know there's more to it, but I couldn't bring myself to play more than halfway through the game. It had plenty of time to get me more invested, and it failed. For that matter, the characters are dull and uninteresting. I do not care when these people die, my reactions to them range from annoying to indifferent. The only interesting guy is Raul, who is kinda cool as Max's sidekick, but he is not enough to hold my interest.
The presentation is different. Gone are the classy and unique graphic novel cutscenes, instead we have normal cutscenes with random cuts between angles as important words flash on the screen, annoying and dull. There are also frequent visual distortions during normal gameplay, the screen flashes or blurs. Annoying and distracting. I don't care if Max is drunk, I'm not, I want to see what I'm doing.
The gameplay is different. Max is severely limited in the amount of weapons he can carry, painkillers and ammo are rare, enemies are more numerous, cover slows down gameplay, and the path between levels is entirely linear. At times this felt more like a rail shooter where I just get to see my character. Quicksaves are gone in favor of checkpoints, so enjoy fighting the same battles again and again and again until you get past them. And you *will* keep trying. I began a game on Medium difficulty and it felt like Hard. I can only imagine how unforgiving Hard mode actually is. There is a single change I liked, where Max does something cool like flip over a table or leap off a balcony, and bullet time triggers so you can shoot the guys in slow-motion as the action is going on. Very cool, but every other aspect of gameplay is terible.
Max is unrecognizable as a character. His narrative metaphors are overdone to the point of parody. I replayed the original Max Payne before this, and this Max is like a caricature of himself with how he talks. Every single line of dialogue he has is a snarky metaphor. Not an exaggeration - every. Single. Line. It wears out quickly. Further, Max repeatedly comments on how he does not like this place, does not like the people he's guarding, does not like the lifestyle they lead, and doesn't want to get drawn into another one-man war against gangs and paramilitary goons. It's as though the character realizes he's been roped into this poor excuse for a sequel and is going along with it under protest.
As I said, they go out of their way to make this not a Max Payne game. Characters and events from the first two games are never mentioned. I think it would be a neat twist if Valkyr had made it down to Brazil and Max had to clean up the drug again, but no. In a flashback Max is plagued by a mob boss whose son he killed, and he fights him with Raul, his old friend from the academy. This is a far more interesting and familiar plot than the one the game insists on focusing on, a pity it's just in one flashback.
This is not only a bad Max Payne game, it's a bad game as a whole. It is simply un-fun, and for a video game to be not fun, the very purpose of the medium, is unforgiveable.

One of my early SQUAD experiences was a cache destruction mission. These can often feel like a really complex game of whack-a-mole. We had a rough idea that one of the caches was located in this small village in a valley to the south of our squad's position. We set out with support from the rest of the company in the valley, while our squad hugged the lower part of a ridgeline. At about 600m we started taking LMG fire, so myself and the other SAW gunner started putting down suppressing fire and letting our team follow our tracers.
At the bottom of the valley there was a small river running perpendicular to our avenue of approach that was proving serious trouble to cross. RPK rounds and RPGs detonating everywhere. The other elements were getting nowhere. Our squad circled around to the right side of the valley to take up firing positions that looked over the village. Myself and one of our medics were prone on this hill with good visibility of the rooftops and quickly spotted several hostiles. At first we just put down suppressing fire but the medic started calling out targets over local comms to me. "Near building, crouching next to the tires." Three round burst. "Next one, building to the west, moving to the stairs." Another burst. Return fire started to get heavy so we were forced to re-position and find a new spot. By this time though the enemy team had sent a small unit up the hill to engage us and it devolved into a messy firefight until the match ended.
We lost but I didn't particularly care. I had just spent an hour and a half of maneuvering, suppressing, and directly engaging equally organized enemies with a bunch of people I had never met before.
10/10 would suppress again.

This is what the puzzle genre is all about. Go take the Bartle test. Did you rank high in "explorer"? Play this game.
You wake up knowing nothing. You're presented with objects that seem incongruous with the surroundings. You try things until you figure out how they work. Things gradually start getting more complex.
But that's just half of it. You come across scraps. Messages. A computer terminal. A voice. They aren't explaining much.
You keep going. The puzzles get a little harder. You start to notice things. There are wierd ways to hack the puzzles. You can sometimes get pieces of them out, or get into wierd places and solve puzzles way easier. You think the game is poorly designed until you find easter eggs and messages in these places. The puzzles were designed to reward you for breaking them.
You read more, you talk to the terminals. The story is finally coming together, you think. Finally it hits you. The pieces all fall into place. You understand why you are. You understand why this place is. You know what you must do.
I'd give it 5 stars, but honestly you shouldn't bother with the stars. It's way too crazy to try and get them all, and the ending you get for it is probably the poorest of the lot. But other than that, highly recommended.

Channeling Tony Scott's Man on Fire, Max Payne 3 departs from its pedigree of graphic-novelesque film noir, in service of a new found penchant for VHS-themed, splice cut madness. Max, the franchise's namesake, is lost and broken, near asphyxiating from a torrent of violence and grief. Seeking respite, he takes on a security contract, protecting a sect of Brazil's well-to-dos. It is at this point that s*** hits the proverbial fan, and Max (and the player) finds himself launched against wave after wave of murderous mad men, ranging from forsaken slum spawn to seasoned and brutally efficient mercenaries.
Rockstar has a torrid, storied relationship with violence, and Max Payne 3 without question earns its place amongst said annals. The degree of Max Payne 3's brutality is exceeded only by its intoxicating degree of style. Bullets tear through the dynamically destructible environments, shredding concrete and flesh alike. Bullet Time, the series' flagship innovation, siphons its duration from the player's bloodlust, challenging the player to execute every maneuver with both grace and angst. The ensuing sensation is undeniably addictive, rendering a cocktail of wanton fury coupled with precision. This is not meant to be an easy game. Throughout the 12-odd hours of playthrough, death is a fearful constant, irking us along a disturbing, albeit visually splendorous travel.
The game's design is purposely linear and unflinching, forcing the player on a singular journey, near devoid of choice-driven moral ambiguity. A common theme throughout Rockstar's efforts, from GTA to Manhunt, Max Payne 3 is an examination into what drives one's virtual savagery.

Pros -
- Beautiful graphics
- Immersive Gameplay
- Heavily Philosophical, written in a way that keeps you engaged.
Cons (with caveats, because I have a hard time with really saying anything bad about this game)
- Repetition, repetition, repetition (though, again, part of the game play)
- Controls aren't exactly intuitive (there are only four or five functions though, so you'll pick it up within a few minutes)
- A little slow paced (though 'dying' certainly can make you jump if you weren't expecting it).

Great story-driven game - one of the better stories I've experienced in a while. I'll try to review this without spoiling anything.
This is a pure singleplayer game, which in itself is all it needs. Story takes you on a long ride and to me, it's crafted out so well, it felt like I was watching a movie at times (even though the cutscenes aren't even that long) because of the depth of the character development. It brings you to another level of gameplay experience, as you can sympathize for the characters and actually feel the way they feel. The immersive storyline kept me away from other games and I plowed through this game in about 3 days (3-4 hours each time). Bringing in a love story, it adds another element to it. Voice acting was nearly flawless. Authentic accents (actually used people from Germany, Russia, and Scotland to name some) provided an amazing feel to the game.
There are times when the game puts you through a very depressing scene, making you ponder how much life is actually worth. Then there are times where they put you through a vigorous environment, only for you to slaughter as many people as you can.
It's hard to stop playing because it's so well written and the gameplay itself is so much fun. You have a variety of weapons to choose from and has something I haven't seen since Halo 2 - dual wielding guns. However, I feel like the weapons are fairly limited. Other than the first part of the game with some gun changes, you only have a choice of like 5 different weapons, only modifications to those weapons afterwards. The game itself ran smoothly on my 660Ti on high, with minimal FPS drops. The gameplay mechanics were smooth and the motions felt good.
The only thing that would stop me from getting the game is the price. I feel like CDN $66.49 is a bit overpriced for this game, since it only has a singleplayer element. I picked it up on sale for something like CDN $16.49 from the summer sale and I can say it was worth every penny. I'd probably pay a max of CDN $40 for it. Singleplayer games that are fairly linear (like this one) just aren't worth it at full price.
Story: 9.5/10 (fantastic)
Gameplay: 8.5/10 (very good with some flaws)
Graphics: 8.5/10 (very good with some flaws)
Voice acting: 10/10 (best I've experienced in a while - authentic voices)
Price: 6/10 (CDN $66.49 isn't worth it - pick it up on sale)

).

The dev team described the game as "Dwarf Fortess meets Firefly" and after playing for several hours, I can agree.
General Concept:
Hands-off unit direction (You give them a task, and someone will get to it.. when they're ready!), as you try to achieve more goals, starting from basic survival, to escaping the planet by building a ship, and dealing with random events that can either help you survive, or make your life hell.
Pros:
- Random Gen World
- Small to Large gameplay areas
- Customizable challenge/gameplay settings
- Easy Start/Hard to Master
- A lot of control over the base building aspects of the game
- Every character has it's own personality, wants, needs and desires that you need to account for.
Cons:
- No direct unit control (w/exception for combat)
- Random Gen World doesn't always spawn with needed resources (you are limited by in-game trade rng)
- Every character has it's own personality, wants, needs and desires, and will take care of them in the order they want, not the order that might make the most sense.
- Maps are currently only a single 'layer'
- Single Player
Gameplay Overview:
Dwarf Fortress is a good example of how the game plays, and what you can generally expect.  If you're carfeul about how you assign tasks, you can 'force' the AI to do certain things first, but at the of the day, if the character wants to sit and watch the clouds more than cook their food.. they're going to go hungry while enjoying the view!
Release 14 introduces new modes expending on the core game, often increasing the challenge to the game (one scenario has you start with 1 character, instead of the normal 3), but ultimately is just a variation on the core game.  14 also introduces intergrated Workshop support for custom scenarios you build, which allows for much easier sharing of the scanrio with others.
Thoughts:
Overall, a fun game to sit down and kill a bit of free time with, but with enough to do to occupy a larger block of time if you have it to spare.  While the maps have various playfield sizes you can choose from, it is still only a single layer map (at least form what I've been able to find - I might just be missing something in the UI/game), but never felt 'small' or confined.  The NPC events (even teh bad events) tend to be fun (or at least as much impact you allow them to be, and provide a very real sense of 'Aw crap, what happened this time'.
One thing I'd like to eventually see in RimWorld would be a variation of the random NPC 'story' archive you get in Dwarf Fortress.  You don't really see the characters 'story' recorded in the development of your colony/camp, and given the nature of the game, I think that could draw you in to the lives of the characters a bit more while increasing your emotional investment in them.
Recommend?
If you enjoy 'god' games where you do more influencing than directly control gameplay - Yes!

A first person puzzle adventure that builds a world around excellent puzzle design with a fantastic and engaging philosophical backstory that wont let go of your interest and curiosity.
From my very first moments of exploring and interacting with the world, I knew I'd found something I was going to enjoy, and while the level of design and subtle mood are all work to set the game up incredibly well, there are some subtle interwoven design choices that make this title something special, and it took me a lot of playtime to figure out why I enjoyed The Talos Principle beyond just being an excellent first person Puzzle game with rich story. Things like the writing work hand in hand with the overlying story to create depth and intrigue at an early stage and make you want to progress more than any other game I've played in recent memory.
The subtle gameplay and level design choices throughout The Talos Principle are so incredibly well done that the first playthrough is nothing short of incredibly engaging fun. You're taught to interact with the world and not take anything for granted which means you're unaware that you're improving and more importantly unaware that you're thinking in a different way and genuinely unlocking different avenues of thought in your own mind.
Terminals, for example, contain short segments of text that serve the overall narrative, but also change pitch every so often, and coupled with the mythological, religious and historical tales and references and things like recordings scattered throughout the world, you'll often unknowingly have expectations of what's expected of you. The writing and design set up a box then encourages you to think outside of it and it makes everything more rewarding.
Other subtle changes like the complete lack of timed puzzles which make up the vast majority of other titles, and the lack of direct linear progression, and lack of any direct demand of the player to continue means we progress in the game of our own accord, and it helps us tie ourselves into the story and feel part of the world.
* The sheer technical design and tuning which show off more of the stellar design is impressive. Cross platform support, console access and inside mod support, outside mod support for Steam Workshop and more all add replayability to an already lengthy title.
* There wide array of configuration options deserve praise, you can adjust almost any aspect of the technicals.
The biggest annoyance of this game is the standard it sets for itself early on, and in not maintaining the incredible level of curiosity and quality of writing up until the end. It's hard to complain about a game offering this much content and length, but when the latter third of the game doesn't hold up as much as the first third, it can feel slightly weary or repetitive at times to continue.
* Due to the somewhat floaty movement and bright colour scheme, it's very easy to feel nausea or motion sickness while playing this game, though there are an impressive set of tools to adjust these settings under an aptly named Motion Sickness sub-menu
Priced at £29.99/39.99€/$39.99 and only 19.99€ in Steam European Region 2, The Talos Principle is at the top range of what I'm personally willing to pay for a video game, and more expensive than related games like Portal 2, and even more than the inflated prices of some of the triple A titles. As a result, I find it hard to call this good value for everyone, but because of the very well designed and polished gameplay and the average play time of at least 16 hours, people paying full price are not going to feel ripped off and if you're the target market, someone who enjoys first person puzzle games with a great backstory and interesting details, it's a good buy even at full price. For the rest of us, I'd suggest it's worth waiting for a sale of -50% or more.
* The
adds four new episodes with much harder difficulty (but by no means cheap in approach, nor needlessly difficult) with an open approach and a different take on the game and an equally great and interesting story/narrative. None of this is just more-of-the-same and it's a great DLC worth buying for people who have already enjoyed the full game. Fairly priced at £10.99/14.99€/$14.99, as with the main game, cheapest from EU2.
* The
adds a Serious Sam character model and a new voice for Elohim and may be worth £1.99/2.99€/$2.99 for Serious Sam fans, but is a waste of time otherwise considering other models and skins are available free within the Steam Workshop.
* The
adds 100+ puzzles, the majority of which are simply recycled designs from the pre-alpha to release of the game. You'll revisit many levels from the main game with flaws or without nice modelling/background and as a result may feel like you're wasting time or being cheated. There is one exclusive world included, and this DLC offers support for many Steam Workshop mods and offers two new Elohim voice-overs. If you can put up with retreading old maps with annoying issues, it may be worth the £3.99/4.99€/$4.99
* A free demo is available on the Store page for anyone still on the fence.
* Check the Steam Workshop after completing the game where you can find a number of skins (Companion Cube Hexahedrons anyone?) and more maps.

This is, without exception, one of the best games I've played in the last decade or so, and is an excellent, unique and pretty addition to the FPS genre. The story is superb, playing out like a mix of Indiana Jones and Oceans 12, where relic hunting is perfectly intertwined with prison break - type planning. The music is excellent, and the artist behind the soundtrack should be given a medal. And lastly, the graphics are positively wonderful, and 10x better than those of any other FPS, not just for reasons of fidelity, but because this is, without exception, the best art design I've seen in a video game since Half Life 2.
There are three minor issues. BJ Blaskowicz has a permanent, half-open mouth and otherwise looks mentally challenged, often nodding instead of giving a verbal response. Second, the weapon selection leaves a lot to be desired. Third, whoever wrote BJ's internal monologue would make Max Payne proud, as, at any quiet moment in-game, BJ never misses an opportunity to say something half-intelligeble, and fully-meaningless.
In conclusion, let me say that this game is worth £100, and is an absolute must-buy for anybody. The Gameplay is stellar, the Graphics are stellar, the Story and Music are Stellar, and aside from a small amount of insignificant detractions, no issues exist.
