No one will read this, but I'll write it anyway.
This game is an affront to the Max Payne series to a point it makes that Marky Mark abomination of a movie feel like an homage. It's plagued with technical instability and endless crashes (even on a top end PC like my own), so much so it seems like one of those pre-release games on Steam in which you can participate to help the developers root out all the bugs before the main release. Except this is the main release.
Rockstar failed to deliver just about every aspect that made Max Payne series what it is. In their eyes, it is all about bullet time shootouts, everything else was lost on the journey to South America. The dark noir atmosphere, the hallmark of the series, is virtually non-existent. What you get are voice overs and irritatingly endless cutscenes of a slob on a binge inbetween shooting people in the face. Predictable story, cardboard cutout characters and lots and lots of repetitive action. You came, you slowed down time, you shoot people in the face, you left. Max Payne 3 in a nuttshell.
One of the reasons Max Payne duology was a success was the bullet time action. Key part of that sentence being "one of the reasons". What separated it from every other game that had "bullet time" or "focus" or "ninja mode" feature, what ever they called it, was the atmosphere.
Max Payne and The Fall Of Max Payne managed to put a player in the shoes of a guy who lost everything, and you felt it down to your bone. You felt it! The setting, the tone, the music, the gloomy atmosphere and the noir approach to telling the story immersed the player in the shoes of Max Payne. You felt like a guy thumbling down the rabbit hole with nothing but a bottle of JD, handfull of painkillers and a gun to keep you company. It was dark, grim and bloody. It was Payne.
Rockstar took the bullet time part and left everything else out with their approach to Max Payne 3. The truly sad part, they show you Max Payne 3 as it could have been, and that is during the flashback chapters of the game which take place in New York. During those chapters you traverse the dark streets, buildings and rooftops of New York while dealing with a Jersey mobster and his goons and you are oh so painfully reminded of a game you could have been playing. But then the chapter ends and you're back in Rio De Janeiro and it all goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥
STORY
Max left the force and spends his days at the bottom of a bottle. A run in with a spoiled son of a Jersey mobster goes wrong and Max kills him. The mobster unleashes his men on Max who, being Max, kills them all but is forced to leave New York. At the same time, a buddy from the academy shows up and offers Max a job down in Rio De Janeiro. A bodyguard to the rich and famous, a wealthy business man, his politician brother, younger party loving brother and their better halves. When one of them gets kidnapped, Max and his "partner" go on a quest to find her, going from one seemingly connected location to the next all the while discovering that there is more to the kidnapping than it seems. You'll guess where the story is going in less than a few hours with only a few quasi twists to make you wonder, but both will be insignificant to the story as a whole. It might make you feel less like an ******* for shooting up half of Rio, if you're one of those morally inclined gamers.
LOCATION, LOCATION, LOCATION
Replacing the cold New York streets with Rio De Janeiro is the first major flop of this game. I get that Rockstar wanted to do a new chapter of Max Paynes' life, but there is no Max Payne without the atmosphere of the first two games and Rio De Janeiro as a setting simply can't deliver this. I get where they saw potential, with all the corruption, poverty and favelas. It is a powerful setting and a game can definetly be made there, but just not a Max Payne game. Who in their right mind takes a dark noir character and puts him in warm and sunny Rio De Janeiro?! Setting is a character in and of itself, in first two games New York was that character and it played its part to perfection. Casting Rio is the games equivalent of casting John Wayne as Ghenghis Khan, Hayden Christensen as Anakin Skywalker or Collin Farrel as Alexander. They don't fit and by default break the immersion. You break the immersion, you break the game.
I would rate the levels as great if it were another game, but for Max Payne game they don't fit. You'll go from fancy office building, a night club, police stations, old on the verge of collapse building, yacht, slum of favelas (which has the most promising atmosphere of feeling helpless) to what I can only describe as the bayoou of South America. You go places, shoot people and move on. Despite Rio beeing a poor choice of setting, the levels are neat enough and do deserve a praise.
GAMEPLAY
Controls got a bit of an overhaul and not necessarily for the better. I loved the simplicity of bullet time in first two games. One button activated the bullet time, the rest of the controls added to it. If you wanted to jump sideways in slow mo, you would hit bullet time and simply jump while moving sideways. Presto, flying Max Payne.
Max Payne 3 has one control to activate bullet time while you're just walking about and another control setup to do something acrobatic while in bullet time. The separation sounds simple and works on paper but it's annoying, unnecessary and really not user friendly while you're in the middle of a firefight. I belive they did it this because there are situations where enemies shoot rockets or throw explosives at you and you can use the former bullet time to slow down time and shoot the projectile. The later is used for John Woo stuff like flying through a door and busting caps before you even hit the floor. I've had moments that reminded me of Max Payne of old, using bullet time to the fullest.
Having recently seen John Wick, I recall a scene where Keanu Reeves takes cover behind a pillar, leans out and sees the foot of an enemy hidding behind another pillar. He shoots the foot, the guy falls out of cover and Reeves pops him in the brain. I literally had that exact scene play out in the game. Cleared the room but one guy was left and he took cover behind a pillar. I shot his heel, he leaned out of cover and I poped him in the head. Reloaded and moved on with cool as Wick swagger. I strugled with controls but they weren't impeeding as I've experienced in some other games, so that's not much of a minus as much as a personal preference.
The physics in the game is a plus. Bodies will fall realistically, either limp as a fish or over objects depending on the way they died. I had a funny moment at the airport where I shot a bad guy and he literally dropped into a chair and remained seated as if waiting for a flight. Office shootouts tend to be hectic as hell especially since everything the bullets hit tends to explode creating a Michael Bay like mess that makes firefights even more chaotic. That is a major plus and adds to the action movie feel. The bad side, it's repetitive, just one swarm of enemies after another. Not to mention the cutscenes. There is more cutscenes than the game itself, it kills the immerson and tends to place you in a bad position before a firefight. Very annoying.
But when all is said and done, Max Payne 3 is a disappointing game. Buy only if it's on discount and if you you really want to know what happens to Max Payne after the second game. Leave every other expectations at the door.

So, I posted a review awhile back once Robocraft' whole descent into mediocrity began, what with the removal of tier-based matchmaking that almost ensured a fair match would be had, the removal of the gradual unlocking and purchasing of the parts you ACTUALLY wanted without worry of RNG and luck getting in the way, removal of Mega-Tier mechs and so on. My previous review also touched base on the downright unenjoyable turn the game has taken. Sure, there's more weapons than before, but it feels like there's an -immense- lack of balance even if there are a few that harp on otherwise that the game, for the most part, is balanced.
Well, after deciding to try starting anew with a fresh account, I'll be making a new review.
Robocraft has, somehow, gotten worse still. That's right. Worse. RNG crates didn't ruffle your jimmies enough? The general feeling that matchmaking has become a joke didn't irk you to high hell and back? Haha, well, guess what; matchmaking may as well be practically non existent. Upon starting up a few simple Deathmatches in game, rather than getting paired with similarly leveled players/CPU mechs, I instead get thrown against a team decked out with a plethora of legendaries. Shields, cloaks, chain guns, plasma bombers and so on, the stuff you'd usually see in CPU 1000+. 'Oh, but, but, b-but, all weapons are fair! Sure, your lowly wasps may not hit as hard, but you'll have a far superior fire rate!' Yes. Whilst I nibble at the mechanical ankles of encroaching, brick-shaped, shielded up death with my dinky, super-hyper fast fire rate wasps, I'll be getting torn asunder in, oh.., I don't know, about 5, 15 or 30 shots depending on the weapon said brick is currently equipped with.
'B-but that's plenty of time to retaliate!' Sure. I'll have broken off all but 15-20 blocks, maybe.., MAYBE broken one of their guns before I'm turned to a pile of spare parts and they're well on their merry way after having stepped on the equivalent of a bug equipped with a rapid fire pea shooter, healing what piddling little damage I've done in a span of ten seconds.
'Well.., y'know, it helps speed up the matchmaking process!' Yeah, it speeds things along towards the next HEAVILY unbalanced, unfair match, whereas I'd rather wait a minute or so to be paired against similarly equipped/skilled players. No, no, yeah, you're right. Please. Throw all the fresh level 1's at level 90+'s. That's sure to inspire players to continue playing and continue getting steamrolled into oblivion.
'..At least you don't have to endure grinding out the parts you want, now that we've got crates!' Shove off. Let's assume the majority of the playerbase is looking to get a particular piece of equipment for their mech. Maybe that sixth spider leg for an arachnid robot, or that left-facing shield to match the right-facing shield. Oh, what's that? You've gone through 20+ crates and STILL haven't gotten the part you'd like to have? Well chin up, champ! ...It sucks to be you. Keep trying.
It baffles me that some people will defend this game even given its current state. They defended it when the crates came along, when the fair tier system was dropped, when the factory was released and pretty much kicked any attempts of creativity to the side because hey; why have a nice looking bought when you can just roll with the current 'meta' and pwn, pwn, pwn!
Myself, I'll be uninstalling Robocraft until it starts properly shaping up, and would suggest others to either do the same, avoid it altogether to begin with.., or keep expectations reasonable, if not somewhat low.

A first person puzzle adventure that builds a world around excellent puzzle design with a fantastic and engaging philosophical backstory that wont let go of your interest and curiosity.
From my very first moments of exploring and interacting with the world, I knew I'd found something I was going to enjoy, and while the level of design and subtle mood are all work to set the game up incredibly well, there are some subtle interwoven design choices that make this title something special, and it took me a lot of playtime to figure out why I enjoyed The Talos Principle beyond just being an excellent first person Puzzle game with rich story. Things like the writing work hand in hand with the overlying story to create depth and intrigue at an early stage and make you want to progress more than any other game I've played in recent memory.
The subtle gameplay and level design choices throughout The Talos Principle are so incredibly well done that the first playthrough is nothing short of incredibly engaging fun. You're taught to interact with the world and not take anything for granted which means you're unaware that you're improving and more importantly unaware that you're thinking in a different way and genuinely unlocking different avenues of thought in your own mind.
Terminals, for example, contain short segments of text that serve the overall narrative, but also change pitch every so often, and coupled with the mythological, religious and historical tales and references and things like recordings scattered throughout the world, you'll often unknowingly have expectations of what's expected of you. The writing and design set up a box then encourages you to think outside of it and it makes everything more rewarding.
Other subtle changes like the complete lack of timed puzzles which make up the vast majority of other titles, and the lack of direct linear progression, and lack of any direct demand of the player to continue means we progress in the game of our own accord, and it helps us tie ourselves into the story and feel part of the world.
* The sheer technical design and tuning which show off more of the stellar design is impressive. Cross platform support, console access and inside mod support, outside mod support for Steam Workshop and more all add replayability to an already lengthy title.
* There wide array of configuration options deserve praise, you can adjust almost any aspect of the technicals.
The biggest annoyance of this game is the standard it sets for itself early on, and in not maintaining the incredible level of curiosity and quality of writing up until the end. It's hard to complain about a game offering this much content and length, but when the latter third of the game doesn't hold up as much as the first third, it can feel slightly weary or repetitive at times to continue.
* Due to the somewhat floaty movement and bright colour scheme, it's very easy to feel nausea or motion sickness while playing this game, though there are an impressive set of tools to adjust these settings under an aptly named Motion Sickness sub-menu
Priced at £29.99/39.99€/$39.99 and only 19.99€ in Steam European Region 2, The Talos Principle is at the top range of what I'm personally willing to pay for a video game, and more expensive than related games like Portal 2, and even more than the inflated prices of some of the triple A titles. As a result, I find it hard to call this good value for everyone, but because of the very well designed and polished gameplay and the average play time of at least 16 hours, people paying full price are not going to feel ripped off and if you're the target market, someone who enjoys first person puzzle games with a great backstory and interesting details, it's a good buy even at full price. For the rest of us, I'd suggest it's worth waiting for a sale of -50% or more.
* The
adds four new episodes with much harder difficulty (but by no means cheap in approach, nor needlessly difficult) with an open approach and a different take on the game and an equally great and interesting story/narrative. None of this is just more-of-the-same and it's a great DLC worth buying for people who have already enjoyed the full game. Fairly priced at £10.99/14.99€/$14.99, as with the main game, cheapest from EU2.
* The

You'll revisit many levels from the main game with flaws or without nice modelling/background and as a result may feel like you're wasting time or being cheated. If you can put up with retreading old maps with annoying issues, it may be worth the £3.99/4.99€/$4.99

The better you become at the game and the higher skill level players become the more the gameplay moves away from awesome battles for the first time and realism firefights to more csgo getting headshot 500 meters away within 1 sec. The "Meta" atm for good matches is rushing everything and run and gunning. Positioning isent that big of a factor in high level games. More your lighting reflexes. A game focusing on being a realism tactical shooter I find this to be abit silly. I myself am a good player but even I find times when the guy I just shot should have killed me.
Other cons..
The content is amazing but as slow as they get. We are all waiting for V10 atm. V10 = Animation update and coreinventory rehaul. Hopefully this will fix in my eyes the csgo gameplay to more slow paced tactical gameplay.
Overall the game is def worth the buy!

Strikes the perfect balance between Mil-Sim and Mainstream FPS, requires teamwork and mic to really enjoy the game. If you don't work as a team and communicate effectively you're going to have a bad time. There is a learning curve, and don't count on seeing the enemy, understanding fire superiority is key to push forward as a squad. Learning how to squad lead effectively is extremely rewarding, nothing is better than getting your guys in perfect ambush position and holding fire until they get out in the open......sweet sweet endorphine rush.
Still quite a few kinks to work through with optimization and anti-cheat, but if you're rig exceeds the recommended specs you should be good to go. Think of it as an infantry only version of Project Reality at this time. The game and the graphics engine are both in early development so this one should really take off in a year, the community is pretty healthy as you need to use teamwork to win. The learning curve is steep, but once you figure it all out it's hard to play anything else.
Tip: Currently Set Shadows to Low (not shadow detail), memory leak or something on that setting and it doesn't really make a difference visually but you'll get back your framerate.

I know you won't hear many people say this, but if you want to kill more Nazis, and have more fun with less messing about, and to pay less for the experience, get The Old Blood instead. I would recommend this game though, but I think that The Old Blood was just better overall, and felt like it had less filler content.

I actually quite like this game. It continues the legacy of the previous two games in terms of gameplay and game elements.
The major change, is that they scrapped the comic book style narration, and replaced it with actual cut scenes. Max will still narrate and serve dry comments in the background, though. It works really well for immersion and storytelling.
I also quite like the story, although it's not quite as linear as the first two games. You will do a bit of jumping backwards and forwards in time, although again, it works really well, because the mystery unravels itself to you in a fine pattern.
Because Max is portrayed very differently in each "time span", the story does not get too confusing.
You will be able to play:
All Max'es are equally alcoholic and bitter, and the variety is refreshing.
The game is great, and even works really well on Mac, but is quite likely that you will not be able to play it a lot of the time. The game features a third party DRM, which you must log in to every time you start the game. Should the service be down, for one reason or another, you are not going to play the game.
This is, sadly, a very common occurence, and the only solution is to force quit the game and try a different day.
The game itself is solid, but you are entirelly at the mercy of the service. It is not worth paying full price for. You might pick it up if it is heavilly discounted, otherwise you are better off putting your money elsewhere. I suggest bourbon, it's what Max would have wanted.

This is literally the only game I've played for the past year, to the tune of 20-30 hours a week on average. I originally "borrowed" a copy of the game from a friend during Alpha 9, and within 2 days I'd bought my own copy and never looked back.
The learning curve is a bit steep at first, but the game is so addicting and possibilities for how to build a colony are near limitless between different biomes, base styles, AI storytellers, difficulty settings, and the inherent randomness of the events (both good and bad). And of course, this latest version has the scenario system which will increase the possibilities even more!
The downside: it's a complicated game. Much easier than Dwarf Forttress, but that doesn't say much. Learning to navigate the menus can take a while, and then learning how to optimize bases for various challenges is a never-ending process. I'm still discovering new ways to improve my colonies after hundreds of hours spent. But maybe that's a good thing?
You might also find your sleep schedule and personal responsibilities start to suffer, so if you can't control your time spent in-game, then maybe RimWorld isn't for you. Put another way... if you find yourself repeatedly saying "just one more turn" in Civ, you're going to have a hard time putting this game down. The game can also be a bit frustrating at higher difficulties due to the fickle nature of RNG, but that's also what makes it so maddeningly fun.
Plus, Tynan can be found personally answering threads on the RimWorld subreddit that only have 5-10 upvotes. He really cares about the total experience players have, and actually listens to player feedback and incorporates it into future releases. He'll also make you care more about a tiny digital pawn than you ever thought was possible.
So if you're ready for a deep strategy game rife with joy, frustration, and everything in between, give this game a shot. The only regret you'll have is that your free time might suddenly disappear faster than you'd like.

So, let's define what a typical video game zombie horde is:

This game is excellent. Buy it.
GAMEPLAY
Basically, it uses a similar format to the Portal games: enter a sealed area and solve it's puzzle by picking up and using certain gadgets to interact with the environment- and it does this VERY well. While it lacks portals, it makes up for this by making the puzzle objects very complex, entertaining and in some cases, quite sophisticated (despite needing only a very simple interface!). The puzzles start simple but become VERY challenging.
STORY and VISUALS
Beautiful. The storytelling is also excellent, teased out in hints as you progress. The environments look great. Level design is open and encourages exploration (you don't permanentaly "die" per se, and you can backtrack easily if you feel the need). The game is structured in a way that the main story is easy to play through and complete- with a more extended story hidden from view that you find by exploring.
MINOR GRIPES (advice to make the game more enjoyable)
1- Multiple endings. Really not necessary as you just do the same puzzles a second time. My advice to make the most out of it- forget the stars and white pieces- just take the "RED" to the place you mustn't go.
2- Hidden stars- while fun at first, don't break your back looking for them, as sometimes the puzzle pieces are put in the most ridiculous places that you have no reason to expect them (one was hidden up a tree).
BUT- these 'issues' are minor- the game was a massive success!
Highly recommended.

Maybe you'll build your batteries outside. When they blow up in the rain, and you watch colonists die in the fire trying to put it out, or run screaming away only to return to desolation, you'll know what you did wrong.
Maybe your colonists just aren't skilled enough to farm and mine basic subsistence, and you watch them slowly go mad as they refuse to do the work necessary to survive.
Maybe you got too lax with the squirrels in your camp, and one goes rabid, biting your best medic, which is the last straw for her - what with the bedroom being too small and the food being too boring - and causes a psychotic break. In her rampage, she gives your best fighters concussions, and you couldn't get anyone to subdue her before they're all bleeding, dying, and the medic is passed out in the wilderness dying of stavation.
Maybe a lightning strike happens to hit the one wire connecting your turret bank, right before a bandit assault. Or angry natives bring a rocket launcher, creating a hole in your defenses that you thought were solid. You survive the attack, but the lack of preperation, injuries and death, and loss of supplies are just too much for your colony to recover from.
Maybe, maybe you'll lay the foundations for a thriving trade outpost. A Deadwood in space. A Babylon 5 on a planet's surface. A spot of stability in the messy frontier of space.
Whatever happens, you will learn what went wrong, what detail you missed, what you can improve for next time, as you watch your colony wrestle survival and sanity, before closing their book and opening another.
Difficulty and story style options, along with previewing and rerolling your colonist(s), helps you start off into the game you want to play.

Ab-so-lute-ly fantastic.
But let's address the reason you're here first, and bust the bubble. There's no cake. Nor anything that resembles cake. There aren't even any drawings of it (unless there's an Easter Egg?) All sugary consumables are gone, except maybe you yourself. But that doesn't mean that the game is bitter or tasteless.
I mean, you get everything you have in Portal, and more. There's even a certain theme in the story that I never imagined there to be, because I didn't even know there would be a new character. But

Sometimes hilarious, sometimes scary, you get to feel a lot of emotions when you play the game. You also get to see a lot more of Aperture Science and learn about its history, at least two new game mechanics, and GLaDOS herself.
As always, you never need to completely restart the level to complete the puzzle, which is something I loved about the original Portal. The visual, music and sound effects are great, as expected.
Unfortunately, I never played the co-op of the game, so I cannot comment on that. Though from the speedrunning at SGDQ it also looks fantastic, and GLaDOS trash-talks as usual. Hope to play it myself though, someday, maybe with Companion Cube.

I played The Talos Principle because of all the praise I heard for its interesting philosophies, but I was a bit disappointed by the game. The abstract concepts in the game weren't bad, but they weren't particularly novel or engaging. That being said, I did have some fun learning about the world of the game.
However, I found many of the puzzles to be mediocre. Most of their difficulty came from having to keep track of the state of many objects, not from having to think in new ways. I ended up looking up the solution for a few of the puzzles, and I did not regret doing so at all. I found these puzzles to be more frustrating than challenging, even though the game's overall difficulty was appropriate.
The Talos Principle is an okay puzzle game that presents somewhat worthwhile concepts in a fairly interesting way, but neither the gameplay nor the plot is compelling enough for me to recommend this game.

So I picked up Wolfenstein: The New Order on Steam Summer Sale and decided to try it out. I like FPSes but generally their Campaigns suck and they tend to be very twitchy or overly stealthy. This was neither. I had moderately high hopes going into the game due to the reviews, and my hopes were exceeded. The story is fun, if really unrealistic. The creators paid a lot of attention to detail. The writing, voice acting and especially the music was superb. The main protagonist (You) tends to have a limited emotional range and so on but honestly I think it works. The story is scripted but it doesn't feel like you should just be watching the movie version instead. The combats can either be Rambo-style guns blazing in or stealth style, or, and here's the best part, a combo of both. I usually start off stealthy but ♥♥♥♥ it up somewhere in the middle and go full rambo from then on out. The game does not punish you for this and that is so damn nice. 'Chapters' are short enough so they are not tiresome but long enough so you feel a sense of accomplishment. and the 'Average' difficulty I am playing on is challenging enough for an older player to fair a few times but not so hard as to truly be frustrating. I have not finished it yet, but I'm very impressed and happy with this game.

After about 1500 hours across all characters, I am still learning this game. I am good, but by no means great at it. That being said, welcome to the Dark Souls of FPS games. The learning curve is brutal, the new player experience is rough, and there are a ♥♥♥♥ton of players like me and better shooting at you from all angles. There is no matchmaking and there is no MMR or Elo to pander to your skill level.
However, I can help make your new player experience a little better.
Step 1. Un♥♥♥♥ your settings. I wont go in depth, but there are a few things you can do right off the bat to make your performance better. Turn flora and shadows off, and turn render distance down to 1500 meters.
Step 2. Join an outfit. Soloing as a new player is the fastest way to get turned off to this game. Find a group you like and get to know them. Teamspeak 3 or mumble is also immensely helpful for this. They will speed your learning exponentially
Step 3. use starter weapons. with the exception of a few outliers, all the starter weapons are really good. Save your certs for suit upgrades and attachments/utility slots. Weapons are mostly sidegrades for different situations/playstyles
Step 4. Start out playing medic. It gains you a lot of easy XP through healing and revives and does not require you to kill get certs. It also teaches you to be a better player by not relying on the heavy assault class' shield.
Step 5. Accept that you will die. A lot. And there is little you can do to avoid it until you learn this game. You will imrpove with time, but it will be frustrating .
Step 6. The game is not p2w. Everything that affects gameplay can be earned for free. Only comsmetic things cost real monies.
Step 7. Koltyr, the new player continent, will probably be mostly empty. You will find better fights (and more people) on Amerish, Indar, Hossin, or Esamir.
This list is by no means comprehensive, but it entails a lot that I wish I had known as a new player, 4 years ago. Of all of these, most critical is finding a good outfit. The rest will likely follow if you have a good group to play with.

After about 1500 hours across all characters, I am still learning this game. I am good, but by no means great at it. That being said, welcome to the Dark Souls of FPS games. The learning curve is brutal, the new player experience is rough, and there are a ♥♥♥♥ton of players like me and better shooting at you from all angles. There is no matchmaking and there is no MMR or Elo to pander to your skill level.
However, I can help make your new player experience a little better.
Step 1. Un♥♥♥♥ your settings. I wont go in depth, but there are a few things you can do right off the bat to make your performance better. Turn flora and shadows off, and turn render distance down to 1500 meters.
Step 2. Join an outfit. Soloing as a new player is the fastest way to get turned off to this game. Find a group you like and get to know them. Teamspeak 3 or mumble is also immensely helpful for this. They will speed your learning exponentially
Step 3. use starter weapons. with the exception of a few outliers, all the starter weapons are really good. Save your certs for suit upgrades and attachments/utility slots. Weapons are mostly sidegrades for different situations/playstyles
Step 4. Start out playing medic. It gains you a lot of easy XP through healing and revives and does not require you to kill get certs. It also teaches you to be a better player by not relying on the heavy assault class' shield.
Step 5. Accept that you will die. A lot. And there is little you can do to avoid it until you learn this game. You will imrpove with time, but it will be frustrating .
Step 6. The game is not p2w. Everything that affects gameplay can be earned for free. Only comsmetic things cost real monies.
Step 7. Koltyr, the new player continent, will probably be mostly empty. You will find better fights (and more people) on Amerish, Indar, Hossin, or Esamir.
This list is by no means comprehensive, but it entails a lot that I wish I had known as a new player, 4 years ago. Of all of these, most critical is finding a good outfit. The rest will likely follow if you have a good group to play with.

You enter a room. You don't remember anything. The world around you isn't familiar. You are given a gun, shown who to shoot and thrown into the fight of your life. You die. And you die again... And again... And again... Alright you get the picture.
Planetside 2 is a combined fire shooter game. You yourself aren't a super hero, you aren't rambo. You're a soldier who is simply there. This game doesn't have a learning curve, it has a learning cliff. It will take hundreds of hours for you to fully comprehend how this game functions. The most important thing you will ever learn is how to survive. Aiming and killing is all outside of your primary skill repertoire. Staying alive is your main objective. Don't run into the enemy time after time. It won't work. And remember you will die. Most of us had to learn this the hard way.
First thing you should do is to check across the internet for guides. Easiest way to do so is to search YouTube for them or read up some forums.
Secondly, in this game you will never be good instantly. You will always start off bad, but like everything else it takes practice and time. You need to be determined enough to grind through the hard times.
And thirdly, you should time your sessions between 1 to 2,5 hours and have moderate breaks between these sessions, because either your nerves won't last or you will notice worsening of performance
It's a great game to play with friends or alone depending on what kind of playstyle fits you best. Some classes are very group centric (medic, engineer) and others are made for pure lone wolfs (light assault and infiltrator), however all have their place on the battlefield.
After DayBreak Games took over the certs have become more than plentiful. Progression is now fast and they are working to make the game accessible to new players as much as possible. And if you decide to support the developers, the cosmetics look very decent and you might also take a look at all the player-made cosmetics, as a part of the profit goes to the creators themselves. The prices of items also aren't that bad, even though some people believe 5€ is to much for a gun, I've seen much more expensive weaponry and cosmetics in other games, so compared to those PS2 is cheap.
It also doesn't hurt to read up some lore of the game, which can make an illusion of cause and motivates you to fight more for certain factions. It also springs up all sorts of faction banter, which is always fun to read or participate in.
Planetside 2 isn't for everyone, but it is a one-of-a-kind experience to which other games cannot even get close to. It is a game that can send chills down your spine when going over the top and it is a game that can reward you with hours of fun if you find the right fight.

I was, at first, a little apprehensive about a $30 early access title, but I recommend this game to anyone who might have any interest in a town/colony management game. It is pretty much finished and bug free, so this review stands even if they don't touch another thing in the game.
It gets compared to Dwarf Fortress often, and I think that's fairly accurate in a lot of ways. It's more like DF was back in the early days before the Z axis was added, minus much of the tunneling.
What makes this game worth your time and money is the strange situations and detail given to character's health and relationships leading to some neat stories and exciting moments. For example, my first colony was going fairly well, everyone got along for the most part except when the town's pet cat was butchered and cooked by (my) accident. Fistfights broke out, farming didn't get done, and there was a food shortage. I sent someone to hunt a doe but it was in a herd, and apparently alien deer are fiercely defensive; the entire herd pummeled the hunter to death and then ran through the main street in my settlement and beat everyone unconscious. Raiders then showed up and hauled off one of the women while the last two survivors wasted away in a coma outdoors. You can get all of this in DF for free of course, but not with this setting, presentation, or nice UI.
Losing is fun in DF, and it's also thankfully fun in RimWorld.

Don't believe the play hours; I've played this game since Alpha 9. This is an amazing colony-builder game where you control and try to survive with randomized colonists as various scenarios happen around you; this means that every playthrough is inherently different and you will evolve as a player as your colonies/tribes evolve. Despite the Early Access status of this game, it is by far and large a fully functioning game with relatively zero bugs. More content is being added by a very supportive development team, and now with this game being on Steam you have much more easy access to new updates and mod support if you wish.
The new scenario system added in this update (Alpha 14) is very interesting, and if you don't like the three vanilla scenarios, you can randomize them and/or find mods for them to make each playthrough even more unique. While the complexity of this game is far short of Dwarf Fortress, this game is still a gem for all players who enjoy the colony-building genre.

Overall, the game is great at what it sets out to be, that is, killing Nazis, and the characters are fairly memorable and engaging, but if you're looking for a compelling drama about you vs a world entirely ruled by Nazis, you won't find it. You won't even find out at the end of the game if you overthrow the Nazis. The last half of the game is a little disappointing, and there are several spots where the difficulty shoots astronomically high (higher than the final boss fight, which is stupid easy, just run to two corners of the room and trigger two things, by accident, then fire all of your rockets at a robot and take no damage.).

TL;DR Bottom
Rimworld... What can I tell you about Rimworld? This game has been under development for years and as such it's seen more than a few significant changes to the overall game. For those who have had bad experiences with early access games, I understand the hesitation. I've been there, I've got a handful of games that I wish I didn't get, Rimworld isn't one of those games. Tynan has worked so hard on this game, and listens to those who are supporting him.  I can say with out a doubt that this is hands down the BEST alpha game that I've spent money on.
Pros:
-- Replay Value; Not every playthrough has to be different, create your own scenario and watch how things unfold.
-- Permadeath mode option; For those who don't want to save scum. Bad♥♥♥♥♥♥happens. It sucks. Something so simple as a cougar could single handedly wipe out your entire tribe (sad experience that was.)
-- Art; it's beautiful for the style that it is!
-- Well optimized; This is a stab in the dark because I've got a high end gaming pc... But the game doesn't lag unless I'm playing on the huge map options, and even then it takes be hollowing out a few mountains and building a big base for it to start lagging.
--Active modding community; Constantly re-re-re-releasing their mods to keep up with the stage of the game. They have a wide selection that can really change how you will play the game!
Cons:
-- Randomness; You could literally be stuck in a 2 year toxic fallout and slowly lose all of the worth in your colony as they slowly start to become worthless and then food grows short until you all die... Not to a raid, not to explosions or illness. But a single map effect that lasted seemingly forever. (Personally I think it's a bit of a pro!)
-- Colony/tribe size;  If you play well you can end up with a tribe or colony too large, with no means to just tell them to leave. Killing them or selling them causes a colony wide mood debuff.
-- Addictive; Yes.. yes I know this seems like a pro as well. But when you spend 3 hours playing and expect it to have been only 30 minutes, that's a con!
I've been with this game for a long time, way before it was released on steam. I've seen the progression and I feel pretty confident in saying that I'll see it to completion.
Long story short; Do I recommend this game? Yes I'd give it a 8.5/10.

A really great game. Been with it since its early alpha stages. I remember staying up all night playing this game when I first heard about it, it's incredibly in depth. You will get attached to your colonists and they will die. Its constantly being updated and the modding community is incredible. You could easily stretch the vanila game to 1000 hours plus. Its easy to get the hang of, but difficult to master. If you're a fan of games like FTL, Duskers, any rpg or rts, this game brings the best of strategy and economy together in an incredibly personal tale of survival and the effect it has on people. All your colonists are by no means trained killers or carpenters, (though some might be) so there will be struggle and effects on their psyche, the mood and relationship system is really good, it gives personality to each pawn (colonist) in ways of permanent traits, and with how they react and talk to each other. conflict can come from your own people as if you slaughter a prisoner, they may become stressed and leave, fight with each other or break down. and I did say prisoners. Your colony doesn't have to be cold blooded murderers. There are many times where you can capture fallen enemies. Talk to them, convince them to join you, or harvest all of there organs and limbs. you can play it however you want. the combat system is pretty RNG, but is based off your colonists skill, with either shooting or melee combat. Individual limbs and organs are all modeled in the system so its very possible to lose an arm, have your leg blown off, get your fingers crushed. This of course doesnt always mean death. prosthetics and medicine can keep them alive, though dont expect "one arm Jim" to be a good crafter. Same goes for little Tessa's running career. damn tortoises. Theres a very in depth growing and hunting system too. food is your number one priority and is not always easy to get. in winter crops will not grow, and theres many biomes to choose from. Ice sheets are difficult, you need heat and greenhouses to survive. Rainforests provide lots of wood and cool temperature, but lots of man hunting animals and infections are there. deserts are blistering hot, but you'll never need to build greenhouses. Over all its a very varied and complex game, I havent even begun to scratch the surface. I Highly recommend this game for anyone who likes resource managment and rts games. seriously get this game.

My squad was pushing up to take the farm compound. The squad leader orders me to stay back and support them with my scoped sniper rifle. While I am watching the roofs I hear a shot behind me. I immediately drop to prone and check the map. Nothing is showing up where I am, and that can only mean enemies. Thankfully I had positioned myself in a waist high poppy field so there is no way they can see me. The thing is though I can see them through the stalks of the flowers running by me. They also must have shot at someone else because they have no clue I am there. What the enemy squad thought was a great flanking route to take on my squad has now turned into their worst nightmare. As they approached me  I radio in my position to the squad leader and let him know of the situation. He cannot spare anyone to come back and aid me, so now it is up to me to keep them occupied. They run past and with their backs to me I get in the kneeled position and shoot two of them dead. I get prone and slink off to their right while they toss grenades into the field. I take no damage. They knew the shots were close but they do not know where I went. Their medic tries to go and revive one of the soldiers and I shoot him dead. They were a smaller squad of seven so I had just killed their only medic. Now I have effectively stalled their attack because there are only four of them left with no way to revive. They toss another grenade and miss again. I'm wishing now that I could hear their radio chatter because I am sure they freaking out trying to locate me. I slowly snaked up to the wall of the field and looked on the other side. I see two more and I take them out, but I get hit in the process and I go down. Moments later the last two are killed as my squad had taken the compound and had returned to aid me. Our medic revives me and I recieve verbal praise from my squad as we go back to occupy the control point.
10/10 Would save the day again.

There are two types of players that play this game:
The player plays competitively amongst other plays on multiplayer. They are always finding new strategies to defeat their opponents, and learning from their own defeats. As their rank goes, up, so does their skill. They either raise from the bottom of the scoreboards to the top, or lose trying.
The other player plays this game with an entirely different tone. They may or may not play multiplayer, but it doesn’t really matter. If they do play multiplayer, it’s usually with their friends. This player doesn’t play to win, but plays for fun. They play singleplayer, and roleplay as kings and rulers of their glorious kingdom, watching it grow from a petty band of villagers to an entire civilization that history ought to remember. This player makes alliances, and tears down other kingdoms as they become the most powerful civilization in the map, or lose trying.
I’m more of the second type, but want I basically said was what types of people would find this game fun. Play to win, or play to have fun? It doesn’t matter, because everyone plays games for one of the two reasons.
TL;DR: It’s a great game for everyone who is into this stuff, either for competition or immersion.
